1930-05-06.text: Liverpool, England, May 5—A terrific explosion in Bibby’s oil cake mill on Great Howard street today killed three persons and injured at least 40 more. Several of the injured had little chance to live.

Bombay, India, May 5—Mahatma Gandhi, leader of the civil disobedience movement by which Indian Nationalists hope to gain independence from Great Britain, was arrested at Jalalpur at 1 a. m. today by British authorities. He was spirited aboard a Gujerat mail train which took him to Borivli station. A waiting automobile carried him to the jail of Yeranda, a town near Poona, where there is a large British garrison. The arrest was made under article 25 of the ordinance of 1827 which provides for maintenance of British authority in India. Under the ordinance the Mahatma, who is venerated by a large section of the Indian masses, will remain in prison without trial during the pleasure of the government. The arrest had been predicted for several days after it became increasingly apparent that in new phases of the civil disobedience planned by Gandhi there was a threat of serious disorders and tr

London, May 5. ()—Armed forces swiftly ordered into action tonight became Great Britain's answer to India’s turbulent factions. While troops camped in Indian cities, Mahatma Gandhi's followers prepared, despite his arrest and imprisonment, to press his campaign of civil disobedience. With excitement and apprehension, England surveyed the situation in her far-off domain. News from Bombay was scanned eagerly. Observers looked for information which would indicate the trend of the independent movement, which with the arrest of Gandhi passed to the leadership of Abbas Tyabaji. Karachi began to take on a war-like aspect. Into the city’s heart trooped a detachment of East Lancaster soldiers. The arming of European banks and mercantile employees by the city government began at once. Machine gun posts were established at prominent corners and upon roofs commanding business and public edifices and

CROYDON, England, May 5 (AP).—Amy Johnson, 23 years old; English aviatrix, whose longest flight has been only 299 miles; started today in a tiny moth plane on a lone flight of 22,000 miles to Australia and return. Her plane is named the “Jason” after the Grecian hero who sought the Golden Fleece. In it the golden-haired miss, a member of the London Aeroplane Club, hopes to beat the record of Bert Hinkler, who flew to Australia in 15 days. Her plane carries no radio, and she will depend upon telegrams to keep in touch with home. She carried a change of dress and other traveling equipment in a light bag behind the cockpit.

BOMBAY, May, 6.- Mahatma Gandhi attained the martyrdom he sought Monday when he was arrested by British authorities for leading the passive resistance campaign against British rule of India. The sixty-year-old Hindu was taken in custody at Surat, 100 miles north of Bombay, and conveyed to Yeroda jail, Poona, for imprisonment under the ordinance of 1827, which means he will be held in jail without a trial. British authorities made thorough preparations throughout India for a possible outbreak of Gandhi's followers and a military occupation was installed at Peshawar, where serious rioting occurred ten days ago. The Bombay Stock Exchange was expected to remain closed for some time, in view of the latest development. News of the arrest did not spread through Bombay immediately, owing to the suddenness with which it was made and the secrecy with which Gandhi was taken to Poona, but officials

ALCUTTA, May 6—(UP)— Serious disorders broke out in the Calcutta district today as mobs of Indian nationalists protested the arrest of the Mahatma 'M. K. Gandhi. The district magistrate and police superintendent were stoned, a police picket was attacked and a mob stoned a strong police patrol. In each case the police were forced to fire on the rioters to scatter them. Stone throwing and hostile demonstrations in which several persons including at least one European were injured occurred in the mill district of Bombay. A group of Europeans living in a suburb were delayed by hostile paraders and rowdy demonstrators when they entered the city by automobile. A mob of 3000 persons attempted to derail a train near Howrah, across the river from Calcutta, and was fired on by police. Several persons, including a British police sergeant, were injured before the crowd was scattered. Riots were repo

LONDON, (CP—King George celebrating the twentieth anniversary of his accession to Britain’s throne, left Buckingham Palace this morning to attend the races at Newmarket today and tomorrow. It was the first time His Majesty has been to a race meeting since his serious illness of 1928-29. King George was up early and attended to some state and official business before beginning his trip. He looked over the flood of telegrams and letters of congratulation on the anniversary, and then participated in the only ceremony of the day, presentation of medals to members of his household staff who had been with the Royal family for a long time. Crowds outside Buckingham Palace watched the picturesque changing of the guards and heartily cheered the King as he drove through the palace gates to the race meeting. It was said that he would remain at Newmarket for the entire meeting, returning to London F

LONDON, May 6.—George Bernard Shaw's cure for poverty would be to kill everyone earning less than $3,000 a year or wanting more, G. Sylvester Viereck quoted the dramatist as saying, in his new book published here yesterday. Viereck’s book, “Glimpses of the Great,” includes a series of interviews with Shaw, former Kaiser Wilhelm of Germany, Henry Ford, and J. Ramsay MacDonald. Discussing poverty, Viereck quoted Shaw as saying: “Tl should prohibit poverty by putting to death every person earning less than $3,000 a year, or asking for more.” Viereck asked Shaw if he wished to be rejuvenated. “TI want, if anything, to be senilized,” Shaw replied. “Ask me again in 30 or 40 years. However, my chief task is done.” “You mean your plays?” Viereck asked. “No,” said Shaw, “my prefaces.”

SIMLA, India, May 6 — (#) —At least thirty persons were injured in clashes with the police during the observance of the complete Hartal or sympathy strike at Jallundhur today. Two of the victims were reported in serious condition. News reaching here from several localities indicated that rioting was spreading in many towns.

Bombay, India, May 6 (UP)—The first effort at violence by independent campaigners protesting the arrest of Mahatma Gandhi broke out in widely spread parts of India today but were met with firm police and military measures. Stone throwing and hostile demonstrations in which several persons, including one European, were injured occurred in the mill district of India. A mob of 3,000 persons attempting to derail a train near Howrah, across the river from Calcutta, was fired upon by police. Several persons, including a British police sergeant, were injured before the crowd was scattered.
[By The Associated Press] DELHI, India—Serious clashes with the police ushered in the second day of the Imprisonment of Mahatma Gandhi: (Continued on Page 4)

Liverpool, May 5 (AP)—An explosion attributed to spontaneous combustion caused the death of five men, the critical injury of four and injuries of various degrees to about 80 others in Bibby’s Oil Cake works this morning. The blast occurred on the eleventh floor of a 12-story silo. About 300 men were in the silo at the time. The clothes were torn off many. Numerous others were burned and blinded by smoke. Later in the evening a number of gas cylinders in the stable yard burst and 13 persons were overcome. They were taken to a hospital but their condition is not believed serious.

LONDON, May 6.+-INS—Unconfirmed dispatches indicating a probable death toll in excess of 6,000 filtered through from India today following a disastrous earthquake and fire which devastated a huge area in the vicinity of Rangoon. Crumpling hundreds of houses in Rangoon and Pegu, about fifty miles north of that city, the quake was regarded by superstitious Indians as a supernatural demonstration over the arrest of Mahatma Gandhi, Nationalist leader now languishing in jail near Poona for his campaign of civil disobedience against British rule. Dispatches to the evening newspapers from Rangoon stated that terrible desolation followed in the wake of the tremblor at Pegu. A tidal wave following the quake was reported to have wiped out scores of lives while fire which swept the homes and buildings demolished by the quake added to the horror. A Central News dispatch from Rangoon stated that seve
‘Many persons were reported killed today in an earthquake at Rangoon, Burma. The city was severely shaken and the residential flats of Europeans and the high court were badly damaged.

CALCUTTA, Bengal, May 6 — () — Fifteen Indians were wounded today at Panchanantala, near Howrah, when police fired on them in a clash growing out of the Indians' attempt to enforce a stoppage of work. The Hartal was in protest against the arrest of Mahatma Gandhi, leader of the civil disobedience campaign. The crowd of Indians, greatly excited, attempted to prevent operation of the electric light and railway plants. The police, intervening, were attacked violently with brickbats. After a warning the police fired, injuring fifteen.

ALEXANDRIA, Egypt.—A tube of serum rushed here from Paris by airplane to save the life of a Cairo baby was in the hands of the child's father, Elie Catz, en route to Cairo Tuesday after a dramatic mile-a-minute race to catch a fast express train. Catz, who received the anti-toxin from an Imperial Airways pilot at the field here, rushed to catch his train but was too late by a few minutes. Police telephoned for the train to wait at Sidi Gaber, a suburb, while the airways manager drove Catz five miles to the station.

MADRID, May 1—(#)—The university of Madrid was closed by government order today and heavy police forces patrolled the streets in an effort to prevent further rioting by students favoring establishment of a Spanish republic. The disorders started last Thursday and were climaxed yesterday by a riot in which one person was killed and at least 35 others were injured. Twenty of the injured were students. Premier General Damaso Berenguer after an extraordinary session of his cabinet expressed regret that the disorders had occurred and declared that necessary steps would be taken to maintain peace. Unofficially it was indicated this would not involve arrest of Don Miguel De Unamuno, returned Primo De Rivera exile and rector of the Almanaca university, whose recent republican speech in a downtown theatre precipitated the first fighting. Don Miguel, while urging establishment of a republic, has b

MADRID (UP).—The most serious rioting since the fall of the Spanish dictatorship had resulted Tuesday in the closing of the University of Madrid and the installation of precautionary patrols by the well-trained Guardia Civil in this city. Madrid was quiet Tuesday, but officials of the university and of the city were determined to allow no grounds for a recurrence of Monday's riotous demonstration, which ended in the death of a laborer and the injuring of scores of students, police, and laborers. Students who joined in the outbreak described it as spontaneous, and said otherwise it would not have been confined to the medical and veterinary schools of the University of Madrid, but would have appeared all over the country. The closing of the university was ordered by the board of governors, but Premier Damaso Berenguer met with his cabinet Monday night to discuss what measures should be ado

Madrid, May 5.—(4)—A clash here today between police and university students brought word from the government of Premier Damaso Berenguer that it would tolerate no further disorder. Two men are dead, both workmen. Many Hurt. At least 40 were injured. Some arrests were made. The trouble began when the students, complaining bitterly at police treatment since Thursday, ran a red flag over the college this morning and adjourned to the campus. Numbering 2,000, they headed for the street. Police and troops, who had assembled at the first sign of trouble, assumed they intended to parade and advanced to drive the collegians back. The students yielded, but not before each man had taken cobblestones from the street, which was torn up for repairs. They returned to the building, barricaded it, climbed to the roof and showered stones on the law's forces. Open Fire. Thereupon the police and troops ope

Tokyo May 68—(P-Advices to Rengo news agency from Seoul today said a dozen fishing boats, each of which carried three to five men, were missing off Mokpho, Southern Korea, as the result of a storm last night.

1930-04-23.text: [BY ASSOCIATED PRESS] Representatives of the five dominant naval powers of the world—America, Great Britain, Japan, France and Italy Tuesday afternoon affixed their signatures to an epoch-making treaty, limiting and reducing the navies of three of them and restricting the navies of the other two. Colonel Henry L. Stimson, American secretary of state, and his colleagues on the American delegation were the first to sign the historic document. M. Briand, French foreign minister, J. Ramsay MacDonald, British prime minister and Admiral Giuseppe Sirianni, with their delegations, followed. Reijiro Wakaisuki, a former prime minister of Japan, and those of the Tokyo delegation who have worked with him through the three months and one day of long and (Continued on Page 13)

LONDON, April 22—(47)—Signed and sealed today by 27 envoys of the five great sea powers, the London naval treaty of 1930 rests in the archives of the British foreign office. With that, the work of the delegates who have labored in London for three long months was over. Secretary Henry L. Stimson and his American co-workers left tonight for South Tanstall, and will sail tomorrow on the Leviathan. The signing of the treaty was enacted under mellow sunshine which streamed through the four tall windows of Queen Anne's drawing room of old St. James’ palace. English springtime had replaced the dogs of January, prevailing when the conference opened, and outside the palace flowers bloomed and birds sang. Beginning at 10:30 a.m., the closing plenary session required nearly three hours for addresses from chief delegates. The actual signing took less than 15 minutes. The moment of historic signific

(By The Associated Press) LONDON, April 22,—By terms of the naval treaty signed today by representatives of the five powers at London, the United States should have achieved parity with Great Britain by the date of its expiration, December 31, 1936. Japan will occupy at that time a ratio of naval power somewhere between the five-five-three capital ship ratio agreed upon at the Washington 1925 conference and the ten-ten-seven auxiliary ship ratio which the Tokyo delegation sought at the beginning of this conference. Nine battleships are to be scrapped, or, in the case of three, converted to training vessels, and a five-year capital ship construction holiday is decreed. The ships to be scrapped are, for the United States, the Florida, the Utah, and either the Arkansas or the Wyoming, while Great Britain will abandon the Benbow, the Iron Duke, the Marlborough, the Emperor of India and the T

Calcutta, India, April 23 (UP)—The Indian civil disobedience campaign became a crusade of violence again today when 11 persons were killed in fighting between insurgents and troops in Bengal. Seven persons were slain in the jungle of Hatazari near Chittagong, scene of the most serious outbreak of the campaign, last weekend. Four others were jailed at Fenis where a band of raiders attacked the police station to seize firearms.

The important results of the London naval conference could not be reduced to writing in the treaty but "remain in the minds of the various nations" to grow toward even greater peace progress in the future, Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson suggested Wednesday in an interview with the United Press. The head of the American delegation to the five-power naval conference discussed the outcome of the London sessions over the wireless telephone, speaking from the S. S. Leviathan, five hours at sea, to the United Press bureau in London. It was his first exclusive press interview since the start of the conference and the conversation inaugurated commercial service from the Leviathan to England. "Leaven" is Planted Secretary Stimson pointed out that the "leaven" planted in the minds of Britain and America at the unsuccessful Geneva naval conference produced a result now achieved at London and e

LONDON, April 23.—INS—The Royal Air Force plane which carried the Prince of Wales from Khartoum to Cairo a few days ago crashed at Heliopolis today, killing all its occupants, according to an Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Cairo. The Prince had utilized the plane for part of his journey back to England from his hunting tour in the African jungles.

CALCUTTA, April 22 ()—British authorities believed tonight the Indian insurgents who raided the Chittagong arsenal Saturday were surrounded and that capture would soon follow. Forty soldiers of the Eastern Frontier Rifles and a troop of Burma Valley Lighthorse engaged a party of about 30 of the rebels on a road a few miles north of Chittagong today, but details as to the outcome were lacking. As to other aspects of the Indian situation, political prisoners in the Alipore central jail, including J. M. Sen Gupta, mayor of Calcutta, went on a hunger strike as the result of an alleged assault by jail officials. They were imprisoned because of their activity in the civil disobedience campaign of Mahatma Gandhi.

One of the girls with the American naval delegation, bound, remarked that London men were the finest she had ever met, and a marine said the London girls were wonderful. No engagements have come to light. NEW YORK — The only man Gienna Collett has designs on is Bull, and she wants to take one of his golf titles. But she is leaving on the same plane with Helen Wills Moody. Gienna was quizzed about her single bliss and so forth. She's clever. She said she had no immediate idea.

LONDON, April 23, GNS)—Four Indian police guards were shot and killed today by Indian Nationalists in a raid on the Fenny Police Station, near Chittagong, it was stated in dispatches from Calcutta to the evening papers. The Indians raided the place in search of arms. They took the police unawares, and were driven back only after a sharp conflict. The raiders also are believed to have suffered a number of casualties.

CALCUTTA, India, Apr 23.—A constable and three other persons were killed at Feni, Bengal, today when a party of men raided the police station to obtain firearms, advices received here said. The raiding party was not identified.

LONDON, Apr. 23.--Their long and tedious task completed, American delegates to the London Naval Conference sailed for home aboard the Leviathan early today. The huge United States liner pulled away from Southampton Harbor just as dawn was breaking over the Solent. The delegates, fatigued and weary, were fast asleep in their staterooms and had been from a few minutes after they boarded the vessel at 8:30 last evening. It was an unusually gay departure, for the new night-club of the vessel had been kept open for the especial benefit of the delegates. Not one of them, however, had the desire for anything else but sleep. Other passengers took advantage of the unexpected entertainment and danced until the early hours of the morning. With the conclusion of the conference and departure of the Americans, the British press launched into an almost unanimous expression of approval over the parley's

BASEL, SWITZERLAND, April 22, (AP) — Gates W. McGarrah of New York, widely known financier, today was elected president of the bank for international settlements. Pierre Quesnay, youthful French financial expert and a member of the French delegation to the Hague conference, was elected general manager.

Basel, Switzerland, April 22. An American bank president, Gates W. McGarrah, New York financier, Tuesday was placed at the head of the bank for international settlements, organized to handle German reparations payments under the Young plan. Delegates of six countries that were belligerents 19 years ago voted for him unanimously. A French financial expert, Pierre Queanley, was elected general manager with only one dissenting vote, that was cast by Dr. Hans Luther of the German reichsbank, who said that the German delegation opposed the election of a Frenchman as general manager in principle but emphasized that such opposition was not personal. The setting up of the international bank is called the final and most de-

TOKYO, April 23 (AP)—Reports received by the navy office here today said Chinese pirates had raided the Japanese freighter Kamioshi Maru, which ran aground about 35 miles off Swatow. The crew of the freighter, numbering about 30, was missing. Japanese warcraft were sent to search nearby shores and islands.

Tokyo, April 2.—The strike of tramway and bus workers of Tokyo which started Sunday, apparently failed yesterday as 4,000 strikers resumed operations at reduced wages, which caused the walkout. Municipal authorities who operated the transportation system predicted that conditions would be normal today in this city of more than two million. Although 12,000 of the 13,000 transportation workers quit work, the authorities maintained a reduced service with the aid of volunteers. In Kobe, 1,300 tramway workers struck in sympathy with the Tokyo strikers, and the strike threatened to spread to Osaka. The Kobe tramways continued to operate but with a small force. Many persons were injured severely in accidents caused by inexperienced crews. There was little disorder caused by strikers.

PARIS, Apr. 23.—(AP)—France experienced possibly the worst week-end automobile casualty list over Easter in the history of motor vehicles. Thirty-six persons were killed and 172 injured in widespread accidents.

1930-03-22.text: London, March 21—(AP)—The American, British and Japanese naval delegations were understood today to be preparing for quick, definite action next week in the production of a limitation and reduction pact. In American circles it was said that the moment the Japanese government indicates acceptance of the proposals now being considered in Tokyo for an agreement among the United States, Great Britain and Japan, France and Italy will be called upon to put their cards on the table in an effort to settle their parity disagreement. If France and Italy still cannot see any purpose in further negotiating on their difference, then the other three powers will quickly frame an agreement along the lines of the Washington treaty and France and Italy will be invited to sign such parts as they wish.

London, Mar. 22—-(AP)—Pending word from the Japanese government regarding the tentative naval agreement worked out between the American and Japanese delegations, the Americans and British, it was said in authoritative circles, will go ahead in the preparation of a draft conference pact. This is on the assumption that no break in the Franco-Italian parity deadlock develops. The Americans and British plan to go ahead with the drafting and leave blank spaces where necessary for the Japanese to fill in later. Presumably France and Italy would be invited to sign this pact but while there might be some clauses to which they could subscribe, it would be virtually a three power agreement. It is understood that it would follow the general lines of the Washington treaty. Thus far it has been kept a secret, but it can now be seen that the Americans brought a draft five power agreement to the confer

London, March 21, (*)—As the five-power naval conference passed its sixtieth day, both the French and Italians, although still deadlocked over parity, authorized statements showing that neither is ready to quit the fight. Conference forces are scattered far from St. James’ Palace and prospects of changes over the week-end are slight. But Prime Minister MacDonald, of Great Britain, waits at Chequers, ever hopeful that either the Italians or the French will present new proposals which will hurry Premier Tardieu, of France, back to London tomorrow night for the conference with Mr. MacDonald on Sunday. With a five-power treaty at stake, Mr. MacDonald is displaying great patience to enable France and Italy to reach some basis of agreement.

DUNEDIN, No. March 22 (Saturday) — Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd announced today that his Antarctic exploration bark, the City of New York, was ready for sea and would begin its return voyage to New York tomorrow with a portion of the expedition.

LONDON, March 22. (AP) — An air of uneasiness hung over the five-power naval conference today. Predictions were that unless there was a constructive development almost immediately, a provisional three-power treaty would be drawn up and the curtain rung down upon the somewhat unsuccessful five-power parley. The British Morning Press in some instances went so far as to say that only a miracle could save the conference. "The nations are standing by helpless while a world tragedy is enacted before their eyes," the Chronicle commented. LONDON, March 22, (—With tomorrow’s meeting at Chequers between Prime Minister MacDonald and Premier Tardieu definitely canceled, the five-power naval conference has reached the point where it is a conference in name only. LONDON, Mar. 22. The naval conference deadlock between France and Italy was described in reliable Italian sources today as so serious that any future attempt to settle their differences might endanger the friendship of the two countries. Delegates of France and Italy have agreed that their differences in regard to naval parity have been made more difficult by the rigid atmosphere of the naval conference and should be worked out more differently than otherwise.

By HARRY R. FLORY International News Service Staff Correspondent LONDON, March 22,—All compromise proposals offered by the oceanic powers—England, America and Japan to France and Italy have been “thoroughly explored” by delegates of the latter countries and none has been found satisfactory, it was said in Italian sources here today: The statement revealed officially for the first time the wide gulf that exists between the Mediterranean powers and the “big three.” It indicated without qualification that as matters stand at present, there is no hope of a five-power disarmament treaty being negotiated at the present conference. Suggestions Needed Unless outside interests make new suggestions forming a possible basis for compromise, further direct conversations are utterly useless, it was said. This was regarded as a definite ultimatum that unless some satisfactory proposal was made in the n

London, March 21 (4)—One of the senators in the American naval delegation received a letter from the United States this morning, asking him to see King George immediately. Thinking the letter referred to the naval conference, the senator read on to find that the writer desired him to arrange a contract for his constituent to reupholster the sofas in Buckingham Palace.

London, March 22 (UP)—France’s temporary withdrawal from London—in effect a veritable ultimatum to the other four powers—left the naval conference today on the verge of comparative failure; world plans for disarmament in their worst plight since the Geneva conference in 1927. In the background appeared two unexpected results of the parley which are of predominant importance although they will not figure in the written results. First is the increase in French and Italian rivalry in the Mediterranean and intensification of the Franco-Italian political irritation. Second is the further tightening up of the unofficial and unwritten Anglo-American ‘entente’ created by Premier J. Ramsey MacDonald and President Herbert Hoover this fall. The Franco-Italian deadlock has brought up a latent bitterness between the two nations. It has revealed and intensified the spirit of co-operation between Ameri

Jambusar, Bombay, India, March 22.—(4')--Mahatma Gandhi, Indian Nationalist, in a speech today at Ankhi severely reproved the villagers for so enforcing the social boycott against policemen that the officials were unable to obtain food. The Mahatma declared it was against religious principles to starve officials and that those who harbored active enmity to the government would be joining enemies even though they should not assault officers. Gandhi said he would suck snake's poison "even from General Dyer" if he should be bitten. General Dyer resigned from the British army after a loud outcry growing out of his order to troops to fire on a crowd of 5,000 Indians in Amritsar. Three hundred and eighty natives were killed and 1,200 were injured. Police attended Gandhi's speech to report it for official reference.

LONDON, March 21. (AP) — Reports in Jewish quarters from Bucharest today said that all the Jewish boys who are born in Rumania next week will be named Balfour and the girls will be named Baltouria. In this manner will the Jewish community commemorate the name of Lord Balfour, who died this week in England, and a week of mourning has also been proclaimed by Rumanian Jews.

Jambusar, Bombay Presidency, India, March 21.—(f?)-—Mahatma Gandhi and his volunteers marching to open the civil disobedience campaign arrived at Gajera tonight with sickness rife in their ranks. Ten of the volunteers, who are suffering from fever, will be taken to the village of Broach, awaiting Gandhi's arrival there on March 26.

MOSCOW, March 22 (CAP).— Buoyed by their hatred of religion, tens of thousands of Soviet citizens, Red soldiers, government employees and school children marched yesterday over Moscow's muddy pavements in protest at intercessory prayers abroad for Christians in Russia. The marchers sang anti-religious songs and carried inflammatory Red banners. They were led by brass bands playing martial and Communist airs. Some marchers carried grotesque effigies of the Pope. There were many banners bearing the familiar Marxian expression: “Religion is the opium of the people.”

SHANGHAI, Mar. 22 (AP)—One hundred bandits and fifty Chinese soldiers were killed and hundreds were wounded yesterday near Haichow in northern Kiangsu Province in a battle between 1,000 bandits and 2,000 soldiers, say advices received today. The soldiers are reported to have routed the bandits after an all day fight.

MOSCOW Mar. 22. (U.P)—Literally hundreds of thousands of workers marched singing through the streets of Moscow last night in a vast demonstration in protest against the foreign religious attacks on the Soviet atheistic campaign. It was estimated no less than 250,000 persons participated—a great throng of singing, shouting, banner-waving men and women. They came through the streets direct from the factories, converging at various points until they had formed several gigantic streams of humanity. Bands played stirring martial airs of the revolution. Thousands on thousands of throats responded. The most popular was an old atheist ballad which concentrates on a sort of chant meaning, “Down, down with monks—down, down with priests.” The paraders concentrated into surging pools as their converging streams came to open plazas where speeches were made. The theaters all over the city were open mu

SHANGHAI, Mar. 22. (AP). Commenting on the announcement from Washington that eleven American Catholic missionaries had been trapped at Kanchow, Kiangsi Province, as the result of Communist disorders, Bishop Sheehan, director of the mission's activities in the northern part of that province, asserted here today that the reports were exaggerated. Bishop Sheehan said the vicariate at Kanchow was in the midst of continual Communist and bandit depredations but asserted that its missionaries were in no immediate danger and were carrying on their work despite the uncertainties. The bishop, a native of Streator, IL, and whose American headquarters are in St. Louis, further stated that the mission's local office on March 19 received a telegram from Hanchow saying conditions were quiet.

1930-03-24.text: LONDON, Mar. 24 — Secretary Stimson and Prime Minister MacDonald got together at 10 Downing Street with the idea of trying to work out some Franco-Italian compromise which will be sufficiently interesting to Andrew Tardieu to draw the French Premier back to London. The American and British delegation chiefs were taking M. Tardieu at his word that he would return to the conference when there was something worthwhile for him to consider. Colonel Stimson was accompanied by Ambassador Morrow and Senator Robinson. An American spokesman told the Associated Press that hope had not by any means been abandoned for a five power agreement. He commented that as long as the five nations represented at the conference were still there, there was still hope. For this reason the Americans were favorably impressed by Dinc Grandhi’s statement last week that he would remain in London a week after everybody

DUNEDIN, N. Z.--(P)—Carrying fifty members of the Byrd Antarctic expedition homeward, the bark City of New York, flagship of Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd, sailed Sunday afternoon from Otago harbor for Tahiti, en route for New York. Admiral Byrd was among a crowd of more than ten thousand that thronged the wharves to say goodbye. He is remaining here for a few days to complete business affairs and will travel by mail steamer homeward, rejoining the City of New York at the Panama canal. He bade his shipmates farewell before the tug took the bark down the channel. Pushing out into a gray mist and bucking a stiff easterly breeze, the Byrd flagship, after sixteen months in the waters under the southern cross, started the expedition's journey home from its conquest of the south pole by air, and its triumphs in the fields of exploration and scientific research. The steamship Eleanor Bolling wil

(Associated Press Staff Write LONDON, March 23.--44’)—Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald came back from a weekend at Chequers tonight to search the somnolent naval conference headquarters for the material with which to build a five-power naval pact of limited scope, but resting on a tri-partite agreement among the Americans, British and Japanese. He will begin the preliminary phases of this work tomorrow, when the Japanese have received word from Tokyo about the tentative Japanese-American arrangements, the fate of the treaty envisaged will be settled, and if the word is favorable, it can be rushed to completion within two weeks.

United Press Staff Correspondent LONDON, Mar. 24—(U.P)—Unless the French and Italian delegates surprise the London naval conference by coming to some agreement on parity, Great Britain, America and Japan will turn, by the end of the week, to the only possible task remaining—a tripartite agreement. Negotiations for the three-power treaty, the United Press learned, will begin as soon as Tokyo’s reply to American proposals is received. It is expected the reply will be delayed until Friday, in order to give the French and Italians time to end the parity controversy. There is every indication that Japan will reject part of the American proposals, and make counter-suggestions. It was learned that the Japanese are somewhat irritated at British intimations that the American project was “satisfactory.” They view this as a form of Anglo-American pressure upon them. The power developed probably will find its way into private hands, to be sold to the public that builds the dam, for all the traffic will bear. Senora Hansen, of Paris, Brazil, has given birth to six children, boys, at one time. London, March 24.—(01)—Prime Minister MacDonald and Secretary Stimson are going to have at least one more fling at developing a five-power limitation treaty from the prolonged negotiations of the naval conference. Their efforts this week will be directed, until such time as they appear futile, toward achieving an agreement between all the powers represented here embodying not only limitation, but possibly paper reduction, and such other points of agreement that are possible. Failing, the two leaders almost inevitably will turn to a three-power pact between Japan, Great Britain and the United States, fixing their naval standings very much in accordance with the Rapidan agreement, and hinging them upon maintenance of the status quo in Europe. TOKYO, March 24, (*)—Japan’s decision whether to accept or reject the tentative agreement of the Japanese and American delegates to the London naval conference is fully expected to be rendered next Thursday. An extraordinary session of the cabinet has been called for the purpose of finally shaping instructions to the delegation. Approval Is Expected There are strong and trustworthy indications tonight that the cabinet will authorize Reijiro Wakatsuki, Japan's chief delegate, to accept an agreement approximating the terms laboriously formulated by Senator David A. Reed of the United States and Tsuneo Matsudaira, Japan's ambassador to Great Britain, as delegates of their respective countries. Pessimism of the past week concerning this agreement has been fading in favor of the widespread belief that a Japanese-American agreement permitting at least a tripartite naval treaty will be announce

Rome, March 23, ()—With Fascist demonstration of party strength and unity in every city and large town, Italy today celebrated the eleventh anniversary of the foundation of the combat units from which the party arose. District secretaries in all regions read a message from Premier Mussolini in which the Duce declared that in 11 years Fascism prevailed over a thousand difficulties, but that many more await it. "We must always pose upon us more the command and the discipline by which the Fascist party should always unite into a single group." "Today the first battle legions find themselves side by side with the young men who have grown up to a life dedicated to a faith which unites two ages and two historic moments, the past and the future of the nation. Let us therefore regard with tranquil security the unfolding of events. Retrograde forces in coalition against young Fascist Italy do not

STUTTGART, Germany, March 24.—(7)—Six persons have died here from a kind of poison believed to have resulted from their eating a bear ham. Many others are dangerously ill, among them the restaurant keeper who served the meat. One patient in high fever jumped out of a sick-room window.

MOSCOW, (UP).—Millions of hitherto cruelly suppressed “class enemies” of the Soviets rejoiced Monday at the removal of restrictions which for years have set them apart, despised, ostracized, and deprived of human rights. In the most important social decree of recent years, the central executive committee has ordered practically every right of communist citizenship—except the franchise—restored to the “non-toilers,” which include remnants of the former ruling class, priests, private traders, “Kulaks” (property-owning farmers) and other disfranchised elements. The decree is regarded as emphasizing the demand of Joseph Stalin for a change in methods and the elimination of force and terrorization as a means of furthering the Soviet's program. The main objective of the government—suppression of the Kulaks and collectivization of industry and agriculture—is in no way altered.

VIGO, Spain, March 23—(P)— Several persons were cut and bruised today in a panic after lightning struck the Roman Catholic church in the village of Salceda near here. The church was crowded with attendants at early mass. None were seriously injured.

Tokyo, March 24.—The capital today began a three day celebration in commemoration of the reconstruction of Tokyo and obliteration of scars of the earthquake and fire of September 1, 1923, which were officially pronounced completed after six and one half years work and the expenditure of 739,000,000 yen (about $369,500,000). Today's feature of the celebration was Emperor Hirohito’s journey of inspection through the restored areas, a five hour progress of 22 miles along broad, new boulevards, equal to the best in the occident. The boulevards were elaborately decorated for his majesty’s visit with bunting, lanterns and flowers, reaching its highest splendor along the Ginza, or Tokyo’s “Fifth Avenue”, which was embowered with artificial cherry trees in full bloom. The Emperor's journey itself was an unprecedented departure of the Mikado’s usual seclusion. He left the palace at 9:45 A.M. in a

BERLIN, March 24 (AP) — The central board of the Reichsbank presided over for the last time by Dr. Hjalmar Schacht, its retiring president, decided today to reduce its discount rate a half per cent to 5 per cent and the Lombard rate a half per cent to 6 per cent.

1930-03-28.text: London, Mar. 28— (2)—Having succeeded in drawing France back into the five-power naval parley, the American and British delegations today turned their attention particularly to Italy with the hope of some sort of compromise from the offer of “security” which will be made to France as the price of reduction of her naval figures and the consultative pact into which the Americans may be drawn continued the principle topic of conversation. Italy Stands Ground But while the situation with reference to France apparently has been greatly eased and now gives promise of possible tangible development in the direction of naval agreement, Italy has stood her ground and reiterated her original contention “parity with any continental power.” France as consistently is maintaining even though this phase of the naval argument is out of the limelight, that they cannot accept parity with Italy and that the

MAES (United Press Staff Correspondent) — London, March 28 — The London naval conference radically changed its course today, and is now headed towards a general European security pact, long the dream of Aristide Briand of France, supplementing the League of Nations covenant. A committee of French and British experts began an examination of the possibility of drawing up an agreement which, without materially increasing British military obligations, would give France the feeling of security she demands before she becomes committed to armament reduction. Briand’s decision not to return to Paris Tuesday, as he had expected, together with the statement of a spokesman for the French delegation who said flatly that the recent announcement of American views towards the so-called “consultative pact” was largely responsible for the new turn in events. London, March 27, (#)—Preparation of a treaty to preserve peace in the Mediterranean began today as an indirect method of bringing France and Italy into a five-power disarmament pact at the London naval conference. An experts committee, including Sir Robert Van Sittart for the British and Rene Massigli for the French, was established to draft the treaty which would guarantee French security anew and still not commit Great Britain beyond obligations already imposed in the League of Nations covenant. LONDON, March 28—Some of the mystery surrounding America’s much-discussed willingness to participate in a European consultative pact was swept away today when it was learned from an authoritative source that two very definite conditions had been laid down governing America’s entrance into such a treaty. The principal condition is that a workable five-power naval disarmament treaty must be formulated before a consultative pact can be agreed to. The other is that France's security demands must be settled before the pact is even discussed. To begin with, International News Service learns that no nation or statesman has yet approached the American delegation. The entire pact question hinges upon reduction of the French security demands, which the American delegation here considers a prerequisite. London, Mar. 28. (AP)—The American delegates have definitely eliminated a type of treaty such as the four-power Pacific pact of 1921 as a basis for a consultative agreement to be framed at the London conference. It was learned on the highest authority in the American delegation today that the Americans are convinced commitments under Article two of the Pacific treaty, if applied in Europe, would cause the United States to participate in discussions over virtually every controversy in Europe whether the United States was interested or not. --- 1921 Treaty Cited. Article two of the treaty, to which the Americans would object in a consultative pact applied to Europe, provides that if the contracting rights are threatened by any other power, those powers signing the treaty shall consult in order to arrive at an understanding. LONDON, Mar. 28—(#)—The Daily Herald, labor organ said today that Lord Byng probably would resign as chief commissioner of metropolitan police and head of Scotland Yard on his return from South Africa soon. Lord Byng has been advised that a return to police duties may bring another breakdown in his health. Lady Byng has also urged her husband to relinquish the position, the Herald said. Former commander of the Canadian corps in France, and later governor general of Canada, Lord Byng became chief commissioner of London police in the summer of 1928.

Tokyo, March 28—(AP)— Seven hundred buildings were destroyed by fire at Komatsumachi, northwest Japan, today. Damage was estimated at yen 1,000,000 (about $499,000). The blaze swept the town hall, police station and schools. One fireman was killed and three others seriously injured when a fire engine turned over.

Ferlin, March 23.—Heinrich Bruening, until recently little known outside the Centrist party, was designated this afternoon as chancellor of the Reich, and was instructed by President Paul von Hindenburg to form a government to succeed that of Herman Mueller, which resigned yesterday. The president, who usually is cited as an incarnation of imperturbability, seemed to have his dander up, and instructed Bruening to work fast, forget party pettifoggings and construct a cabinet which above all can put through the budget and financial reform programs. Shortly after departure of Bruening from Hindenburg’s quarters, the president received his political enemy, Dr. Hugenberg, leader of the extreme Nationalists, to persuade him for his country’s welfare to give up his opposition at this point. Dr. Hugenberg was asked to permit Martin Schiele, former minister of agriculture, to accept that portfoli

TOKYO.—(/)—Continuously repeated earthquakes have rocked the Izu peninsula, particularly Ito, 40 miles southwest of Yokohama, the past fortnight. Inhabitants have become panic-stricken. Although the disturbances at present are local, their persistency is regarded as ominous since they are near the epicenter of the 1923 earthquake.

Calais, Mar. 2 (AP) — Nearly 20,000 persons marched thru the streets of Calais today in a huge demonstration to protest against the new American duties on lace. Another 40,000 gathered from over the countryside to watch the orderly procession, headed by the entire municipal personnel, local magistrates and members of the chamber of commerce. They marched to the city hall to present resolutions of protest to Mayor Louis Vincent. “I would like for you to emphasize that this demonstration is in no way aimed against the United States or its government,” Mayor Vincent told the Associated Press correspondent. “We simply want to bring home to the French government, in the most forcible way, what the new tariff means to the industry of Calais.”

BERLIN, March 27 ()—The coalition government of Chancellor Hermann Mueller, after surviving the stormy seas of post-war German politics for 21 months and recently bringing the Young reparations plan safely through the Reichstag, crashed today on one of the many rocks threatening it in its financial program. The cabinet resigned when its component parties failed to agree on an unemployment insurance question. President Von Hindenburg accepted the resignation, requesting the ministers to remain in office until a new cabinet could be formed. Dr. Heinrich Bruening, a centrist member of the Reichstag and one of the outstanding leaders of his party, was reported to have been suggested by Chancellor Mueller for the task of forming a new government. The resignation of the Mueller cabinet was far from being unexpected; political circles had long believed that all that was holding it together was

BERLIN, March 28 UPi— Heinrich Bruening, Centrist leader, was asked by President Von Hindenburg today to form a new cabinet to replace that of Chancellor Hermann Mueller, which resigned yesterday. Herr Bruening accepted. Herr Bruening made it clear to Von Hindenburg that he would form a new government within 24 hours.

| BERLIN, March 28. ~ President Paul von Hindenburg today called on Heinrich Bruening, leader of the Catholic Center party, to form a new German government. The president's invitation to Bruening had been forecast by unofficial reports that an attempt would be made to form a cabinet with the Centrist group dominating, and with the possible exclusion of the Social Democrats who brought about the collapse of the Hermann Mueller government yesterday. In his audience with Dr. Bruening, the president emphasized the difficulties of the present parliamentary situation which, he said, rendered the formation of a cabinet without regard to parties or party coalitions desirable. Dr. Bruening agreed, and informed Hindenburg he would attempt to construct a government on a nonpartisan basis.

Shanghai, March 27. (?)—Fears for the safety of 16 American Catholic missionaries at Kanchow, Kiangsi province, continued tonight in missionary circles here notwithstanding reports from Canton and Nanking that the bandit and communist armies besieging the city had been dispersed by Nationalist government troops. Mission headquarters here also were anxious regarding three Finnish women missionaries, captured by Chinese bandits, February 3, in Northern Kiangsi, and reported killed. Supporting the belief that the communist forces still surround Kanchow, missionaries here said their Kanchow colleagues informed them a month ago that they would report the dispersal of the Reds whenever it took place. Telegraph wires have been controlled by the besiegers, cutting off communication with Kanchow.

BERLIN, Mar. 28 (.—Unmoved by President Von Hindenburg’s appeal for harmony, the extreme nationalists of the Reichstag today declined to participate in the new government which Dr. Heinrich Bruening is attempting to form, demanding dissolution of the Reichstag and new elections. Dr. Bruening nevertheless offered the ministry of agriculture to Martin Schiele, a nationalist leader, who agreed to accept. Herr Bruening, in accepting the presidential mandate, gave President Von Hindenburg to understand he would form a new government within 24 hours. The president told him expressly that he did not want him to confer for a long time with the parties and secure their approval in advance. Instead he said he should construct a cabinet without definitely binding the parties to a coalition. Herr Bruening agreed. The new cabinet is to succeed the one which steered the Young Plan and Polish agreement
By The Associated Press. CALAIS, France, March 28.— Nearly 20,000 persons marched through the streets of Calais today in a huge demonstration of protest against the new American duties on lace.

1930-04-13.text: LONDON, April 12—The first draft of the London naval agreement was prepared today with a view of its submission to the delegations by midnight. It was indicated that it would be possible to conclude a rough draft for consideration by the various delegations over the weekend. Several points of difference are yet to be cleared up, including the so-called safeguarding clauses to protect the navies limited under the treaty in the event that neighboring countries should begin what might be regarded as excessive building. The expert reports now being used as a basis for the pact, no doubt will be approved.

LONDON, April 12.—The London naval treaty, which in large measure will eliminate world competition in naval building for the next five years, today began to take shape in definite written form. A draft was rushed into shape by the drafting and expert committees throughout the day, in the hope of submitting it to the delegates by midnight, so it can thus be studied over Sunday. So far, the jurists responsible for writing the treaty are holding their own in their race against time to make possible formal signature on Thursday and the departure of the American delegation homeward on the liner Leviathan on April 22. The committee assigned to the task worked all through the day and into the night. They were aided by special treaty experts under Sir Maurice Hankey, secretary-general of the conference. The experts waited outside the committee’s room in St. James Palace ready at a moment's notic

BOMBAY, India, April 12.—“The passive resistance” strike on the great Indian peninsular railway flared into violence today when bombs exploded in two Bombay stations, injuring two persons. Leaders of the strike movement hitherto have confined their activities to obstructing the passage of trains by lying down on the railroad tracks, and have blocked the way to stations and offices of the railroad company, defying arrest.

London, April 12.—(Saturday)— The Daily Mail this morning states that “the most appalling weapon of war ever devised by man, defying all defense and raining merciless death from the skies,” is now being forged in secret in England. This new war terror, says the Mail, is a giant airplane torpedo, operating without a crew, its engine and course controlled by clockwork and its hull a mere receptacle for bombs. The clockwork control is set beforehand to operate at a certain moment and a specific place. ‘On arriving at the appointed moment the engine stops and the whole machine with its deadly load crashes to the earth.

LAINDON, April 10 — Ten persons were burned to death and more than 100 injured when fire destroyed 200 houses in the town of Ment, Kafr El Sheikh, according to news dispatches today from Cairo. Ment is on the Nile delta, 100 miles north of Cairo.

SIMLA, India, Apr. 12. -—-(Reuters) —— Reports from various districts affected by Mahatma Gandhi's civil disobedience campaign show that the first effects of the government’s patient and carefully controlled policy have been to disorganize the forces of the resisters and bewilder them by the query of ‘what next?’ The government calculated that it would not tolerate any breach of the law, however technical or minor, and that all and sundry among the violators would be thrown into jail. They hoped thus to fill the jails to overflowing and face the government with a problem and a test of strength. Things have turned out differently from Gandhi’s expectations. He and his followers find the government is dealing with each local situation on its merits. This has led to a striking change in the Gandhi program. The Mahatma had said several times that he would win freedom for his country or his d

LONDON, April 12.—Part of the American naval delegation left here for home today, traveling by bert train from Waterloo station to board the George Washington at Southampton. The party included Admiral Moffatt, Admiral and Mrs. Pringir, D. W. Bergman, and Mrs. W. U. Hopkins Beck.

London, April 12 (/P)-Hundreds of woolen operatives in the great Yorkshire textile industry have ceased work in protest at wage reductions, notices of which have just been posted by employers. It will not be possible to measure the extent of the defections until the rolls are called on Monday. The reductions posted by the employers amount to 9.24 percent for time workers and 8.76 percent for piece workers. The National Association of Unions in the Textile Trade proposed a reduction of 5.4 percent for time workers and 5.34 percent for piece workers, but the employers’ council rejected the schedule and substituted their own.

Bombay, April 12 (P)—One week ago tomorrow morning, Mahatma Gandhi opened the Nationalist civil disobedience campaign by entering the waters of the Gulf of Cambay near Dandi and defying the government’s salt monopoly by crudely making salt from sea water. After six days of agitation, the Nationalist campaign tonight continued with apparently unabated vigor despite arrests of many prominent Gandhi lieutenants and the meting out of rigorous prison sentences. The Mahatma is still at liberty. He spoke today in the Sarat district. The chief centers of activity in the campaign today were Calcutta, Lahore, and Bombay, three of the great cities of India, and there was agitation and the menace of violence in all three. At Calcutta Mayor J. M. Sen Gupta, campaigning vigorously again after his release from imprisonment at Rangoon, Burma, for seditious utterances, was once more arrested, this time w

PUTNEY, Eng, April 12.—Three spectators at the Oxford Cambridge boat race on the Thames today were believed to have been drowned soon after the finish when a rowboat in which they were following the crews capsized. Eight other persons who were in the craft, a large sea-going type rowboat, were rescued.

SHANGHAI, April 12. (AP)—Chinese press dispatches from Canton today reported that “a private Lungchow (Kwangsi Province) letter stated that since January 1 Reds have been scourging districts along the French Indo-China border, climaxing their activities March 25 by raiding and burning the French Consulate at Lungchow, driving away the French consuls and occupying the Lungchow customs officers.” “The raid resulted in the French sending 300 soldiers and five airplanes, assisting Kwangsi (Chinese) troops in defeating the communists of whom 500 were slain. Five Russians were captured with many Chinese Communists. The Chinese soldiers executed the Russian and Chinese prisoners with machine guns.”

BERLIN, April 12.—(C.I.N.S.)—Another governmental crisis in Germany was averted today when the Reichstag voted 217 to 206 in favor of the budget of Chancellor Bruening’s cabinet. This test vote averted the dissolution of the cabinet which Dr. Bruening had threatened if the Reichstag did not back him up in his government's financial and agricultural programs.

By United Press MARSEILLES, April 12. — Jean Mermoz, French navigator who intends shortly to fly to South America, broke the world’s seaplane distance record over a closed circuit at 5:45 a. m. today, when he completed 2618 kilometers of flying in 18 hours. Mermoz's record knocks down the previous mark of the Americans, O. J. Connell and H. C. Rood. Mermoz intends to fly to South America by way of Senegal and Natal.

PARIS, April 12—(U.R.)—Dieudonne Coste said today he would be ready in a month for another attempt to fly from Paris to New York. Coste and Bellonte attempted a trans-Atlantic flight last July. They started July 12 for New York, via Spain, the Azores and Halifax, but were forced by storms to turn back. They landed at Villa Coublay, near Paris, the morning of July 14, having flown 3,350 miles in 28 hours. Last autumn, Coste and Bellonte made a record-breaking distance flight from Paris to Eastern Siberia.

Berlin, April 12 (UP)—Chancellor Heinrich Bruening’s government won a victory in the Reichstag today on its agricultural and financial program and avoided the necessity of dissolving the German parliament. The Reichstag, by a vote of 217 to 207, endorsed the cabinet motion to couple the agricultural program with the finance reform bill. The government won through the nationalists who were permitted by their party to support the government or to do as their conscience dictated.

BERLIN.—(?)—The cabinet of Chancellor Bruening, aided by a threat of new elections, again steered safely between the Nationalist opposition on one side and the Communist and Socialist opposition on the other in the Reichstag Saturday. By a vote of 217 to 205 Nationalist attempts to hold out on the government in matters of taxation were defeated. As a final gesture of defiance Saturday afternoon, the Communists introduced a motion of no-confidence but this was voted down 222 to 229.

Need Home Approval Approval by the home governments of the American-Japanese settlement which closed yesterday was said to be the only thing remaining to enable these three delegations to write finis to their naval conference difficulties. Observers said that what this amounted to was that if this agreement is approved by the home governments, the United States, Great Britain and Japan will be in a position to sign a three-power pact at any minute if this should seem desirable. There remains the crisis surrounding France and Italy and the next move would seem to be up to these two. LONDON, Mar. 15. — (®) — Great Britain's Queen knows considerably more of beer, bartenders, and bar-rooms today than she has ever known before. Yesterday she visited a British public house, counterpart of the old American saloon, and found out for herself some of the things of which so much has been written and spoken here and abroad. Her comment upon leaving the bar-room was: “I have enjoyed myself tremendously. I think it is a splendid place, so cozy and homey.” The silence of astonishment and bashfulness fell upon the men in the crowded public house when her majesty, wearing a mauve gown, appeared behind the bar and looked round her with a friendly smile. The men doffed their hats but said nothing until an elderly man whispered to his neighbor: “Ain’t she lovely?” The compliment did not escape the queen who laughingly acknowledged it and in so doing set the whole party at ease. London, March 15 (4)—The fate of the London naval conference is considered to be hanging on the conversation of Prime Minister MacDonald and Premier Tardieu at Chequers tomorrow. The French premier arrived from Paris tonight and spent the evening with M. Briand, French foreign minister, and other French delegates. Early tomorrow, he and Briand will go to the country retreat of the British prime minister for one of the most important meetings of European statesmen since the World War. When they come back to London tomorrow night, Tardieu and Briand will carry the knowledge whether there is any use in the five-power delegations staying in London in the hope that France and Italy can liquidate their naval stalemate. (United Press Staff Correspondent) London, March 15. — Terms of an agreement between Japan and America, now in the hands of the two governments for approval, give Japan 60 per cent of the American battleship strength, 70 per cent of her heavy cruiser tonnage, and equality in submarines, it was learned today from American sources. The agreement, worked out of a long series of inter-delegation conferences, would apply to the two navies until 1936, when the next conference is called. Within the next six years, Japan is to be permitted to build her cruisers armed with 6-inch guns to a total of 108,000 tons, and the United States will agree not to lay down her last three cruisers of that class until 1933, 1934 and 1936 respectively. Since these ships could not be completed before the next conference, the agreement thus virtually assured the far eastern nation of a 70 per cent ratio in that cl

LONDON.—Hope of achieving a five-power naval agreement at the 1930 conference rested Saturday on the conference to be held between Premiers J. Ramsay MacDonald and Andre Tardieu at Chequers Court Sunday. There was little question that the United States, Great Britain and Japan would reach a three-power agreement, but the French-Italian deadlock made a general treaty of any consequence extremely dubious. Premier Tardieu left Paris at noon Saturday for this momentous conference.

Shanghai, March 15. (4) — Five American and two Chinese steamers, attacked with heavy machine gun and rifle fire by Chinese bandit soldiers late yesterday, beat off their attackers and escaped from one of the most dangerous rapids in the Yangtse river. Hidden among rocks of mountainous cliffs between which roars the Hsingtang rapids, the bandits fired from both banks where the great river is narrowed to sixty yards. The attack was made fifty miles above Ichang and more than one thousand miles from the sea. The brunt of the attack was borne by the American steamer Chipping whose American guard under command of Lieut. C. M. Winslow, of the U. S. navy, fired more than 3,000 bullets at the hidden foe and passed through the rapids to Ichang. Casualties of the Chinese could not be learned. Winslow, son of a fighting father, Rear Admiral Cameron McR. Winslow, retired, was struck in the left leg

The Soviet party leaders ordered restitution of property unjustifiably confiscated by officials, the reopening of churches illegally closed, and the punishment of those guilty of using terrorism to carry out the major government policies. Berlin, March 15.— The criminal court today sentenced a pedestrian to imprisonment for causing a traffic accident. Testimony showed that the defendant, Herr Semester, showed negligence in not getting out of the way of a cyclist. The cyclist, forced to swerve, died under the wheels of a motor truck.

1930-03-14.text: London, March 14.—(AP)—The American and Japanese naval delegations were said in well informed quarters this afternoon to have achieved an agreement which is only dependent on confirmation from the home authorities. Senator Reed and Ambassador Matsudaira, two old friends who have been threshing out the complicated difficulties between the two countries, met again this morning and observers were led to believe that they had discussed final details. The big task which they are reported to have all but accomplished included settlement of the Japanese claim for a 70 per cent cruiser ratio. This has been the outstanding stumbling block since the beginning of negotiations. While this was not amplified, observers assumed it to refer to the all-day conferences which have been in progress in an effort to reach a solution of the crisis growing out of the French demands. These same quarters said that while the situation undoubtedly was grave, the conference has not entirely reached a deadlock. Henry L. Stimson, head of the American delegation, and the British prime minister held a further conference this evening. The delegations of three countries at the conference were adhering tonight to the position that some solution was possible despite the crises growing out of the French big navy demands. BOMBAY, INDIA, May 16.—Indian peace prospects brightened today when announcement was made in liberal quarters of an early expected government move for negotiations with Mahatma Gandhi, civil disobedience prisoner. A government meeting at Bombay and a secret session of the all-India congress, held simultaneously, presaged decisive action in some direction, it was declared, before the weekend. While these reports were going abroad, Mme. Sarojini Naidu, successor of the Mahatma and Abbas Tyabji, was arrested early today for attempting a salt raid at Kharasana and shortly afterward set at liberty. Mme. Naidu and her band of volunteers had sat-in the road outside of the village since yesterday forenoon, when halted by police. Mme. Naidu Released Some of her followers were detained after her release. LONDON, Mar, 14.-()——The government of J. Ramsay MacDonald, victor in one fight with its opposition, today looked forward to an impending more dangerous tilt 1 week from now when the coal mines controversy is resumed. The conservative motion of censure blaming the government for the general depression failed to pass the House of Commons last night after a lengthy debate by vote of 308 to 235, a majority of 73 for the government. In opening the debate Stanley Baldwin, conservative leader, predicted that the government probably would win, and about 25 conservative members absented themselves from the House just before the division was taken. Sir Samuel, speaking for the liberals, in an opening address announced his party would support the government, but he predicted that unemployment would "wash away" the government. LONDON, March 13.—(®)—The labor government tonight beat off a conservative attack in the House of Commons, defeating a motion of censure brought by former Premier Baldwin, conservative leader, with a margin of more than 70 votes to spare. The figures were 308 to 235 in the division. After six hours of debate in which Winston Churchill, former Chancellor of the Exchequer, led the Tory attack, about a score of liberals filed into the government lobbies and voted with labor. The labor strength of 287 votes, however, would have been sufficient alone to defeat the Tories, the figures indicating many abstentions among both opposition parties. London, March 13,—(4)— The London naval conference is fighting for its life, and apparently with hope of success. Tonight Prime Minister MacDonald of Great Britain authorized a statement that he was encouraged by the day's events. Aristide Briand, foreign minister and head of the French delegation, received the world journalists just to show them that he is not so gloomy as he is supposed to be. He is confident the conference can achieve definite results in the general interests of peace. The events of the day to which Mr. MacDonald referred were a series of conversations held at No. 10 Downing Street. He began this morning with Reijiro Wakatsuki of the Japanese delegation. Dino Grandi of the Italian group followed. Then came M. Briand, who stayed an hour and three-quarters. Lastly came the American's secretary Henry L. By The Associated Press. LONDON, March 13.—Former Premier Baldwin, conservative leader, opened an attack on the labor government late today, moving a vote of censure, but took most of the sting out of it by declaring that the government in all likelihood would win on the vote. At the same time he asserted that eventually the cold fact of unemployment would mean the defeat of the MacDonald ministry. LONDON, March 13.—The House of Commons votes tonight on a conservative motion of censure of the government of J. Ramsay MacDonald. If the censure is successful, resignation of the labor prime minister and ministry might be expected. Neither Mr. MacDonald nor his fellow laborites, however, despite their defeat on an agreement to the coal mines bill Tuesday, expected the House to go against them, although a close vote was forecast.

London, March 14—An attempt will be made this weekend to salvage the five power naval conference from the stalemate into which it has fallen. Delegates hope to find the way for a limitation treaty which will not involve such high figures as in reality will constitute a building program agreement. Engagements Cancelled Golf matches and other weekend engagements are being cancelled in the belief that conversations seeking a solution to the problem presented by French demands will be continued tomorrow and Sunday. A new factor will be present with the arrival of Andre Tardieu, French premier. Intensive efforts to lead the conference out of its difficulties actually began yesterday with a round of private meetings and later a statement by Premier MacDonald that he was encouraged by the day’s events. Aristide Briand, French foreign minister, announced also that he was not discouraged and that

Bombay, India—P—Two policemen and 50 strikers were injured Thursday during a fight in the railway shed at Byculla, where the Great Indian Peninsula Railway maintains a large force. The workers attempted “passive resistance” by lying prostrate and obstructing the loyal workmen. Police arrested two of the strike leaders on charges of unlawful assembly and trespass and then attempted to disperse the prone workmen with clubs. The workmen arose and stoned the police and the free-for-all fight ensued. Ahmadabad, India—/—Mahatma Gandhi and his ‘party of 79 devotees left Aslali at dawn today on the second stage of their march to the salt fields at Jalalpur in inauguration of the campaign for Indian independence. Unlike Wednesday, when thousands bade him godspeed outside his college at Ahmadabad, there was no crowd Thursday outside the rest house where the party spent the night and when the party

London, March 14.—Henry L. Stimson, secretary of state and head of the United States delegation, who shared the task of pulling the naval conference from the brink of deadlock with Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, of Great Britain, yesterday, was assuming an even more important role this afternoon in the direction of the negotiations. A meeting between the secretary and Dino Grandi, foreign minister of Italy, featured renewed energies of the conference. Grandi later conferred with Aristide Briand, foreign minister of France. From all directions pressure was being brought to bear on the Franco-Italian deadlock. MacDonald went to Chequers, country home of prime ministers, this afternoon, and tomorrow he will attend the annual British-Scottish Rugby game in London. Sunday has been set aside for an important conference with Premier Andre Tardieu, of France, at which the British and French st
