If the censure is successful, resignation of the Labor Prime Minister and Ministry might be expected. Neither Mr. MacDonald nor his fellow laborites, however, despite their defeat of an amendment to the coal mines bill Tuesday, expect the House to go against them, although a close vote was forecast. The motion of censure is that prepared several weeks ago by Stanley Baldwin, Conservative leader and former Premier, and Winston Churchill, former Chancellor of the Exchequer. It states the case against the government in the following terms: "That the House deplores the depression in trade and the increase in unemployment resulting from the policy of the present government and regrets the refusal of the government not only to extend safeguarding or imperial p

BOMBAY, (UP).—Mahatma Gandhi and his pilgrim-revolutionaries reached the Katra district, stronghold of the civil disobedience movement Friday in their march towards Jalalpur where they will defy the British laws forbidding private refining of salt. Gandhi's campaign in Katra was particularly effective, and it was there that Vallabhbhai Patel, before his arrest by British police, did his most intensive work of propaganda. Arrival of the 70 crusaders in Katra was signalized by their leader's address to village chiefs, urging them to join the independence movement and demonstrate their faith by resigning their official positions as a protest at Patel’s arrest. Affected by Gandhi's pleas, three of the police, a number of minor officials and several headmen surrendered their offices. It is the revolutionists’ intention thus to paralyze the government's organization in Indian towns and village

London, March 14.—(INS)—Thrown overboard in a frantic attempt to ‘save the five-power naval disarmament conference from failure, the so-called parity agreement between the United States and Great Britain went into the discard today. While the principle of parity between the two English-speaking naval powers will be maintained, the level will be considerably higher than that agreed upon tentatively some weeks ago. According to present indications, the figure will be nearer 1,300,000 tons, representing an increase over the tentative program of approximately 100,000 tons of warships. The American delegation to the parley, although reluctant, is prepared to accept this augmented figure and let the earlier program of 1,200,000 tons go by the board. This decision has been necessitated by the final realization by both British and American delegates that it is impossible to persuade France to re

Calcutta, India, March 14— J. M. L. Sengupta, mayor of Calcutta who is under arrest on a charge of sedition, left his home in a motor car procession today for the docks where he embarked on the steam Sirdhana for Rangoon. He must answer the government's charges there.

LONDON, Mar. 14—(?)—The Lancet, British medical journal, today announced discovery of what may prove to be the germ of “disseminated sclerosis,” a degenerative disease of the brain and spinal cord. The discovery was by Miss Kathleen Chevassut, a young pupil of Sir James Purves Stewart, widely known British medical authority. If substantiated, the Lancet believes that it will rank among the foremost achievements of bacteriology. Disseminated sclerosis is often responsible for paralysis. It usually steadily progresses, chronic nephritis or tuberculosis frequently developing, causing death. Its causes hitherto have been obscure and its treatment unsatisfactory. The Lancet said experiments are being made in treating the disease with vaccines prepared from cultures of minute bodies which Miss Chevassut discovered.

Poona, Bombay, India, Mar 14 (AP)—A “war” council of eleven members was appointed by Indian Nationalists today to organize passive resistance to the British government in Poona and this district. One hundred volunteers enrolled and decided to march to a suburban district of Bombay on the seacoast and manufacture salt in violation of the British monopoly.

London, March 14, a.f—American and British efforts to hold the London naval conference together by main strength until it can show some tangible results have been temporarily successful. Hurried inter-delegation conversations following indications that the conference was on the verge of a breakdown lulled the storm raised by France's refusal to modify her tonnage demands unless she was given a security pact insuring her against aggressors. Both England and the United States appear determined to reach an agreement in one form or another.

London, March 13.—(Special Dispatches to The Daily Mail from Bombay, India, today said that the villagers of Bareja showed only a faint interest in the pilgrimage of Mahatma Gandhi and his 79 volunteers when they passed through the village. According to the Daily Mail correspondent, most of the peasants in the district round about paid no attention to Gandhi's march of civil disobedience and continued unconcernedly at work.

LONDON, Mar. 14--Commissioner Catherine Booth of the Salvation Army, daughter of the late General Bramwell Booth, will leave the army but not voluntarily, to write the biography of her father. Mrs. Bramwell Booth, the general's widow, declared today. Mrs. Booth said her daughter wished to continue her work and write the book also, but that General Higgs, new commander of the army, had decided that she could not do both.

Dunedin, New Zealand, March 14— (AP)—Rear Admiral Byrd and his associates in the Antarctic are enjoying a well earned rest. Several have gone into the country for short trips prior to departure for the United States and home. The City of New York and the Gleanor Bolling are being prepared for sailing Friday, over a tentative route including Tahiti and Panama. The City of New York's hull is in capital shape despite severe buffeting by the ice. Rear Admiral Byrd today addressed 6,000 school children, who gave the explorer a remarkable ovation.

BERLIN, March 13, (#)—President Von Hindenburg today signed the Young Plan a few minutes after it had been approved by the Reichsrat with an urgency clause, making it immediately effective as far as Germany is concerned. The associated liquidation agreements have not yet been signed as the president is formally obliged to investigate whether any of these agreements are in conflict with the institution.

BORDEAUX, France. —(P) Swollen by ceaseless rains the Garonne and its tributaries, and rivers south of here are rising rapidly again. Pau, in the lower Pyrenees, is in the center of a flooded district; at the watering place Salies-de-Bearn, picturesque low quarters are flooded to a depth of six feet. Authorities have taken measures to evacuate part of the population in the Basque country. The Nive river, rising four inches an hour, menaced Camboles-Bains and St. Jean-Pied-de-Port, the famous golf course at St. Jean-de-Luz was partly submerged.

Cassel, Germany, March 13. (P)—A woman lion tamer’s heroic attempt to separate a battling lion and bear in a circus menagerie wagon proved fatal to herself and to the beasts today. The tamer entered the cage armed only with a wire whip and succeeded in wrenching the bear from the lion's deadly claws. Suddenly the lion leaped upon the woman and clawed her fatally. Her dying cries attracted attendants who succeeded in dragging her from the cage only after shooting the lion. The bear also died from his injuries. The battle between the beasts started after the lion crushed a wooden partition in the cage.

13(A.B) —F eenichn official circles in Paris feel that practically all hope must be abandoned of a five-power naval reduction treaty, especially if such a treaty hinges upon further concessions from the French delegation. It is felt here that some sort of agreement may be patched up to save the face of the London conference and not to have it go down in history as a complete failure, Official circles here express the feeling that France has stated her position clearly and that she cannot recede now from the stand she has taken.

Paris, Mar, 14.-(P)—A Brussels dispatch to the newspaper Intransigeant says that the bodies of the three French airmen Roux, Caillot and Dodemont who left Madagascar last January for Paris, have been found beside their wrecked plane in the Belgian Congo. The men left Madagascar Jan. 10 and were last seen on the 13th near Port Franqui fighting high winds. They were found in the Great Kasai.

1930-04-05.text: London, April 4.—(AP)— Signing of a three power pact by the United States, Great Britain and Japan and quick adjournment of the naval conference was said in an authoritative quarter late today to be quite possible. This would involve leaving the knotty questions of French security and Franco-Italian parity to be signed in other fields, and would provide so that France and Italy would be in a position to sign as soon as these difficulties have been ironed out.

Lewy wwe, Londen, April 4 — Having achieved their major objectives at the conference in an American-British-Japanese naval agreement, Col. Henry L. Stimson and the rest of the American delegation today reserved cabins on the Leviathan for the homeward journey April 22. Hope for a five-power agreement is being abandoned and the belief is that the conference cannot last longer than that date. It is understood that the American-British-Japanese agreement will cover a five-year period from the expiration of the Washington disarmament treaty in 1921. Announcement that the Americans were preparing to buy their steamer tickets came during one of the tensest days of the conference and indications tonight are that a crisis exists which may end Continued on Page Three

London, April 5.—(A.P.)—The five power naval conference hurried on today to what generally was considered its inevitable end. Unless the situation changes greatly in the next day or two, observers believed, the negotiations will be concluded before Easter. The American delegation has engaged space on the Leviathan leaving England April 22, two days after Easter. The French and Italian delegations may leave as soon as the plenary session is held next week: Three Power Pact Likely, It was expected that a three power treaty between America, Japan, and Great Britain would be drawn up in the remaining days of the parley, with Prime Minister MacDonald said to be the only man among the naval delegates who still has much hope of a break in the impasse which seems definitely to exclude France and Italy from agreement. The French and Italians themselves, patience apparently frayed by the long argu

Bombay, India, April 5.--(4)—Police and striking railway men clashed here yesterday during which 30 persons were injured and reports this morning indicated that the incident has hastened threatened civil disobedience on the railway lines. At meetings today of strikers on this railway, it was decided to “paralyze” train service by groups of strikers prostrating themselves on the lines, this is a means of tying up service that has been used by the Indians previously. It was estimated that 7,000 persons volunteered for such action. The Bombay police today claimed that the slogan “brickbats for batons” had in effect been given the strikers. If molested by the police the strikers were said in the police report to have been instructed to retaliate with “Indian bullets,” otherwise stones.

BOMBAY.—(4)—Police Friday fired on a crowd of striking Indian railway men, injuring thirty persons, including two European bystanders. A police sergeant and Miss B. Hay and H. B. Burley were taken to the hospital. The encounter occurred outside the Victoria terminal of the great Indian Peninsular railroad where 2,000 strikers were demonstrating. The natives forced their way into the station and demanded to be taken to the station of Byculla, in the environs of the city. Railway officials replied by shutting the platform gates, an action that so incensed the strikers that they burst into an uproarious disturbance. The police were sent for, but when they arrived the strikers received them with a barrage of stones. They retaliated by opening fire. Order has been restored and the police were on guard Friday night around the station. Railway employees on the Great Indian Peninsular line have

BOMBAY, India, April 6. (P) - Thirty persons were injured when police fired into a crowd of striking railwaymen here yesterday. A police sergeant, a woman and a man were seriously wounded. Two thousand native strikers demonstrating outside the Victoria terminal of the Great Indian Peninsula railway forced their way into the station and demanded free transportation to a suburb. When police interfered they were stoned. They opened fire in retaliation.
LONDON, April 4.— (U.P.) — The United States delegation to the naval conference was said in American sources today to have made tentative reservations to sail for home on the Leviathan April 22.

BRUSSELS, Belgium, April 4—Thirteen men were killed and eight injured in a fire-damp explosion in a coal mine at Elouges, near Mons, last night. Two of the injured men were seriously hurt and were taken out by rescue crews who worked desperately throughout the night. The explosion took place as an electrically controlled dynamite charge was detonated. The miner in charge of the operation declared that all precautions had been taken and that there was no trace of fire-damp before the accident. King Albert has requested by telegraph a complete report on the causes and circumstances of the tragedy.

Rome, April 4—(?)—Queen Victoria of Sweden, long an invalid, died here today. The queen, who had been sinking for some time from a complication of pulmonary illnesses, took a sudden turn for the worse today and King Gustaf, who had been visiting in Naples, returned to Rome to be at her bedside. The queen was 68 years old.

ROME, April 5 (AP)—Officially Rome was in deep mourning today for Queen Victoria of Sweden, who died yesterday at her villa Svezia here after a heart attack. She had been ill for more than 20 years. This city knew the Queen almost better than her own capital, Stockholm, since it was here that she spent a considerable part of her time during the long bronchial illness. The Swedish court physician, Axel Munthe, attended her. The Queen died with King Gustav and almost all the Royal family, including Prince William, at her bedside. King Gustav held her hand as life ebbed. She died calmly and without apparent pain. Her body lay in state today at her villa, from which it was to be transported to Sweden for interment after services at the German Lutheran church here.

ROME, April 4.—Queen Victoria of Sweden, 68, long an invalid from a bronchial ailment, died calmly here today in the winter home that was her refuge every year from the rigorous climate of Sweden. King Gustave, who returned yesterday from a trip to Naples, and Prince William, were at her bedside. Queen Victoria had been sinking in vitality for a long time from a pulmonary complication. Yesterday her condition was disquieting and King Gustave was summoned. The queen died as though she were falling asleep. Only Doctor Munte, who has attended her for more than thirty years, realized she was dead. Aided by nurses, Doctor Munte clad the body in burial garments of black and laid it out on the bed, over which were strewn roses from the garden that the queen had loved and personally supervised. She used to say that it was the sight and perfume of flowers in sunny Italy that kept her alive. By co

Rome, (UP) — The queen of Sweden died today after a lingering illness. Death occurred at 7 p. m. The queen, who was 67, had been in failing health for years. Her final illness began some months ago in Rome, where the climate was better suited to her condition. The king and other members of her family have been constantly with Queen Victoria during her long illness.

Berlin, April 4. (P)—A Berlin court has granted a decree to a wife who, while her husband was away on business in England, happened to see a newsreel of a football game played in that country. Among the spectators accidentally shown in closeup during the photographing of the game was the absent husband, obviously more interested in his woman companion than in the game itself. The injured wife persuaded the manager of the picture theatre to give her a little of the incriminating celluloid. She brought it into court, and the divorce followed.

MOSCOW, Apr. 4. (AP)—Pravda, official organ of the Communist party, today said that revolutionary feeling is steadily developing among the masses in the United States, asserting that this was proved by the events of March 6, the international unemployment demonstration day, which caused riots in a number of American and foreign cities. The American Communist party, it adds, is being converted from a mere propagandist unit into a cohesive group. After telling its readers that the American Communist party in the past has led many bitter class struggles, including the textile and mines strikes in 1927 and the recent trouble in the Gastonia mill regions, Pravda regretfully announces that only an insignificant number of new members have entered the party, the present membership being only 15,900. American Communists are endeavoring to correct this weakness, it explains, by an intensive recrui

HAMBURG, Germany. April 5 UP, - Commodore Hans Ruser, former skipper of the south polar exploration ship Gaus and the liners Imperator and Vaterland, died today aged 68. It was while commander of the Vaterland that Commodore Ruser was interned in New York during the war.

BY United Press. GENEVA, April 6.—Sinister intrigue and royal poison plots enter into accusations now in the hands of the League of Nations secretariat against Ras Tafari, sole ruler of Abyssinia since the death of his cousin, the Empress Zeoditu, two days ago. Ras Tafari is accused by Dr. Alexandre Garabedian, former physician to the Abyssinian court, of having twice urged the poisoning of the empress and of Waiziro Sehin, her niece and Tafari’s mother-in-law. Because he refused to obey the royal commands to put out of the way the woman who blocked Ras Tafari’s sole autocratic sway over the black empire of Africa, Dr. Garabedian claims he was subjected to persecution, raids on his hospital, imprisonment and exile.

PARIS, April 4.—(C.I.N.S.)—Pre- mier Andre Tardieu, who collapsed in the chamber of deputies yesterday from a sudden attack of indigestion, spent today in absolute rest and quiet. His physician said he had quite recovered from the attack and probably would be able to resume work in the chamber tomorrow.

BERLIN, April 5.—A solemn warning to beware of the lure of the pyramids, the Sphinx in the moonlight, or the starlight on Egypt's desert was sounded by Gordon C. Thorne of Chicago and his wife, formerly Mrs. Marion Bolin, of Hammond while here on a visit. Mr. Thorne is a son of the late William C. Thorne, one of the founders of Montgomery Ward & Co. 'Things may sound romantic to camp at the foot of the pyramids on the desert, but for us it proved a ghastly experience,' Mr. Thorne said. 'When in Egypt I heard that many others had had similar and worse encounters, but I never read about them and I think the public ought to know about them. THE THRILLS OF CAMPING 'We were taking part in a Mediterranean cruise. The folders told us all about the thrill of a night in camp at the foot of a pyramid and the entire cruising party dutifully pitched camp to enjoy the thrill. Dark figures hovered in

YOKOHAMA, Apr. 5.—(P)—The Chichibu Maru, new motor liner of the Nippon Yusen Kaisha, today interrupted her maiden voyage across the Pacific to answer a distress call from an unnamed Mexican vessel off the coast northeast of here. The Chichibu Maru left Yokohama for San Francisco at 3 p.m., yesterday and picked up the call a few hours later. Radio advices said she had altered her course and was standing by the Mexican ship. Hopes of her breaking the transpacific time record

1930-05-05.text: BOMBAY, India, May 5.—(?)— The Indian government today caused the arrest of Mahatma Gandhi, thus for the moment halting the civil resistance campaign upon which for more than two months it had looked with patient eye and effectually preventing entry of "The Holy One" into Bombay. Gandhi’s arrest, made early today, was followed by a silence upon the part of his followers so intense as to give no indication of what their attitude would be. The Mahatma himself was mute. Whirled away to Poona, where for the third time in his eventful career prison doors closed behind him, and made no statement, voiced no threat. Mrs. Gandhi alone spoke for him. "I fervently hope India will show her mettle," she said, "and give a fitting reply to the government’s unwarranted action." Bombay, India, May 5—(UP)—Strong forces of British and Indian troops were ordered mustered for any emergency in the chief cities of India today as the Mahatma M. K. Gandhi was put in a British jail—his most dangerous battle front in the Nationalist campaign for independence. Bells tolled in Bombay, signifying a Nationalist call for a day of mourning as the man whom India’s millions call the “Great Soul” was placed in Yeroda jail in Poona for an indefinite term. No formal charge was announced. Hartals—days of cessation of work which are tantamount to paralyzing strikes—were declared in many cities. All shops were tightly shut and barred. Only muslin and some factory workers hesitated to join the Bombay hartal, which was started under the eyes of heavy patrols of soldiers. Troops Patrolled Cities Troops and armored cars patrolled Ahmedabad, where a hartal paralyzed business; Peshawar was t

CROYDON AIRDROME, LONDON, May 6.—Miss Amy Johnson, 29, began a solo flight from London to Australia at dawn today. Miss Johnson planned to make her first stop tonight at Vienna. The young woman was flying a gypsy moth plane and said her route would take her to Constantinople, Aleppo and Baghdad.

Jalapur, India, May 5.—(Monday)—(AP) — Mahatma Gandhi, leader of the Indian civil disobedience movement against British rule in India, was suddenly arrested in this village this morning. Gandhi was taken to the central jail at Yerroda, a town near Poona. Poona is a British military stronghold and the headquarters of an army command. Rescue Forestalled Elaborate precautions were taken by the authorities to prevent violence or attempts at rescue. At Yerroda, Gandhi will be detained without trial. Under the terms of a regulation more than a century old, the idol of the Hindu masses will remain in prison at the pleasure of the government of India. His arrest, following a week of comparative tranquility since the riots at Calcutta, Karachi and Peshawar, which were disavowed by Gandhi, had been heralded by many rumors but finally came with a shock of surprise. LIVERPOOL, May 5,—Six persons were killed and at least 100 were injured, some of them seriously, when a terrific explosion partially demolished an oil cake factory here today. The victims were trapped in the building by the blast. An immediate investigation was launched in an effort to determine its cause.

LIVERPOOL, Eng., May 3.—-(U.P.) —A terrific explosion extensively damaged the Bibbys Oil Cake mills in the central part of the city today, setting fire to the three upper stories. At least 100 persons were believed to have been injured. All traffic in the district was suspended and stretcher bearers removed the injured to ambulances and private cars. One of the injured men's clothes was torn off and his skin blackened. Officials at the factory said six persons were believed dead in the explosion.

Worcester, South Africa, May 4. — Four mulattoes and one negro native were killed and 17 other persons injured in a three-cornered battle with police today. Constable Barter was struck with a hatchet during the fight in the streets of the town, and his condition is critical. The police intervened during a row between mulattoes and negroes and were finally forced to open fire when stoned by the mob. Los Angeles — Walter Schuyler, 56, wealthy retired corporation lawyer, died.

By The Associated Press Bombay, May 5—(Monday)—Mahatma Gandhi, Nationalist leader whose arrest in the civil disobedience campaign has been frequently predicted during the past week was taken into custody today at the village of Jalalpur. He was arrested under regulation 25 of the laws of 1827 and will suffer imprisonment for as long as the government decrees.

Poona, Bombay India May 5. (UP) Mahatma Gandhi, leader of the Indian civil disobedience campaign, entered the Yeravda prison at 11 a.m., three motor cars carrying him and his police escort arriving from Borivli shortly before that time. He seemed in good health and spirits and told the correspondent that he was pleased with the arrangements which had been made for the journey and that every comfort had been provided for. It was understood the government shortly would issue an order providing a definite allowance for him of 100 rupees (about $36) monthly for food with a food allowance for his subordinates.

LONDON, May 5.—The greatest crisis in the history of Britain's turbulent protectorate over the Indian peninsula reached its sensational climax today with the arrest and “indefinite detention” of Mahatma Gandhi, the “Holy Man" of India's Nationalist cause. Rudely awakened from his sleep at 2 o'clock this morning, Gandhi achieved his long-sought martyrdom with incarceration in the Yeroda jail, while threats of nation-wide strikes and the possibility of general uprising followed in the wake of his prison van. An exchange Telegraph dispatch from Bombay gave vivid details of the Mahatma’s arrest at his temporary home in Surat, 100 miles north of Bombay. After long and serious consideration, the Bombay government, with the sanction and authority of the British crown, decided Gandhi's doctrine of passivity had failed to hold in check the violence of many of his followers. (By The Associated Press) Madrid, May 5—A battle be- tween rioting students of the San Carlos Medical College and police today resulted in casualties unofficially reported as one dead, a workman, and 17 injured. The authorities would give no official information regarding casualties or arrests.

MADRID, May 5. (UP)—Student rioting at Madrid university was renewed today when anti-monarchist demonstrators clashed with police. At least one student was killed and nine others critically injured in the fighting. Seventeen other students were less seriously injured in the clash which occurred at the school of medicine when police opened fire on the students.
GLLDER, Germany, May 4—(} The well known German parachute Jumper, Lange, was killed today in a jump from an airplane flying at an altitude of about 1600 feet. The parachute did not open.

MADRID.—(CP)—Three different riots, a number of arrests and several injuries Sunday marked a speech calling for a Spanish republic by Prof. Miguel de Unamuno, of the University of Salamanca, one of Spain’s republican leaders. Repeating in a large theater his appeals for the supplanting of the monarchy by a republic, he again proved himself a storm center in Spanish politics. Fighting started inside the theater before he even had a chance to speak. It was resumed in the street after the meeting, and continued in front of his hotel when he went home. A group of a dozen monarchists opened the republican demonstration by rushing down the aisles of the theater shouting, “Long live the king!” The professor's republican followers, shouting in reply, “Long live the republic,” forcibly expelled the intruders after vigorous fist fights. Civil guards finally restored order in the meeting, which was

BASEL, Switzerland, May 4.— (AP)—The pilot and one passenger of an airplane were killed today in a wreck near Dornach. The pilot, Willy Storrer, was forced to make a landing, but in doing so one of the plane’s wings struck a tree and the three occupants were hurled to the ground. The other passenger was seriously injured.

1930-06-06.text: Bombay, June 6,—(A.P.)—Three hundred policemen with lathis or staves, and fifty armed police all under the command of thirty European police with revolvers today surrounded the headquarters of the All-India National Congress here and raided the premises. It was the third police raid since the launching of the civil disobedience campaign. Six members of the Bombay Congress committee's “war council” were arrested, including President Joshi. The police conducted a thorough search of the premises as well as of the Jinnah public hall which adjoined the congress headquarters. Picketing of European shops in the fort or foreign quarter of the city began today in accordance with the decision of the All-Indian National Congress. Two volunteers, dressed in khaki shorts and wearing Gandhi caps took their positions in front of each of twelve European shops and urged Indians not to enter. Europeans we

Cambridge, Eng., June 5. (AP)—Ambassador Dawes tonight addressed a dinner given by the Masters and Fellows of Trinity College during which he paid tribute to the American Gold Star mothers and made caustic reference to American social seekers in Great Britain. The ambassador was responding in behalf of 17 noted persons who were given honorary degrees by Cambridge earlier in the day. The ambassador himself received the honorary degree of Doctor of Laws. He referred only indirectly to those Americans who seek social preference, bringing this up in connection with a recent visit of the Gold Star mothers whom he referred to as “the best representatives of my people.” “We have recently had in London,” he said, “a body of American travellers representing a cross section of the American people, representing the heart and soul of the American people, representing the bone and sinew of the Americ

BOMBAY, June 5—(AP)—Hostile episodes on the northwestern frontier have taken the spotlight from the Nationalist salt raiders in troubled India. A warlike Lashkar (Tribal force) consisting of Afridis and Zakka Khels tonight was advancing on the key city of Peshawar, and while authorities here felt that troops of the northwestern area would be adequate to deal with this advance, there was some consternation here. The Peshawar region has been in a troubled state for some time; the crisis arose on the night of May 28 when Nari Khwar, an outpost, was fired upon. On the same day some 3,000 Kuki Khel Afridis, carrying a red standard, assembled at Mardan, where they were joined on May 30 by contingents from the Malikden Khel Kamber and other Kuki Khels.

Good news announces navy contracts for 52 fighting planes, torpedo and bombing airboats. They will cost, for the 52 ships, $3,000,177. For the price of one modern battleship, with coalers and other equipment, the navy could buy 1,040 such fighting planes. Altogether, they would require crews smaller than one battleship crew and would cost far less in the upkeep than one battleship. And one such bombing plane could sink any battleship or other ship afloat. This nation needs, at the least, an air fleet of 5,000 fighting planes, with an adequate fleet under waters. Peshawar is a long way from Buckingham Palace, and once it would have been painful, slow work subduing natives in those far-off valleys. But now, the dull thud of exploding Royal Air Force bombs is heard in the hiding places of Hall and his Mohammedan tribesmen, rebelling against Britain. And Hall's forces are melting away. Allah

Simla, India, -June 68, WQ— The British government in India has no intention whatever of compromising with Mahatma Gandhi’s movement for independence, and is ready to take even more stringent measures than in the past to check its development, the United Press learned from an authoritative source today. The government realizes fully that the rebellion is a serious matter, and that it may yet lead to violence, the United Press informant said, but it has every confidence that the forces now in India will be able to cope with whatever situation occurs. Gandhi's objectives in the passive resistance campaign so far have not been changed.

Bombay, India, June 6. (UP)—Four persons were sentenced to death today in Sholapur for the murder of several constables killed during the recent rioting there. Sentence was pronounced in sessions court by Judge Nijivadia, a native jurist.

LONDON, June 5 (CAP) — Prime Minister MacDonald informed the House of Commons today the government had decided against the construction of the proposed English Channel tunnel. BOMBAY, June 5. (AP) — A hartal, or cessation of work, was observed by Indian nationalists here today in mourning for Mahatma Gandhi who today ended his first month's imprisonment at Yeroda jail, Poona. Several minor disturbances occurred as processions in commemoration of the day were carried out.

Bombay, June —(A.P.)—Picketing of European shops in the fort or foreign quarter of the city began today in accordance with the decision of the Bombay "war council" of the All-India National Congress. Two volunteers, dressed in khaki shorts and wearing Gandhi caps took their positions in front of each of twelve European shops and urged Indians not to enter; Europeans were not molested. A humorous touch was added to the proceedings by one European firm of outfitters which provided stools on which the Nationalist volunteers might sit. FEAR FIGHTING. British forces in the northwest frontier province, centering about Peshawar, were believed today to be sufficient to meet an advance of frontier tribesmen against the city but the situation was such as to cause some apprehension of serious fighting. A large force of war-like Afridis and Zakha Khels was understood to be moving upon Peshawar. Unre

Seville, Spain; June 5 - Fresh from her seventh crossing of the Atlantic, the homeward bound Graf Zeppelin landed here at 12:04, eastern standard time, this noon to disembark several passengers and then continue to Germany. The Graf, after fighting unfavorable weather conditions off the European coast, arrived over Seville at 10:20 a.m. and circled over the city for a while before making a landing. The flight from Lakehurst to Seville took 59 hours and eight minutes.

FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, Germany, June 6 (AP)—The Graf Zeppelin, home from her 18,000 mile voyage to South America and the United States, landed at Friedrichshafen at 7:22 p. m., (1:22 p. m., EST). The Graf thus completed a cruise lasting 19 days during which she made landings in Spain, Brazil and the United States and flew over the North African coast. The Graf left her home port of Friedrichshafen on Sunday, May 18 and since then made her sixth and seventh crossings of the Atlantic. She left Seville, Spain, on May 20, arrived at Pernambuco, Brazil on the 23rd, visited Rio De Janeiro and left Pernambuco on May 28 for the United States, arriving at Lakehurst on May 31. Two days later she was off again for Seville, arriving there yesterday and remaining just 31 minutes. She discharged some passengers and took on supplies. Her voyage from Seville to Friedrichshafen, which lasted 24 hours and 47 mi

Lyons, France, June 6 A lent storm area was descending from the northeast today on the Rhone Valley where the Graf Zeppelin was maneuvering in an effort to find clear sailing en route to the home port, Friedrichshafen. The weather bureau here warned Hugo Eckener four times that the storm was approaching but received no word from the dirigible. An aviator en route from the north to Marseilles also signalled Dr. Eckener, who began swinging his ship around to escape the fierce storm which was creating havoc with trees and roofs in Lyons. The dirigible turned about from Valence toward Montelimar and Dr. Eckener was expected to make a detour around the storm. The aviator who warned the dirigible of the coming storm before he landed at Bron Field, near Marseilles, said the Graf Zeppelin was maneuvering easily at the time and was swinging about in its course. FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, Germany, June 6 — (U.P.) — The Graf Zeppelin, completing its spectacular flight to North and South America and return, landed at its home port here at 7:23 tonight. A large crowd cheered the Zeppelin and its commander, Hugo Ickener, on returning from the most ambitious journey since its flight around the world.

BERLIN, June 6.—(#)—Germany’s bachelors and bachelor girls will have to shoulder an additional burden of taxation as their share of efforts to meet Germany's heavy obligations if a proposal of the cabinet is approved by the Reichstag. The cabinet has agreed upon an additional ten per cent tax on incomes of unmarried men and women, which means more than double the present rate. The increase, while startling, compared to the income tax of Americans without wives or children, is not likely to exceed the high level already reached on British income taxes.

| Seville, Spain. June 5. (7)—The Graf Zeppelin and a wobbly, storm-shaken group of passengers made port here between storms today and in half an hour whirred away toward Friedrichshafen, seventh and last stop of their historic tri-continent voyage of nearly 18,000 miles. After flying around for several hours over southern Spain, Dr. Hugo Eckener, the Graf's master, directed the huge craft to its depot, discharged passengers, literally snatched supplies from the ground and made off for home in just 31 minutes, demonstrating the express nature of the passenger craft. It was a pale, haggard party of laggard adventurers that arrived, after being tossed about in storm after storm during the last night of their journey here. They had little sleep last night, but gamely asserted that the experience was worth their discomfort. Dr. Eckener said the airship stood the terrific weather splendidly.

PARIS, June 6—A letter requesting that attention of the United States government be called to anxiety of French industry at proposed increases in American tariffs has been sent the French minister of commerce, M. Flandin, by the French Federation of Industries and the National Association for Economic Expansion. The letter characterized the proposed new duties as a prohibitive barrier to most of the principal French industries and predicts a tariff war as "dangerous alike to world prosperity and peace." The letter further refers to statements of American economists that high tariffs will increase prices in the United States with resultant dangers to the country’s prosperity. "It is not for us to re-echo these dangers but we do intend to call the attention of the American government and congress to the repercussions which the American economic policy will have upon American commercial rel

Friedrichshafen, Germany, June 5 (P)--The dirigible Graf Zeppelin, which left Seville this evening and turned toward her familiar berth at the Zeppelin plant here, was flying along the Mediterranean coast of the Southern Route. - At midnight mid-European time (6 p. m. E. S. T.), the Zeppelin radioed that it had just flown over Cabo de Gata. That point is on the Mediterranean about 200 miles southeast of Seville. The position indicated that the Graf either was making slow time or else was cruising around to avoid bad weather, for the 200 miles was made in something like six hours.

Naples, Italy, June 5.—(#)—Warning that the present eruption of the Vesuvius may be serious and immediate construction of earthworks is necessary to avert possible disaster was made today by Professor Malladra, head of the Vesuvius observatory. He said former earthworks were destroyed in a previous eruption, leaving a free path for the flow of lava which may come at any hour now. “The mountain is increasing its ‘eruptive activity and innumerable burning stones and rocks already have collected in the crater,” he said.

CUNEO, Italy, June 6. (AP)— The eleventh arch of a great bridge now under construction over the river Stura collapsed today causing the death of eight workmen. Three men were seriously injured. The cause of the collapse has not been determined.

By United Press PARIS, June 6—A bomb concealed in a package addressed to the Baroness De Rothschild exploded in the main post office today. There were no casualties. The package was addressed to the Baroness Robert De Rothschild, the former Mlle Beer. Baron De Rothschild is administrator of the Northern Railroad Company and of the P. L. M. Railroad, and other lines.

The naval dispatches said the nationalist defenses had reorganized near the strategic railway line, and that a sharp engagement was still going on at the time they were filed, late in the day. SHANGHAI, June 6. (AP)—Hard pressed on four major battle fronts, the Nationalist government was considered today to be facing one of the most serious military crises in its short and turbulent existence. In addition, many government civilian officials here were seeking to strengthen its sorely strained finances, resulting from the military’s demands, paralyzed trade and depreciated currency. The American consul at Tsinan, Shantung Province, said Japanese advices today urged Americans to evacuate Tsinan, against which the northern rebel armies were marching. By the Associated Press. Shanghai, China, June 5.-The Nationalist government armies retreated today in Hunan and in Shantung provinces before victorious rebel onslaughts on widely separated battlefields. On two other fronts—central Honan north of Hankow, and along the Haichow-Tungkwan railway in northern Honan, the Nationalists were in a precarious condition after a month of fighting with 400,000 men engaged in the opposing sides. Because of civil war and banditry, conditions have become so unsettled that foreign consuls in Hankow were reported today to have decided to urge foreigners to leave the provinces of Hupeh, Hunan and Kiangsi. Moving northward through Hunan province, 80,000 Kwangsi province rebels, joined by a horde of bandits, swarmed into Changsha, chasing northward the 10,000 Nationalists who made feeble resistance. Lyons, France, Today.—The Graf Zeppelin, which had been expected over Lyons this afternoon, turned before a terrific electric storm raging in the Rhone Valley and flew southward again from Valence. At 3 o'clock this afternoon (9:00 A. M., E. T.) the Graf again appeared over Montelimar and it was expected that she would cut straight across France to escape the storm, heading straight in the direction of Basel. The Rhone Valley, which is such a convenient course for the Graf Zeppelin from South France to Friedrichshafen, once before presented difficulties for the great dirigible in May, 1929. The Graf had to fight strong head winds with several of her five motors out of commission. The Graf had started on a flight to the United States and was well over the Mediterranean when her motors went bad and she was forced to abandon the Atlantic crossing and to turn back to Friedrichshafen.

The Associated Press Lyons, France, May 18.—The Graf Zeppelin, making for the Mediterranean on her way to Seville, passed over this city at 11:15 p.m. (5:15 p.m., E.S.T.) and headed down the Rhone valley. She was flying at an altitude of 1800 feet and traveling rapidly.

Shanghai, China, June 6, URE Thousands of refugees were fleeing today from the walled city of Tsinan, capital of Shantung province, as a result of continued bombardment by northern troops, dispatches received here said: Government troops apparently were beginning to withdraw to Yenchow nearly half way to Hsuchow, a junction of the Tientsin, Pukow and Lunghai Railways. Hsuchow, which is of great value as a base, probably will be defended at all costs. Recent reports that the government suffered reverses along the Lunghai line apparently were substantiated but a rally of the troops was considered possible.

Shanchai—(A—A I though the artillery fire of the fighting northern and nationalist troops was plainly heard, the native population of Tsinan, capital of Shantung province, continued normal activities today, said Japanese advices received tonight by way of Tsingtao, Shantung seaport. The dispatches said many Japanese women and children were arriving at Tsingtao from the west, as well as numerous wealthy Chinese merchants. The northern allies forced their way across the Yellow River yesterday about 60 miles east of Tsinan and reached a line near the Tsinan-Tsingtao railway before the nationalists halted their retreat and reorganized their defenses. It was felt in foreign circles here that the fall of Tsinan was only a matter of time.

FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, Germany, June 6--(UP)— Friedrichshafen was ready today to welcome the Graf Zeppelin home from a tour which covered three continents. The serial wanderer was plodding the last stage of its long voyage today. At 8 A.M., the ship radioed it was passing near Marseilles, France, at barely 40 miles an hour. It was expected to arrive here about 1 o'clock this afternoon. The Graf paid a hasty visit to Seville, pausing only long enough to discharge passengers destined for that city, and take onboard Jesus Herraiz, a Guenaca attorney.

LE BOURGET, France, June 6—The Graf Zeppelin informed the wireless station here at 3:37 p.m. (9:37 a.m. e.s.t.) that she had reached Lons Le Saulnier in the Jura department, fifty miles from the Swiss frontier, having avoided the storm in the vicinity of Lyons. The town of Salins is northeast of Lyons and is approximately 200 miles from Friedrichshafen. The Lyons report would indicate that the Graf had not swung as far south as previous advices had indicated but had taken a northeast course from the region of Valence directly toward the Swiss border in order to avoid a terrific electric storm in the Rhone valley in the Lyons region.

Another plenary session will be held Thursday for signing, if it is possible to prepare the prospective treaty by that time. Should it be impossible to get the treaty ready by Thursday the signing probably will be deferred until after Easter. London, April 11.—-(A.P.)—Happy as the bride of a 21-year-old British newsboy, Vivienne Huntington, 27-year-old New York heiress will leave tomorrow with her husband, Alfred Cecil Durban, on the liner Montrose for Toronto, where they hope to make their home. Mrs. Durban is the daughter of the late Charles Pratt Huntington, architect of New York, and a cousin of Archer Milton Huntington, New York author. The groom, until his marriage March 1st, earned his living selling newspapers outside Folkestone station. His father drives a butcher's cart.

EAST GRINSTEAD, Sussex, Eng., April 12. (AP)——Lord Dewar, widely known distiller, died suddenly at his home here yesterday, aged 66. Lord Dewar was born in Perth, in 1864, was managing director of John Dewar and Sons, Ltd., distillers, and also was director of several other distilling companies. He was unmarried.

Bombay, India — (f)—Twenty-two persons were injured in rioting outside the courthouse here Friday when a number of Satyagrahis, who yesterday offered passive resistance during a police raid on national congress headquarters, were sentenced to various terms of imprisonment. A large crowd attempted to get at some of the prisoners, as they were removed, for the purpose of hanging garlands on them. The police fought them off and the Indians changed from passive resistance to reply with a shower of sandals and stones. Ten policemen, of whom three were Europeans, were injured. The police then charged the crowd with their bludgeons, scattering them. There were 12 casualties among the Indians. Thursday's raids by the police resulted in the destruction of pans which had been set up in the congress hall for the illegal manufacture of salt.

LONDON.—CP—The London naval conference will be wound up next week with a three power agreement forming the backbone of a skeleton five power pact which France and Italy can join even before they settle their differences on parity. The way was made clear Thursday when the United States, Great Britain and Japan, after nearly three months of negotiating, sealed their naval accord. And a dramatic last minute move by the American delegation salvaged the five power treaty. When the conference seemed doomed as far as general agreement on any points was concerned, Secretary Stimson, Ambassador Morrow and Ambassador Gibson made proposals to the French and Italian delegations which will enable the skeleton five power pact to be drawn, and the big five, or delegation chiefs, will meet in St. James’ palace to approve the plan. LONDON, Apr. 11. (U.P)—The five-power conference which convened January 21 to limit the world’s great navies will end its sessions late next week, probably Thursday, without having achieved its purpose but with its chief delegates “very well satisfied.” A treaty limiting the navies of the United States, Great Britain and Japan, until 1936, and pledging France and Italy to certain principles formulated at the conference, but not to limitation, will be signed at a plenary session Monday. The heads of the delegations decided furthermore to appoint a committee of jurists to draft the treaty which will be signed. A committee of experts under the chairmanship of the secretary general of the conference, Sir Maurice Hankey, will assist the jurists. The arrangements were made at a meeting of the five chief delegates at St. James Palace this morning, where the chairman reported the results of rece

BOMBAY, India, (UP).—With India’s salt rebellion spreading through the provinces, Mahatma Gandhi intends to spread the active gospel of resistance to British rule by preventing the sale of taxed liquor and foreign cloth, as the next step in his program of defiance, it was announced Friday. The Mahatma called a conference, to meet Sunday, of women adherents to his civil disobedience campaign, at which picketing of shops selling foreign cloth or taxed liquor will be discussed. Abid Ali Jaferbhai, secretary of the provincial congress committee, active promoters of the present campaign, was sentenced to nine months imprisonment Friday by a Bombay court, on charges of inviting the people to disobey the salt-tax laws. Jaferbhai was arrested in a spectacular raid on the congress headquarters Thursday. His sentence is one of the heaviest yet meted out to any of Gandhi's followers.

LONDON, April 11.. The London naval conference moved rapidly toward a close today as the delegates worked on the wording of a treaty which appeared certain would be signed by all five of the nations represented. The heads of the naval delegations have agreed if possible to hold a plenary session next Thursday afternoon for the purpose of signing the treaty and ending the conference. A public session also will be held Monday at which the report of the so-called first committee will be received. The plenary session will open at 12:30 p. m. It will have achieved agreement among the United States, Great Britain and Japan on a battleship building holiday until 1936 when another naval conference will be held. The principle of naval equality between the United States and Great Britain will have become a fact, both agreeing to maintain a navy of equal strength in the future.

JALAPUR, BOMBAY, INDIA, April 1—(#)—Mahatma Gandhi, who yesterday had to curb his salt making because of high blood pressure, asserted today that his health was excellent "except that I have received a warning from kindly nature that I must hasten slowly if I don’t wish to court a breakdown." He said that if his health permitted he would concentrate his attention on Gujarat, which he said has not given his movement of civil disobedience its deserved support, but could go no further despite an embarrassing number of invitations to visit other parts of India. Accompanied by Miss Maniben Patel, daughter of Vallabhai Patel, who was speaker of the legislative assembly, Gandhi today proceeded to Karadimatwad, where he announced a conference of women would be held at Dandi Sunday. They will consider the possibility of concentrating their civil disobedience campaign there on the picketing of liq

LONDON, April 11.—Work went ahead speedily today to get the London Naval Conference "out of the trenches" and send its delegates home with a complete three-power pact and a five-power treaty "framework." Heads of the five delegations met for an hour and a half this morning, appointing a "drafting committee" to formulate the five-power agreement. This "framework" will include all items on which the five delegations are in harmony, leaving blank spaces to be filled in when and if the remaining differences are reconciled. It is hoped the results of the conference can be put on paper and signed at a plenary session next Thursday, but it is more probable the signing will take place shortly after Easter. Tokyo, April 11—(#—The British steamer City of Peking struck the rocks today 15 miles northeast of Port Hamilton Island, South Korea. Passengers and members of the crew, numbering 81, were rescued by a passing trawler and landed on a small island off the river path. A dispatch from the Rengo news agency in Shimoneski said the City of Peking struck at 5 p.m., while en route from Vladivostok to Dairen. Reports were that a portion of the steamer still was above the rocks, but that it was believed a total loss. A salvage boat was sent out from Moji.

TOKYO, April 11.—Japan’s economic difficulties reached a critical stage today with the suspension of trading on the Tokyo stock exchange. The bear-ridden market opened well below yesterday's closing and the resulting confusion caused the directors to announce a one-hour suspension, which later was extended. At 1 p.m., the exchange attempted to open again but when a selling stampede was threatened it closed for the day. Despite the near panic here the Osaka exchange continued orderly trading throughout the day, the leading stocks dropping slightly. The economic crisis is the result of a long period of decline in trade and industry which recently was accentuated by adverse elements in the export market.

ROME, April 9.—(#)—Funeral services for Queen Victoria of Sweden were held this morning in the German Evangelical church here in the presence of her husband, King Gustav, Prince William and Princess Ingrid of Sweden, the king and queen of Italy and Premier Mussolini. The body of the queen was not at the services, but was carried later from the Villa Svezia where she died Friday at the age of 68 to a special funeral train, which, with King Gustav, Prince William and Princess Ingrid aboard, departed for Stockholm.

A90V FHOVENIE SY - TOKYO, April 11—The Ellerman liner City of Peking went aground today with 150 passengers and crew off Port Hamilton and was reported so badly damaged that salvage will be difficult. Fishing boats are reported to have taken off the passengers and crew, but many of the latter are believed to have been injured when the City of Peking struck. The liner’s hull is seriously damaged, with its bow fast aground and its propeller above the surface. The salvage vessel Kalyo Maru went to its aid from Moj!

PARIS, April 11.—-(4)—Satisfaction was expressed in official circles today at the way the naval conference was winding up. The fact that France and Italy will be left in a position to continue negotiations is particularly stressed, as it had been feared that the conference might leave these two countries in a disagreeable situation that would increase the tension which has existed for some time.

(A) — U.S. conference pessimism over the success of the Anglo-French negotiations concerning a security pact was expressed in American conference circles this afternoon. It was generally understood the British and French have virtually reached an impasse. Secretary of State Stimson visited Foreign Minister Briand of France during the afternoon and expected to see Prime Minister MacDonald this evening. The nature of his discussions with the French foreign minister was not divulged. French conference circles also were extremely gloomy late today. Foreign Minister Briand, however, thus far has declined to put himself on record as being pessimistic. LONDON, Mar. 31.—(#)—A sharp repercussion was produced in French headquarters by the statement issued by a British official spokesman yesterday in which it was declared absolutely impossible for Great Britain to undertake any further military commitments in connection with the proposed French security pact. Foreign Minister Briand himself this morning indicated disapproval of the issuance of this statement on the grounds that it had been agreed no statement of any kind would be made while the Franco-British negotiations were proceeding. The French foreign minister, speaking to French newspapers, said he hoped he could believe that the statement issued last night had no authorization. He understood it had been agreed no statement of any kind would be issued while these conversations were continuing and he felt publication of this particular statement was scarcely suitable at this time. - NEW DELHI, INDIA, Mar. 31.—Prohibition of baby brides becomes effective throughout British India at midnight. Henceforth it will be illegal for mature men to marry girls of 7 and 8 years of age. Specifically, the new law forbids the marriage of girls less than 14 and boys less than 18 years of age, but the law was aimed at the greater marriage evil which brought upon its Indian proponents the condemnation of many westerners. A fine of 1,000 rupees or imprisonment of one month will be imposed upon any person solemnizing a union which comes under the ban of the child marriage act. Tiny brides have been rushed to the altar by thousands during the last five months in an effort to forestall the law which was passed last September by the legislative assembly to become effective April 1. In one recent case the age of a little bride was only two years; hundreds of cases have been reported in G

Lerwick, Shetland Islands, Mar. 31—Seven men who had been clinging to the rigging of the Aberdeen steam trawler, Ben Doran, which struck a reef in the West Shetland group Saturday, had disappeared with their ship today and it was feared they had perished. Trawlers and drifters which left the mainland this morning to rescue the imperiled crew of the Ben Doran returned several hours later and reported that the trawler had broken up and disappeared. There was no sign of life anywhere.

LONDON, March 30—(@)— The profits and losses of disarmament at the Five-Power naval conference will be made known to the world during the coming week. Through what proved to be one of the best week-ends of the long negotiations, the delegates pored over their ledgers, and tomorrow the Big Five delegates, as chief accountants, will meet at St. James’ Palace to confer on what is to be publicly and "officially announced at the plenary session on Friday. When that session comes round, Prime Minister MacDonald, Secretary of State Balfour, Ex-premier Wakatsuki, Foreign Minister Grandi, and Foreign Minister Briand, acting for Premier Tardieu, will declare just how much of the task that brought them here two and a half months ago has been accomplished. Over the week-end the delegates still continued heroic efforts for world-wide naval reduction by the five great sea powers. The general opinion t

INTERNATIONAL NEWS SCENERY LONDON, March 31.—Amid cries of "resign," the government of Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald sustained an adverse vote in the House of Commons today on a motion of the premier to permit late sittings of Parliament. The vote was 183 to 179. It was the second adverse vote the MacDonald government had sustained within the past three weeks. The other was on the conservative amendment to the government's coal bill. While the issue was an important one, it did not affect the government’s fate, as the bill was only in the committee stage. Conservative and liberal opponents of the prime minister took advantage of today’s defeat to demand MacDonald’s resignation.

CALCUTTA, India, March 31.—-(U.P.)—Hundreds of Hindu boys and girls, some of them less than 10 years old and a few of them still at the cradle age, have been married within the past 24 hours in "orthodox" circles of India. Hundreds more, before midnight, will have been bound by their parents to involuntary marriage, in an endeavor to beat the new British law forbidding child marriages, which goes into effect tomorrow. One of the most amazing customs, to western eyes, and one of the most sacred to Indians, comes to an end with the operation of the act. The new British rule, which is certain to be disobeyed quietly, raises the marriageable age of "women" and "men."

LONDON, March 31. — Great Britain, Japan and the United States will be ready to draft a three-power naval agreement with. known today after the five worried nation leaders conferred at St. Swithun Palace. From reliable sources it was learned that the reservations Japan was reported as desiring on the proposals submitted to Tokyo will meet no objections from the United States. The Japanese will not be prevented, at the expiration of the projected three-power treaty from resubmitting their claims to a 70 per cent ratio in cruisers and inch guns. It also is pointed out that at the same time America may claim the right to withdraw from future negotiations any concessions made to Japan at the London conference. Today's session of the principal delegates was brief and concerned the subjects for discussion at next Friday's plenary session. Another session will be held Wednesday.

London. — Political discussions between Great Britain and France, aimed at giving the latter nation sufficient security guarantees to enable her to reduce her tonnage demands, have virtually ended in failure, it was reported on good authority today. Experts of both nations, it is understood, are now drawing up an official report admitting their inability to reach an agreement. Further “last minute” efforts are expected, but present indications are that the death-knell of the London naval conference as a five-power body has been sounded. Heads of the various delegations met for fifteen minutes today, following which the American contingent held an hour's conference. Spokesmen for the American delegation...

NANCHANG, March 31.—(4)—Foreign dispatches from Nanchang, capital of Kiangsi province, today said the menace of bandits was increasing and that a general evacuation of foreigners was anticipated. Possible general evacuation of Kiangsi by missionaries and other foreigners because of the steadily increasing menace of bandits and communists seemed indicated in various reports from the northern part of the province. These advices, coming from foreign sources, or from official and missionary quarters, stated that the communistic bandits which previously had confined their depredations to southern Kiangsi were steadily moving northward and that the whole province now is menaced.

Shanghai, Mar. 31—()—Captured by brigands who Thursday raided and looted Yuanchow, western Kiangsi province, three foreign workers of the British China Inland Mission today were the object of an intensive search by fellow missionaries. Dispatches reporting the Yuanchow outrage were confirmed by the mission at Changsha, Hankow Province, and by a mission representative at Sinyu, Kiangsi. Much concern was felt for the safety of the trio, the Reverend and Mrs. R. W. Porteus of England and Miss N. E. Gemmel of Girard, Kan., since they were believed to have been captured by the same bandits, who on February 3 kidnapped and presumably murdered three Finnish missionaries. Mrs. Porteus was formerly an American and resided at Kirkhoyer, Minn. Her maiden name was Emma Forsberg. She came to China in 1894. The dispatch said those who escaped were two British missionaries and one American, the Rev. R.

SHANGHAI, March 30—The British North China Daily News correspondent at Changsha, Hunan Province, reported today that Kiangsi Province bandits had captured three more foreign missionaries, two women and a man, at Yuanchow, Western Kiangsi. Three others, two women and a man, are reported to have escaped by fleeing into the mountains. The bandits, the correspondent said, are considered to be the same ones who on Feb. 3 carried off and presumably murdered three Finnish missionaries, raided Yuanchow and after looting the city carried off the three representatives of the British China Inland Mission. Those captured were the Rev. and Mrs. R. W. Porteus of England, who have been in China for almost a quarter of a century, and Miss N. E. Gemmell, an American. Miss Gemmell has been in China since 1919. The dispatch said those who escaped were two British missionaries and one American, the Rev. R.

(By The Associated Press) Rome, March 31.—Donna Maria Sarto, only surviving sister of Pope Pius X, died yesterday. She had been ill for several weeks. Donna Maria accompanied her brother on many of his pastoral missions before his election as Pope in 1903. Recently she had lived in a small apartment overlooking St. Peter’s Square.

TOKYO, MAR. 31. (AP).—It was understood here today that Baron Shidehara, foreign minister, had completed a draft of instructions to the Japanese delegation at the London five-power naval conference authorizing the acceptance of the Japanese-American formula without material alteration of the figures involved, but seeking the assent of the other powers to two or possibly three reservations attached to the Tokyo acceptance. It was authoritatively promised that the end of the Japanese fortnight of indecision regarding the Reed-Matsudaira formula would come tomorrow.

ROME, Mar. 31.—Samuel Insull, Chicago multi-millionaire, today was received by Premier Mussolini at the Venezia Palace. The premier praised Mr. Insull for his public benefactions, especially his work in aiding the Chicago Civic Opera. Mr. Insull was accompanied by the musical conductor, Signor Polacco. Mr. Insull left tonight for Milan.

Vienna, Mar. 31—(2)—Advices here from Ohrid, Jugo-Slavia said that ten occupants of a motorboat were drowned when the boat upset on the lake there yesterday. The boat was making an excursion tour of the lake. Those drowned included Colonel Protic, the military commander at Ohrid; the Greek consul at Korcha and his wife, the Czecho-Slovakian consul at Korcha, a Greek physician of Palena with his fiancée, the secretary of the Jugo-Slavian consulate at Korcha with his wife, the sub-prefect of Ohrid and one sailor.

PARIS.—(4)—The first memorial service for Myron T. Herrick, American ambassador to France who died at his post before one year ago today, was held Monday afternoon at the American Pro Cathedral. The same prayers were said and the same hymns sung which were Mr. Herrick’s favorites in his lifetime——"O Paradise,” and the twenty-third psalm, just as at the services a year ago before the French government sent his body home on the cruiser Tourville.

| SHANCHAL March 21.—Three more foreign missionaries, including Miss N. K. E. Gemmell, an American, have fallen into the hands of the feared Communist bandit horde that has been terrorizing Kiangsi province for many weeks. Besides Miss Gemmell, who has been in China since 1919, her friends and co-workers, the Rev. and Mrs. R. W. Rorteus, of Venezuela, were captured. They were taken in a raid at Yuanchow. The bandits are reported to have looted the city. Two other British missionaries, one a woman, and an American (R. H. Glazier), were said to have escaped into the mountains. Yuanchow is a day's journey northwest of Kanchow, where sixteen American Catholic missionaries were captured by the bandits. Because of the interference of communications by the bandits' armies between here and points in Kiangsi, little if any authentic information is available. The fate of the captives has not been

Rome, March 31.—(UP)—The renewed status of the Holy See as a sovereign temporal power will bring before the great ecumenical council of the church, announced for 1931, three questions involving the entire civilized world. At the meeting, which will be attended by archbishops and bishops from every Christian country, the following issues will be considered: The position of the church towards the League of Nations. Doctrines upholding the supremacy of state over church. Settlement of a fixed date for the celebration of Easter. In connection with the Easter question, it is recalled that the League of Nations sounded out the Vatican on the matter some time ago, receiving a reply that the Holy See considered the question prematurely, since it would be examined by the ecumenical council. Work of Council. A papal bull convoking the council outlined its purposes, broadly, as follows: “To conside

Berlif, April 5. -— A nicotineless tobacco leaf which produces both salad oil and cigars will be exhibited in the traveling fair which will begin at Cologne on May 27. Although attempts have been made to extract the nicotine from tobacco, it is believed here that this will be the first exhibit of tobacco grown without nicotine. The salad oil is said to be of fine flavor and the nicotineless cigars to have a pleasant aroma.

BERLIN, Mar. 30—(AP)—President Von Hindenburg today signed the list of cabinet members proposed by Chancellor Bruening. He also appointed Gottfried Treviranus, previously named minister without portfolio, as minister for occupied territories, and Hermann Dietrich, minister of economics, as vice-chancellor.

1930-04-27.text: | BOMBAY, India, Apr. 26 (AP)— Further disorders at Peshawar increased apprehension here today that grave events may be shaping themselves in the Buffer northwest frontier province. Lahore dispatches to the London Daily Mail said a mob paraded the streets yesterday and taunted troops on guard. A British officer, facing the ringleaders with a drawn revolver, tried in vain to persuade them to disperse their followers. When an armored car which had been sent for arrived, a machine gun was trained on the mob, which then scattered. Earlier the Indians had paraded with “corpses” of those slain in Wednesday’s rioting, in which, it is said now there were fifty casualties. Upon investigation it proved the Indians seeking to enlarge the death reports, had placed live men in the coffins. Arrival of two companies of British infantry and two machine gun sections created a feeling of security among Eu

- LONDON, April 26—*)—Tens of thousands of Londoners who once knew the roar of the wartime zeppelins, today watched the dirigible Graf Zeppelin as she circled the capital on a voyage of good will. The British dirigible R-100, which is housed in Cardington, made her first appearance over London shortly before four o'clock. She was accompanied by six airplanes. The Graf sailed over the football field at Wembley where thousands had gathered for the football cup final, then passed over central London. The Graf arrived over Cardington shortly after 5 o'clock.
LONDON, Apr. 26.—(AP)—The body of Robert Bridges, poet laureate of England, was cremated yesterday at Golder’s Green with such secrecy that even the closest friends of the family were unaware of it.

Bombay, India, April 26. (&).— Mahatma Gandhi announced a stronger move in his campaign of civil disobedience today, asserting he soon would lead a group to take possession of the government salt depot at Dhareana. Previous manifestations sponsored by the nationalist leader have centered around the manufacture of salt illegally. Gandhi is prepared to offer his head for the cause, he told a crowd at Charvada. He said he would take with him both men and women, but only those who wore home-spun cloth and had given up liquor. He concluded by saying that breaking of the salt act alone would not bring independence, asserting that other acts would have to be violated to attain the desired end. News from other parts of India showed the country more quiet than recently.

LOD "DON, April 26. --Reports of a sensational incident involving Josef Stalin, chairman of the Central Executive Committee of the Communist Party, and the widow of Nikolai Lenin, leader of the Bolshevist movement in Soviet Russia were contained in a dispatch from Riga to the London Daily News today. The incident occurred, according to the dispatch, when Mme. Lenin sought to criticize Stalin's policy of collectivization. The communist chief, according to the reports, drew a revolver and threatened to shoot Mme. Lenin. Several other communist leaders were present during the altercation between Stalin and the widow of the man chiefly responsible for the overthrow of the imperial regime in Russia. One of them quickly snatched the weapon from Stalin’s hand, the report declared, while another escorted Mme. Lenin from the room. Stalin recently greatly expanded the collectivization policy which

HAMBURG.—(4)—The American liner President Harding, inward bound and making for the mouth of the Elbe river, collided in a fog off Helgoland Saturday morning with the British collier Kirkwood, which sank. The President Harding rescued all of the Kirkwood's crew with the exception of one fireman who was missing. The President Harding, proceeding to Hamburg, found the fog so dense she was compelled to anchor off Elbe light ship No. 1. No one was injured aboard the American liner and the United States Lines later stated that the damage to her was of very slight nature. The President Harding was able to continue under her own steam toward Hamburg.

BERLIN, April 26—The U.S. President Harding rammed and sank the English coalship Kirkwood in a fog off Heligoland today. The President Harding of the United States lines was not damaged. The crew of the President Harding saved all of the Kirkwood's crew except one. The Kirkwood was a 2,789 ton vessel. The President Harding was en route from New York to Cuxhaven, having disembarked passengers at Cherbourg yesterday. The Kirkwood, which sank almost immediately, was a new vessel, built in February of this year. The collision was the second accident to befall a large transatlantic liner in the last two days. The North German Lloyd’s Bremen rammed the tanker British Grenadier in the English channel off Dungeness Thursday but the tanker made port safely.

[INTERNATIONAL NEWS SERVICE] HAMBURG, April 26.—In an almost impenetrable fog in the North Sea off Heligoland, the United States liner President Harding today collided with and sank the small British collier Kirkwood. One member of the Kirkwood's crew is missing and feared to be drowned. The remainder were picked up by the President Harding before the collier sank a few minutes after the collision. The President Harding was slightly damaged. No one aboard is believed to have been injured.

HAMBURG, Germany, April 26—The United States liner President Harding, groping through a dense fog off the German coast, today rammed and sank the British collier Kirkwood, according to reports received here. The collision occurred near Heligoland, the island used as a German submarine base during the war. The crew of the Kirkwood was saved by the President Harding soon after the crash. The President Harding was proceeding to Hamburg from Southampton at the time of the collision. It is not known whether the American liner was seriously damaged... Latest word, however, stated that the vessel continued toward Hamburg after picking up the crew of the Kirkwood. The accident was the second serious collision in less than three days caused by the heavy blanket of fog which has shrouded the entire coast of Europe.
