1930-05-09.text: Sholapur, Bombay, India, May 8 — (AP) — Twenty-seven or more police and natives were killed in desperate rioting which, starting last night, was resumed at dawn today and had resulted at noon in seizure of this city of 120,000 inhabitants by the adherents of Mahatma Gandhi. Resisting the local authorities who had forbidden their assemblage, the angry natives maintained attacks which threw the city into chaos. The local police were powerless. Citizen reserves who joined them soon were thrown back by the rioters. Troops rushed into this textile community likewise proved unable to cope with the situation. More Troops Are Called At noon today the officer commanding the auxiliary forces of India sent out a call for more troops. His request stated that he considered the single detachment already provided would not be enough. Six police stations and the magistrate’s court were burned down durin

BOMBAY, India, May 9 (AP)—Sholapur was cleared of all European women and children today and ready for eventualities which might follow yesterday's reign of terror. Special trains guarded by troops today carried the last of the refugees to Poona and nearby towns. Police at Sholapur today said three policemen were burned by the mob, five others were missing probably murdered, and another five, mostly natives, known to be dead. There were 24 wounded in yesterday's Sholapur rioting; however, exceeded all outbreaks since the inception of Mahatma Gandhi's program of civil disobedience, both as to life and property losses. The authorities looked forward anxiously for tomorrow's coming, Saturday being the Moslem feast of Bakrid, which even under normal circumstances is likely to produce disorders. Dr. Gopichand, general secretary of the Lahore all-India congress committee was arrested under the

BOMBAY, India—Police and independence demonstrators clashed in a prolonged battle at Sholapur today, where 25 persons were killed and approximately 110 others wounded. The rioting at Sholapur, which is the capital of the district of the same name, broke out suddenly during picketing of liquor shops by a mob of demonstrators. It was the most serious outbreak of the present independence campaign and came shortly after it had been revealed that Mahatma Gandhi, who was arrested Monday, was secretly removed from Yeroda jail Wednesday night and taken to the Purandhar military sanatorium. Sholapur, which has a population of 120,000, is about 220 miles southeast of Bombay. Gandhi's removal was said to have been due to excitement which his presence aroused among natives at Poona City and to the desire of authorities to provide him with surroundings most favorable to his health. Four rebels were k

London —(#)— John Masefield the celebrated English poet and writer, Friday was appointed poet laureate. The new poet laureate is known as the “hobo poet.” He has roamed the world hobo fashion and once was a porter in a New York saloon. He is 65 and has a wife and two children.

By FRANCIS LOW (United Press Staff Correspondent. BOMBAY, May 9—The most stringent precautions for the protection of Europeans in India were taken by the government today as rumors of impending attacks by independence seekers were received in Bombay. The center of the disturbed area appeared to be in the vicinity of Poona, where Mahatma Gandhi was imprisoned after his arrest near Surat last Monday. All European inhabitants of Talegaon, 30 miles from Poona, were warned to evacuate the city before noon today, reports received here said. The warning was issued by authorities after they learned an Indian mob planned a raid on a glass factory. Two trainloads of European women and children arrived at Poona today from Sholapur, where the most serious rioting since Mahatma Gandhi began his passive resistance drive for Indian independence broke out yesterday. They reported 50 persons were killed

LONDON, May 9. (Friday) (P)—Unofficial reports reaching here early today say that yesterday’s riot at Sholapur greatly exceeded any disturbance since the beginning of the civil disobedience campaign. One dispatch said three policemen were murdered and that their bodies then were soaked in kerosene and burned on a street. Reports of casualties among the rioters differed greatly, the highest placing the number of killed at 23 and those injured at 100. At one time, during the height of the rioting, the police were hopelessly outnumbered and withdrew toward headquarters. The mob, composed mostly of millmen, followed with gathering strength and spread terror en route. They concentrated on stray policemen, liquor shops, police stations and other buildings. The district courthouse and several police stations were burned, the rioters firing them with kerosene looted from the shops. The Sholapur

INDIA, May 9—One hundred and fifty European women and children arrived here today, terror on their faces, from Sholapur, which they left yesterday as three Mohammedan policemen were being burned to death by an angry mob of Indians. They said the three policemen, all Mohammedans, were captured by the mob and bound together. Their uniforms were then soaked with kerosene and set afire. The outrage took place near the sessions court building which was also burned by the mob, which had begun its demonstration in behalf of the civil disobedience campaign and in protest at the arrest of Mahatma Gandhi. The refugees carried with them what they could snatch from their houses after the evacuation order was given. Some had their dogs, canaries, and cooking utensils. They all appeared to have been badly frightened and could give only incoherent accounts of what had happened. Official explanations of

BOMBAY, May 8 (By A. P.)— Hope of an early end of difficulties with the cohorts of civil disobedience went down in blood and ashes tonight while cavalry forces rode upon Sholapur where twenty-seven were killed during a strike that lasted all day. Nightfall did not bring quiet to the scene of the most severe clash since the internment of Mahatma Gandhi signaled the seeming end of passive resistance. With its lists of dead and probably more than a hundred wounded, Sholapur this evening sent out calls for troops and more troops. It was evident that a stubborn encounter still was in progress. Leave. Thirteen European women and children tonight had been evacuated from the city. They were removed to a point of safety said to be Poona, where earlier in the day it had been reported and denied that the Mahatma had been spirited from his internment quarters to a fortress at Purandhar. London, May 8—(UP)—The new radiotelephone service between England and South America started off in good old-fashioned style yesterday with a wrong number. The London Daily Express, wishing to be the first to use the new service, put in a call to La Nacion, Buenos Aires newspaper. A few minutes later the Express’ editor found himself connected with a Mr. Smith of Santiago, Chile. “Comfortable pioneering,” the Express observed in commenting on the experience.

LONDON, May 9.—With violence and terrorism riding rough-shod over India, the British government took decisive steps today to protect European residents from death or injury at the hands of Nationalist rioters. Simultaneously with the publication here of statements from refugees that at least 50 persons had been killed and hundreds had been injured in the two-day rioting at Sholapur, Bombay presidency, all European residents of Talegaon, 30 miles from Poona, were ordered to evacuate the city before noon today. Reports had been received that the independents, whose campaign of passive resistance has suddenly flared into violent rebellion, planned an onslaught on that city. In the face of stories told by hysterical refugees from Sholapur, the British authorities issued an official statement in Bombay today asserting that the casualty reports had been greatly exaggerated, according to an Exc

London, May 8.— (#P) —— Ellen Wilkinson, member of parliament, tonight took up the battle for short skirts at a meeting of women clerks and typists to discuss the length of skirts. The knee-length skirt won, for a vote after the meeting showed only one woman held out for the dress that reaches the ankle. Miss Wilkinson said she regarded the introduction of long evening skirts as “a cloud on our female horizon.”

(By United Press.) SHANGHAI, China, May 9. - A great horde of bandits devastated the Yung-Yang district in Honan province and slaughtered thousands of residents, according to delayed advices received today. The newspaper Sin Wan Pao said that approximately 15,000 persons were killed by the raiding outlaws. The bandits swarmed through the district for four days, starting April 23, killing without mercy; they slaughtered women and children and pillaged their homes, the advices said. The raid was the worst of many reported in recent months. There were about 3,000 bandits in the band. Almost every home was looted or burned and residents who did not readily give up their goods were tortured and slain. Many small villages were desolated in the attack. After three days of pillage, the bandits rounded up 600 prisoners, forced them to shoulder the loot and marched them off to be held for ransom.

| SHANGHAI, May 9 (Pr) Climaxing China's unparalleled banditry in recent months, 15,000 Chinese of Yungyang, Hanan province, were killed April 23, said unverified dispatches appearing today in Chinese newspapers. The dispatches said the looting, burning and killing lasted four days. The outlaws held 500 townspeople for ransom. The town was obliterated. This, said the dispatches, explained the delay in the carnage becoming known.

Paris, May 5—(A. P.)—A protocol putting into effect the Young plan today was signed at the French foreign office by Premier Briand, and the foreign ministers of Great Britain, Italy and Belgium. The signing took place at 5:45 pm. The last minute arrival of the necessary documents from Great Britain and Italy and their deposit in the French foreign office made the signing today possible. Premier Briand was the host of Arthur Henderson, British foreign minister at luncheon. The diplomats discussed questions concerning the forthcoming Geneva council session. They made announcement afterward that they were in complete accord.

ROME.—Italy is ready to resume immediately the naval limitation negotiations interrupted at London, Foreign Minister Dino Grandi told the chamber of deputies Friday in expressing willingness to continue efforts toward an understanding with France. Grandi discussed the work done at the London conference, including the positions of France and Italy whose failure to agree prevented them from joining the other powers in a limitation treaty.

MADRID, May 5 (Reports published in Paris of an attempt by two Spanish generals to establish a dictatorship were denied here today. All is quiet in Spain. PARIS, May 5 (—A Havas dispatch from Madrid today says Premier Berenguer has taken measures against an attempt by Generals Anido and Barrera to reestablish a dictatorship in Spain.

1930-04-19.text: Calcutta, Bengal, India, Apr. 19.—A group of 100 Indian nationalists today attacked the police armory at Chittagong, across the Meghna estuary east of here, and killed six of the defenders. The dead include one sergeant major. Before attacking the armory the insurgents cut telephone and telegraph lines leading out of the city, which is of about 30,000 population, and derailed a train about 40 miles away, blocking the railroad line. A detachment of eastern frontier rifles under command of Lieutenant Colonel Dallas Smith was ordered from here to Chittagong to handle the situation. They left Calcutta this morning. In Calcutta strong guards were established at all gun shops, while armored cars and armed police took up positions in strategic locations. The authorities ordered an immediate search of the city for arms and ammunition. The headquarters of the All-Indian National Congress committe

London, April 19—(4)—The “safeguarding clause” of the naval treaty being drawn up here which the naval delegates themselves have kept rigorously secret until after final approval of the home government was revealed today in dispatches from Tokyo. The clause provides for an increase in the navies of either Japan, America or Great Britain—the three signatories to the projected limitation treaty—if the building program of non-signatory nations be considered excessive. Consultative Idea Dropped Conference observers noted that in the safeguarding clause the consultative idea is omitted altogether. For a nation which considers its position endangered by the building program of another to abrogate the figures of the treaty it will be necessary only to notify the other two nations which would be allowed proportionate increase in the same category. London, April 18 ().—The committee drafting the London naval treaty today polished the sentences, crossed the T’s and dotted the I's of the document which envoys of the five great sea powers are expected to sign Tuesday. They worked in the peace of Good Friday, when Londoners in general are on holiday, and the courtyards of St. James's Palace were as quiet as they were centuries ago when Henry VIII built the edifice as his country house. Thus far no new prospect of delay has arisen to interfere with the carrying out of the final plenary session as planned.

DUNEDIN, NEW ZEALAND, APR. 18. (AP).—Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd, Antarctic explorer, returned here today from his visit to Wellington and will remain in Dunedin a week before sailing for Panama on his homeward journey. Byrd returned without his famous dog Igloo, which became separated from him at Ashburton on the return trip. Igloo wandered away from the Ashburton railroad station while Byrd was being made a member of the Aero Club during a short train stop. Admiral Byrd arrived here in a commodious railroad coach accompanied by Mr. Tatley, his New Zealand business manager. For his last week in New Zealand, Admiral Byrd has only one official engagement—a lecture to assist the fund for endowment of a university chair of obstetrics. Byrd said his northern trip had been wonderful, but he appeared tired after the extensive traveling during which he was acclaimed on all sides. He feels that

BOMBAY, India, April 18.—India as a whole remained comparatively quiet today both as regards demonstrations and arrests, but there were some signs tonight of restlessness. At Calyan, a suburb of Bombay, the police arrested Jamnadas Mehta, formerly a prominent member of the legislative assembly who recently joined the civil disobedience movement. Gandhi, addressing 500 followers during the afternoon, again expressed surprise that he was still at liberty while many of those whom he instigated to break the salt laws have been cast into jail. Reaffirming his civil disobedience doctrine in another speech, he said: "We must be prepared to sacrifice men of pure character. If swaraj (independence) is built on their backs, it will be a glorious structure. I would dance for joy if you tested bullet wounds in your bare chest, but if you were guilty of violence, tears of blood would come to my eyes.

Tokio, April 19—The Japanese government today approved the entire five-power naval treaty. Reijiro Wakatsuki, chief of the Japanese delegation in London, was instructed by cable to sign the document for Japan when it is presented at the plenary session next week.

Warsaw, April 19—(f}=-Two persons were killed and 19 wounded yesterday in Zaewiercte, a large industrial center, half-way between Warsaw and Kralow in a clash between unemployed and the police. The unemployed were promised doles Tuesday but the city did not receive the money and postponed payment until Friday. The unemployed learned that only a small sum of money had come, just sufficient for a few of them. Eight thousand then gathered and marched to the city council room and demolished it. The police intervened and a riot took place. Six policewomen were among the wounded.

Moscow, April 18.-(7)—Despite recent onslaughts upon religion by the atheist societies and prohibition of public sale of Easter eggs, candles, cakes and other paschal articles, the Easter holidays are being celebrated by Russia’s Christians with only slight variations over those of previous years. In most cases Russian housewives overcame the government’s objections to the public sale of paschal tokens by making these articles at home themselves. As Easter is the biggest holiday in the orthodox calendar many families borrowed money to enable them to entertain their friends at home with true Russian hospitality. Good Friday was observed today throughout the country in the traditional orthodox manner without any molestation on the part of Soviet authorities and atheistic organizations. Considerable surprise was caused today by the announcement that the trade union authorities had decided t

1930-05-26.text: LONDON, May 26.—The Church of England was in mourning today for the Archbishop Lord Davidson, archbishop of Canterbury, who died at 1:00 a.m. yesterday after a lengthy illness. He was 82 years old. Funeral services for the former primate, who was the first of his long line to die in retirement and who held the first temporal title—that of baron—extended to an English churchman, will be held Friday at Canterbury cathedral. Death came peacefully to the archbishop after he had lapsed into unconsciousness several hours before. Lady Davidson was present. There is no heir to the barony which Lord Davidson had conferred on him in 1928, the peerage therefore becoming extinct.

London, May 26—(#)—Lord Randall Thomas Davidson, former Archbishop of Canterbury, who died in his sleep early today, will be buried with impressive ceremonies in Canterbury Cathedral on Friday. The services will be conducted by Lord Davidson's successor in the See of Canterbury, Archbishop Cosmo Gordon Lang, primate of England. King George will be represented.

LONDON, — (PF) — Queen Mary Monday celebrated her sixty-third birthday in the privacy of Buckingham Palace where all the family was gathered with congratulations and presents. Most importance was attached to the visit of the grandchildren—Princess Mary's two sons and little Princess Elizabeth of York—whose presentation of gifts to grandma was made with impressive enthusiasm. There was no national celebration except for the firing of artillery salutes at London, Windsor, and naval and military stations.

Bombay, India, May 26.—(UP)—The Nationalist civil disobedience campaign was intensified today by renewal of violence in widely separated areas and by appeals of certain independence leaders for a resort to armed struggle. The most serious outbreak was at Rangoon, in Burma, where independence agitators were held responsible in part for inciting striking dock workers to a riot. Twelve persons were killed and more than 50 wounded. Strikers fought police and imported strike breakers with stones and sticks. The salt raids in the Bombay area were renewed today when volunteers clashed with police again at the Wadala works, 12 miles from Bombay, and carried away 50 pounds of salt. Forty-three of the 83 raiders were arrested. The Bombay district raids have continued for almost 24 hours, being centered at Wadala and Wadia. BOMBAY, India, May 25.—Seventeen persons were injured, seven seriously, and more than 100 were arrested today during attempts of Mahatma Gandhi's volunteers to raid the salt depots at Wadala, near Bombay. The riot was precipitated by a party of 100 volunteers who crept close to the depot early in the morning. The police were waiting for them, however, and fought them back with their staves. Adopting guerilla tactics, the raiders rushed past the police and obtained a considerable quantity of salt, but in the end the police routed them, arresting 54 volunteers and 47 spectators. The injured included a police sergeant who was struck with a stone. Noted Cyclist Arrested. Bhumgarn, a noted cyclist, who was accompanied by a number of Parsi members of the Zoroastrian religion, was among those arrested. LONDON. May 26. — Violence broke out anew in India today, with communal rioting in Rangoon taking a toll of at least 10 dead and 300 injured, while hundreds of others were hurt in attempted new raids on the government salt depots in various Indian centers. The Rangoon clash, according to a Central News dispatch from that city, resulted from an attempt by authorities to halt the serious dock workers strike by the importation of strike breakers. Street fighting occurred all along the waterfront, and police were helpless in their efforts to preserve some semblance of order. Time after time they charged the scuffling groups with drawn batons. Many of the injured are in a serious condition. Scores were injured when a band of Nationalists attempted a new raid on the Wadala salt pans. Port Darwin, Australia, May 26. (Monday) — Miss May Johnson, who has leaped into fame as Britain's premier aviatrix by her 19-day flight from England to Australia, left here at 7:30 a.m. today for Sydney. She landed here yesterday from the island of Timor and was given an ovation. Sydney is nearly 2,000 miles southeast of this city. Miss Johnson will not attempt the flight in a single jump.

N A TINY MOUNT FIS, one small engine, Amy Johnson, 23 years old British girl has flown from England to Australia. — Fighting storms, forced to land in Java, starting on again without help, the young girl flew the 10,400 miles from England to Australia in less than 20 days. YESTERDAY MISS JOHNSON, with three planes escorting her, was to fly over the wilderness between Port Darwin and Brisbane, later flying on to address the Parliament at Canberra. She will come to this country to meet her father and mother. And this country will be “pleased to meet her.” England reports that “king and commoner are thrilled.” No wonder. Flying offers wonderful opportunities to young women. It requires courage, good nerves, intelligence, in all of which they excel. 4 Russia's Communists may be wrong in their social and economic theories, but they are right in their attitude toward their own country’s defens

(United Press Correspondent) BOMBAY, May 26.—National Congress volunteers renewed their raids on the Wadala Salt Works today, and successfully made away with approximately 56 pounds of salt. Thirty of the 83 volunteers participating in the raid were arrested, bringing the total prisoners taken by British guards of the Wadala Works in the past two days to 145. The raid was the third the Satyagrahis had made on the Wadala Salt pans in the past 24 hours. The first raid occurred early Sunday morning and resulted in injuries to twenty persons, including five European policemen, besides the arrest of 115 raiders. A strong police force dispersed the raiders after several hours and the volunteers reformed their lines and made a second raid in the late afternoon. The police met the volunteers with their bamboo and injured sixty. A raid before the Wadala Salt Works, near Ahmednagar, resulted in in

PARIS, May 26. (AP) —— The first serious illness among the American gold star mothers visiting France was reported today, officials of the pilgrimage announcing that Mrs. Mary Reynolds of Damascus, Ohio, and Mrs. Florence Williams of Portsmouth, Ohio, were “gravely ill.” The officials added that some fear was felt for their recovery. Mrs. Reynolds, who was taken to the American hospital yesterday suffering from what at first was believed to be indigestion, was found to have acute peritonitis. Her daughter, Mrs. W. I. Barber, of Damascus, has been notified and will be kept informed of her mother’s condition. PARIS, May 26. (AP) —— Gold star mothers today were beginning to feel the reaction from the emotional strain of their last week's activities, when they visited the battlefields wherein are the graves of their sons who died in the great war. Most of the first group remained over the we

Paris, May 25. (AP)—The American Gold Star Mothers of the first group to cross the Atlantic on a pilgrimage to the graves of the American war dead, today said good-bye to their boys in the battleground cemeteries. Their pilgrimage is almost over. They have left behind Verdun, Nancy, Chateau Thierry, Soissons and St. Quentin, cities they knew from wartime dispatches, and are coming back to Paris along the roads made famous by their soldier sons.

Shanghai, May 29.—(P) — Dispatches received here Sunday from Amoy, Fukien province, said eight were killed and many wounded in a mutiny of prisoners at the Amoy jail. One hundred and fifty of the prisoners were said to have escaped. Amoy officials blamed the reds, advancing the belief that arms were smuggled to prisoners captured in recent anticommunist raids here. The coup was made suddenly by the prisoners, who rushed and disarmed the guards, assuming control of the exits after a sharp fight.

PARIS, May 26.--Communists of Paris clashed with police today and also had a little quarrel among themselves during the annual parade to the Pere Lachaise cemetery in memory of those shot against the cemetery wall for their part in the “commune” of 1871. About 340 persons were arrested, One policeman was injured and a score of communists were bruised when the marchers refused to obey police orders to keep the red flag furled outside the cemetery.

Shanghai, May 26. — The Nationalist government of China today was fighting with its back to the wall. Struggling with civil war in north China, harassed by bandit and red armies in numerous provinces, the government imperatively needed money for military operations while confronted with an economic crisis. T. V. Soong, government minister of finance, who is in Shanghai, it was authoritatively learned, telegraphed President Chiang Kai-Shek, at Kewiteh, Honan province, where the president is commanding Nationalist forces, that a speedy Nationalist victory was imperative. Otherwise, said Soong, grave detrimental developments within the Nationalist government would be likely. Soong’s message stated that nationwide communistic and bandit ravages, depreciated silver, crop failures and paralyzed business were combining to constitute the gravest menace the government had been called upon to face
NAUEN, Germany, Feb. 22 (2). Two persons were wounded and four others arrested during a clash between communists and members of a nationalist society at the village of Lietzow last night.

PARIS, May 26.—(CU.P.)—The first group of American Gold Star mothers visiting French battlefields returned to Paris today in preparation for departure for home Thursday. The various groups of visitors started back from the cemeteries where their sons are buried early this morning, stopped en route at such historic places as Fontainebleau, Beauvais and Chateau Thierry. For the second group of mothers, which arrived here Saturday, a reception and tea at which the mothers will be guests of Gen. John J. Pershing and Ambassador Walter E. Edge, was arranged.

PARIS, May 10. Ian today recognized the American gold star mothers as messengers of peace on earth and goodwill toward men. Today, with all France watching the visitors reverently, there was abounding evidence that their pilgrimage across the sea had served to give impetus to the world movement for the outlawry of war. The dolorous and unostentatious visit of the American mothers to the graves of their sons has revived sadness in thousands of French towns which were made desolate by the war, but observers believed it had also resuscitated the determination of the masses to wage battle unflinchingly for peace. "Mysterious indeed are the workings of Providence," said a distinguished Frenchman today, "Who can fail to be struck by the fact that these mothers come to us when France, and all the foes of warfare, are seeking to fashion a durable fabric of peace?"

VIENNA.—(P)—Archduke Rainer Karl of Hapsburg-Lorraine, eldest son of the Archduke Leopold Salvator and of Princess Blanche of Castile, died of blood poisoning Sunday in the Vienna hospital. He was thirty-five years old and a brother of Archduke Leopold, who is living in the United States.

1930-04-22.text: LONDON, APR. 21. (AP).—The heads of the five delegations to the naval conference met today and formally approved the draft treaty which was then sent to the printers. Announcement was made at St. James Palace that the last plenary session of the five power naval conference would be held at 10:30 a.m. tomorrow. The treaty drawn up here, a three-power limitation pact with some five-power sections, will be filed at that time. On the strength of the announcement the American delegation here happily concluded their sailing arrangements for the trip back home aboard the Leviathan which may be held at Southampton until Wednesday morning for them. Most of the delegation were in their quarters superintending packing after the three months in London while Colonel Stimson bade farewell to his country home at Stanmore and said good-bye to his household staff here.

The London naval treaty is ready to be signed and sealed tomorrow. Three months ago today the five-power disarmament negotiations were inaugurated by King George and tonight the results are contained in a document of approximately 7,000 words which rests at St. James’ palace where the final plenary session will begin tomorrow morning. As final arrangements were made this evening for the windup session, Colonel Henry L. Stimson broadcast from London his interpretation of the parley’s accomplishments, his words being directed to the luncheon of The Associated Press in connection with the annual meeting and being carried over the United States by a radio network. Colonel Stimson stripped disarmament of technical terms on tons and guns to probe deep into the underlying problems of world diplomacy and the progress of civilization in relation to national defense. LONDON, April 21.—(AP)—Announcement was made at St. James's Palace this noon that the last plenary session of the Five-Power Naval Conference would be held at 10:30 A. M. tomorrow. The treaty drawn up here, a Three-Power Limitation pact with some five-power sections, will be signed at that time. The American delegation will be the first to sign the historic document, Colonel Stimson as its head, leading off. The powers will sign according to their English alphabetic order, America, France, Great Britain, Italy and Japan. Following Colonel Stimson will be Ambassador Dawes, Secretary Adams, Senator Robinson, Senator Reed, and Ambassadors Gibson and Morrow. The treaty drafting committee took final survey of the treaty this forenoon and pronounced their work done. Bombay, India, April 22. (P)— British police made an unsuccessful attempt to break through a nationalist volunteer cordon around the salt pans at Bhatia Baag today. Three people were injured during the scuffle. The constabulary made several arrests, including Professor Gharpure, president of the “war council,” and two joint secretaries of the Bombay provincial congress committee. A large crowd watched the proceedings. K. M. Munshi, who recently resigned his seat in the legislative council to join the civil disobedience movement, today was convicted of incitement to disobedience of the salt laws and was sentenced to six months simple imprisonment and fined 600 rupees (about 210 dollars). If he fails to pay the fine he must serve two months longer.
LONDON, April 21 - Robert Bridges, poet laureate of England, died here today. Mr. Bridges, who had been poet laureate since 1913, was 86 years old. His works were known all over the world.

By Associated Press. WINDSOR, England, April 21.—A tiny golden-haired girl usurped the British throne this morning and for a brief spell ruled her native land with charming grace which brought delighted plaudits from her subjects. This day belonged to Princess Elizabeth, daughter of the Duke and Duchess of York and beloved granddaughter of King George and Queen Mary, for it was the fourth anniversary of her birth. Bright and early little “Lilybet,” as she calls herself with delighted laughter, seized the scepter beneath which the grey-haired king-emperor, his queen and all the royal family bowed in pleased submission. There was a wonderful birthday party in old Windsor castle—such a party as the fairy books record for children to read all over the world. There were presents galore including a mysterious package from Uncle David—the Prince of Wales—sent from the heart of the hunting field

LONDON, April 22.—(AP)—The five power naval conference adjourned at 1:18 p.m., after delegates of the five nations had signed a treaty limiting and reducing the navies of Great Britain, the United States, and Japan, and setting restrictions on those of France and Italy. The adjournment came after three months and one day of long negotiation, during which many times the parley seemed on the verge of almost complete failure. Colonel Henry L. Stimson, American Secretary of State and delegation head, was the first to sign the treaty.

CALCUTTA, April 22.—(I.N.S.)— Local police aided by British troops today continued their round-up of Indians suspected of complicity in the raid on the Chittagong arsenal in which seven defenders were killed. To date 105 persons have been arrested in various parts of Bengal, The Chittagong raid, according to a new version, was engineered by an Indian leader who disguised himself as a Briton.

LONDON, April 22——The address of Colonel Henry L. Stimson, American secretary of state and delegation head at the London naval conference, before the conference plenary session this forenoon, follows: “Mr. Chairman, I wish to congratulate you on the successful conclusion of this naval conference and to take occasion at the same time to thank you for the sterling qualities of your leadership which have contributed so effectively to that end. “I do not propose to elaborate on this subject, but I can not refrain from a personal word to tell you how deeply we appreciate the unwearying patience, skill and tact with which you have led us through these difficult weeks. CALCUTTA, April 2. (AP)—Government activities in the Indian situation today still centered on pursuit of the insurgent group which raided the police arsenal of Chittagong Saturday and killed six of the defenders. Troops and auxiliaries are searching for the raiders, but as yet have not captured them. Reports from Bombay, Madras and Karachi today indicated that an atmosphere of tension pervaded those cities, but only in Karachi was any large scale demonstration staged. It caused no trouble, several hundred women merely marching through the streets carrying pots of contraband salt on their heads. Mahatma Gandhi, leader of the Nationalists and father of the civil disobedience movement, remained in Gujerat today. Interviewed regarding the Chittagong incident, he declared it “sad news,” but added, “however serious the situation becomes there can be no suspension of the fight; there can be no

LONDON, April 22.—The London Naval treaty took its place in the world’s library of peace today. Exactly thirteen weeks after its glittering and resplendent opening in the House of Lords on January 21, the Conference met in Plenary Session in Queen Anne’s drawing room in ancient St. James's palace, and the chief delegates of each of the five nations affixed their signatures to the latest document composed to further the cause of disarmament. The signing session opened at 10:32 a.m. (4:32 a.m. Eastern Standard Time.) The delegates of the five powers grouped themselves around a crimson-covered horseshoe table, and of all those who participated in the brilliant opening three months ago only Foreign Minister Dino Grandi of Italy and Premier Andre Tardieu of France were absent. SHANGHAI, April 21.—A letter received here from one of 16 American Catholic missionaries, who for weeks have been held prisoners in the Kiangsi Province City of Kanchow, said that Communist and bandit besiegers had threatened "when Kanchow falls, to kill every foreigner within the walls for robbing us of our prize." Although the walls continued to halt them, the Reds, according to the letter, which was dated April 4, had notified Kanchow authorities that they considered the foreigners responsible for their failure to capture the city. Defense of Kanchow, the missionary said, continued unchanged with no immediate danger of its capture. Meanwhile the Reds have withdrawn part of their forces from the siege and "while awaiting Kanchow's fall are busy plundering the surrounding country, looting villages and kidnapping hostages. 1930-04-15.text: LONDON, APR. 14. (AP).—One week from tomorrow, barring mishaps representatives of the five great naval powers will affix their signatures to the historic pact which has evolved from the London naval conference after long weeks of difficult negotiations. Announcement to this effect was made at a 24-minute plenary session of the conference in Queen Anne's drawing room in old St. James’s Palace this noon, Prime Minister MacDonald officiating as general chairman of the conference. This announcement was the principal development in the whirlwind session, the first complete meeting of the conference since February 11. It originally was planned to try to get the treaty drawn up so that it could be signed next Tuesday, but the Prime Minister announced that this was impossible of achievement. As it is, it will be a race against time for the drafters to get the document ready for the meeting Tuesd

London, April 15. —The American and British naval delegations today reached agreement regarding the so-called safeguarding or ‘escalator’ clause for the naval treaty by which powers signing the tri-lateral limitation pact may protect themselves against competitive building by non-signatories. The clause, it was understood, will be considerably broader than Article XXI of the Washington treaty, designed for a similar purpose. By its provisions the navy of any of the three signatory powers may be increased to meet increases in navies of non-signatory powers, with resulting raising of the levels of the other two signatory powers. An American spokesman described the agreement as “virtually completed.” He said it was reached by Secretary Stimson and Prime Minister MacDonald just before the premier left for Scotland to spend the Easter holidays. Bombay, India, April 14.—(A.P.)— Striking hard in defense of its sovereignty in India the British government today took into custody leaders in the Indian nationalist "civil disobedience" movement captained by Mahatma Gandhi. Gandhi himself was not molested. Of importance, however, and almost tantamount to arrest of Gandhi, was the incarceration and sentence a few hours later, of Jawaharlal Nehru, president of the all-Indian national congress. Nehru was sent to prison for six months after conviction on a charge of violation of the salt act Friday. He was arrested at Cheoki Station and temporarily detained in Nairi provincial jail, both places near Allahabad. News of his arrest spread like wildfire through Bombay, and within a few minutes the cotton, bullion, seeds and share markets suspended business. Under the rules only one speech was allowed for and against the bill. After Foot had spoken for 10 minutes advocating the measure, Frederick A. MaeQuisten, Conservative member from Argyll and a lawyer who sometimes acts professionally for the liquor trade, opposed the bill in a speech filled with humorous remarks.

(Associated Press Staff Writer.) LONDON, April 14.—(/)— Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, his iron-gray hair tousled, his workaday spectacles hooked over his ears, and his hands full of papers, stood like a schoolmaster today as he called the delegates of the London naval conference into plenary session at St. James’ palace and rushed through, in 24 minutes flat, adoption of technical reports which form the raw material for the London naval treaty. But the naval conference held the spotlight only briefly in London today, for Mr. MacDonald hurried from St. James’ to parliament to hear the budget speech of Philip Snowden, chancellor of the exchequer. The ordinary Briton is thinking more of the additional sixpence levied on him for income tax than of the nebulous £70,000,000 saved in British naval expenditure. CALCUTTA, India, April 15.—Several deaths and a number of casualties were reported after a renewed outburst of rioting between revolutionary demonstrators and police today. A mob that had attacked tramcars, burning four of them and wrecking five more, became completely unmanageable, and after armored cars and troops had been called to the rescue of embattled police, the officers were forced to fire into the mob.

London, April 15. (4¢)—After three months negotiations with representatives of five nations, speaking four languages—Col. Henry L. Stimson’s French has improved until he hardly has need of an interpreter. Senator Reed knows some Japanese. Reijiro Wakatsuki, Japanese chief delegate, has incorporated “battleship,” “destroyers,” “holiday,” “replacements,” “honorable secretary” and “honorable senator” into his vocabulary although he spoke very little English when he left Japan early six months ago. Dino Grandi, Italian foreign minister, has learned to speak English with no vestures and almost without an accent. Ambassador Morrow however admits his French grows worse day by day, while Jacques-Louis Dumesnil, French minister of marine, contends it is impossible for him to learn English.

London, April 15.--(UPI)—All five powers participating in the naval conference have virtually agreed on all points on the treaty which will be signed next week, the American spokesman announced today. Agreement includes accord on the contingent clause and the global pelegory transactional methods, he said. The contingency clause provides protection for the United States, Britain and Japan against any large building of navies by another country, permitting them to increase their navies if forced to do so by competition of a non-signatory nation. The clause was especially demanded by Britain, which desires to maintain the “Two-power standard” in Europe. The transactional clause, first suggested by the French, provides the method by which limitation of navies shall be achieved. CALCUTTA, GAL. April 15. (INS.)—The “evidence” campaign of Mahatma Gandhi, which has been smouldering for weeks, blazed forth into violent fury today with a bloody demonstration in the streets of Calcutta. After a heated skirmish during which stones and brickbats were thrown, reports showed that 26 had been wounded, some of them seriously. Among those taken to hospitals was an unidentified European woman, severely cut and bruised when the rioters hurled stones through the windows of a streetcar. It was the most serious riot since that in Bombay last week when five Indians were killed. The outbreak occurred as part of a city-wide protest against the incarceration of Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, president of the Indian National Congress, who was sentenced to a six-month jail term for aiding Gandhi in his violation of the British government's salt laws. The bandit Jawaharlal Nehru, president of the All-India Congress, Monday was sentenced to six months simple imprisonment for violation of the salt law, while J. M. Sengupta, mayor of Calcutta and president of the Bengal civil disobedience committees, was sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment on charges of sedition, conspiracy and obstructing the police. Members of the Bombay Congress committees immediately decided to observe the day of mourning, and the nationalist “war council” decided to send out 500 volunteers as salesmen of contraband salt. LONDON, April 15.—(U.P)—A bill under which Great Britain could co-operate actively in suppressing liquor smuggling into the United States had its first reading in the House of Commons today. The bill would enable the Board of Trade to suspend or cancel the certificates of any master, mate or engineer engaging in the illicit importation of liquor into the United States. The bill, proposed by Isaac Foot, laborite, was read amid shouts and an almost continuous uproar until a division was called. The House voted 215 to 142 in favor of granting permission to introduce the bill. “Gesture of Friendship” In introducing the measure, Foot said: “The bill is aimed to assist the United States government to contend with many formidable difficulties, the object of which is to defeat its constitutional policy. Unfortunately, in the efforts to defeat that policy, many British subjects have been concerne

LONDON, April 15 — Liberal support for the budget of Chancellor of Exchequer Phillip Snowden was believed assured today with most of Mr. Lloyd George’s party either indulgent or probatory of its provisions. This Liberal support apparently made passage of the measure certain. Conservative opinion was definitely hostile, declaring it an attack on capital, a burden of industry and bound to increase unemployment. Lady Astor, Conservative, described it as the most unimaginative budget of British history. Gleanings from the press and individual commentators seemed to show that aside from those interests specially affected it would neither be popular nor unpopular.

LONDON, April 1st——-Savage rioting through the city of Calcutta was occasioned by the arrest and conviction of the young extremist, Jawaharlal Nehru, necessitated the use of firearms today by police. There were casualties among the rioters, according to Central News dispatches. Street cars and automobiles carrying foreigners were stoned by the rioters. Armoured cars and strong detachments of police restored a semblance of order at noon, but the situation was still serious. A white woman, occupant of an automobile, was severely injured and taken to a hospital. Six European firemen were injured, two seriously. Nineteen natives were seriously wounded. The hospitals were opening emergency wards, according to dispatches to London evening newspapers. In the afternoon serious fighting was reported to have broken out in the northern section of the city.

By United Press CALCUTTA, India, April 15.—Rioting which was started by Indian revolutionaries who demonstrated in the streets of Calcutta was quelled late today after a vigorous offensive by police. About 170 persons, including 15 European police and 11 firemen, were injured. A mob that had attacked tramcars, burning four of them and wrecking five more, became completely unmanageable, and after armored cars and troops had been called to the rescue of embattled police, the officers were forced to fire into the mob. The rioters made a vigorous attack with stones, and casualties among the police forces were reported heavy. The riots followed proclamation of a “hartal” throughout the city in protest against the convictions of Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru and Mayor Sen Gupta. Earlier, an indignant mob of demonstrators barricaded the section around the Kalighat Temple, and then fell upon a number

Friedrichshafen, Germany, April 15—(AP)—The dirigible Graf Zeppelin this afternoon started on a cruise with 20 passengers to Seville, Spain. Rain was falling at the start of the flight but good weather was reported over France. The Graf was in command of Captain Ernst Lehmann, second in command on the world flight with Captain Hugo Eckener. The dirigible will stay only a few hours in Seville and then will turn homeward, being expected back in her hangar at Friedrichshafen Thursday evening.

Berlin—(/)—The Reichstag today approved the government's bitterly contested agrarian program on its third and final reading by a vote of 250 to 204. Promulgation of the program, however, was made dependent on whether the tax bills presented by the ministry also are adopted. How close the fight was, was shown by the fact that the sugar tax bill was approved with only a minority of six, the vote being 230 to 224 with no abstentions. Today's vote was looked upon as giving the government the first round in the voting skirmish on the finance and agrarian programs.

(By The Associated Press.) Washington, Apr. 15.—The love of two widely known Russian actresses drove Vladimir Mayakovsky, leading proletariat poet and playwright, to shoot himself through the heart, his friends believed today. Despondent at the failure of his last two plays, "Red Bug" and "Bat Hose," which were criticized as "ideologically unsound," the poet, who was 36 years old, found himself unable to choose between the two beautiful women, and took instead a quick effective way out. In a dramatic farewell letter addressed to "everybody" he begged his mother, sister, and comrades to forgive him. Lily Brik, one of the two actresses, then is mentioned, and a plea made to her to love him.

FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, April 15 (M6) The Graf Zeppelin, which shortly is to make a transatlantic flight to Rio de Janeiro, left here at 11 a.m. today for Seville, Spain. There are 16 passengers aboard the airliner, which is commanded by Captain Ernest Lehmann.

PARIS, April 15.—(UP)—The chamber of deputies gave Premier Andre Tardieu's cabinet a vote of confidence today by a majority of 319 to 260. The vote of confidence was taken on a motion of Deputy Leo Bouysson, a Radical Socialist, demanding an automatic increase in pensions for retired officials.

Licata, Sicily, April 15 (AP) — Funerals will be held for 15 boys, aged between 12 and 18, who were killed yesterday in a stampede in a moviehouse after a film had become ignited. Three others were injured seriously and five slightly hurt.

"y ine tates PF ress. MOSCOW, April 14.— Vladimir Mayakovsky, regarded by many as Soviet Russia’s greatest poet, killed himself today. Mayakovsky visited the United States in December, 1925, and on his return to Russia pictured the United States as money mad.

Licata, Sicily, April 14.—(/P)— A fire breaking out in a crowded moving picture theater here tonight caused the death or injury of 15 persons. Three of the injured are in a serious condition. There were many children in the audience. The causes of the fire could not be immediately learned.

Paris, April 15. (4/P) Frederic Stork, wealthy Dutch shipping man, today asked the Paris police to investigate the alleged airplane kidnapping of his seven-year-old daughter, Margareta. He especially asked them to interrogate his divorced American wife, the former Christian Kramer. He alleged that his former wife and her present husband met the girl as she left school in Laren, Holland, November 19, and took her by air to Elberfeld, Germany and from there to Paris. Police said the three left their Paris apartment before officers arrived.

IFNNA, Apr. 14. — (AP) — The American authorities are investigating an unconfirmed rumor from Constanza, Rumania, that two American girl tourists aboard the steamship Oceuna were arrested for taking photographs of the harbor as the vessel was entering the port. They were alleged to be spying.

1930-04-08.text: Dandi, Bombay, India, April 7—(®—Police and a party of followers of Mahatma Gandhi engaged in a scuffle on the beach this morning while volunteers engaged in the civil disobedience campaign were collecting salt in defiance of the government monopoly. While so engaged the police arrived and demanded the salt which the volunteers refused to hand over. While the altercation was in progress villagers arrived at the beach and also began to collect salt. The police then arrested the captain of the volunteers and others who had told the volunteers not to give up their salt. In the scuffle which followed two Nationalists were reported slightly injured. Mahatma Gandhi, who opened the civil disobedience campaign himself yesterday, arrived at Aat on the beach from Dandi shortly after the scuffle to observe his usual Monday silence and meditation. Bombay, India, April 8.—(A. P.)—Most of the Hindu and Parsi shops in Bombay City suspended business today in response to the hartal or strike call of the Bombay Congress Committee of the Indian National Congress. The hartal is in protest at the arrest of K. Y. Nariman and Jamunlal Najaj for their activities in behalf of Mahatma Gandhi’s salt law violators. Nariman, who is a most prominent Swadeshi, or Indian Nationalist, was sentenced to one month’s simple imprisonment for infringing the salt laws. Most of the local shops closed, but a number of Moslem shops remained open. Two thousand school boys threw down their books and joined the hartal.

London, April 7.—(AP)—Dissatisfaction in scattered sections of the house of commons over the trend of Anglo-French security discussions in connection with the naval conference tonight resulted in a move to debate the whole question openly. Prime Minister MacDonald was able to check it only by taking the floor himself and pledging full information to party leaders any time they sought it. It was the first attempt of the British parliament to check Mr. MacDonald's free hand in the disarmament negotiations. The motion, if it had been voted on and had resulted in the government’s defeat, would have constituted a vote of censure and called for Mr. MacDonald's resignation. Tomorrow the Anglo-French negotiations undoubtedly will come to a head, and it was reported in London tonight that M. London, April 8.—(A.P.)—The Big Three of the London disarmament conference—the chiefs of the American, British and Japanese delegations—today raised the banner of a tripartite naval agreement for the world to see. Secretary Stimson, Prime Minister MacDonald, and Reijiro Wakatsuki at noon went into conference and it was understood they began discussing the outlines of a pact to bind their three countries in a new effort towards disarmament and peace. Heretofore their meetings have been for the purpose of trying to achieve a five power agreement which would include France and Italy. They still cling to the hope, even though it may be slight, that these two neighbors may see their way to sign with the rest. But observers considered it significant that for the first time the Big Three today were closeted in order to debate the actual terms of a tri-partite treaty. Foreign Minister Briand of

The Nationalist leader himself remained at liberty, and in spite of a scuffle that took place between his followers and the police near Dandi today, announced that he would come in person tomorrow to collect salt with the volunteers. Several minor encounters occurred at widely scattered points between Gandhi followers and the police, but there were no disorders on a large scale. LONDON, April 8..(U,P).-The greatest plague of locusts in modern times has descended upon Egypt blocking trains and devastating hundreds of acres of cultivated land, dispatches from Cairo revealed today. The swarms, making the skies black between Trans-Jordan and the Nile valley, have become so menacing that the Egyptian government has voted $250,000 to fight the plague, and has mobilized 140 flame throwers, using 200 tons of liquid destroyer in the afflicted region. An army of 75,000 men has been in Transjordan to fight the plague.

Bombay, India, April 8.—Mahatma Gandhi fulfilled his pledge today to visit the little village of Aat, scene of a scuffle between police and rebels yesterday, in defiance of threats that he would be arrested. He was not molested by the police. Three thousand devoted followers of the Mahatma flocked into Aat from neighboring villages to hear the leader of India’s revolt against the salt taxes urge the nation to defy British rule. There was some disappointment, especially among Gandhi's followers, that his act of defiance today did not bring about the immediate arrest anticipated by the Mahatma.

WELLINGTON, New Zealand, April 8. — Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd and a group from his Antarctic expedition were entertained at a civic reception here tonight following their arrival from Dunedin. Admiral Byrd said in a speech that he wished to convey sincere thanks to the government and people of New Zealand for invaluable assistance to his expedition. He added that he was proud to have New Zealand's cooperation and that no government in the world could have aided him more. The party also is making preparations to embark at the next sailing for the

OMBAY, India, April 8—(UP)—The government ordered military reinforcements sent to the gold mine areas of Mysore and Oorgaum today as disorders spread simultaneously with the civil disobedience campaign of the Mahatma M. K. Gandhi. After a clash yesterday when soldiers fired on a crowd of strikers at the Southern India mines in Mysore province, it was revealed that 16,000 workers in five mines were striking. The reinforcements were dispatched from Bangalore. Although Gandhi again defied authorities at Aat and was not molested, there was no cessation of measures taken against his chief lieutenants and followers who have participated in the breaking of government salt laws. Gandhi's son, Ram Das, was sentenced to six months imprisonment at Surat and a large crowd demonstrated when he made an anti-government speech in the courtroom. | Bangalore, Mysore, India, April 7—()—Police today fired on workmen in the Mysore gold mines, who got out of hand during a strike and stoned local officials. There were 50 casualties, A squadron of the Mysore lancers, as well as police reinforcements, have been rushed to the mines, where 6,000 workers have gone out, causing a complete stoppage of work. Fox strangled his mother, a charming gray-haired woman of 66, as she lay in bed at their hotel at Margate last autumn, and then set the room afire. Evidence showed that he desired the money so that he could go to Australia and join a wealthy beautiful blonde woman with whom he had a love affair.

Maidstone, England, April 8 (AP) Within less than three weeks after his conviction of the murder of his mother, Sidney Fox was hanged in jail here this morning. The crowd, which gathered outside, dispersed when a notice was posted that the erratic youth had paid the penalty for his crime. There were no bells tolled, no flag hoisted, and prison routine went on as usual. Fox strangled his mother, a charming gray-haired woman of 63, as she lay in bed at their hotel in Margate last autumn, and then set the room afire. The son previously had insured her life for considerable sums. Evidence showed that he desired the money so that he could go to Australia and join a wealthy beautiful blonde woman with whom he had a love affair.

MAIDSTONE, Kent, England (UP).—Sydney Harry Fox, 31-year-old "confidence man" and forger, was executed Tuesday morning for the murder of his widowed mother. The pleasant young man, once known, because of his engaging smile and cherubic face, as "Little Lord Fauntleroy," went to the gallows at 8:15 a.m. He protested his innocence of the crime—England's first case of matricide in 50 years—to the end. Fox's death marked the final episode in the sensational "Room 66" case. The tragedy occurred October 23, 1929. Fire broke out in room 66 at the Metropole hotel, Margate, Kent. Mrs. Rosaline Fox, a woman of 63, was in the room asleep. Her son, Sydney, had an adjoining room. He gave the alarm, but other guests in the hotel entered the room and found Mrs. Fox dead. The performance of the R-100 may determine whether Britain will carry out its plans for a fleet of dirigibles linking the far-flung units of the empire by air. LONDON (UP).—An authoritative French source said Tuesday night that France and Britain had reached an agreement for interpretation of Article XVI of the League of Nations covenant, based on Annex F of the Locarno treaty. — Interpretation of the article to meet French security demands has been the chief obstacle in naval conference efforts to reach a five-power treaty. The new basis for discussion was announced soon after the return of Aristide Briand, French foreign minister, from Paris, where the failure of Britain to meet French demands for security guarantees was discussed with Premier Andre Tardieu and the cabinet, The Franco-British discussions were resumed at the same time the three-power naval pact among Britain, Japan and the United States was brought near. Bombay, India, April 8 (AP)— While some of his chief lieutenants have been arrested and his son sentenced to six months’ imprisonment for breaking the salt laws, Mahatma Gandhi, Indian Nationalist leader, has yet to be molested by the police in his civil disobedience campaign. The Mahatma, who began the campaign by the illegal manufacture of salt on Sunday, produced salt again today, but there were no police at the scene near the village of Aat on the Gulf of Cambay. A crowd of about 8,000 had gathered in the belief that Gandhi might be arrested but when no attempt was made to interfere with him, the throng dispersed. Advices from Surat said that Ram Das Gandhi, son of the Mahatma, had been sentenced to six months’ rigorous imprisonment for breaking the salt laws at Bhimrad. Four companions were given similar sentences. Some of Gandhi's chief lieutenants have been sentenced to imprisonme

TOKYO, April 7. (P)—The railway ministry today announced that 17 persons had been killed and seven seriously injured in an explosion aboard a train near Oita, Kyushu prefecture. The explosion was officially attributed to dynamite, which was believed somehow to have become mixed in the coal used in the engine. All the dead were passengers. A majority of the 17 apparently lived for several hours after the explosion. The blast started a forest fire which burned throughout the night.

FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, Germany, April 8.—(/P)—Reports from Brazil that Dr. Hugo Eckener had been removed from command of the giant dirigible Graf Zeppelin for her coming Brazilian flight were denied by Captain Ernst Lehmann at the Zeppelin works today. “There never was the slightest doubt about Dr. Eckener’s commanding the South American flight,” said Captain Lehmann. “Somebody apparently has an interest in throwing a monkey wrench into our machinery, but he will not succeed. Dr. Eckener will be in charge of the South America flight just as he has been our leader on all other Graf expeditions.”

Bilver Dell A. b, bureau write. SHANGHAI, April 5.—Police of the international settlement here shot to death one student and wounded another today during a student demonstration allegedly the outgrowth of recent similar occurrences at Nanking. Police riot squads were held in readiness in the event of further trouble.

PARIS (UP)—Madame Fraya, famed French seeress who predicted in an exclusive interview with the United Press at the first of the year, the ending of a European dictatorship, the death of one of the most prominent political leaders in the world and the recent flood disasters in southern France, advises you to take your vacation late this summer if you want to get sunburned. Madame Fraya is not a pessimist, but she sees nothing but black clouds ahead. The nefarious influence of Saturn dominates 1930, and she does not think much good will come from it. There is even the menace of war in the offing, but Madame Fraya sees it cleared up without bloodshed. The weather of early summer will be particularly distressing. NAPLES, Italy, Apr. 8 (AP)—The Duchess of Apulia, who was born Princess Anne of France, yesterday gave birth to a daughter in Capodimonte Palace, the residence of her father-in-law, the Duke of Aosta.

Alexander, British first Lord of the Admiralty, and Aristide Briand, French foreign minister, and a whole crew of experts and advisers ranged beside them, the French and the British premiers negotiated to bring together the viewpoints of France, Great Britain and the other powers. The conversation is believed to have changed the whole complexion of the conference. New avenues have been opened for bringing France and Italy into a general agreement on armaments, which has already been achieved by the United States, Great Britain and Japan. London, May. 17 (UP)—The naval conference deadlock on the issue of France’s heavy tonnage demands appeared to have been broken today, and the delegates resumed their conversations with more confidence than at any time since the fall of the French cabinet, four weeks ago. In a conference at Chequers, Premier Andre Tardieu yesterday arrived at “new terms” which will be the basis for discussion, with the possibility that France's demands may be cut. The Sunday meeting is described in some quarters as “the most important of the entire conference.” It appears, at least, to have given the parley a new lease of life. Acting with MacDonald in the conversation yesterday was A. V. Alexander, first lord of the admiralty. ANAND, Bombay, India, March 17—(AP)—Mahatma Gandhi, the Indian nationalist leader, passed today in silence as he and his 79 devotees rested from their grueling four days’ march in behalf of Indian independence from Ahmadabad to the sea. The Mahatma has maintained silence one day each week for years, conveying his wishes by means of signs and the written word. It is a self-disciplinary measure the nationalist leader imposes on himself. Tomorrow morning he and his procession of fellow Swarajists will continue on their way to Jalalpur on the bay of Cambay, where in defiance of the British monopoly they will manufacture salt, thus inaugurating their campaign of civil disobedience to the British crown. The confidence and optimism were not shared elsewhere. Many felt that unless M. Tardieu made considerable concessions—and it was indicated he did not—the differences between France and Great Britain, and France and the United States, are too essential for ready compromise. They could not see how, other things being what they were, the gulf between the two viewpoints can be bridged. M. LONDON, March 17.—Albert Y. Alexander, first Lord of the Admiralty announced in the House of Commons today that the government had decided to suspend its submarine program temporarily. Alexander made his statement introducing the naval estimate. He valued attention to the fact that this year’s estimate of 52,789,000 pounds sterling was 4,126,000 pounds below 1929. He said the figures however did not reflect the real amount of saving because it was the net amount achieved in the face of new commitments which it had been impossible to avoid.

LONDON — (A.P.)—Death of the Countess of Coventry yesterday four days after the decease of her husband, the 9th Earl of Coventry, awakened sympathetic emotions among the public today. The aged lady—she was 87—within an hour of her bereavement said: “I do not wish to live any longer” and took to bed almost at once with evident consciousness that her wish would be granted. She was not, her physician said; she merely lost the will to live since she was separated finally from the man whose companion she had been for 65 years. “Always try to appreciate one another's point of view and never quarrel,” the Earl gave recently as the golden rule of a happy married life. Both seemed to find it easy to follow. They are being buried today side by side in the family vault.

PARIS, March 17.—The hand which ruled Spain firmly for nearly seven years today was stilled in death. Garbed in the sack cloth and sandals of a Carmelite monk, the body of Don Miguel Primo de Rivera y Orbaneja was in an unpretentious suite of a modest Latin quarter hotel. Tonight a train will take it back to Madrid, where in life Captain General Primo de Rivera was dictator of Spain. The end came in exile in Paris, the same city of exiles to which during his seven years of power he doomed many of his fellow citizens. Death came to General Primo de Rivera on the eve of his departure for Wiesbaden, Germany, where he was to take the cure. He had planned a farewell tea for yesterday afternoon, at which his friends in Paris, including Marshall Petain, had been invited. General Primo de Rivera was a devout Catholic. Madrid, March 17. (/P)—Tossed about by a black bull with wide sharp horns, Sydney Franklin, Brooklyn bull fighter today was in a hospital injured seriously, although probably not fatally. In a second off guard, as he whipped his maddening red cape in front of the enraged beast’s eyes, he turned his back on the animal which impinged him and bandied him about like a plaything for several minutes. Dr. Crespo, his physician, predicted he would live but said it would take him 40 days to recover. Franklin is the son of a Brooklyn policeman. He received his early education in the bull ring in Mexico City where his proficiency led him to go to Madrid where after an apprenticeship he made several public appearances and acquitted himself well. The spectacle of an American in the bull ring won him many Spanish admirers. He recently said he hoped to inaugurate bull fighting in the United States.

| United Press Staff Correspondent. PARIS, March 17—Spaniards of every walk of life, many of them sworn enemies of the six-year dictatorship of Miguel Primo de Rivera, today flocked to the little hotel on the left bank of the Seine to pay tribute to the man who died yesterday, six weeks after he laid down his power. The body of the former dictator, who died in exile here, lay on the deathbed of his apartment. He wore the brown robes of the order of Carmelite monks, to which he subscribed as a layman. This is permitted by Spanish custom. Two nuns constantly prayed by his bedside, while candles were massed around the bier. The body will be removed at once to Spain, and burial will be in the family vault at Gerez, near Seville, in accordance with his request. (By The Associated Press) Paris, March 16. — Primo de Rivera, 60, former dictator of Spain, died of heart disease in his hotel room today. General De Rivera, who bore the title of Marquis De Estella, came to Paris shortly after he resigned his office last January 28, ending six years of almost supreme power in Spain. He was in poor health for some time, but was believed to be recovering. The former dictator died alone in his hotel room. His two daughters found the body when they returned from church. They summoned their brother, who called the family physician. The doctor said De Rivera had been dead half an hour. Believed Improved. Death called General Rivera on the eve of his departure for Wiesbaden, Germany, where he was to take the cure for diabetes. His condition had so improved that his physician consented to let him give a farewell tea at his hotel for a few friends. His two daugh

PARIS, March 16.--(44)—Miguel Primo de Rivera y Orbaneja, Marques de Estella, Spanish grandee and for seven years dictator of Spain, died today in the modest Latin Quarter hotel where in the 1890s he spent what he always considered the happiest days of his life as a student at the Sorbonne. The former dictator was stricken by heart disease this morning and died alone in his room at 11 a.m., less than seven weeks after relinquishing the supreme power in Spain. Death broke his voluntary and temporary exile in Paris.

MOSCOW...—While millions in other lands prayed Sunday for Russia's legions of Christian faithful, the militant atheist society of Russia, the league of the Godless, prepared for a more intensive assault against God and the churches during the approaching Easter period. The Russian government itself, however, has noticeably moderated its attitude toward religion. It now discountenances the forcible closing of churches or the tearing down of church bells without the consent of the overwhelming majority of the population and the formal sanction of the central government authorities. Even so great an atheist as Joseph Stalin, “the strong man of Russia,” has issued strict orders that any communist party worker, or village soviet official found guilty of using violent methods in the party's fight against religion shall be severely punished. Franklin drew a large crowd to the arena today and received a great welcome on killing his first bull. The second bull was an unusually large and fierce one, but Franklin attempted to play a few fancy tricks with it. Caught Off Guard He was caught off guard by a sudden charge of the bull, which got its horn into a thigh. He was badly wounded and fell to the ground unconscious. MADRID, March 17. (AP)—The Spanish cabinet met in extraordinary session today to consider plans for the funeral of former Premier Primo de Rivera Wednesday with high military honors and government tributes. King Alfonso will be represented by members of the royal household and perhaps his second son, Don Jaime. Premier Berenguer and members of the cabinet probably will attend in a body. The special funeral train from the French frontier is expected in Madrid Wednesday morning.

MOSCOW, Mar. 17—(UP)—In an effort to counteract the pope's prayers on behalf of Christian Russians Wednesday, “The Godless One,” official Soviet atheist, today ordered all atheists to mobilize their strength on that day for massed demonstrations against religion and foreign intervention. Declaring that Pope Pius had taken advantage of religious fanaticism for the purpose of inciting “the backward masses against the Soviet Union,” this anti-religious publication, which has nationwide circulation, used particularly abusive and violent language in criticizing the pope. The paper declared that hooligan bands were being organized in Italy, Poland, Bulgaria, and other countries for an attack upon the crusade of capital against the first Soviet proletarian republic.

Tokyo, March 16. (P)—Differences between the naval and civilian elements of the Japanese government, it became known today, must be reconciled before Tokyo can approve the provisional Japanese-American agreement, which the delegates at the London conference have submitted. The Japanese naval element is known to hold strong misgivings concerning the big cruiser and submarine sections, but the Associated Press has no reason to believe that civil officialdom favors acceptance of the agreement.

MADRID, March 17.—Spain today mourned the passing of General Primo Rivera, until a short time ago its military dictator. The friends of the military leader who died suddenly yesterday in Paris, joined hands today with his former foes, to pay him homage in death and bestow upon him the honors due a faithful soldier. Some of the men who had been his most bitter political enemies expressed keen regret at his untimely death, lauding him as a “great fighter, unrelenting in the support of his principles.” The news of the former Dictator’s death was a distinct shock. There being no Sunday newspapers in Spain, the general public learned it only through reports in the streets. Then it was announced in the churches.
