1930-06-09.text: DUBLIN, Irish Free State, June 9. (*)—Capt. Charles Kingsford Smith decided this afternoon not to attempt a start of the Southern Cross Atlantic flight tomorrow morning owing to unfavorable weather forecasts. Captain Saul, the navigator, has insured his life for the trip, and is paying a premium of 400 pounds sterling (about $2,000). The capital sum involved has been kept a close secret, but it is believed to be 5,000 pounds. He is a master mariner and has crossed the Atlantic many times.

LONDON, JUNE 9. (AP).—Madame Magda Lupescue, former companion of Prince Carol during his exile in France, is reported by the Interlaken correspondent of the Sunday Chronicle as taking her parting from Carol very much to heart. “Ours is a union of love,” the correspondent quoted her as saying. “There is deep pain in every thought of final separation from him. I am an exile; an outcast, extirpated from the land of my birth, the land I love. Carol is my only happiness, and now I shall see him no more. My grief is almost too much for me to bear.”

London, June 10 (UP)—The Daily Express said that Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald planned to fly to Canada aboard the British dirigible R-100 in the autumn, if the political situation would permit his absence. The report said other political leaders would accompany the prime

BOMBAY, June 8,—(AP)—With the subjugation of northwest frontier tribesmen by British airplanes and with the coming of the rainy season lessening the activities of Nationalist salt raiders, the Indian situation offered little of an exciting nature today. Nationalist political activity continues, however. At Jalapore, a conference of civil disobedience volunteers was held under the presidency of Mrs. Gandhi, wife of the Mahatma, and adopted plans for a stiffening of the civil resistance movement. The conference passed a resolution urging the non-payment of land revenue and a social boycott of government servants, both of which are forbidden in recent ordinances promulgated by the viceroy. The working committee of the All-India National Congress concluded the sitting which began last Wednesday at Allahabad. Its activities were kept secret.
Bombay, June 10—Ten members of the Bombay National Congress War Council were sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment each today on charges of issuing congress bulletins in violation of the law.

United Press Staff Correspondent. BOMBAY, India, June 9,—(P) Serious riots between Hindus and Moslems broke out Monday at Kapadwanj in the Kaira district as a sequel to a religious observance by Shias, a Mohammedan sect. Four hundred persons were injured. The district magistrate and police superintendent, accompanied by a force of police, hurried to the scene from Kaira. The Shias, one of the two chief Mohammedan sects, were holding a Muharram procession in observance of the first month of the Moslem year, beating their breasts as they walked through the streets. The riot which followed was only one of several incidents that caused anxiety to British officials during the day. Because of a slump in cotton prices, due to workless periods and nervousness resulting from the civil disobedience campaign, the East India Cotton Association declined to fix minimum prices for the various classes o

LONDON, JUNE, 9. (INS.)—The amalgamation of Hungary and Roumania under King Carol II within a very short time was foreseen here today by Barbu Jonescu, powerful friend of the new monarch and wealthy Roumanian businessman who has a residence in London. “In two or three months, I shouldn't be surprised to hear of definite movements aimed at the amalgamation of Hungary and Roumania under Carol,” Jonescu said, “Such a fusion would be quite possible because both countries require a stable government and amalgamation under a single crown would serve a useful and practical purpose.”

(By Associated Press) London, June 9--India dispatches today indicated a definite improvement in the situation in the northwest frontier province where British military forces have been engaged in putting down an invasion of tribesmen from the outlying districts. Repeated bombings and shelling from British airplanes and guns, apparently, it was said, have satisfied the invaders that British power is not defunct as they allegedly had been led to believe. The general quiet in India was attributed in some quarters to the attitude of Indian nationalists of awaiting publication of the first report of the commission of Sir John Simon on Indian statutory reforms which are due tonight.

SHANGHAI, June 9—()— One hundred passengers and crew of the Chinese steamer Litung were drowned today. The Yangtse river vessel struck a rock off Tungchow on the north shore of the river’s mouth and sank. The ship was winding its way among the small islands of the estuary between Twsungming Island and Tungchow when it struck the rock. It was not known immediately whether any foreigners were on board. The north channel in which the Litung was sunk is generally avoided by ocean-going vessels, the south channel being considered safer.

Shanghai, June 8.—(AP)—An official statement issued today said that the rebel losses in the recent battle near Sincheng were heavy, with 20,000 killed, 10,000 taken prisoner and 15,000 surrendering voluntarily. Meanwhile, the government has concentrated seven gunboats at Yochow to co-operate against the Kwangsi rebels who are reported to be advancing from the southward in the vicinity of Changsha.

De Valera had planned to continue his tour here until after Easter. “If I am selected by the Dail, which chooses president and council, to succeed Cosgrave,” de Valera said, “I would form a Fianna Fáil government. Cosgrave, for the past eight years president of the Irish Free State, would be re-elected to that office—from which he resigned Friday—when the Dail Eireann meets next Wednesday. Two candidates will oppose him in the Dail Wednesday, one of them long a stormy figure in Irish Free State politics, Eamonn De Valera leader of the Fianna Fail, or Irish Republicans, which are the leading party in the opposition minority. The other will be T. J. O'Connell, parliamentary leader of the Labor party. Mr. De Valera is in Chicago, His hope of election to head a new Irish

DUBLIN, March 28 (UP)—President William T. Cosgrave’s government resigned today after a defeat and the Fianna Fáil accepted responsibility for forming a new cabinet. Sean O’Kelly, acting leader of the Fianna Fáil, announced that the party was ready to nominate Éamon de Valera, who is now in Chicago, to form a new cabinet. De Valera has been a leader of the advocates of complete independence of Great Britain.

| DUBLIN, Irish Free State, Mar. | 28—(AP)—William T. Cosgrave, president of the executive council of the Irish Free State and head of the oldest ministry in post-war Europe, announced the resignation of his government today as a result of its defeat by two votes on an opposition pensions bill in the Dail Eireann last night. The Dail then adjourned until next week. | The prevailing opinion in political circles tonight was that he almost certainly would be reelected president of the council when the Dail reassembles Wednesday. Under the novel, and still experimental, ministerial system of the Free State, the way is open for his reelection. Resignation of a government does not necessarily result in a general election, since Mr. Cosgrave’s voting strength in the Dail was not really inspired by his defeat yesterday there will be no call to the country. The chief opposition party, the Fianna

Melbourne, Victoria, Mar. 29. (AP)—Opponents of the extension from Melbourne and its suburbs of the prohibition of alcoholic liquors throughout the state of Victoria, second largest state in Australia, tonight were leading in returns on a compulsory referendum. With 750,000 of a total of 1,029,222 votes counted, the position of those in favor of the proposal was considered hopeless although the drys had several individual majorities. The figures just before midnight were those opposed to extension: 422,581, and those in favor of it 326,553.

London, March 28. (P)—While the American delegation to the naval conference today was busy making clear its position regarding the proposed consultative treaty and Mediterranean security pact, British and French experts continued seeking a formula which will satisfy France's security demand without increasing Great Britain's European obligations. Formal conference meetings today included a talk between Secretary Stimson, Ambassador Gibson, and Prime Minister MacDonald at No. 10 Downing Street this morning. Foreign Minister Briand, meanwhile, visited the foreign office to continue discussion of the French security problem with Arthur Henderson, British foreign minister. Tonight, after the Lord Chancellor's reception to the naval delegation at the House of Lords, MacDonald went to Chequers for a weekend rest. Stimson retired to his country place at Stanmore. To Work Over Weekend Experts wh

London, March 29 (4P)—Naval conference circles heard persistent reports this morning that negotiations between the French and British to work out a scheme for a suggested security pact have met failure thus far. One report had it that a complete deadlock had been reached. French circles were reticent in discussing the reports but said there was undoubtedly a certain amount of pessimism in some quarters. Jacques-Louis Dumesnil, minister of Marine, left this morning for Paris. Foreign Minister Briand of France and Rene Massigli of the French delegation had lunch with Arthur Henderson, the British foreign secretary, and it was assumed that the situation came up for discussion. Indications that the experts were still struggling with the security proposal in an effort to reach some kind of an agreement were shown by the fact that Sir Robert Van Sittart and other British foreign office officia

| LONDON, March 2 (UP)— Negotiations between French and British delegates for a pact which would break the naval conference deadlock reached a difficult situation today, with the French delegates extremely discouraged. French and British experts met at the foreign office and compared formulas drafted by each group outlining their respective ideas of the possibility of a pact offering security to France in return for reduction of her naval tonnage claims. The ideas were based on interpretation of articles 8 and 16 of the League of Nations covenant. French sources represented the British and declined to agree to a sufficiently strong interpretation of the league articles to provide security which France demands. Thus the deadlock between England and France over interpretation of the two articles—a deadlock which has existed in international negotiations for eight years—appeared to be so fa
_{Cairo, Egypt, Mar. 29.—(AP)—It was understood here today that the Prince of Wales would leave Khartoum, on the upper Nile, April 1 by plane for Cairo.

LONDON, Mar. 29. (—The current English review, The Spectator, today published an interview with Henry Ford in which the American automobile manufacturer makes another answer to the question, “What is wrong with British industry?” Mr. Ford is quoted as declaring that what it needs to save it is birth of a new spirit of enterprise and initiative among its leaders and that higher industrial wages would give that new stimulus immediately. “The main trouble with industry everywhere,” Mr. Ford said, “not only in England but also in the United States, is that leaders of industry do not properly interpret their difficulties as notices to change their methods.” The Spectator said their interview was obtained eight weeks ago by John Dugdale, former member of the Spectator staff. Mr. Ford does not think England's case is by any means hopeless,” but it will need a complete change of outlook among yo

Dublin, March 29.—The combination of political circumstances that defeated William T. Cosgrave’s Irish Free State government will result in sending the same government back into office again, in the opinion of political observers today. Cosgrave was defeated by a coalition of Labor, Independents, and the Fianna Fáil (De Valera party) but in order to prevent raising De Valera’s issue of Republicanism again, an issue which is not popular with those outside the Fianna Fáil, it is probable Cosgrave will be returned to office by the same labor and independent votes that were cast against the government Thursday.

Jandon, March 29. — The political negotiations between Great Britain and France struck a snag today. The French delegation has yet to be known that it considers the security concessions Britain is prepared to make entirely unsatisfactory and insufficient. The negotiations, however, are continuing. An expert attached to the French delegation visited Ambassador Dwight Morrow today and explained the present status of the negotiations. His report was pessimistic. ‘The British and French are trying to work out a security arrangement which will enable France to reduce materially her tonnage demands.

SHANGHAI, Mar. 28 (AP)—Word that 200 communists and 100 Fukienese soldiers were killed in a battle Wednesday between 3000 communists and 2000 provincials near Taiping, reached here today in Chinese press dispatches via Swatow. The scene of the battle was 25 miles south of Lungyenchow, headquarters city of the communists in Fulien province. The soldiers were reported to have routed the communists, arrested 50 women reds and captured and burned the communists headquarters and school in the provincial effort to end radical depredations in southern Fu.

Canton, March 28 (/P)—Further concern for the sixteen American Catholic Missionaries at Kanchow, Kiangsi province was shown today when it became known that authorities believed Nananfu, 50 miles from Kanchow, had fallen into the hands of communists and bandits who have been pillaging and killing throughout the southern part of the province for weeks. Although Chinese officials continued to maintain that the red siege on Kanchow had been lifted, missionaries expressed doubt, saying missionaries at Kanchow had said they would report dispersal of the bandits as soon as it took place. Meanwhile attempts to communicate with cities of Southern Kiangsi proved fruitless, with the bandits controlling telegraphic facilities. Mission headquarters reported that three Finnish women missionaries had been captured February 3 in northern Kiangsi and reported killed. Missionary dispatches said they had b

Berlin, March 29. -- (P)— Dr. Reinrich Bruening, leader of the Centrists, today succeeded in forming a cabinet to take the place of the resigned Mueller ministry. Julius Curtius, who succeeded the late Dr. Gustave Stresemann as minister for foreign affairs in the Mueller cabinet, will hold that same post in the new Bruening ministry. Dr. Paul Moldenhauer, who was minister of finances in the Mueller cabinet, will become minister of economics while Hermann Dietrich will take over the finance portfolio.

Calais, France, March 29.—(UP)— A silent procession of 20,000 marched in protest of the increased lace duties in the new American tariff measure and to picture to the French nation the seriousness of the threatened industrial crisis. While this one-third of the population marched the other two-thirds lined the streets in front of the closed stores and cafes. The parade was quiet—not a banner was flown, not a shout was heard. And afterward a delegation called upon the American consul to reiterate that there was no thought of hostility toward the United States, but that the demonstration was a simple cry from the heart of a people who were menaced by sudden ruin of their industries. The spokesman said half of the 50,000 persons employed in the lace and allied trades would be out of work if the increases went into effect. The parade started from "Place Crevecoeur," which means "heartbreak p

WARSAW, Poland. March 29. (2)—Yan Pilsudski, brother of Marshal Pilsudski, who has been trying to form a ministry, today declined to continue further because of the impossibility of achieving his policies, indicated by the attitude of the opposition. “This afternoon Colonel Slawek, head of a bloc in the diet which is collaborating with the government, was entrusted with the task of forming a cabinet.” The diet held a session today despite tense feeling between the government and opposition parties which had led to threats by the government deputies that they would prevent the session by force if necessary.

BERLIN, March 29.—(I.N.S.)— Twenty-five arrests were made when police swooped down today on the headquarters of an international congress now under way here under communist auspices. Delegates from seventeen countries attending the congress were stripped of their passports. All those not possessing passports were taken into custody.

BERLIN, March 28 (By A. P.)—Dr. Heinrich Bruening, new chancellor of the Reich, set about today choosing ministers on a personal basis and without dealing with parties in his efforts to form a cabinet succeeding that of Hermann Mueller. That was demonstrated when Dr. Bruening offered the ministry of agriculture to Martin Schiele, a Nationalist leader, who accepted despite the fact that his party earlier declined to participate in the new government and demanded dissolution of the Reichstag and new elections. The Nationalists decided on their course of opposition even after their fiery leader, Dr. Hugenberg, had been asked by President Von Hindenburg to give up opposition at this point for the country's welfare. The president also instructed the new chancellor to forget party pettifogging and construct a cabinet which above all could put through the budget and financial reforms. It was af

PARIS, March 29, (®)—Premier Tardieu made a strong appeal to the chamber of deputies today in a speech asking unanimous approval of the Young plan measures, so that the world would understand that France was united on its foreign policies. / The premier was applauded by virtually the entire chamber at the conclusion of his address. Reviewing the history of the reparations problem and looking into the future, the French premier paid his respects to the late President Wilson. He said commercialization of the debt had been discussed soon after the peace treaty and added: “President Wilson, who had an excess of popularity and an excess of injustice, considered it, but the treaty was not ratified and he suffered a shock that brought about his death.”

TOKYO, Mar. 28. (AP)—Fire swept the fishing village of Komatsu today, destroying seven hundred of its flimsy wood and plaster houses, the homes of 3,500 Japanese poor people. The loss was estimated at 1,200,000 yen (about $588,000). One firefighter was killed and three others injured. Their machine overturned. Approximately one fourth of the villagers lost their homes. Komatsu is on the shore of the Japan Sea and is in Ishikawa prefecture of the main island of Japan.
Paris, March 20 (AP) — The French chamber of deputies, answering a vigorous appeal by Premier André Tardieu, tonight ratified the Young plan by a vote of 530.

BERLIN. — (®) — Germany's poverty-barometers—the municipal, state and national pawnshops—indicate that the present period of depression is weighing heavily on shopkeepers and other small business men. In Germany pawnbroking is the business of the city, the state and the nation, as well as of any individuals who care to engage in it. Thus the annual report of the state loan office sheds an interesting light on the situation. Not only did the number of loans in 1929 exceed those of 1928 by 11 per cent, but the largest borrowers were people “in business for themselves,”—shopkeepers, independent craftsmen and farmers. These accounted for more than 40 per cent of the year's loans. Another 27 per cent went to persons receiving state compensation for wartime or inflation-period losses (elderly people for the most part) and to women of no occupation. Skilled workers, apprentices, waiters and oth

BERLIN, Mar. 13—(45—The airplane is trying to shed its tail. Tail-less experimental planes already have been flown, and eventually a tail may be as hard to find on an airplane as a buggy whip to a modern automobile. Why the trend is toward more wing and less tail is explained by Robert Kronfeld, one of the foremost exponents of tail-less flying. So long as airplanes were small, fragile craft with paper-thin wings, says Kronfeld, the development of a fuselage capable of carrying passengers and cargo seemed highly desirable. Now, however, in the days of huge planes with hollow wings, such as the recently-built Junkers “G-38,” the long fuselage is losing its excuse for existence. It is dead weight; it contributes no lift and it means costly wind resistance that cuts down speed and raises the fuel cost. The “G-38,” of course, is not a tail-less plane, but the design by giving the wings funct

Vienna, March 28 (#)—The body of Dr. Hermann Ernst Watzl, Cleveland chemist and inventor, who shot Mary MacGranahan, the wife he married bigamously, and then committed suicide in the Hotel Sacher here on Sunday, was cremated today in the presence of members of his family, and many of his close friends. The public, who expected that in keeping with their last wish the couple would be cremated together, were disappointed. A cable of protest was received by an uncle of Mary MacGranahan from the girl’s mother, Eva Horvath, Cleveland. Mrs. Horvath said that cremation was offensive to her religious sentiments. Her daughter’s body accordingly will be consecrated in church and buried tomorrow in the Central cemetery of Vienna.

1930-04-07.text: LONDON, April 7 (AP) — Secretary of State Stimson began assembling his material for a naval treaty today thus signaling the approaching end of the London naval conference. The secretary was aiming at a three power pact among United States, Great Britain and Japan, which will be so constructed that France and Italy can join later if they overcome difficulties which have blocked a five power treaty. The American secretary of state came to London from Stanmore this morning to consult his delegation, but expected to return to his country home during the afternoon to continue work on the intricacies of a naval pact. No Admission No one among the various delegations has been willing to admit officially that a five power treaty is not still possible and work to that end is continuing. Unofficially, however, there are expressions that there is small likelihood of the French and Italian problems

(United Press Staff Correspondent) London, (UP)—The United States, Japan and Great Britain are ready at a moment’s notice to convert their tentative agreement into a real three-power treaty, excluding France and Italy until such time as they compose their differences. In the authoritative speech of Ambassador Hugh S. Gibson, broadcast from England yesterday, observers at the London naval conference read two messages. One was to prepare American public opinion for a three-power pact instead of the hoped-for five-power treaty. The other was a “warning” to France and Italy that the three-power agreement was virtually in existence, and a hint that the way was still open for adherence to a major agreement if the two continental powers would end their quarrel on naval parity. Gibson reiterated, however, that an ultimate agreement by the world’s major naval powers is probable, if not at this co

BOMBAY, India, April 7.—(U.R)— The force of the British Empire descended today upon disciples of Mahatma Gandhi, India's "peaceful rebel," and threw scores of revolutionists into jail for their deliberate defiance of English law. Seventy-one disciples of the Mahatma, including his son, Ram Das Gandhi, were hustled into prison in the first twenty-four hours of Gandhi's gesture of revolt against the laws forbidding manufacture of salt, and against the burden of the salt taxes. It was thus successful, in that it produced the effect for which the revolutionist had prayed. It was an overt act against British rule, and it brought instant retaliation from the government. The Mahatma himself was untouched, although it was he, at the salt marches of Dandi, who signalized the beginning of the revolt and his disobedience campaign by scooping the first dipper of salt-laden water from the sea, while

London, April 6.—In the common sense language of dollars and cents, which every American taxpayer can understand, Ambassador Hugh Gibson of the American naval conference delegation this evening broadcast from London to the United States a clear cut analysis of the American-British-Japanese naval agreement. This is a definite achievement of the conference, no matter what fate befalls the final efforts now being made to bring France and Italy within the scope of a naval armaments treaty. Means Vast Saving. Americans who listened in to Gibson’s speech did not have to understand parity, naval ratios, global tonnage, political formulas for security, or any other of the hobgoblins of the disarmament negotiations, to comprehend that a three-power pact in the item of battleships alone means a saving to the American, British, and Japanese governments of between $800,000,000 and $900,000,000. Gibs

[INTERNATIONAL NEWS SERVICE] TOKIO, April 7.—Seventeen persons were killed and many seriously injured today when the engine of a passenger train exploded at Kyushu. Dynamite believed to have been mixed with the coal in the engine’s tender by accident, was shoveled into the firebox.

SHANGHAI, April 6—Chinese press advices received here today said 500 bandits had captured, looted and burned numerous villages in the neighborhood of Sunkiang, Kiangsu province, kidnapping 50 school children for ransom and killing three constables and a magistrate. Sunkiang is 25 miles southwest of Shanghai. The plundered district borders the Shanghai-Hankow railroad. A similar dispatch stated that pirates raided 10 cargo junks at the mouth of the Yangtse river and escaped with their loot to the northward. Further information regarding the three missionaries kidnapped in raids of Yuanchow, Kiangsi, was not available today. They included Miss Nina E Gemmell, formerly of Girard, Kan., and Rev. and Mrs. R. W. Porteus of England. Information regarding the besieged city of Kanchow, Kiangsi, where 16 American Catholic missionaries have been held for several weeks, was forthcoming, however, wit

Berne, Switzerland, April 7. (AP)— Switzerland, voting in yesterday's referendum for revision of its alcoholic legislation, has undertaken heavy taxation against strong liquors with the avowed object of social reform. All political party organs except those of the communists favored the revision on the theory that the Swiss were drinking too many Schnapps, which are highly alcoholic drinks distilled from fruits, and occupy a position in Switzerland analogous to whiskey in America. Heretofore only alcohol made from potatoes has been taxed. The new law will tax from one gold franc a liter upwards all alcohol, brandies, and similar high-proof liquors, with the exception made that the people have a right to brew their own liquor solely for their own consumption without taxation.

SHANGHAI—(4)—Chinese press dispatches Monday reported that bandits were threatening Kiukiang, Kiangsi province, where foreign missionaries have been concentrating for safety. An American gunboat on the Yangtse river has been ordered to proceed from Hankow to Kiukiang to protect missionaries and observe conditions. Numerous villages near Sungkiang, Kiangsu, were reported to have been looted and burned by 500 bandits who kidnapped 50 school children and held them for ransom. Three constables and a magistrate were said to have been killed by the outlaws. A letter, dated March 21, from a missionary at Kanchow, Kiangsi, said the city was surrounded by communists but that they had been unable to force entrance to the town, Sixteen American Catholic missionaries have been unable to leave Kanchow for several weeks because of the communist siege.

BY PRISCILLA RING Associated Press Correspondent Istanbul, Turkey, April 6.— ‘Once royal dispenser of terror and mystery to the mystery-loving world, Istanbul is now selling the last of her secrets. Tomorrow, by order of the Turkish republic, the doors of the imperial harem of the Seraglio palace of the Ottoman sultans will be thrown open. Then infidels and followers of the prophet alike may pass, for the price of 25 cents, the threshold whose crossing would once have cost them their lives. Jealously Guarded For almost two years, repairs have been under way to make ready this last portion of the Seraglio palace for opening to the public. For four and a half centuries this was the most jealously guarded corner of the vast palace and of the vast Ottoman empire. Great walls, heavy bronze gates, thousands of soldiers without and hundreds of eunuchs within kept inviolate the mystery of the im

SANTANDER, Spain, April 7.—(P)—Forty miners were reported missing in a cave-in in the Dicibo Iron Mine in the village of Miono today. A thousand men were at work at the time of the accident. Advices received here said that the cave-in took place after the midday shift had been charged. Mine guards, observing signs of a collapse, ordered the occupants to leave but forty could not be accounted for and it was feared they were entombed before they could escape. Rescue crews from nearby towns late today were digging furiously in an effort to reach the place where the men were believed cut off by heavy dirt deposits. The governor of the province left Santander immediately to take personal charge of the rescue efforts.

Shanghat, Apr 7, Um—Fifty children, kidnapped by a band of 500 Chinese pirates, escaped from their captors in the Kiangsu province, it was revealed today, after the marauders had created a tale of terror throughout the district. Three small towns were looted and burned, three constables were murdered and all telegraph lines were severed.

Shanghai, China, April 7.-(UP)— Bandits have released Miss N. E. Gemmell, of Girard, Kans., American missionary kidnapped at Yuanchow, Kiangsi province, advices said today. Miss Gemmell was kidnapped with two British missionaries on March 30. The brigands had demanded about $10,000 each in ransom.

1930-04-10.text: LONDON, April 10—(4)—Naval conference experts are understood to have been put to work this afternoon drafting a five-power disarmament treaty which Foreign Ministers Briand of France and Grandi of Italy have tentatively agreed to sign as the outgrowth of American intervention this morning. Complete agreement was reached today between the United States, Great Britain and Japan at the conference, and the way is clear for a three-power pact. All outstanding minor points of difference were settled at the morning meeting, including definition for use of training ships. The last vestiges of hope for a five-power pact were not entirely abandoned, but it was expected that the conference would know tonight definitely whether such a treaty was possible. The ministers of Italy and France were being informed for a quick decision, either to stay in or get out.

The Japanese withdrew their request that they be allowed to transfer 20,000 tons from destroyers to submarines this afternoon and thereby reached a complete accord with the Americans and British on all points excepting a minor definition concerning training ships. This development took place this afternoon at a meeting attended by Secretary Stimson, Prime Minister MacDonald and Reijiro Wakatsuki. It disposed of the Japanese government’s tentative reservations to the tri-partite agreement recently submitted to Tokyo. Conference circles said today’s action meant that the three major naval powers were now in a position to proceed with the drafting and signing of a tri-partite pact if the attitude of France and Italy should make a five power pact impossible. The minor training ship question is expected to be adjusted tomorrow at another meeting of the three chief delegates.

London, April 9——Indications are that all constructive progress in the naval conference ended tonight and the end appears to be a matter of days. Secretary Stimson, Prime Minister MacDonald and Reijiro Wakatsuki reached full agreement today on all questions necessary for five-year naval treaty among the United States, Great Britain and Japan, but France's position continues to be a deadlock on issues as efforts toward solution. Thus it is held likely that the final plenary session will be held early next week—probably Tuesday—and the delegations will prepare to leave soon thereafter. Foreign Minister Briand of France bore out that conclusion tonight, when he gave the American-British-Japanese agreement his blessing but said if the Italian position remained unchanged tomorrow the only thing to do was to part friends and continue the Franco-Italian negotiations later.
