LONDON —(?)— The civil disobedience campaign of Mahatma Gandhi, Indian nationalist leader, is reported here to be growing rapidly in strength. Indian police are said to be finding it increasingly difficult to handle the situation provoked with open violation of the salt laws, although the constabulary nowhere has been overpowered. One of the principal difficulties has arisen from Gandhi's order to his devotees to hold on to their contraband salt at all costs, even if the bones of their hands are broken. This is just what has happened in some cases, and authorities fear violence may result if harsh measures are implemented.

Bombay, India, April 10. Two hundred civil disobedience volunteers, including six Mohammedans and three women, brought sea water to the steps of Congress House today for the manufacture of salt in violation of British law. A large number of women figured in the salt making today, many of them, mostly from Gujarat, bringing the sea water to their homes where they violated the law. The violations of the salt law represented the first step in the campaign for civil disobedience by which Indian Nationalists hope to win independence for their country.

LONDON (UP).—The American delegation abandoned hope of a five-power treaty for limitation of navies Thursday and attempted to salvage from the wreckage of the naval conference an agreement on certain principles to which the five powers have subscribed. The proposed five-power agreement would include the accepted proposals for humanization of submarines, a battleship holiday until 1936, classification of aircraft carriers and a global category transactional proposal. The transactional proposal would limit the tonnage of each class of ship but permit transfer, within limits, from one class to another. Such an agreement would mean some scrapping of vessels on which all five powers have agreed. In addition, the three-power treaty among the United States, Britain and Japan has been achieved. Secretary Stimson decided the five-power limitation deadlock could not be broken after he had conferre

London, April 10. (INS)—The London naval conference to-day scored its first great movement—a final and complete agreement on disarmament between the United States, Great Britain and Japan. At a meeting of the heads of these three delegations this morning, all details of the three-power agreement were decided upon. These final negotiations necessitated a compromise by the British and Americans. They were forced to concede to Japan the right to retain the battle-cruiser Kouso, which was to have been scrapped within two years. The vessel will be converted into a training ship. The Americans retained the right to convert one of her battleships which otherwise would have been scrapped in the near future, into a training ship also. The British made a similar proviso, so instead of scrapping five battleships, she will retain one for training ship use. According to the agreement with the Japanes

BOMBAY, India, April 10—-(LP)— While Mahatma Gandhi lay ill and tired today from his efforts to unite India against British rule, thousands of his people rioted in caste warfare against one another at Nasik, a religious center 100 miles northeast of Bombay. Scores of casualties were reported today as the result of riots at Nasik involving the so-called ‘untouchables’ and caste Hindus. The fighting broke out yesterday and today the tension continued. A band of 4,000 of the miserable untouchables camped on the riverside in a locality inhabited by caste Hindus. They were rounded up and escorted by police to a place of safety two miles away. Hindus lined the route and as some of the untouchables left the procession, they were mercilessly beaten by the Hindus. Armed police patrolled Nasik today and maintained order but feeling ran high. The riots began when the caste Hindus attempted to take

BOMBAY, April 10—Mahatma Gandhi called a halt today in his tour of the district north of Dandi because of illness. The rigors of his work have weakened the frail leader of the Indian independence campaign. He has made a valiant attempt to carry on his campaign but seems physically unable to the task. The independence movement throughout British India inspired by Gandhi has reached a high degree of enthusiasm. Demonstrations have increased in size and fervor and have met with little police resistance as long as they remained orderly. The independence leaders have been arrested, however, in all cases where violation of the salt manufacturing laws was concerned. The situation at Nasik where many were injured last night in a clash between high caste Hindus and “untouchables” continued menacing today. Police rounded up more than 4000 “untouchables” encamped in the locality and moved them to s

BOMBAY, April 5.—Mahatma Gandhi's movement in defiance of the British government’s salt monopoly continued today to spread in various districts. Another of his sons, David Das Gandhi, was arrested and charged with sedition. The nationalist leader remained free from police molestation and obviously surprised at the official indifference toward him personally. Others close to him said he was disappointed.

| Bombay, India, April 19—(AP) —More than 100 Indians were injured in a riot yesterday at Masik, about 100 miles northeast of Bombay, between caste Hindus and “untouchables,” who are not allowed to enter the temples or participate in any Hindu religious ceremonies. Although not directly related to the independence campaign of Mahatma Gandhi and the India National Congress, the affair had some significance in view of what some regard as the implied promise of improvement of the lot of “untouchables” should Gandhi's movement succeed. The rioting began when caste men took two chariots containing images to be drawn by 5,000 devotees from the temples. Thousands of “untouchables” rushed to aid in pulling on the ropes alongside the caste men, who resisted and provoked a free for all fight.

LONDON, April 10—(INS)—After one last final attempt, the chief delegates of France and Italy decided this afternoon that further attempts to reach a conclusive Italo-French naval agreement here were futile. Foreign Minister Aristide Briand of France and Foreign Minister Dino Grandi of Italy conferred for an hour and a half in the latter’s sick room at a London hotel. They found it was absolutely impossible to reconcile their wide differences at the present time. LONDON, April 10.—With apparently only a few more days to live as a five-power organization, the London naval conference today scored its first real achievement—a final and complete agreement on disarmament between the United States, Great Britain and Japan. At a meeting of the heads of these three delegations this morning, all details of the three-power agreement were decided upon. These final negotiations necessitated a comprom

London, April 10. Settlement of all outstanding problems in the 3-power naval treaty among the United States, Great Britain and Japan was announced today by the British spokesman. The settlement was reached at a meeting of the chief delegates of the three countries this morning, the spokesman said. The treaty, which was assured yesterday when the naval experts achieved agreement on Japan's reservations, was believed likely to be the chief product of the five-power naval conference. London, April 10. American delegates to the naval conference made a final effort today to achieve a five-power agreement. Secretary Stimson and Dwight W. Morrow were understood to have made new suggestions to the French Foreign Minister, Aristide Briand, at a hurried conference at the Carlton hotel where Briand was called from the meeting.

| London. April 10, 192—The passengers and crew of the mail steamer Saint Sunniva have been saved, the steamer Earl of Zetland reported today. Lloyds reported the Danish steamer Island Filk wirelessed she was standing by the grounded Saint Sunniva, off Mousa, on the west side of the Shetland Isles.

ROME, April 10 (AP)—Popolo Di Roma’s Vatican city correspondent today said that Pope Pius would start his own money during the second half of 1930, the series being of gold, silver, nickel and bronze. One side of the coins will bear a half bust of Pope Pius, while the other side will carry the Papal seal with date of emission and the year of the pontificate.

| BERLIN, April 0— Beer today threatened to wreck the new government of Chancellor Bruening. President Von Hindenburg was forced to intervene in an attempt to save the situation. The Bavarians, in the budget committee, declined to endorse a 10 percent beer tax demanded by Finance Minister Moldenhauer. A Bavarian deputy complained that it was becoming the custom in the Reichstag to poke fun at beer taxation. He advised the Reichstag to take the matter seriously, since in Bavaria, beer is a primary constituent for the nourishment of the inhabitants. President Von Hindenburg summoned the Bavarian leader, Fritz Schäfer, for a conference in the hope of swinging him into line. It was believed a compromise would be reached as a result of the president's intervention.

1930-05-29.text: London, May 29.—(A.P.)—By the grace of its own dissenters and 50 liberals who did not vote, the Labor government of J. Ramsay MacDonald still was safely in the saddle today. The ministry last night defeated by a vote of 270 to 241 a conservative motion of no-confidence, asking reduction of the salary of J. H. Thomas, lord privy seal and minister for unemployment. Twenty-three of the 29 left wing laborites who refused to voice confidence in Mr. MacDonald at last week's parliamentary labor party caucus voted with the government. Had the government been defeated conservative victories in two bye elections of the past few days would have been a factor in predictions of the result of a general election.

Rio Janeiro, May 28—(P)—The Graf Zeppelin today forged northward at a 60-mile speed 700 miles at sea off the mouth of the Amazon river. Dr. Hugo Eckener took the airship across the equator at 40 degrees of west longitude at exactly 10:00 p.m. (7:00 p.m. C.S.T.) last night, according to a radio dispatch received here this forenoon. Natal was the last Brazilian city sighted on the voyage and even the coastline dropped out of sight about an hour after the dirigible flew over that port, the dispatch said. The Graf was expected to reach Havana some time Saturday, remain there two or three hours and fly on to Lakehurst, where the ship will be moored Sunday. From Lakehurst the Graf will take off Tuesday or Wednesday on the last leg of its 18,000-mile trip to Friedrichshafen, which it is expected to reach by June 9 at the latest. From Pernambuco to Havana is about 4,500 miles and from Havana to

BRISBANE, Queensland, May 29,—(4)—Miss Amy Johnson, who flew from England to Australia without a mishap of consequence, cracked up her plane at Eagle Farm aerodrome this afternoon while en route from Port Darwin, North Australia, to Sydney: She was not injured. The plane, carried by cross winds over the edge of the aerodrome, hit a fence and turned turtle. Miss Johnson, who is 23 years old, was thrown clear of the machine, but beyond a shaking up was not hurt. The propeller of the machine snapped off and both its wings crumpled, but the undercarriage was not damaged. It will be repaired as quickly as possible to enable her to continue her flight to the southern states.

By The Associated Press. Bombay, May 28.—Turbulent India was much quieter today than yesterday, when disastrous riots in four large cities piled up a toll of 82 dead and more than 800 injured, but tension still existed despite the fact there were few casualties. Two new flare-ups occurred at Rangoon, the Burmese capital, where bloody fighting grew out of a dock laborers’ strike Monday and Tuesday. One conflict developed when police opened fire on Moslems who had held up a streetcar and assaulted Burman passengers. Two persons were killed and many injured, the rioters meeting the police fire with stones. The police opened fire on another occasion when a band of Burmans attacked residents in the vicinity of the contagious diseases hospital, but dispatches reaching here said it had not been determined whether there were any casualties.

BOMBAY, India, May 29. (UP) The disorganization of Indian business resulting from the independence campaign impelled the federation of Indian chambers of commerce and industry today to solicit Viceroy Lord Irwin for a promise of immediate dominion status. Only by granting dominion status, the federation of 22 important commercial organizations said, can peace be restored. There is no hope, it said, for collapse of the movement inaugurated more than two months ago by Mahatma Gandhi. "Two courses are open," read the letter to Lord Irwin. "They are either to rule by sheer force or to conciliate." Reports of disorders were limited today to Rangoon, Burma, where three days of communal rioting have brought the list of dead to at least 100 with another 900 injured. The national congress committee here adopted a new line of attack when it dispatched 27 volunteers to Sholapur to defy the martial

(By Associated Press) LONDON, May 29, — The Labor government weathered another attempt by the opposition to upset it. Opponents of the government failed by 28 votes to pass a motion calling for a reduction in the salary of J. H. Thomas, Lord of the Privy Seal and unofficial minister of unemployment. The motion was introduced for the purpose of obtaining a debate on England’s unemployment problem.

Brisbane, Queensland, May 29.—(Thursday)—The airplane of Miss Amy Johnson, British aviatrix, in which she had flown from Croydon, England, to this continent, crashed today as she was coming here from Charlesville. Miss Johnson was unhurt and has arrived here safely.

Surat, Bombay, India, May 29 (B) -- One year of rigorous imprisonment was the sentence imposed today upon Chimanlal Chinchy, president of the Surat National Congress Committee and leader of the League of Youth of India for inciting salt raids. Chinchy was awakened from sleep before daybreak and charged with inciting members of his party to join the civil disobedience campaign and with leading them in the raid on the Dharasana salt depot. Chinchy, taken before the city magistrate, entered a plea of guilty, in accordance with the custom of the followers of Mahatma Gandhi. After his arrest, a cessation of industry, in mourning for the loss of another leader, began throughout this district. Dharasana, India, May 29 (P) — One hundred nationalist volunteers arrived here this forenoon from Bulsar intent upon raiding the government salt pans. All were arrested and interned at Dunvari.

Bombay, India, May 29—(A.P.)—Twenty-nine Nationalist volunteers left here today for Sholapur where they will defy martial law regulations prohibiting display of the Nationalist flag. Several arrests already have been made there. Bombay Nationalist Congress members last night paraded the city calling upon the people to join today in a procession with the body of a non-volunteer salt raider who died of injuries received Sunday in the raid at Wadala. In the view of some observers there has been a remarkable revival of the Nationalist Congress energy since outbreaks in the Bhendi Bazaar district, Moslem quarter, the first of the week, in which Moslems attacked police. Four persons were killed and more than 50 wounded.

LONDON, May 29.—(DN.8.) — Approximately 170 Moslems and Burmese have lost their lives and countless hundreds have been injured in the rioting at Rangoon, India, during the last few days, it was stated in a Central News dispatch from that city today. Sporadic rioting continues, the message said. Heavy detachments of troops are on hand to quell any disturbances. Additional loss of life is feared.

By The Associated Press. PARIS, May 29—The hundred and twenty-seven gold star mothers left Paris this forenoon in a special train for Cherbourg, where tonight they will board the steamship President Harding for home. Two of the mothers, one from the north, and one from the south spoke their thanks at leaving for the courtesies they have been extended here and for the government’s part in arranging their trip. Four of the mothers of this first group to come to France remained. Mrs. Florence Williams, of Portsmouth, Ohio, is still at her hotel at Verdun, but today she was further improved although restless during the night the doctors do not say she is out of danger but they are increasingly confident of her ultimate recovery. Three others remained to tour France and other countries. They were Mrs. Ada C. Verges, of Columbus, Ohio; Mrs. C. A. H. Cahoon of Cleveland, Ohio, and Mrs. G. Lewal

Madrid, May 1 (AP) - The missing Spanish aviators, Burguete and Nunez, lost for several days in the wilds of Africa, have been found. They are safe and well with tribesmen in the interior of Rio de Oro. General Burguete and Nunez were forced down during the flight from Cape Juby to Spain.

FLORENCE, Italy, May 28. (AP) — Miss Helen Gee, an American girl, whose home is in Denver, Colo., and Miss Ruth Henderson, 32, a Canadian nurse, employed in Johns Hopkins Hospital, Baltimore, Md., were killed today in an automobile accident near Ronta, 48 miles from here. The automobile in which the two women were traveling collided with an automobile driven by Pietro Giarizzo of Rome who was proceeding toward Ronta. The automobile of the Americans left the road and plunged 250 feet down a ravine, finally coming to a stop at the edge of Razzolo cemetery. Giarizzo summoned assistance and climbed down into the ravine where he found the women dead. Their automobile was loaded with suitcases which showed that they were touring Italy. The police marshal at Ronta said the accident appeared to be the fault of neither party but was due to the narrowness of the road. Joseph R. Haven, American con

Paris, May 25 (4)--One hundred and sixteen American Gold Star Mothers today rejoined the sons and husbands they kissed good-bye thirteen years ago and never saw again. The second group of war mothers reached the Mecca of its pilgrimage at the graves of the great battle front cemeteries. Tonight they slept in towns the war made famous: Soissons, Chateau Thierry, St. Quentin and the long besieged Verdun. Tomorrow they will go on beyond these towns to where lie the doughboys, each with his little white marble cross and robe of green. Up and down the beautiful green slopes peace reigns. Here and there a withered tree stump or a crumbled wall gives mute testimony to the passing of the Apocalypse. The mothers will have several days in the region. Afterward they will return to Paris—a woman's Paris, where the delights of shopping for little gifts to dear ones still remaining to them will comple

Shanghai, May 28.—~-(#)——The Northern Alliance rebels claimed today to have captured 50,000 prisoners in a crushing defeat of Nationalist government troops in North Honan province. The Nationalists admitted they had suffered a reverse west of Lanfeng, which they evacuated in a retreat eastward. The government asserted, however, that its air squadrons had executed damaging raids behind the enemy’s lines between Kaifeng and Cheng Chow. Penetrating the Northerners’ territory as far north as the Yellow River, the planes bombed the railway bridge, damaging piers. Said Advance Halts This stopped the movement of the rebels southward, it was said. Flyers also bombed the northern arsenal at Kunghsien on the Haichow-Tungkwan railway, west of Chengchow, destroying a power plant.

Las Palmas, Canary Islands, May 29—UP)—The silence of the Sahara last night was broken by the roar of airplanes seeking two Spanish aviation officers, their mechanic and a Moorish chieftain, wrecked and presumably held for ransom by Nomads of the sandy wastes. Across the desert trails camel trains moved through the surrounding rim of African coast back-country near Cape Juby. Picked scouts sent out by the Spanish and Moroccan governments vainly hunted for Comandante Ricardo Burguete, Captain Nunez Maza, Vincente Ferrer and their Moorish companion. The lost party, in two planes, were forced down a week ago. Save for the vaguest reports of their whereabouts, mystery since has enveloped them.

BRUSSELS, Belgium, May 28. —(#)— This war-swept country today opened wide its arms to the Americans who were among its defenders and the women whose sons spilled their life blood upon its soil. Tired after three strenuous days in England, the gold star mothers and veterans of the 27th division arrived after a quiet channel crossing.

- (By Associated Press) Canalejas, Spain, May 29.—While several coast guard cutters and mail boats patrolled the African coast; messengers were sent inland from Spanish military posts in the hope of releasing Commandant Burguette and Captain Maza and companions, believed held as hostages in the Sahara desert by wild tribesmen. The two Spanish officers with a mechanic and Moorish chieftain have been missing for a week after their two airplanes were forced down in an unlocated spot. Spanish scouts conducted authorized government representatives into the wilds to arrange for the release of the captives.

MOSCOW, May 29.—Belated advices received here today said 45 persons were burned to death in a fire on a passenger train near Domodedovo. At least 23 others were seriously injured. The accident occurred May 16. It was said a passenger spilled methylated alcohol which was ignited by a discarded match.

1930-03-19.text: London, Eng., March 18—(?)— Secretary Henry L. Stimson himself today undertook the role of mediator in the Franco-Italian naval dispute, seeking to solve the problem of naval relationship between the two countries which is threatening failure of the five-power naval conference. Colonel Stimson invited Dino Grandi, the Italian foreign minister and confidant of Premier Mussolini, to meet him privately in what was said to be the first consultation of its sort held between these two delegation heads since the naval conference started. Italy claims the right to absolute naval parity with France, although professing willingness to disarm, even completely, if other nations will follow her suit. France, on the other hand, has set a total projected naval tonnage far in excess of what other powers think fit, and has refused with finality to grant Italy parity.

London, March 19. (®)—The American delegation to the naval conference sticking persistently to its slogan "never say die" met today to discuss among themselves the Franco-Italian parity stalemate. Ambassador Morrow and Commander Harold Train, technical expert who have been specially working on this situation which threatens to cause at least partial wreckage of the conference, submitted ideas which they thought might afford the basis of discussion between the two European neighbors. But the difficulty is that the Americans could not with propriety volunteer their services as mediators between Italy and France. The American delegation is understood to be hoping that it will be invited to intervene by one or the other of the two nations. Observers say the big problem now is to get the French and Italians to face each other across the conference table. Neither has budged from its original s

By The Associated Press London, March 18.-As the endurance deadlock between France and Italy over naval parity wore on today, the opinion grew in naval conference circles that neither side was prepared to yield. If the present situation lasts through Sunday, when Premier Tardieu of France will return for another conference with Prime Minister MacDonald of Great Britain, authoritative quarters see the end of negotiations within two weeks. A limited five power treaty may be the result in that case, and within its scope will be complete agreement among the United States, Great Britain and Japan. That this treaty would be what MacDonald has called a “good” agreement, fulfilling the expectations of those who have fully realized the difficulties of the five power negotiations since their inception two months ago, is the belief of the responsible sources from which this information is derived.

Hobart, Tasmania, March 19. (UP)—An 18-inch shell exploded under a seaplane which was flying high above Norfolk Bay during naval gunnery practice today. Although the plane was 1,000 feet above the warship, the explosion of the great shell brought it down. The wireless operator, Macgowan, was drowned, and Lieut. Elliott and Warrant Officer Grant, the other occupants of the aircraft, were injured.

LONDON, March 19 ~ A spokesman for the American delegation to the five power naval conference today characterized as “simply foolish” reports printed by the Daily Express that there had been a breach of harmony in the naval conference over matters connected with the American-Japanese negotiations. In addition, Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald specially instructed the British spokesman to deny the story. The American delegation continued to profess hopefulness, but outside of this delegation there was expressed little if any expectation of a five power agreement based on the original thesis of limiting and reducing the world’s huge naval armaments. There was almost no activity among the delegations yesterday and there were indications private conversations scheduled for today were more for moral effect than with hope of achieving results. As it stands there probably will be little of conse

Loudon, March 19.—(UP)—Italy's only reply to the pressure brought upon her naval delegation to recede from her demand for "parity with France" is a refusal to retreat, even at the cost of preventing a five-power agreement on armament. The Italians insist that Aristide Briand and other parties to the Washington conference of 1922 accorded them equality at that time. They see no reason for abandoning that ratio. Accordingly, it appeared today, the deadlock which has occupied the conference for a week was no nearer solution than ever. There are two possible solutions in the opinion of observers. First, a four-power treaty, excluding and "isolating" Italy might be achieved. Second, a three-power agreement, omitting both Italy and France until they find some basis for adhering to the pact, might be reached. The British spokesman told the press today that the Italian-French deadlock still was

Tokyo, March 20 (Thursday), (P). Dispatches to Rengo News Agency today said that 76 persons were killed, sixteen were missing and scores injured when fire destroyed a moving picture theater at Kirin, Manchuria. The fire, caused by the explosion of film, occurred Tuesday night. All the victims are believed to have been Chinese, including the relatives of several prominent officials.

Moscow, March 18—(AP)— An official announcement today said that fifty-six churches in Moscow and vicinity would be closed "upon demand of the people and public organizations." This is the largest number of churches ever closed by the Soviet government at one time. The announcement said that these churches would be converted into cultural and educational institutions, schools, workers' clubs, libraries, museums, mess halls and workshops.

MADRID, March 19. — Spain's “benevolent dictator” as former Premier Primo de Rivera was often called, was buried in a modest grave in the family plot at San Isidro cemetery today with the highest of funeral honors that King Alfonso and the Berenguer government could give. Great crowds, massed in all directions as the solemn cortege passed, cheered for the king and Spain. The monarch attended mass in the railroad station chapel where Primo rested in state, but did not march behind the caisson which carried the coffin to its last resting place. Don Fernando Bourbon, a cousin, followed the coffin as a representative of his majesty.

Bremerhaven, Germany, March 19. (#)—The north German Lloyd liner Europa, twin sister ship of the Bremen, blue ribbon liner of the Atlantic, left here at 1 p.m. today for the channel ports and New York. The Europa started on her maiden voyage to New York amidst howling factory whistles along the Weser Estuary and the salutes of other ships while thousands of spectators lining the shore cheered. The new ship outwardly is similar to the record holding Bremen except that she draws two feet more and has oval funnels instead of streamlined. Fair weather on leaving was regarded as a good augury of a fast voyage on which, despite the company's statements to the contrary, it is generally believed she will try to establish a new world record for the crossing of the Atlantic. The Bremen on her maiden voyage established a record on the westward crossing of 4 days and 17 hours.

Shanghai, March 18. — Organized bandits have massacred 2,000 persons in Fuan, Kiangsi province, said reports here today, and other robbers are said to be planning to renew attacks upon American and other foreign shipping in the middle section of the Yangtse river. The massacre in Kiangsi province was reported in Chinese press dispatches to have taken place early this month. The magistrate at Kiangfu appealed to the Nationalist government officials at Nanking to send troops against the gangs of bandits who were overrunning Kiangsi, robbing and slaying thousands. Bandit hordes were reported also 1,000 miles up the Yangtse and its tributaries, threatening another attack upon foreign shipping similar to that of Friday when five American and two Chinese steamers were fired upon above Ichang while struggling in the dangerous Hsintang rapids. American and British and Japanese gunboats are patro

With religious services abroad for the welfare of Russia's millions of Christians, Soviet workers and atheistic groups participated in anti-religious meetings and demonstrations in various parts of the Soviet Union today. At the same time several thousand members of the Society of Militant Atheists were preparing for the opening of the anti-God Congress tomorrow. Tonight many thousands of anti-religionists will conduct an attack against the Pope at the Moscow planetarium. Today’s newspapers are unrestrained in their denunciation of the Pope for leading the worldwide prayer movement against the Soviet Union. Pope Assails Soviet. Vatican City, March 19 (AP)—Pope Pius XII, this forenoon made solemn and dramatic protest against mistreatment.

BERLIN, Mar. 19 (AP)—The Tabe- reported today that the illness of Leon Trotsky, exiled Soviet leader, has taken a critical turn at Constantinople. The former Russian chieftain has been ill since before his exile in 1924, but despatches last December indicated that he was recovering. When first he arrived at his island home in Turkey he appeared a sick, pallid down and outer, but later he recovered much of his mental and physical vigor from activity around his island retreat in the Marmora Sea.

BERLIN, March 19.--(4)—Communists were charged today with attacks on church edifices in Berlin during the night. A large illuminated Bible text over the door of a Protestant church in North Berlin was smashed, and a Catholic church was daubed with huge red paint inscriptions deriding religion. It was said here in dispatches from Moscow that the anti-religious campaign would be extended to America.

Moscow, March 19.—Arrest of some of the highest officials of the Kharkov government on charges of conspiring to foment a counter-revolution was announced today. The Soviet secret political police has disbanded the organization with which they are accused of working. Included in the list of arrested officials are some of the highest executives of the Commissariat of Agriculture of the Ukraine, the Ukrainian State Planning Commission, the Agrarian and Co-operative banks, the Institute of Economy of the Ukraine, the Agronomical school, the Ukranian Lumber Trust, and others. Today’s announcement disclosed that for several years, some of the most important posts dealing with the agricultural life of the Ukraine have been occupied by members of an organization which aims to tear down the agrarian policies and strengthen the position of the Kulaks (well-to-do farmers).

Tokio.—(UP) — Many were killed and injured by a film explosion at a Chinese motion picture house at Kirin, Manchuria, last night. Searchers had recovered 76 bodies today, including those of 23 Chinese policemen who lost their lives trying to stop the panic and fight the fire caused by the explosion. The injured numbered 126.

MADRID, Mar, 18—(AP)—From the town of Irun on the Franco-Spanish frontier to the capital of Spain crowds gathered today at railroad stations along the route taken by the funeral train bearing home the body of General Mituel Primo De Rivera. A state funeral will be held in the city where he ruled as a dictator for more than six years. At some of the larger stations along the route, it stopped for brief formalities and the rendering of homage to the former Spanish dictator. The center of many political storms while living, Primo De Rivera in death was received by Spain with all the official honors that can be conferred upon a premier dying in office and a captain-general dying at his post. His opera will be an official tribute proceeding in pomp and solemnity only by that given to the kings of Spain. When the body arrives in Madrid tomorrow morning, it will lie in state for about four hour

PARIS, March 19 — (AP)— Prince Danilo of Montenegro, brother of the queen of Italy, has been awarded 100,000 francs damages (about $4,000) against Metro-Goldwyn for an alleged libelous picture of him under the title of "The Prince of Monteblanco." The prince had brought suit for 500,000 francs objecting to the "scandalous character and conduct" of the character in the film which he declared was supposed to represent him. He and his family, he asserted, had been humiliated. Paul Boncour, the prince's attorney, laid stress on the fact the film was directed by Eric Von Stroheim who had been Austrian military attaché in Montenegro before the war. He told the court that there could be no mistaking the references to the prince and Montenegro under the thin disguise of Montehienro.

Paris, March 19.—(A.P.)—A 19-day hunger strike by Marthe Hanau, jailed woman financier, ended against her will today when officials at the Cochin hospital carried out a forcible feeding operation. Despite her weakness, Madame Hanau objected strenuously and it required eight attendants to place a tube in her throat. Madame Hanau was arrested 15 months ago and an investigation started into her vast financial enterprises. While the investigation has been going on Madame Hanau has been held without bail.

MADRID (UP).—The body of Miguel Primo De Rivera, grandee of Spain, captain-general of her armies, Marques of Estella, and former dictator, received simple sepulcher Wednesday in a little family plot of the San Isidro cemetery. The homecoming was in vivid contrast to the magnificence that surrounded him in life. The funeral coach came to the north station and was taken at once to the temporary station-chapel with its somber drapery. The honors paid the Marquis D’ Estella were those of a soldier and a grandee—not those of a once powerful ruler. Burial of the statesman-soldier is in the same grave with his sister, Ines Primo De Rivera Pemartin, and his sister-in-law, Maria Luisa Retgui Primo De Rivera.

1930-04-06.text: (By The Associated Press.) London, April 5—Prime Minister MacDonald and Foreign Minister Briand continued efforts today to find a solution to the French security claim. At the end of their talk at St. James Palace the French foreign minister rushed away to Paris for the weekend saying he was returning Tuesday to resume the negotiations. As he was dashing off to the train he remarked somewhat cryptically: ‘I think the end of next week will see the finish of it one way or the other.’ The assumption was that he was referring to the proposed security pact. Shortly afterward Prime Minister MacDonald arrived at American headquarters and had lunch with Secretary Stimson and Dwight W. Morrow. It was presumed that the British prime minister planned to report the result of his morning’s meetings with the French to the American delegation.

Bombay, India, April 5.—(A.P)—Mahatma Gandhi, Indian nationalist leader, arrived today at Dandi, where tomorrow at 6:30 a. m. he intends to break the British salt laws and begin the campaign of civil disobedience which he hopes ultimately will bring his country’s independence. — With him were those devotees, (Continued On Page Fourteen.)

LONDON, Apr. 5. WP—The American delegation to the London Naval conference will go home April 22 with a treaty between the United States, Great Britain and Japan as the sole result of their labors since January, unless unexpected developments occur within the next few days. The repeated refusal of Italy to recede from her demand for absolute naval parity with France, and the seeming inability of the powers to reach a satisfactory understanding on French security unquestionably led to the decision of the Americans to bring the conference to an end. Under present plans, they will leave England two weeks from next Tuesday on the Leviathan.

(By The Associated Press) London, April 5.—The London Naval Conference is being kept alive by a weekend reprieve which will carry negotiations over into the twelfth week. Aristide Briand, the French Foreign Minister around whom centers efforts to produce a five power disarmament agreement, today left for Paris for a conference with his chief, Premier Tardieu. Prime Minister MacDonald, of Great Britain, bade M. Briand goodbye, then rushed off to American headquarters for lunch with Secretary Stimson and Ambassador Morrow to acquaint them with the latest developments in the hunt for a security formula which will satisfy French claims. Briand will be back in time to continue negotiations Tuesday. His present cross channel mission is considered by conference observers to be the last for the purposes of the present negotiations. The chase for the elusive phrases which would satisfy French fea

N. S. Staff Correspondent LONDON, Apr. 5.—The expected withdrawal of France and Italy from the London Naval Conference was postponed for a few days today. Foreign Minister Aristide Briand of France left for Paris this afternoon to consult with Premier Andre Tardieu. He announced he would return on Tuesday for one last fling at clearing away the obstacles preventing formulation of a five-power treaty. Decision to give the conference another few days’ lease on life as a five-power body was reached by M. Briand, Premier MacDonald and Foreign Secretary Arthur Henderson at a long meeting at St. James’s Palace this morning. They agreed to devote a few days more to political negotiations in the faint hope of agreement. Unless success rewards their efforts by the end of next week, negotiations for a five-power London treaty will be definitely abandoned. Before leaving for Paris, M. Briand declar

JALAPOR, India, April 5 (P)—Tomorrow is the long awaited day for the leaders of the civil disobedience campaign in India. At 6:30 o’clock in the morning, Mahatma Gandhi and a group of his faithful planned to wade into the waters of the Gulf of Cambay at Dandi, near here, and begin the manufacture of salt in opposition to the government monopoly. Nearly a month has passed since the Mahatma and a little party of followers left Ahmedabad for the 240-mile march to the sea. The party stopped in villages at night and at each one the venerable nationalist leader, whose title means ‘the holy one,’ gained supporters and obtained resignations by village headmen. The Mahatma ate little bits of dried fruit on the march, as is his custom, while some of his followers were stricken with smallpox and other diseases, but the little band of survivors kept on. At Dandi tonight, they were preparing for the

United Press | LONDON, April 5—Lieutenant Colonel Oskar von Hindenburg, son of the German president, was thrown from his horse yesterday and severely injured, according to the Exchange Telegraph Company. Von Hindenburg’s foot caught in the stirrup and he was dragged several yards.

Bombay, April 5.—(INS)—Bending his long and fatiguing march from Ahmadabad, Mahatma Gandhi arrived with 82 faithful followers today at his destination on the shores of the Bay of Cambay and pitched camp to rest until tomorrow when he intends to defy the government and manufacture salt. The independence leader set up his camp in the small and ragged town of Bandi, a collection of ramshackle buildings in the salt marshes, accessible only by a rough and bullock cart routed road. On the last leg of his march, he was accompanied by numerous sympathizers who rode in gaily bedecked and placarded bullock carts. A check-up today disclosed that more than fifty, including several police, were hurt in yesterday's riots here when police were forced to charge into an unruly gang of demonstrating strikers. The railroad station where the clash occurred is heavily guarded today.

(By The Associated Press) Rome, April 5.—A Swedish warship will bear the body of Queen Victoria of Sweden, who died last night in Rome, back to the kingdom she served for many years. Funeral services for the Queen will be held at 11 o'clock Wednesday morning and on the same day a special train will carry the royal funeral party to some German port, whence a Swedish naval vessel will then complete the journey to Stockholm. In the funeral party will be, among others, King Gustave, Prince William and Princess Ingrid. Rome was in mourning today for Queen Victoria, who had spent many years in the Italian capital because of illness. Premier Mussolini ordered flags on all public buildings throughout the kingdom to be carried at half mast. Members of royalty, public officials, diplomats and others flocked today to the Villa Svezia, where the Queen died, to sign the register. Messages of sympathy

PARIS, April 5.—The Senate ratified the Owen D. Young reparations plan and the Hague court today by a vote of 284 to 8. The Young plan and its accompanying accords had previously been ratified by the chamber of deputies.

ROME, April 6.—Services were held at the German Church today for Queen Victoria of Sweden, who died yesterday in the villa here where she has been wont to come for years to escape the rigorous climate of Sweden and look upon her favorite garden of roses. The queen long had been a sufferer from a bronchial ailment and for months she had been an invalid. She was 68 years old. King Gustav and Prince Wilhelm, her youngest son, were at her bedside when she passed away. Premier Mussolini sent a guard of honor to the villa last night to remain on duty until the queen’s body is placed on a special train to start on the journey back to Sweden. King Victor Emanuel and Queen Helena went to the villa where in company with King Gustav they paid homage to the dead queen. The queen, since she ascended the throne with Gustav in 1907, had travelled far and wide seeking an agreeable climate, sometimes in

1930-04-30.text: Calcutta, Bengal, India, April 29 —(AP)— One hundred and ninety-two passengers aboard the steamer Condor lost their lives when that ship sank in the river Jamuna in eastern Bengal, the ship's owners said today. Only eighteen of the passengers were saved. The disaster occurred about five P.M. Sunday during a severe storm. The ship at the time was in an isolated district, from which news of its loss traveled slowly. It is now lying in about three fathoms of water. The Condor was carrying mail from Serajgang chat to Coalundo. No trace of the postal officials or the mail bags has been found. The ship belongs to the River Steam Navigation Company. It was built in 1897 and rebuilt in 1926. It left Calcutta last month after being overhauled.

LONDON, Apr. 30 (*)--Prime Minister Ramsey MacDonald lifted a telephone in the cabinet room at No. 10 Downing Street at 8:30 a.m. today and talked to Prime Minister Scullen of the Australian Commonwealth, at Canberra, 12,000 miles away. The conversation was an inauguration of telephone service between England and Australia which will be available to the public at a price of 6 pounds or about $29 for three minutes. The two labor premiers talked for a quarter of an hour.

LONDON, April 30.—— (UP) Wholesale arrests and sporadic violence marked the preparation of Central Europe today for threatened Communist disturbances on May Day. The Balkans offered the greatest threat of outbreaks. Several hundred Communists were arrested in Roumania, Hungary, Bulgaria and Yugoslavia. Police, acting under a defense of the real act at Sofia, arrested 50 Communists charged with subversive propaganda and many other arrests were made in the Bulgarian provinces. Several Communist leaders were arrested at Bilbao, Spain, charged with inciting a violent Communist uprising and at Lodz in Poland, 12 persons were wounded in an unemployment rioting.

(By The Associated Press) London, April 30—The duchess of Bedford, 64-year-old aviation enthusiast, today completed a round trip to Cape Town and landed at Croydon airport this evening. The duchess, accompanied by two pilots, left Sofia, Bulgaria, where she had been forced to make a landing yesterday because of a broken oil line this morning. She left England for the South African city April 10 and hoped to make the round trip in 19 days but was forced to take 20 days by the breaking of the oil line.

BOMBAY, April 29 (By A. P)—With unrest apparently slumbering in India today, no riots or sensational incidents being reported, Mahatma Gandhi took occasion at Bilimoria to denounce "British dictation" in the course of a statement on the revival of the native press censorship law by the viceroy. "I hoped for a time that submission to dictation from our British rulers had gone forever," he said. "Whether we realize it or not we have been living under a veiled form of martial law for some days past. Gandhi said new provisions of the revived press censorship act were "more severe than the original." He is understood to have told the publishers of his newspaper, "Young India," to let the government seize the press rather than deposit the security demanded for a permission to continue publication. The reported disaffection among the government's native troops at Peshawar, on which an official

SHANGHAI, April 29.—(AP)—Authorities of the international settlement, French concession and Chinese district of Shanghai prepared today to forestall May Day disorders, made more threatening by the strike of tramway and bus workers. Meanwhile unverified reports were circulated that Russian propaganda and gold were flowing into Shanghai and south China to aid Communists to overthrow the Nationalist government of China. Making this assertion, the British-owned North China Daily News said that the Soviet government had agents in Shanghai to overthrow constituted authority. By other foreign sources, usually reliable, it was stated that large numbers of Russians were in southern China and in alliance with Chinese Communistic armies which have seriously menaced the Nationalist government. These armies for many months have looted and burned towns and killed their inhabitants in the provinces of

Tokyo, April 30—(4)—The Japanese freighter Luzon Maru which drifted on the rocks near Cape Inubo, Chiba prefecture, was breaking up today under the pounding of high seas which foiled the attempts of rescue ships to remove her crew of 39. The wreck was only a quarter of a mile offshore and the distress signals displayed by the men aboard the freighter were easily seen in nearby villages. Fishermen tried in vain to approach the wreck in small boats. A naval plane from the Kasumigaura base circled overhead, unable to help.

Paris, April 29.—(®)—Reports at the Villacoublay field today were that Dieudonné Coste, noted French flier, tomorrow will begin trial flights in his renovated plane Question Mark in preparation for a trans-Atlantic trip to New York. It was said Coste hopes to take off shortly after the full moon May 12. Coste’s test flights were said to have been spurred on by a report that the airplane Southern Cross, commanded by Captain Charles Kingsford-Smith of Australia, was expected in Le Bourget from Amsterdam in a few days and would be ready to take off for New York at the same time as Coste.

| PARIS, April 30, (AP)—Nelson Morris of Chicago today won his suit against the managers of the Palace Music Hall who had disregarded his statement forbidding his wife, Jane Aubert, famous actress, to appear on their stage. The court awarded $2,000 damages, rejecting the managers' plea that the Morrises were married in the United States where the wife is not obliged to obey the husband. The court held that all persons living in France were obliged to observe the French legal principle that the wife must obey the husband. Beside the damages the court ordered that the managers should be subject to additional damages of $120 for each performance hereafter at which Miss Aubert appears without her husband's consent.

PARIS April 30 —(CINS.) —In France, at least, a married woman must obey her husband’s orders, the Paris court ruled today in returning a verdict favorable to Nelson Morris, Chicago packing millionaire, in his damage suit against the Palace Theatre here. Morris sued the management of the theatre, claiming it had no right to employ his wife, the former Jane Aubert, muse hall star, as he had forbidden her to appear on the stage while his divorce action against her was pending. The court ordered the Palace Theatre to pay Morris damages of 50,000 francs (about $2,000.) In their verdict, the magistrates ruled as follows: “The court considers that a French woman is obliged to obey her husband regardless of what his rationalities may be. “Therefore the court condemns the Palace Theatre for allowing Mile. Aubert to play despite her husband’s orders.” Morris’ suit against the Palace Theatre has be

1930-04-28.text: Karachi, India —/Pi— While a British war plane hovered overhead, 8,000 Indian nationalists Monday burned a pile of foreign made cloth 15 feet high in inauguration of a new phase of civil disobedience and passive resistance. The protesters first paraded the streets of the city, three camel carts filled with the cloth accompanying them. A mass meeting was held and resolutions adopted condemning the government for firing on "peaceful citizens" in Peshawar. The ceremony ended with lighting the bonfire. Appearance of the war plane above caused a slight panic among the women, but nothing serious developed. The women sang hymns of sedition while the pile blazed, the refrain being heard throughout: "If we walk with Mahatma Gandhi, we will surely gain swaraj."

LONDON, May 3.—More than 200 lives are feared to have been lost in severe storms sweeping the coast of southern Sakhalin, Japan, according to Tokio dispatches to the evening newspapers here today. Many fishing boats have been swept to sea. Most of the victims were fishermen whose craft were swamped by mountainous waves.

- United Press Staff. Correspondent BOMBAY, India, April 28—Renewal of hostilities between caste Hindus and the untouchables, who have vigorously supported Mahatma Gandhi's independence campaign, was reported from the Nasik district today. The untouchables in several villages asserted their right to admission to the temples. One group of 50 caste Hindus attacked a smaller band of untouchables and beat men, women, and boys. Orthodox Hindus also attacked picket lines of untouchables at the Kalarem Temple gates at Nasik, throwing stones. In the meanwhile, Mahatma M. K. Gandhi continued his plans today to extend his civil disobedience campaign, undisturbed by further denunciations of his movement from Muslim sources. The Mahatma added the announcement of a proposed raid on a private salt depot at Dharasana to his previous pleas for a boycott of foreign cloth and liquors, apparently despairin

Coach On Canadian Train. By The Associated Press, London, April 27—London tonight was on one end of yet another new development in communication’s methods, which during this century has piled marvel upon marvel. Telephone messages were exchanged between an ordinary desk phone here and a phone in a rapidly moving train on the Canadian National railways lines between Toronto and Montreal. Shortly after 3:30 p.m. (2:30 p.m. EST) C. J. Smith, European vice-president of the Canadian National, picked up the telephone in his office to answer a call and in the twinkling of an eye was in communication with Sir Henry Thornton, president of the railway, speeding from Toronto to Montreal aboard the “International Limited.” A few minutes after the President and vice-president had exchanged greetings and chatted about the weather, two correspondents of the Associated Press on different sides of the oc

CRISTOBAL, Canal Zone, April 28 (AP) — Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh rested here today after having written in a 10 hour and 31 minute flight from Havana yesterday another chapter in Man’s conquest of the air. Leaving Havana at 5:33 a. m., Colonel Lindbergh set his big Sikorsky plane down at Puerto Cabezas, Nicaragua, at 11:37 a. m. and 35 minutes later took off for France Field, here, arriving at 4:04 p. m., several minutes ahead of the schedule he had set for himself. The distance was 1,033 miles. His route was directly across the Caribbean Sea to a point on the Nicaraguan coast, instead of to Yucatan, and then down the coast to the refueling point. The saving thus effected in distance is one of the short cuts enabling the seven-day airmail between New York and Buenos Aires, in inauguration of which the flight was made.

| SHANGHAI, April 28.—(—) Chinese press dispatches received today stated 1,900 men, women and children, Chinese country folk, were massacred, and 1,990 more captured Saturday by bandits, who looted and burned the town of Kinesuchen on the northern border of Kiangsu and Anhwei provinces. The bandits, said the advices, displayed ferocity unparalleled in the annals of banditry in China, which is now taking place on a gigantic scale. One hundred mounted bandits set up 30 machine guns and raked the street, mowing down the helpless villagers. Captives were forced by departing brigands to carry the loot. The outrage occurred about 166 miles north of Nanking, Nationalist government capital of China. The report of the massacre was definitely confirmed late today.

Cristobal, Canal Zone, April 27.—(AP)—With characteristic swiftness, Col. Charles A. Lindbergh today blazed a new airmail route across the Caribbean Sea, linking New York and Buenos Aires in a seven-day mail schedule. Leaving Havana, Cuba, at 5:33 a. m., eastern standard time, today, the flying colonel split the famous Lindbergh Caribbean circle route, striking the Central American mainland at Cape Gracias Dios, Nicaragua instead of at Yucatan, on his old route. He landed at France Field at 4:04 p. m., completing his flight of 1,033 miles from Cuba in 9 hours and 58 minutes. He was not scheduled to arrive here until 6 p.m. Carries Heavy Mail The plane brought 215 pounds of mail, destined for various parts of the Southern Americas. Postoffice employees here were prepared to work all night, if necessary, to prepare the mails for the southward journey, which will be resumed at dawn tomorrow

Shanghai, April 25.—(AP)—Because he was refused permission to marry a maid in the same establishment, the male cook in a Chinese household today, armed with a meat axe, went from room to room and hacked to death his employer, his wife, their two sons, aged 6 and 3, two servant maids and a man servant. He then escaped with his sweetheart,

CRISTOBAL, Canal Zone, April 28—Colonel Charles A. Lindbergh and his two aides who completed a new mail route flight here from Miami, yesterday, rested today before making preparations for a return flight, Thursday morning. Stops on the new route included Havana and Puerto Cabezas, Nicaragua. Arriving here, Sunday afternoon at 4:04 p. m., the flyers completed the last leg of their trailblazing flight in 3 hours and 40 minutes. Bas Rowe accompanied Colonel Lindbergh as co-pilot, and D. E. Denicke was radio operator of the twin-motored Sikorsky amphibian. The plane carried 211 pounds of mail which will be relayed by other pilots along the new New York-Buenos Aires mail system which extends down the west coast of South America. Colonel Lindbergh said that excellent weather conditions had prevailed during the entire flight. The plane was in frequent radio communication with ships and shore s

By United Press; April 28.—A severe thunderstorm in Silesia killed five persons today. A man and his two sons were killed by lightning at Luneburg and a cloudburst flooded the village of Brosshartmansdorf, drowning two persons.

FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, Germany, The South American flight of the Graf Zeppelin will begin May 18, it was definitely announced upon the return of the world-girdling dirigible here Sunday. The Graf Zeppelin landed at 6:40 a. m., after a successful, uneventful flight over England and return.

By The Associated Press PRZEWORSK, Poland, April 28.— Forty-three houses in this little town, near Lwow, were destroyed by fire which was started by candles during services in the synagogue. Seven hundred persons were left homeless and were housed in tents. The historic town hall, dating to the Middle Ages, was saved.
FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, May 14— The German dirigible Graf Zeppelin will start on its flight to South America by way of Seville, Spain, on Sunday afternoon, it was announced by Captain Ernst Lehmann today.

1930-03-15.text: London, March 14.. (4)—The naval conference was cheered today by the news that an American-Japanese naval agreement moved a step nearer. Only one more step appears necessary—final approval of the home authorities, particularly Tokyo—for the compromise which is said to satisfy fully the desires of each country, including a solution of Japan's demand for a 70-per cent. ratio of American strength. Senator Reed and Ambassador Matsudaira met again today to handle the situation. While there was much talk today of the agreement, nothing was made available as to whether its terms would be announced immediately after approval or held until included in the general framework of the five-power treaty that is the goal of the parley. Meanwhile, the Franco-Italian deadlock remains the most critical phase of the conference, and the delegation hopes that Andre Tardieu, the French premier, will bring some

London, Mar, 15—(A P.)—Indications today were that the five power naval conference would know at least by Monday just about what the results of its eight weeks of effort to limit naval armaments will be. Highest importance was attached to a meeting of Andre Tardieu, French premier, and Ramsay MacDonald, British prime minister and chairman of the conference, at Chequers Sunday. Tardieu alone has the power to modify the French stand for a larger navy or guarantees of French security which has thrown the conference into near deadlock. TARDIEU ARRIVES M. Tardieu arrived in London late today from Paris, and probably will return to his capital Monday. Paris dispatches insisted he comes to London convinced of necessity of continuing insistence upon the right to build up to 724,000 naval tons by the end of 1936. London, March 15.—(UP)—Queen Mary yesterday paid what was probably her first visit to a public house. She inspected Anchor Inn in Somerstown, a slum district in north central London. The public bars were full of men and the queen spoke to them. She also visited the cellars and saw the modern methods of storing beer. Anchor Inn is a “model” establishment conducted by the Rev. Basil Jellicoe, cousin of the famous Ad.

LONDON, Mar, 15 — Although official confirmation is still unavailable, there was good reason to believe today that the American and Japanese delegates at the naval conference have come to a compromise agreement, the details of which are now before the Japanese government for approval. The agreement gives Japan an approximate fleet ratio of 63 percent, a three percent increase over the 5-5-3 ratio agreed upon at the Washington conference. It can be stated fairly accurately that the compromise provides that the United States shall have eighteen eight-inch gun cruisers, totaling 180,000 tons while Japan shall have twelve such vessels totaling 108,400 tons. In six-inch gun cruisers, it is believed the compromise provides for 144,000 tons for the United States and about 100,000 tons for Japan. SHANGHAI, March 15. (4)—Lieutenant C. M. Winslow, commanding the United States naval armed guard aboard the American Yangtse Rapids Steamship Company's steamer Chipjing, was wounded in the leg by a machine gun bullet during a clash between his guards and lawless Chinese soldiers roaming the north bank of the Yangtse river, 60 miles above Ichang yesterday. The wounding of Lieutenant Winslow was the result of a particularly vicious attack by lawless soldiers in which the latter used field pieces and machine guns, heavily bombarding several steamers, both Chinese and American, and paralyzing river traffic for several hours. None of the other Americans aboard the ship participating in the skirmish was injured, although three Chinese members of the crew were seriously wounded during the harangue.

MOSCOW, March 15 — The Central committee of the Communist party today placed a definite curb on too vigorous anti-religious and socialization activities. Severe punishment was threatened to those violating the order of the committee, which formulates the policies of the Russian government. The committee pointed out that in some cases local officials attempt to justify closing of churches by saying that it had been done "by the voluntary desire of the population." Today’s order forbids forcible closing of churches, mosques, or synagogues without the consent of an overwhelming majority of the population in each case and the formal sanction of the central authorities.

eA, Otaren ib (UP)— President Ignacy Moseicki today accepted the resignation of Premier Cusimir Bartel’s cabinet, but requested the premier to remain in office provisionally, until a new cabinet can be chosen.

Warsaw, Poland, Mar. 15.—(?)~ Premier Bartel, whose government was defeated on a vote on censure of the labor minister yesterday, presented the resignation of his cabinet to President Mosticki at noon today. The president withheld a decision. The defeat is said to have been caused by general dissatisfaction on the part of the diet.

NEW YORK, March 15—(AP)—Leading Japanese newspapers today issued extras featuring dispatches that reported an American-Japanese preliminary agreement giving Japan "almost seventy per cent" of American auxiliary naval strength. Official circles withheld comment, but a more hopeful atmosphere was noticeable. Japanese correspondents in London were virtually unanimous in reporting that one of the features is the undertaking by America to build only ten 10,000-ton cruisers prior to 1936, although the general treaty will allow her eighteen. Further, it was intimated, America accepts submarine parity with Japan. The correspondents allege Great Britain adheres to this agreement, assuring at least a tripartite naval treaty.

1930-05-27.text: London. May 27—Inness of King George will present his attending the third court of the season tonight at Buckingham Palace, it was officially announced today. It was said his majesty was suffering from inflammation of the right hip. On May 14 and May 15 he presided at the first two courts of the season, the first he had attended in two years due to his previous illness. The Prince of Wales deputized for him during the preceding season. The following announcement was issued at Buckingham Palace: "For some days the king has been suffering from a painful although localized rheumatism of the right hip. His majesty has been advised not to be present at the courts tonight and tomorrow, but hopes to be able to fulfill his engagements later in the week."

It broke out between different bands of coolies when laborers were imported to replace striking Burmese dock workers. The latest reports gave 26 dead and nearly 700 injured. All bazaars were closed and cavalcades of mounted police clattered through the streets in large patrols. Detachments of the Cameron Highlanders and the Punjab regiment were on the alert and ready to intervene if necessary. The rioters were brought under control by a vigorous display of force late in the day, but none of the officials could guarantee how long the relative calm would last. As a result of the rheumatism, the King has cancelled his attendance at the third and fourth royal courts to be held tonight and tomorrow.

Serious disorders at Rangoon, India, growing out of a dock strike today had rolled up casualties of 40 dead and 740 injured. The disturbance between Burmans and Hindus was continuing with hospitals filled to overflowing and every available police officer on duty. Apparently the disorders had no connection with the civil disobedience campaign. Troops today ruled the Bherd bazaar district of Bombay, where yesterday's rioting cost three lives and 53 were seriously wounded. Moslems took part in the disorders. Police were obliged to fire three rounds into the mob of 5,000 or more natives to halt their activities. Several hundred troops today patrolled the area. Rangoon, India, May 27. (AP)—Sixty deaths were reported officially tonight in two days of disorders attending a dock strike in this Burman capital. May 27, (LP) —Twelve persons were wounded today when British police fired a volley of buckshot into a crowd of Mohammedans who were stoning the Sandhurst road barracks. Police resorted to the buckshot volley after four shots were fired into the air as a warning to the mob to retreat. The shots had no effect whatever on the Mohammedans.

Bombay, May 27 (UP)—Police clashed repeatedly with Moslems today in outbreaks of violence in the central Dhendi Bazaar here and at Sandhurst Road barracks. Guns were fired into the mob on several occasions and the rioters attacked the police with stones. Casualties were placed at six dead and 45 wounded by gunfire in a statement by Red Cross volunteers of the Indian Congress. A dozen others were left seriously wounded. About 12 police and several British officers were injured. The total casualties in the fighting throughout India the last two days was estimated to reach 53 dead and hundreds injured. A partial Hartal was called in Bombay with Hindus and independence volunteers joining in. The situation remained dangerous at mid-afternoon when a huge crowd of demonstrators gathered at the Sandhurst barracks and shouted at the police. LONDON, May 27—King George has been suffering from an attack of rheumatism in the right hip for the past several days, it was announced at Buckingham Palace today. The bulletin was entirely unexpected and considerable concern was felt throughout the country over his majesty’s indisposition. A palace official declared, however, that the attack of rheumatism had no connection with the King’s previous illness. The bulletin reads: “For some days past, the King has been suffering with painful though localized rheumatism in his right hip. “His majesty has been advised not to be present at the Courts tonight and tomorrow night, but he hopes to be able to fulfill engagements later in the week.” *

BOMBAY, May 27.—(?)—Police, suppressing renewed attacks by moslems in the Bendhi Bazaar district, fired three times into the mob this forenoon, injuring seven Moslems. A police sergeant was accidentally shot in the arm and taken to a hospital. The crowd persistently stoned the police and military, the situation not easing until midday when prominent Moslem leaders visited the locality and succeeded in pacifying the rioters. Their visit was the outcome of a call by a deputation on the police commissioner who agreed to withdraw military pickets from the thoroughfares into the police station compound. Tram and other vehicular traffic held up two hours resumed running. Total casualties thus far in the Bhendi Bazaar rioting number three dead from gunshot wounds, and 53 persons in hospitals with other injuries. The 20-year-old son of Major H. B. R. DUBLIN, May 27.—(UP)—The first definite date for an attempted westward crossing of the Atlantic Ocean by airplane this season was announced here by Capt. Charles E. Kingsford-Smith, pilot of the airplane Southern Cross on its California to Australia flight. Captain Kingsford-Smith said he planned to leave from Curragh, County Kildare, near the end of June with New York as his destination. He will follow a more southerly route than that used by the late Baron Von Huenfeld and his companions in the German airplane Bremen. Captain Kingsford-Smith said he planned to fly from New York to San Francisco, thereby completing the last lap of a round the world flight. Three companions will accompany Captain Kingsford-Smith. They are Capt. J. P. Saul, of the Royal Air Force, a native of Dublin, a master mariner; Assistant Pilot Van Dyk, of Holland, and Radio Operator Stannage.

1 onangnal, May co— sre jm. The Nationalist government of China tonight faced another crisis menacing its safety. President Chiang Kai-Shek, Nationalist commanding government forces in Honan province, which since May have been attempting to turn back the Northern Alliance rebel armies, was informed by Finance Minister Soong that immediate victory was imperative to prevent grave developments within the government. Backing his appeal for the quick defeat of the rebels who have fought a series of battles with Uliung's troops, the minister’s telegram stated that communistic and bandit depredations throughout China, failure of crops and demoralized business were conditions to present the gravest menace the nationalist government has encountered in its brief and turbulent existence. PARIS, May 26.—(AP)—General Henri Gouraud, the one-armed hero of the Dardanelles, stood in reverent silence today under the Arc de Triomphe while the American Gold Star mothers of the second group began their pilgrimage with homage to the unknown soldier of France. The American women placed five wreaths on the tomb prior to starting tomorrow for the battlefield cemeteries to see for the first time the graves of their sons and husbands. At a reception later General Gouraud welcomed the women in the name of his government and told them how greatly touched he was by their tender mission. Mrs. Margaret Forsythe, Akron, O., was among those placing wreaths. Ambassador Edge Speaks - Ambassador Walter E. Edge spoke at the reception, assuring them that their sacrifice had not been in vain and reminding them that their sons and husbands were cared for with tender hands. Father Barker of St. Joseph

PARIS, May 27. (P)—Condition of two Gold Star Mothers who have been seriously ill here while on pilgrimages to graves of their sons, who died in France during the war, was considerably improved today. Physicians felt that while they were not yet out of danger there were good chances for their recovery. Mrs. Florence Williams of Portsmouth, O., who is suffering from pneumonia at Verdun, spent a comfortable night and was considerably better this morning. Mrs. Mary Reynolds of Damascus, O., who is at the American hospital at Paris, with peritonitis, also spent a comfortable night. Her pulse and temperature dropped to normal and her general condition is much better.

Paris, May 27 (#)—Warm sunshine bathed the battlefront region when the second contingent of Gold Star Mothers today set out by bus to visit the cemeteries in which their soldier sons lie in peace. The trip was made in leisurely fashion with frequent rest stops. Their first visits to cemeteries will be made tomorrow. Mothers of the first American contingent today remained in Paris. Now that they have had a chance to recover from the fatigue and strain of last week’s travels they are anxious to see more of Paris. Many arose early for sightseeing expeditions. This was their last full day in the French capital. On Thursday they will sail for home.

(By Associated Press) Shanghai, China, May 27.—Niimerons independent dispatch reported tonight that Northern Alliance rebel armies had severely defeated Nationalist government troops in the battles of the past three days in northern Honan province. The Northerners, numbering 200,000, were reported to be delivering crushing onslaughts against the Nationalists who were giving away. News Of Fighting Suppressed Nanking, May 27.—Military headquarters of the National government at Nanking suppressed all news of the fighting for issuing a statement that the Nationalists are rushing reinforcements to the front lines causing expectations of still more sanguinary fighting. The rebels are claiming victories in battles which have never been fought, said the statement, in order to bolster the morale of the Nationalists.

SAN SEBASTIAN, Spain, May 27. (AP)—Seventeen persons, including two policemen, were injured in rioting this noon following a demand for resumption of gambling in the San Sebastian Casino. None of the injuries was serious. Casinos were suppressed under the Primo de Rivera dictatorship. The people protested that they lost much tourist trade when visitors went to Biarritz and other resorts where gambling was permitted. Twenty thousand persons joined in a parade to ask the king and Premier Berenguer to resume the old custom. They became disorderly when mounted police attempted to disperse them. The crowd was composed mostly of youngsters who were in short trousers when the war was on. They knew nothing of it save what they had heard. There was an orderly crowd which watched them depart. 1930-03-20.text: London, March 19 (4).—Indication that a way has been found to break the Franco-Italian deadlock over naval parity, a deadlock which threatened the very life of the five power naval conference here, was seen tonight in a surprise meeting between Ramsay MacDonald, prime minister of Great Britain and Aristide Briand, foreign minister of France. The two talked at French headquarters in the Hotel Carlton. Their conversation lasted two and a half hours, and after it M. Briand said: "We have been talking about means to bring the conference to a successful conclusion and we are going to apply those means as quickly as possible." This afternoon M. Briand had informed Mr. MacDonald that he was going to Paris tomorrow for a conference with Andre Tardieu and would return with the French premier when the latter came here for the weekend. LONDON, March 20.—(l)—Memorial services for the Earl of Balfour will be held at Westminster Abbey Saturday, the day set for the funeral of the Victorian statesman at his Scottish home, Wittingehame. The Duke of York will represent King George, and leaders of state will join with other prominent persons and those of humble rank in paying homage to his memory.

LONDON, Mar. 20—Naval conference circles today wondered just what significance to attach to an obviously impromptu meeting of Prime Minister Ran MacDonald and the French minister Aristide Briand, at the Hotel Carlton last evening. At the conclusion of the conference, which lasted two and one half hours, M. Briand, smiling and jovial, told papermen: "We have been talking about means to bring the conference to a successful conclusion and we are going to apply those means as quickly as possible." There were those, hearing M. Briand’s words, who imputed to them a prospective solution of the Franco-Italian naval ratio problem, one of three or so major problems which may bring disruption of the conference activities. Others recalling that the French idea of what would constitute conference success has always been at variance with that of the United States and Great Britain were dubious. Arrang

LONDON, Mar. 20,—(#)—The Bank of England reduced the bank rate today from four to three and one half percent. Downward trend of world money rates fostered by central banking institutions—owing to fall of commodity prices and trade depression—reached a point especially in New York and London permitting reduction by the English central bank from the mark which was established only a fortnight ago. The authorities were rather forced by the way discount rates declined out of proportion to the official minimum since the collapse of the Wall Street boom to ease the monetary stringency.

LONDON, March 20. (AP) With the Franco-Italian parity deadlock still holding at the naval conference, Foreign Minister Briand of France went back to Paris today to see Premier Tardieu, while Prime Minister MacDonald arranged a meeting with Foreign Minister Grandi of Italy. The British prime minister who is now beset by numerous vital problems in connection with the conference, was relieved to a great extent from domestic worries by announcement of the liberals that they would not press amendments to the coal bill while the present conference crisis was on. Lloyd George, the liberal leader, said that his party, having regard for the present position of very important affairs, did not feel that it ought to undertake the responsibility of defeating the government or even putting it in a humiliating position while the very important naval conference was hanging between life and death. London, March 20.—(U.P)—Diplomatic phrases—the use of cleverly chosen words disguising the real meaning of naval parity—may be the solution to the Franco-Italian deadlock which has threatened a five-power agreement on curtailment of armaments. The British delegates, the United Press learns, are seeking some formula in which any suggestion that France admits Italy’s right to equality, or Italy officially consents to French superiority, will be scrupulously avoided. Whether such a vague agreement would be acceptable to either nation remains a question, but it has been stated repeatedly in reliable French quarters that while France is unwilling to “admit” Italian parity with France, she has never actually considered she had the right to “deny” such equality.
