Berlin, Mar. 20.—(P)—The newspaper Tempo today published rumors from Riga, Latvia, that Joseph Stalin, secretary of the central committee of the communist party, had been deposed. Joseph Stalin, known as the strong man of Russia since the death of Lenin, who was chairman of the central committee, has held the dominant position in the communist party despite attacks by the opposition which he crushed. Leon Trotsky, one time leader of the red army, was one of Stalin's chief opponents but he was deprived of his power and finally sent into exile. Trotsky is now in Turkey. Riga has long been a sort of clearing house for news coming across the border from Soviet Russia, and reports from there have not always proved reliable. While Stalin has his opponents, particularly on matters of policy, there have been no recent reports from Moscow that his position was in any way threatened.

Madrid, March 19 (P)—Primo de Rivera rests in a soldier's grave, honored with the highest tributes a nation can bestow. The body of the man who ruled Spain as a dictator for six years, then went into exile, was placed beside the body of his wife in San Isidro cemetery today. Premier Damaso Berenguer and foremost dignitaries of the country, including King Alfonso, participated in the funeral. The King did not march in the procession to the ceremony, but attended the mass in the North station before the funeral march began.

SHANGHAI, March 18.—(AP)— Bandits and Communists, said delayed Chinese reports received here today, attacked and captured Fuan, a town near Kianfu, central Kiangsi province, massacring all Fuan officials and 2,000 men, women and children, early this month. After slaying the populace, continued the reports, the bandits looted the town, carrying their plunder into the mountains of western Kiangsi. The outrage was reported by the magistrate of Kiangfu. He said the people of Fuan were paralyzed with fear and were afraid further to oppose the bandits, who were depicted as subjecting Kiangsi province to a merciless deluge of robberies and wholesale killings. The magistrate appealed to the nationalist government at Nanking for military assistance.

(International News Service) WARSAW, March 20.—Numerous armed uprisings among the peasants and grave labor discontent are causing the Soviet government serious concern, it was revealed by travelers from Russia arriving in Poland today. Clashes of a sanguinary nature have occurred, they reported, resulting in hundreds killed both among the Soviet troops and rebel forces. At least six insurrectionary movements have taken place in the last few weeks, the voyagers declared. In each of them, Soviet troops were forced to go into action to quell the uprisings.

Rome, March 20—(AP) Information reaching officers here from London is to the effect that the United States, Great Britain and Japan have virtually concluded an agreement for naval reduction while a plan for a naval holiday, acceptable to both France and Italy, is being studied, thus leading to hope the five powers can still agree. London, March 20—(AP)—Aristide Briand, head of the French delegation to the five power naval conference, left London this afternoon for Paris. His trip was understood to be for the purpose of consulting Premier Tardieu about the conference. He said he expected to return to London with M. Tardieu at the weekend. PARIS, Mar. 20. (U.P)—Andre Maginot, France's good-natured, giant-statured minister of war, is planning to protect France's rich northern frontier from enemy attack—with water. Should France be menaced again from the north by a German army surging across Belgium, a simple twist of a switch and the entire northern border would be flooded with millions of tons of water. In a few hours the rich farming and industrial region from the port of Dunkirk to the manufacturing city of Lille would be turned into a sea. Only the hills and prominent plateaus would remain above the water, but each will be fortified with artillery and anti-aircraft guns capable of commanding the entire flooded region. The attacking army's infantry and cavalry would be thus instantly halted while bombing planes could only fly over the flooded region at great danger. The deadlock of the French and Italians has resulted in a practical suspension of the five-power conference. MOSCOW—(/)— Official warning to be moderate in carrying out the anti-religious campaign of the Soviet government and the communist party was the interpretation gained Friday from speeches before the opening of the all-union congress of atheists. A succession of speakers told the congress that their propagandists must abandon the idea that religion can be exterminated in Russia overnight. They declared that excesses committed by atheistic workers and village officials in the war on religion must forthwith cease.

(By Associated Press) FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, Germany, March 21—Capt. Lehman informed the Associated Press that the takeoff of the Graf Zeppelin on its first South American flight will be between May 10 and May 15 with return by way of Lakehurst, N. J.

Paris, March 21—(4)—Premier Tardieu said today that he planned to go to London when something definite at the naval conference seemed to require his presence. The attitude of the French government remains unchanged, it was said in official circles regarding rumors that Premier Tardieu was not going back to London. It was added, however, that it does not depend on France alone to find a solution of the present difficulties of the conference, Prime Minister Briand and his colleagues will cooperate in any effort to accomplish something, it was said, but it must be cooperation and not one-sided sacrifices. "The French figures have been put through detailed study, it was remarked, and there was no reason seen here why everybody else interested did not submit their figures to the same test.

SHANGHAI, March 4. Ties less soldiery between Hankow and Ichang today attempted to pirate a Standard Oil Company of New York steamer which was nearing Itu, midway between the two towns. Due to the combined efforts of the United States Naval guard aboard the steamer and the guard aboard another American ship which was nearby, the marauders were repulsed.

CHERBOURG, France, March 20,-(/)—Off for New York on her first Atlantic crossing, the new North German Lloyd liner Europa, sister ship of the blue ribbon Bremen, steamed out of port into headwinds and westerly gales tonight. She remained in the roads only 65 minutes, a call record breaking for its shortness. A hundred miles out, the big liner wirelessly that she had run into violent headwinds. Nautical men here believe that she will hardly be able to break the Bremen’s record for the crossing, if the westerly gales hold for several hours. Officials of the North German Lloyd line have declined to comment on reports that the Europa would try to better the Bremen’s time of four days, 17 hours and 24 minutes. TOKYO, March 21, —An agreement was reached between the Japanese and Soviet governments for interchange of military officers between their governments. The interchange of military officers will be between the two armies, whereby Japanese officers will be attached to certain Soviet units and vice versa.

1930-05-10.text: BOMBAY, India. May 9.—(AP)—The British lion showed its teeth today to the unruly followers of Mahatma Gandhi's civil disobedience campaign. While 40 airplanes were dispatched on a warning flight over the Peshawar district, where restive natives were suspected of preparing for a raid, the home government took occasion to announce that Great Britain has 226,000 troops ready to answer a call to arms in India. The semi-official totals of yesterday's Sholapur casualties rested at 20 dead and upward of 100 wounded. The outstanding fact of the clash was the burning by natives of several police, bound together and soaked in oil, and made into torches to illuminate the terror-ridden night. Apparently the natives burned only dead officers, sparing the wounded. Accounts of the injured ranged from 60 to 400, the latter figures being supplied by horrified wives of police officials who reached Bombay

London, May 9— (#) —John Masefield, who has sung the glory of Britannia’s merchant marine and her fox-hunting and steeple-chasing, today was appointed poet laureate of England by King George. Masefield, who succeeds the late Dr. Robert Bridges, in his 55 years has roamed the world in the carefree fashion of a hobo. He went to sea as a boy and for many years thereafter covered the Seven Seas as seaman and ship’s cook. At various times he would leave the sea and work his way across countries he decided to study. On one occasion he traveled from New York to the Pacific coast, working as a farm hand and doing odd jobs en route. He returned the same way and for a time was porter in a New York saloon run by Luke O'Connor.

LONDON, May 10.-All available troops in Sholapur, Bombay Presidency, were rushed out in full force today following a report an unruly mob was marching on the police arsenal, according to dispatches to the evening newspapers. The report proved to be without foundation. The city, however, remains in a state of extreme nervous tension. All mills are closed and business is at a standstill. The entire port of Rangoon has been paralyzed by a strike of dock hands, according to an exchange telegraph dispatch. The strikers were led by Nationalist agitators, the dispatch said.

TOKYO May 10—(#)—The House of Representatives today passed a bill permitting women 25 years of age or older to vote in elections for municipal and prefectural assemblies. Although the measure is likely to be defeated in the House of Peers, advocates of women suffrage hail it as a victory presaging full enfranchisement of women in a few years.

The reports followed closely unconfirmed advices received here yesterday from Chinese sources saying 15,000 persons had been slaughtered by 4,000 bandits at Yungreng, also in Honan, and that 500 residents were carried off after the slaughter had been completed and the town burned. FA MAG, MAY 1. Young plan for payment of reparations, reducing Germany’s obligations for damages caused during the World War from something like $25,000,000,000 to about $9,000,000,000, went into effect this afternoon. A protocol registering the decisions of the Hague conference, which adopted a plan January 20, was signed by the ambassadors of Great Britain, France, Belgium, Italy and the French minister of foreign affairs after a tea served by the French foreign minister, Aristide Briand. The signing was made possible by the arrival today of necessary ratification papers from Great Britain and Italy. Ratification by Germany and four creditor nations was required, and ratification documents already had been deposited by Germany, France and Belgium.

ROME, May 9.—(4)—Premier Mussolini sat in the chamber of deputies today and heard his foreign minister, Dino Grandi, affirm that Italy is ready to enter forthwith into final naval negotiations with Great Britain and France. The premier remained throughout the entire reading of Signor Grandi's speech, which went fully into the London naval parley and Italy's participation in the Hague conference. Although he touched upon the Young plan, Grandi confined himself chiefly to expressions of satisfaction with what had been done toward naval disarmament, first in Washington and then at London. He called attention to Italy’s efforts to effect an agreement with France before the recent parley, and had notes between Rome and Paris. He declared Italy went to London not merely for limitation but for definite reduction of naval strength. (Continued on Page 2, Col. 7)

SHANGHAI, May 10— (P) —The Nationalist government and the northern alliance armies have been locked in a big battle for two days with heavy casualties on both sides. Conflicting reports from the battle front between Cheng Chow, Honan province and Suchow, Kiangsu province indicate the result is in doubt. The Chinese populace, said the dispatches, was fleeing from the area, while the Japanese already had gone to places of safety. Hankow messages said military preparations were proceeding on all sides and large bodies of troops had departed northward. 1930-05-17.text: BOMBAY, India, May 17. (AP) — Four hundred civil disobedience volunteers this evening began their march upon the salt works of Wadala. The procession started from Congress House, Pandit Mukund Malaviya, son of Pandit Mohun Malaviya, led the volunteers. The procession marched past one of the largest concentrations of armed police mustered since the beginning of Mahatma Gandhi’s campaign for civil resistance. Six hundred officers, 190 of them with firearms, were stationed at Jacob Circle and elsewhere on the route to the salt depot seven miles from Bombay. Elaborate preparations for arrests if necessary to thwart an actual raid included preparation of quarters in the development department buildings of Worli, around which is a barbed wire barrier through which electric current can be circulated.

Formby, England, May 16---Diana Fishwick, 19 year old English girl, today won the British women's golf championship, defeating Glenna Collett, American champion, four up and three to play. Miss Collett was not the player today that she was as she moved through the championship to the finals nor the player who forced Joyce Wethered to play sensational golf to defeat her in the championship last year. She was five down in the morning and although she played a better game in the afternoon she never was able to reduce her young opponent's lead to a point where the American could be considered a contender. An erratic putter brought about the defeat of the American. She failed to hole reasonable putts all day.

Bombay, India, May 17. — Growing unrest among the Mohammedan population of India was viewed with concern in European circles here today. Coupled with the progress of the Hindu civil disobedience campaign, the situation provided a particularly disquieting outlook. Muslims, who for weeks have abstained from participation in the civil disobedience campaign, now appear to be drawing near the nationalist leaders through agitation of a cause entirely exterior to India itself—treatment of Muslims in Palestine. Muslim quarters here observed a hartal or day of protest, Friday, in sympathy with the Arabs of Palestine. BOMBAY, India, May 16.--(®)— Two women today held in their hands the destinies of millions of India’s native population. They are Madame Sarojini Naidu and her sister-in-law, Mrs. Kamaladevi Chattopadhyaya, leaders of Mahatma Gandhi's civil resistance movement. Madame Naidu spent her day sitting in the hot and dusty Dharasaana roadway until, in a truck with the police, she and her salt-raiding comrades withdrew from the scene. In removing her from the Indian political picture the police took occasion to make public a long list of illegal activities attributed to her. Grave news came from various sections of India. Indicating strict censorship, a dispatch was made public for the first time telling of a riot at Mymensingh, Bengal, Wednesday, in which 90 persons were injured including a considerable number of police. BOMBAY, India, May 17, (UP)— Passive resistance volunteers were rounded up in wholesale lots as the British government took up the advantage it gained when it crushed Mrs. Sarojini Naidu’s first move as Mahatma Gandhi's successor. The volunteers, however, were not depressed by Naidu’s failure to effect a raid on the thrice threatened Dharasana salt works. Another group of fifty, some of them among the party which had remained with Mrs. Naidu throughout a 38 hour siege near the Dharasana works, left their camp at Untadi again this morning in an attempt to effect the raid. They were stopped by the alert native police at almost the exact spot where Mrs. Naidu was halted Thursday and once more volunteers and police sat opposite each other in passive resistance.

LONDON, May 17—(UP)—The American embassy issued a statement here today denying intimations published in the United States that Ambassador Charles G. Dawes would resign soon. ‘The ambassador will not apply for his regular leave of absence until next September, when he will go to Chicago for a month in connection with his duties as chairman of the finance committee of the Chicago Century of Progress Exposition,” the statement said. “At the end of his leave, he will return to his duties in London.”

London, May 17—(INS)—Police once again imitated the policies of Mahatma Gandhi's disciples today in India in meeting "passive" resistance with "passive" opposition, according to a Central News dispatch from Bombay. At Dharasana, where police sat it out for twenty-eight hours yesterday with Mrs. Sarojini Naidu and her followers, constables met a new party of volunteers who wished to conduct a raid today on the salt pans in the city. Both parties continue to eye each other, according to last reports. At Shiroda, however, police charged volunteers attempting to raid salt depots and several were injured. Two hundred were arrested. Two thousand volunteers left the congress house in Bombay and marched toward Gowarl this afternoon, where they plan to spend the night, according to an Exchange Telegraph dispatch. Bombay, India, May 16.—(AP)—Their patience exhausted after hours of vigil in the blistering Indian sun, police today arrested and then released Mrs. Sarojini Naidu, new leader of the civil disobedience campaign in succession to Mahatma Gandhi and Abbas Tyabji. The police action thwarted the first attempt of the Indian nationalists to raid the government operated salt depots at Dharsaana. Mrs. Naidu was withdrawn by the police from the cordon they had drawn around the salt raiders, and sent back to the nationalist camp, about half a mile away. Those of her followers who had remained within the cordon throughout the night with her, then were treated similarly. The depth of feeling aroused against the government's participation in the liquor traffic was shown by the rioting at Memensyngh, in Eastern Bengal, Wednesday, in which more than 90 persons were injured when a crowd attacked a cart, surrounded by armed guards, which was delivering liquor from the government depot to liquor shops. The government derives considerable revenue from the taxation of native liquor made from the coconut, which resembles fiery cognac. Cherbourg, France, May 16.—This wartime port of American debarkation this afternoon greeted 231 Gold Star mothers of the United States who arrived on the steamship America. The liner was escorted into port by two French military planes. An enthusiastic reception was given the party. All the mothers arrived in fine health and spirits, greatly affected, however, by the tumultuous welcome. Officials representing the government and the port administration met the mothers as they came ashore and gathered on the railway station platform adjoining the dock. Four short addresses were made, after which the visitors boarded a train for Paris.

Friedrichshafen, Germany.—(P)—Several Americans, some of them veteran Zeppelin flyers, will be on the Graf Zeppelin when the great German dirigible heads over the South Atlantic Tuesday on its trip to South and North America. George Crouse of Syracuse, N. Y., who has crossed the ocean before on the Graf, will be on board Sunday when the big ship takes off for the first stop in the journey, Seville, Spain, and it was reliably reported Mrs. Mary Pierce of New York would join the airship at Seville. Mrs. Pierce participated in last May’s ill-fated voyage, when the Zeppelin became crippled over France and had to land at Cuers. Her husband and relatives were much against her taking the flight and even attempted to have the American ambassador talk her out of it. But she went and her husband said that if she ever took another airship trip he would go along. He is in Europe now. Another America

Paris, May 16, (4)—The body of William J. Locke, British novelist, who died at his flat here last night, will be cremated tomorrow at Pere-Lachaise cemetery in conformity with his last wish. The ashes will be taken to England where funeral services will be held Tuesday at Saint Martin’s in the Field Church, London. Locke, who created “The Beloved Vagabond,” died quietly, and never realized that death was approaching. He was 67.

PARIS, May 17—(AP)—Paris looked her most beautiful today for the first contingent of 6,000 Gold Star mothers here to visit graves of sons who died in the World War and see for themselves the things they used to write about. These first Gold Star mothers have come to France when the country, and the capital particularly, are at the height of their spring-time perfection. This morning most of the 233 women who arrived yesterday from the liner America contented themselves with short trips in the neighborhood of their hotels, or resting for the ceremony at the Unknown Soldier’s tomb this afternoon without military representations.
PARIS. May 17. Premier Tardieu today gave orders for progressive evacuation of the last bridgehead on the Rhine.

PARIS, May 17—The bank for international settlements, which will act as trustees for the creditor powers in the final liquidation of the world war reparations problem, came into being officially today in an old hotel building in Basle, Switzerland. Headed by Gates W. McGarrah, of the United States, and Pierre Quesnay, of France, the international bank will serve as the chief business instrument of the Young plan. The bank will receive from Germany and her former allies more than $35,000,000,000, and will supervise its distribution among the allied and associated powers. More than two-thirds of the money is destined to pay inter-allied war debts, and about $10,000,000,000 will go to the United States for credits advanced during and after the war. Early in the day, the Gold Star mothers were about seeing the sights of Paris and, more important, shopping. 1930-04-24.text: London, April 24 (Thursday) (P)—Sudden extension of the anti-British movement in India to far away Peshawar, the great gateway of the Northwest near the Afghan border, has roused disturbing thoughts here. The Lahore correspondent of the Daily Mail sent a version of developments in Peshawar which dwarfed earlier reports. The dispatch said that a serious outbreak was suppressed only when troops poured machine gun and rifle fire into a riotous mob, killing 20. The mob, inflamed by recent propaganda and speeches by leaders of the Indian National Congress, had held up an armored car, poured kerosene on it and ignited it, the two occupants being burned to death. It was related further that a British sergeant had been pulled off a motorcycle in the bazaar and attacked with an axe. It was reported that he had died of his wounds. SOUTHAMPTON, England, Apr. 23.—(AP)—The Leviathan sailed from Southampton harbor at 7:30 a. m. today taking with it Colonel Henry L. Stimson, American secretary of state, and others of the American delegation to the London naval conference. Departure of the steamer was delayed more than 19 hours in order that the naval delegates might complete the work of the conference with signing of the treaty. They came aboard at midnight, after a rail trip from London, but the ship had to await better tide conditions before attempting the difficult harbor channel. Dawes Remains Accompanying Colonel Stimson are Ambassador Morrow, Senator Robinson, and Secretary Adams, what was left of the clerical staff of the delegation, the naval experts, and American newspaper men assigned to the conference. Senator Reed remained for a visit with Ambassador Gibson in Brussels. Ambassador Dawes is remaining in Lond

Dover, Eng., April 24—(AP)—The giant German liner Bremen, sister ship of the record-breaking Europa, was in a slight collision with the tanker British Grenadier just off Dungeness in the English channel this morning. The Bremen, which was outward bound, was reported to have proceeded on her way to Southampton after a search for the tanker in a dense fog in which the crash occurred and was apparently little, if any, damaged. The tanker, however, was badly battered on her port side and although not requiring assistance wirelessed that she was putting into Deal to land a man requiring immediate medical attention. The tanker, in addition to damage on her port side, lost large quantities of oil, the sea over a wide area being covered with crude oil. The tanker was reported late this afternoon anchored in the Deal roads.

LONDON, (UP).—The British tanker Grenadier advised by radio Thursday that it was badly damaged in a collision with the North German Lloyd Liner Bremen, a Lloyd's dispatch from North Foreland said. The tanker said it collided with the Bremen at 9:26 a.m., and was proceeding to Deal, England, where it would land the supernumerary, who "is requiring medical attention." The tanker reported she did not require assistance, although tanks number four and five, the bridge, and parts of the ship on the port side were damaged badly. The tanker's message did not say whether the supernumerary was injured in the collision. Before advising that assistance was not needed, the British Grenadier had reported that tanks four and five were leaking. The British Grenadier is a steel tanker of 6,888 gross tons and is owned by the British Tanker Company. A Lloyd's dispatch from Dover Thursday said a report had

CALCUTTA, April 28. (AP)—Officials announced today that 12 insurgents were killed and two seriously wounded in a fight near Chittagong last night between the group which raided the Chittagong police arsenal Saturday and British troops. Fourteen arrests were made. No soldiers were injured. The insurgents were posted in a strong position on a hill and attacked by detachments of the eastern frontier rifles and the Burgma Valley light horse. The main body of the raiders was still at large following the engagement but military operations were continuing.

(By The Associated Press) London, April 24.—It was reported from Cardington that the huge British dirigible R-100 was damaged while being brought out of her shed today, one of her starboard fins catching against the side of the shed and buckling slightly.

LONDON, Apr. 24—(UP)—British troops and police maintained an uncertain outward calm in half a dozen of the largest cities of India today as the nation-wide independence campaign of the Mahatma M. G. Gandhi smouldered again after 24 hours of violence, At least 24 persons were killed and a large number were wounded in fighting yesterday and last night. The situation was desperate at Peshawar until troops with machine guns and bayonets and backed by armored cars, beat off a native attack. The city remained under strict patrol today. Entry of Europeans into Peshawar City was strictly prohibited because of the fighting there, the exchange telegraph reported today. Congress leaders who were arrested there this morning were removed to Peshawar fort because ‘they incited other jail prisoners to revolt.’ The Check Up . The following cities, scattered all over India, were affected by the outbreaks

Dover, England, April 24 (2P).— The German steamship Bremen, one of the two fastest liners on the seas, collided with the British tanker British Grenadier, off Dungeness Light in the English Channel at 9:56 a.m. GMT today, badly damaging the tanker. The Bremen, which was due at Southampton at noon from Bremen, was not believed to be badly damaged, and was thought to have continued on her way after seeking the tanker to render assistance. — The tanker radioed that she did not require assistance. The Bremen left Bremen, Germany, yesterday afternoon on its usual trip to New York, intending to dock at Southampton at noon to pick up passengers there. The collision occurred in a dense fog which made navigation in the Channel perilous.

DUNEDIN, New Zealand, April 24 (C.P.) Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd left Dunedin today for Wellington, whence he will sail for New York. The crowd at the station was so thick that Byrd almost had to fight his way to the train. Admiral Byrd paused at the War Veterans’ Memorial on his way to the station long enough to lay a wreath in tribute to New Zealand's soldiers in the World War. Before departing, Admiral Byrd issued a farewell message to Dunedin. It said: “I had rather say Au Revoir to Dunedin than Good-bye, for I am looking forward to coming back. “One thing never sufficiently emphasized is the great debt the expedition owes to the New Zealand contingent who volunteered to get ships south to us. There was not one of them who did not show himself a gentleman, played the game, worked hard, and contributed greatly to our success.

Calcutta, India, April 23—Conditions of unrest in India increased in gravity today. The day’s events included information that 12 persons were killed yesterday when troops clashed with the insurgents who raided the Chittagong arsenal Saturday; a demonstration by thousands in Calcutta; the shooting of five persons at Feni, and the death of a British soldier at Peshawar. The 12 deaths resulted when detachments of light horse dislodged a band of the Chittagong insurgents from a strong position in the hills. In addition to those killed two were seriously wounded. Fourteen were arrested. No military casualties were reported. The main body of the rebels escaped and the soldiers were concerned. The demonstration in Calcutta followed upon yesterday's announcement that political prisoners in Alipore jail had gone on a hunger strike in protest against treatment by jail officials. Police ultimately

| ROME, April 24. (AP)— Benito Mussolini, premier and dictator of Italy, this morning gave his daughter Edda in marriage to Count Gaietto Ciano, secretary of the Italian embassy at the Holy See and son of the minister of communications. The church of St. Joseph, which is Il Duce’s parish church, was crowded with dignitaries. It was decorated for the occasion with beautiful tapestries from the Capitoline Palaces, and with palm flowers. The wedding and attendant ceremonies were without show and ostentation, in keeping with Premier Mussolini's policy of keeping his private life and family as much in the background as possible. Guests included United States Ambassador John W. Garrett, and Mrs. Garrett. The bride is 19 years old, and the groom 27. Their engagement was announced February 15, the Roman papers hailing it at the time as uniting two of the most illustrious families of the new regi

CANTON, China, April 24,--Two American missionaries, who arrived from Sinfeng in Kiangsi province, said 16 American Catholic missionaries are in grave danger of falling into the hands of Red troops and being executed: Anchoo is near surrender to Communists and bandits who have besieged the city since early last month, they said.

ROME, April 24.—Edda Mussolini, daughter of Premier Benito Mussolini, became the wife of Count Galeazzo Ciano, secretary of the Italian legation accredited to the Holy See, at 11 a.m. today. The marriage vows were read by Mer. Giovenale Pascucci, priest of Mussolini's parish, in the Church of St. Joseph, one of the less imposing churches in the City of Rome. The ceremonies were simple, in accordance with the orders of Duce, but the profusion of flowers about the altar, in every part of the church, and the gorgeous tapestries and carpets that had been placed for the occasion, lent an air of grandeur. Automobiles brought the wedding party to the church, a two-minute drive from Mussolini’s Villa Torlonia. They dismounted while Maestro Germani of Augusteum concert hall played Bossi’s Wedding March. Signorina Mussolini entered, on the arm of the groom's father, Count Costanzo Ciano, Italian M
BR Sipe eee re, Friedrichshaven, April 24 (AP).—The Zeppelin works announced today that the South American flight of the Graf Zeppelin has been postponed from May 10 to May 15.

A. N. N. S. Staff Correspondent Rome. — In the presence of a small but distinguished gathering, Edda Mussolini, 19-year-old daughter of Italy’s premier, today became the wife of Signor Galezza Ciano, handsome young secretary of the Italian embassy at the Vatican. Guided by the simplicity which has characterized Premier Benito Mussolini’s regime, the wedding took place in the small parish church of St. Joseph, a few steps from the Villa Torlonia, home of Il Duce and his family. While the church was magnificently decorated with crimson damask tapestries and trans-

1930-05-22.text: London—/—The ministry of J. Ramsay MacDonald, second labor government in the history of Great Britain, girded itself Thursday for a battle for its existence. It was expected that at a meeting of the parliamentary labor party Thursday night the prime minister will ask for a vote of confidence in the ministry’s unemployment program. Failing to achieve it, he probably will ask King George to dissolve parliament and then will take the question to the country. The situation is the outgrowth of the resignation of Sir Oswald Mos- (Continued on Page 12)

BOMBAY, May 22.—-(#)—British troops—a contingent from a Hyderabad regiment—were sent today to the government-operated salt depot at Dharasana to prevent further raiding by Indian nationalists' volunteers. Simultaneously nationalist headquarters there announced that the next mass raid would take place Sunday. Hitherto only police, some armed, but principally armed with laths, or staves, have been depended upon to maintain order at the salt depots. Police and troops raided the nationalist camp at Untadi, near Dharasana today, and destroyed it, remaining in complete control of the area. At Wadala a party of 100 raiders divided themselves into two batches, and were arrested. Of a second party 18 were arrested but the remainder succeeded in getting away with some salt. Alarming news came from the northwest frontier, a report from Peshawar saying that severe casualties had been inflicted by Br
|By The Associated Press. LONDON, May 28.—The projected flight of the new British dirigible R-100 to Canada has been postponed until the end of June or the beginning of July.

LONDON, May 22. (WP) A dispatch to Lloyd's today said 100 persons were believed to have perished on the Fabre Line’s (French) Steamship Asia, which caught fire while transporting 1,500 Muslim pilgrims from Jeddah and Mecca to Jibouti, on the Gulf of Aden. The Lloyd's dispatches from Sudan said the steamer was abandoned and still burning in Jeddah harbor. The fire was said to be beyond control and it was impossible to approach the ship.

By The Associated Press London, May 22.--(Thursday) Lloyd's received a message this morning from Port Sudan, Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, saying that the French steamer Asia was afire with 4,900 pilgrims aboard.

BOMBAY, (UP).—The British government sent its military forces to the base of the passive resistance campaign Thursday evacuating the 'Satyagrahis' from their camp near the Dharasana salt works and occupying Dharasana itself. As a result of the newest move on the part of British authorities in India, the Satyagrahis war council decided immediately to suspend its operations for two days. The occupied camp was located at Dungri, three miles from Dharasana. It and the camp at Untadi had been the center of passive resistance activity for many days, and from them the mass raid on the Dharasana salt pans was made Wednesday.

LONDON, May 22.—(I.N.S.)—One hundred persons were believed to have lost their lives today when the heavily laden French steamer Asia, carrying Moslem pilgrims to Mecca, burned and sank in the Red Sea, according to messages to evening newspapers. The Asia was carrying about 1,500 Moslem worshippers, most of them from French territory under Mohammedan influence. Details of the catastrophe were lacking, but it was believed most of the survivors had been picked up by rescue vessels.

Dharasana, Surat District, India, May 21, UPI—(Delayed by Censor)—Prayers said as white-clad volunteers knelt in the moonlight and an impassioned speech by the Poetess-leader, Mrs. Sarojini Naidu opened the mass attack of 2,500 independence demonstrators today on the Dharasana Salt Works. The poetess, wearing a rough, homespun robe and soft slippers but no stockings, exhorted her followers to the raid in which 260 of them were injured and which brought about her own arrest. “Although Gandhi's body is in prison, his soul goes with you,” she cried in an impassioned voice as she sent the volunteers to the attack. The cry of “Gandhi Kai Jai” (Long Live Gandhi) answered her from the dark ranks of volunteers huddled together in the dim light of early morning. As she finished speaking and af-

| London, May 22.—The Dericoy agent at Port Sudan has received a telegram from Jeddah stating that about 100 lives were believed to have been lost on the French steamer Asia, which is now afire in Jeddah harbor. This information was contrary to advices given by the Fabre Line, owner of the vessel, at Marseilles, quoting the captain of the ship as wirelessing that all passengers and crew had been saved. London, May 22 (Thursday) — Lloyd’s received a message this morning from Port Sudan, Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, saying that the French steamer Asia was afire with 1,500 pilgrims aboard. “We fear some loss of life,” it added. It said that the pilgrims bound for Red Sea ports embarked Wednesday and that the

LONDON, May 21 (P)—The Great British dirigible R-100 sailed majestically over London early tonight and, passing low above Covent Garden, dipped its nose in salute to King George and Queen Mary on their way to a theater. The airship made a test flight today preparatory to its departure soon for Canada. It maneuvered over London for some time, accompanied by six airplanes, one of which aided the show for the spectators by looping the loop. Just when the R-100 will start its transatlantic voyage has not been decided.

LONDON, May 22.—(Thursday) (UP)—The French steamship Asia, of 5,890 tons’ burden, was afire with 1,500 pilgrims aboard, on its way to ports in the Southern Red Sea, according to a report from Lloyd's correspondent at Port Sudan, Jeddah, early today. The correspondent said it was feared there would be loss of life. The fire was reported to have begun at 8 p. m. last night (Wednesday), he said.

(United Press Staff Correspondent.) BULSAR, Surat District, India, May 21 —(UP)—More than 200 persons were injured in a massed advance on the Dhara-Sana salt works today as Indian Surat police beat unarmed volunteers with laths. The national congress claimed their wounded had reached more than 250 by noon. The police kicked and prodded the non-violence raiders who swarmed the depot. Paris—-?)— Ambassador Claudel of France, and General John J. Pershing, for the United States, today voiced the sympathies of their nations to the more than 200 Gold Star Mothers who are visiting military cemeteries where their boys are buried. The ambassador and the soldier who commanded the American Expeditionary forces in France joined their tributes at public ceremonies which today provided a tender climax to the pilgrimage of the mothers from the United States. The consecration, which was spontaneous, occurred at a luncheon given by the American club in Paris to Ambassador Claudel, who had been invited to speak on the French influence in the United States, One of the largest companies in the history of the club was present, with General Pershing among the notable guests. After welcoming M. Claudel as a “great ambassador,” General Pershing turned immediately to the pilgrimage of the A

PARIS, May 17.—Gold star mothers and widows of the United States, who have come to France to visit the graves of their war dead, wept today at a tribute from the officer who directed their men in battles of the world war. When General John J. Pershing, his own eyes moist, thanked them in simple words for the mother love which sustained the American expeditionary forces twelve years ago they gave way to emotion. General Pershing’s talk was the highlight of a reception which followed the ceremony of laying a wreath on the tomb of France’s unknown soldier at the Arc de Triomphe. At this ceremony Mrs. Sarah Thompson of New York laid a laurel wreath on the tomb, uttering the words: “I present this wreath from the gold star mothers of America to the unknown soldier of France with reverence.” Attending the ceremony were many kindly French war mothers; General Gouraud, military governor of Paris

Romagne - Sous - Montfaucon, France, May 21, (#)—Spring rains mingled with the tears of American mothers today to freshen the graves of Yankee boys who fell in the great war. The mothers, more than 200 in number, reached the goal of their voyage from the United States this afternoon and spent a day that was all too short in the six vast military cemeteries wherein their sons lie buried. With tears and prayers they consecrated the resting places of the heroes they had elected to leave upon the battlefields where they gave their lives to democracy. Over nearly all of the cemeteries, the sun broke briefly through a leaden sky for that simple, solemn moment when the mothers knelt beside their boys. Here, where sleep 14,000 of America’s war dead, 108 mothers saw the graves which they had longed to see for twelve dreary years. Another fifty went to Seringes-Et-Nesles, near Soissons and a score

Havre, France, May 22,—Harry K. Thaw landed here today from the Ile De France on a pleasure trip which he said would take him to Paris, Switzerland, and other countries on the continent. He did not attempt to land in England yesterday. There were reports that a previous ban against him denying him admission because of having been involved in an extraditable crime would still be in force.

PARIS, May 22. — (U.P.) — The Fabre line offices at Marseilles were advised today that its liner, Asia, caught fire in the Red Sea while transporting 1,500 Moslem pilgrims from Jeddah and Mecca to Jibouti, a port on the Gulf of Aden. Complete information was lacking, but it was learned that all the passengers and crew were removed safely. Advices reaching the owners merely stated that the ship was afire, and that all aboard had been removed. They did not say whether the fire was extinguished.

MARSEILLES, France, May 22 The Fabre line, owners of the steamship Asia, which is afire in the Red Sea, said today that the captain of the ship had wirelessed that all passengers and crew had been saved by rescuing ships. Other vessels, he said, came promptly when the Asia sent out an S. O. S. signal. The Asia was temporarily abandoned. There were 1,500 pilgrims (presumable Moslems) aboard bound for Jeddah.

PARIS, May 8—(#)—The undisguised hope of the French, albeit tinged with alarm, that General Pershing would hop aboard the Clemenceau-Foch controversy beyond the tomb, in which former President-Premier Poincaré recently joined, was dashed to the ground when the commander of the A. E. F. landed at Cherbourg recently. “I have nothing to say,” General Pershing told reporters, “and if I did have something to say I should prefer to say nothing.” Interviewers pointed out that two entire pages of Clemenceau’s book “Grandeurs and Miseries of Victory” described the state of affairs behind the American Army's lines in the Argonne, as “chaos” but General Pershing refused to comment. A few days after Marshal Foch died, a book written by M. Raymond Recouly, a noted French author, purported to quote Foch in some statements which left no doubt as to the allied commander-in-chief’s opinion concerning Geo

GENEVA, May 22.— (LN.S.) — A sensational story to the effect that the arrival of Premier Benito Mussolini in Milan resulted in a state of virtual siege in that city, with hundreds of arrests and armed control of all public offices and institutions, was published by the socialist newspaper “Le Travail” here today. The newspaper declares the story was smuggled across the Italian frontier by a correspondent in the face of a rigorous censorship.

1930-04-16.text: (By The Associated Press) Calcutta, Bengal, India, April 15. —Nineteen persons were injured seriously in fighting between Nationalists and police which developed around burning tram cars near here today. A mob demonstrating against the arrest and imprisonment of Mayor J. M. Sen Gupta yesterday stoned a fire brigade attempting to subdue the flames.

LONDON, April 16—Agreement on the so-called contingency clause of the naval treaty—the last outstanding obstacle to drafting of the pact—was reached today by the United States, Great Britain and Japan. Reijiro Wakatsuki, chief Japanese delegate, informed Prime Minister J. Ramsey MacDonald of Japan's acceptance. The British spokesman announced that the delegates expect to finish drafting the treaty Thursday and to sign it Tuesday, permitting the American delegation to sail for New York April 23.

LONDON—(?)—Rapid progress in drafting the London naval treaty continued Tuesday, and the important "safeguarding" or "escalator" clause was agreed upon in principle by the American and British chief delegates. This section will protect the United States, Great Britain and Japan against possible competitive naval building by nations not signatory to the tripartite agreement. A signatory power may, if its building program is threatened by a non-signatory power, build to a higher level than that provided in the three power treaty. The levels of the two other signatories will rise at the same time. It is understood that a clause broader than article 21 of the Washington treaty has been accepted. In reliable American quarters it was thought that the consultative element of article 21 would be eliminated, the London treaty clause providing for a simple declarative statement from any of the thr

LONDON, April 16,—Prime Minister MacDonald, Secretary Stimson and Reijiro Wakatsuki of Japan today reached an agreement on safeguarding the clause which had been left in abeyance overnight to enable the Japanese to study the proposed clause. The wording of the clause which is designed to protect the three big naval powers in event non-signatories begin a naval building program is being cabled to Tokyo by the Japanese delegation.

BOMBAY, April 15 — A tense situation prevailed today as the city observed the Hartal—day of mourning—ordered yesterday by Congress officials in protest against the conviction and imprisonment of Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru and Mayor J. M. Sengupta of Calcutta on charges of violation of the salt law. Armored cars patrolled the streets and additional police were posted at important centers.

Bombay, India, April 16 (UP)—The campaign of civil disobedience which the Mahatma K. Gandhi inaugurated on a muddy beach at Dandi less than two weeks ago threatened to become a crusade of violence and bloodshed today, with sporadic outbreaks from the Bay of Bengal to the Arabian Sea. Although Gandhi urged only passive "resistance" in the campaign for independence, demonstrations against British authorities in Calcutta, Bombay, Allahabad, and Karachi developed into rioting and threatened momentarily to burst into violent conflicts. Fighting was worst in the streets of Calcutta where approximately 80 persons, including nine European officials, were injured in riots growing out of protests against the imprisonment of Mayor J. M. Sen Gupta, a Gandhi supporter. At Karachi, a mob angered by the trial of leaders of the national congress on charges of violating the salt laws stormed the courtroo

Calcutta, April 15, (P).—Rioting and arrests marked today's progress in the civil disobedience campaign although the leader, Mahatma Gandhi, tonight was still free. Observance of a hartal (day of mourning) in protest against the arrest and conviction of Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru and Mayor J. M. Sengupta, of Calcutta, both leaders in the Gandhi movement, caused serious riots in Calcutta. Minor outbreaks north of the city resulted in many persons being sent to hospitals and in much destruction.

LONDON, April 16. — The Exchange Telegraph company in a dispatch from Bombay said there was danger of serious trouble there later this evening. Three hundred Nationalist volunteers marched from congress house at noon with the deliberate object of raiding the government's salt pans and depots at Wadal, eight miles away.

London. (INS) — New outbreaks of violence, forcing the British authorities to use stern measures of repression, took place in various places in India today as Mahatma Gandhi's campaign of civil disobedience continued to spread throughout the country. Developments in the situation today were as follows: 1. A riotous mob stormed the magistrate’s court at Karachi. (Continued on Page Five)

(Associated Press Leased Wire) CAIRO, Egypt, April 15.—The Prince of Wales at dawn today started his flight from Khartoum, upper Egypt, to Cairo, from where he will take a ship back to England. He has been absent since the first of the year on a hunting trip in British East Africa.

BOMBAY, India, April 16.—(U.P.)—Three hundred volunteers from the national congress marched out of the congress house at noon today for the declared purpose of raiding the government salt pans and depots at Wadal, eight miles from Bombay.

NEW DELHI, STALLS (A.P)—Rioting on the streets of Calcutta last night spent itself finally before dawn today in a full-scale attack on the presidency of the General Hospital to which nine Europeans injured in yesterday's clash had been taken. Of the nine Europeans in the hospital, two were women. One was injured seriously, while another man was in grave condition from the night's fighting. Of fifty injured in the disturbances beginning yesterday, fifteen were police and eleven were civilians. Police finally quelled the mob and arrested 20 of their number, nine being found on rooftops with piles of bricks and stones beside them. The city was quieter today after the renewal of the clashes last night when Europeans driving home after an evening out were stoned. Streetcars were stoned and several wrecked.

Rome, April 16. (4)—A solemn Procession in the church of St. Mary Major, otherwise known as the Liberian Basilica, this morning ushered in the ceremonies attendant on Rome's observance of the Wednesday of Holy Week. In mournful cadences the chanting priests recounted the story of the passion, as told in the gospel of St. Luke, preceded by two lessons taken from the Prophet Isaiah foretelling the sacrifice of Christ. The afternoon was marked by the signing of the office of “tenebrae,” so-called in remembrance of the darkness said to have spread over all the earth at the moment of Christ's death on the cross. As in all Catholic churches throughout the world there was a ceremony of gradual extinction of all but the last of the 15 candles, placed on a triangular candlestick to the left of the altar. The last candle, which is also the highest, was carried to the church sacristy at the conclus

SEVILLE, Spain, Apr. 16 (AP)— Spaniards tittered today at the prank played by their sovereign, King Alfonso XIII, upon the Duke of Spoleto, youthful nephew of the king of Italy, who, rumor has it, soon will become engaged to the Infanta Beatriz, Alfonso’s eldest daughter. In the presence of the Infanta Beatriz and other members of the Royal family, King Alfonso led the young man to a trick bench in the palace gardens of Alcazar, where the family and their suite are remaining during Holy Week. The Duke was invited to sit on the bench and did so, his weight releasing a spring which controlled a concealed fountain. He was drenched with the water from the spray, while King Alfonso, the Infanta, the Duke’s mother, the Duchess of Aosta all laughed merrily. Even the discomfited Duke, brushing water from his eyes and trying to wring out his waterlogged clothes, grinned with the rest and made lig

GENEVA, April 16..—(UP) --The League of Nations’ Child Welfare committee today continued to keep secret, formally at least, details of a report handed it yesterday picturing the United States as a mad, decadent nation undermined by prohibition and lack of family life. Mile. Marie de Meonie Chaptal, president of the international council of nurses, made the report. The committee allowed Mile. Chaptal to describe her experiences but refrained from discussing her findings. It was kept secret for fear of injuring the sensibilities of the United States but certain of the criticisms have been known. Mile. Chaptal attributes what she regards as the total decadence of America’s youth, the United Press understands, to these things: 1. Prohibition laws, which children see violated constantly by their parents. 2. Divorce, whereof she quoted figures showing that in certain years 65 per cent of Ameri

SEVILLE, Spain, April 16—The giant dirigible Graf Zeppelin, which is preparing for a flight to Brazil, landed here today after flying from Friedrichshafen, Germany, which she left yesterday afternoon. The airship had made several ineffectual attempts to land, flying low over the field.

DARMSTADT, Germany, Apr. 16—(#)—Johannes Nehring, Germany's foremost glider pilot, was killed today when the plane he was flying crashed near the Island of Kuehkopt in the Rhine. His observer Steinhaeuser saved himself by jumping with a parachute. Nehring was in a Junkers plane taking a regular daily weather observation flight. He reached a considerable altitude when his motor failed and his steering gear went wrong.

SEVILLE, Spain, Apr. 16. (U.P)— The dirigible Graf Zeppelin making a test flight in preparation for a trip to Brazil and the United States in May, arrived today at 1:10 p. m. The royal family and a great crowd which had been arriving here for two days, greeted the big dirigible which will use Seville as its terminal for the South Atlantic flight.

PARIS, April 15.—(—Often heard but rarely seen, the German dirigible Graf Zeppelin, flying from Friedrichshafen, Germany, to Seville, Spain, sailed a steady diagonal course across France today. She was flying low through rain clouds and her progress was slowed down by head winds. There were no untoward incidents reported. The big airship entered French territory near Basel, Switzerland, at 4:05 p. m. (10:05 a. m., E. S. T.) and headed towards Besançon. Avoiding the Rhone valley, where strong headwinds were blowing, she struck southwest from Dijon toward Poitiers, keeping south of the River Loire.

SHANGHAI.--The situation of foreign missionaries remained uncertain Tuesday in bandit-infested provinces of south China, where telegraphic communication was disrupted. Stirred by foreigners’ protests, the nationalist government dispatched airplanes from Canton to drop bombs upon communists and bandits ravaging cities and the countryside along the border of Kwangtung and Kiangsi provinces. Captured April 9 at Fowchow, province of Szechwan, C. A. Bridgman, Canadian United Church missionary from Winona, Ontario, was taken by bandits to the mountains of the upper Yangtze river and held for ransom of $200,000. The British consul at Ichang has requested the nationalist government to obtain Bridgman’s release and that of a Chinese pastor captured with him. Bandit forces swarming over Kiangsi province have severed telegraph wires, keeping fast the secret of the fate of sixteen American Catholic

SEVILLE, Spain, Apr. 16 (AP)— The huge dirigible Graf Zeppelin, which left Friedrichshafen yesterday, flew over the outskirts of the city of Seville shortly after 1:00 p.m., as great crowds gathered at La Tablada air field. The rooftops throughout the city were dotted with spectators, many of whom climbed the famous Moorish tower of Giralda, the highest in Spain, adjoining the Cathedral.

(Associated Press) Seville, Spain, April 16—The dirigible Graf Zeppelin, carrying 20 passengers on a cruise from Friedrichshafen to Seville and return, circled repeatedly over this city today amidst the cheers of enthusiastic crowds. After circling Seville several times, the Graf headed toward Cadiz but was to return to Seville again. King Alfonso sent radio greetings to the Zeppelin while it was over the city. It was not definitely decided whether the Zeppelin should land or, after cruising over the region, head back to Germany. Weather reports were being received by the Zeppelin, and it was dependent upon these whether the dirigible would land or would lose no time starting for home.

1930-06-11.text: London—A—Great Britain’s problem in India was before the empire Tuesday in as complete a statement and as exhaustive a form as it has ever been presented. For recommendations of the investigators for solution of that problem, it will be necessary to wait, however, until June 24. On that day the commission on Indian statutory reform, headed by Sir John Simon, will publish the second volume of the report of their two-and-one-half-years’ inquiry into Indian affairs. The first volume of the report, dealing with the situation, was made public today. There was, in the final paragraph of Tuesday's offering, perhaps, a promise of what the second volume—of recommendations—will contain. LONDON, June 10 (AP)—Discussion of the first volume of Sir John Simmons’ Indian government report today overshadowed all other developments in the Indian situation. The Indian press did not take as kindly to the initial installment, which was a thorough analysis, as had been hoped. Hindu leaders criticized it severely. The immediate result in the United States probably will be the offering of the American share of $98,250,000—or nearly one-third of the entire loan—to the people shortly. HEIDELBERG, Germany, June 10 (P)—Dr. Adolf Von Harnack, widely known as leader of the modern German school of theology, died today at the age of 79. He had been ill for the past two weeks. Dr. Von Harnack, who was one of the most noted of German theologians, was widely known both in Europe and the United States. He visited the United States in 1904 and lectured at various cities in the East and Midwest. He was the founder of the Kaiser Wilhelm Society for the advancement of science and of the evangelical-social council. His chief work was “The History of the Christian Dogma.”

1930-03-13.text: London, March 12. (#)—Aristide Briand, foreign minister of France, is gloomy over his failure to get a security pact for his country out of the five-power naval conference. Tonight he gave the parley only another fortnight of life. The head of the French delegation received French newspapermen, but rigidly excluded reporters of all other nationalities. The French writers came out of the conference convinced that Briand was depressed. They quoted him as saying: "I have finished my role and tomorrow the whole thing will be handed over to the delegations." Briand declared the delay in reaching conference decisions had not been due to the French attitude in demanding security pacts as a price for reducing their program of naval buildings, but to the fact that Italy had not produced any tonnage figures at all, but had insisted on their right to parity with any continental European power.

London, March 13 (UP) — Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald threw all his personal influence into an effort to save the five power naval conference today. The British spokesman said MacDonald, sensing a serious crisis, was stepping in to do all in his power to settle the differences among the delegations. MacDonald caused postponement of the regular daily meetings of the “Big Five” at 4 p. m. to permit him to hold personal conferences with the French and Italian leaders. He saw the chief Japanese delegate during the morning and arranged to see Dino Grandi, the Italian foreign minister, at 3 p. m., and Foreign Minister Aristide Briand of France at 4 p. m. He made no plans to confer with Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson since the differences between Great Britain and the United States are almost nothing.

Berlin, March 13.—President Paul Von Hindenburg today signed the Young agreement and the Hague economic treaties, bringing to an end the reparations controversy that has upset the economic balance of Europe for ten years. By an act Germany is bound to make annual payments to the allied nations until 1988, through the new bank for international settlement. Penalty for non-fulfillment of the agreement will be re-occupation of the German territory by allied soldiers. President Von Hindenburg affixed his signature to the agreements only after overcoming the gravest conscientious objections to the terms, and after 1,000 of his wartime comrades including a host of his former generals, resorted to every possible persuasion to induce him to refuse his approval. By The Associated Press. BERLIN, March 13.—President Von Hindenburg, Germany’s venerable president, today set his hand and seal to the Young Plan despite the urgent appeals of his one-time followers—many of them men who had fought shoulder to shoulder with him and others who had helped elect him president. The president, who otherwise is extremely punctilious about not mixing in political situations, cast aside his reserve at this critical hour and penned a declaration in which he gave clear indication of his devotion to his duty as he saw it. His present declaration, in which he made an appeal to all Germans for cooperation in the common task and to unite in one thought “Deutschland über alles,” was looked upon as one of the most important documents in German history and as a great force in uniting the German people.

PARIS, March 1 — (INS) — Premier Andre Tardieu won a sweeping victory in the Chamber of Deputies today when his government’s budget was adopted by a vote of 416 to 112 after a tiresome 24-hour session. The vote on the budget at 9:30 a.m. today followed spirited debate and a series of minor rebuffs to the premier which he squelched only by asking for and receiving a vote of confidence which turned the tide in favor of the government. The confidence vote, won 320 to 260, gave the premier a majority of 60. Premier Tardieu’s first government fell on February 17 on a minor budget question which brought out the full strength of the Left wing. The budget of his present government, somewhat revised during debate upon it, won hearty support from the majority of the Left wing.

Friedrichshafen, Germany, May 16. - The Graf Zeppelin’s historic first attempt to cross the equator and reach South America by dirigible will begin Sunday some time between 4 p.m. and 6 p.m., if weather permits. The first lap of the journey is to Seville, Spain, which the Graf expects to reach late Monday by way of Lyons, Marseilles and Gibraltar. After an all-night stay there the great ship will rose out over the Atlantic Tuesday morning for the flight to Pernambuco, Brazil. On the first lap the Zeppelin will carry 22 passengers. Of these six will go only to Seville, where four others will be taken aboard in their places, bringing the total for the trans-Atlantic and trans-equatorial flight to 20, besides the 42 officers and men of the crew. TOKYO, May 20.-In the tense atmosphere surrounding the return of Admiral Kotora Takarabe, minister of marine, from the London conference, and his first conferences with the cabinet and senior naval officers a sensation was created today by the suicide of a high naval officer which the press is exploiting as an echo of the navy’s bitter opposition to the London pact. Lieut.-Commander Eiji Kusakira, attached to the naval staff, slashed his abdomen with a sword aboard a train between Kobe and Tokyo. He died at a hospital at Numazu. PARIS, May 20.—(AP)—All of the American Gold Star mothers excepting the Suresnes group tonight were out in the old battle zone, at the end of their pilgrimage. Tomorrow they will kneel beside the graves of their sons in five American military cemeteries and breathe the blessings so long delayed. The 16 mothers of the Suresnes party remained in Paris tonight. Tomorrow will mark their third pilgrimage to Mount Valerien, where their war dead lie. It drizzled nearly all day in Paris and much of the region traveled by the mothers, but as they were carried in large and comfortable sightseeing buses the rain made little difference.

Moscow, May 21 (UP)--A passenger train collided with a freight train on the Moscow-Kazan Railroad Monday, killing 28 persons and injuring a number of others, delayed advices said today. The train wreck occurred at the station of Tchornt. At least 26 persons were seriously injured. The employees of the road who were believed directly responsible for the wreck were arrested and an official investigation started.

LONDON, MAY 15. (AP).—Prime Minister MacDonald opened debate on the London naval treaty in the House of Commons today, praising it as a significant step for disarmament while Winston Churchill, prominent Conservative, declared his party "cannot accept the slightest responsibility in connection with it." Mr. Churchill said the pact was not a treaty of parity with the United States in the sense that Great Britain and the United States should be equal on the seas but was a formal acceptance by Great Britain of definitely inferior sea power. Mr. Churchill's speech followed one by Prime Minister MacDonald which praised the work of the conference. The Conservative leader remarked that the anxiety of his party regarding the treaty had not at all been removed by the agreeable and lucid speech of Mr. MacDonald.

London, May 15.—(UP)—London’s social season was opened at Buckingham Palace last night when King George and Queen Mary held the first of five royal courts scheduled for 1930. Eight American women were among the hundreds from all nations who were presented to the king and queen. The American women presented were: “Miss Frances Hutchinson, Philadelphia; Miss Griselda Forbes, Boston, Mass.; Miss Charlotte Dorrance, Camden, N. J.; Miss Katherine Bunice Bennett, New York City and Oxford University; Miss Eleanor Edwards, Cincinnati; and Miss Elizabeth Kent, Philadelphia. The royal court began at 9:30 P.M., when the king and queen, heralded by trumpets, appeared at the doors of the throne room and advanced to the two golden thrones. It was the first appearance of the king at a royal court since his serious illness. As soon as the monarchs were seated, King George signalled for the presentations
Auckland, New Zealand, May 15, OH—Writing with shaking hand on what is believed to be the death bed, Sir Joseph Ward, aged Premier of New Zealand, resigned today.

By The Associated Press. Shanghai, China, May 14—The nationalist government forces defeated the Soriherr Alliance rebels in a six-day battle, taking 10,000 prisoners and driving the enemy out of Anhwei province, the government announced tonight. Although casualties were not stated, the severity of the struggle was attested by previous dispatches, which said the nationalists wounded in the first two days of fighting numbered 20,000. Pursuing the retreating rebels, the Nationalists attacked their new base at Ewelteh in Honan province. Capture of that city, the Nationalists asserted, would force the Northerners to fall upon Kaifeng to consolidate their scattered forces.

PARIS, May 15—(U.P)—Three hundred gold star mothers and widows, the first contingent of 6,000—who will visit the war cemeteries of France at the expense of the United States government, arrived at Cherbourg tomorrow morning from New York. Their arrival aboard the United States liner America marks the commencement of the first organized pilgrimage of its kind ever attempted by the United States. Sixteen other liners will bring similar groups throughout the summer and for two weeks they will visit the chief American war cemeteries and points of interest around Paris. Special liaison officers and trained nurses of the United States army will greet the pilgrims tomorrow when they first place foot on French soil. Representatives of the French government and Franco-American patriotic organizations will also tender a welcome.

Geneva, May 1— (AP.)—The council of the League of Nations adjourned today after approving the personnel for a special commission which will study the historic problem of the wailing wall in Jerusalem, so often the center of dispute between Jews and Arabs. The commissioners are M. Elliel Loefgren, former Swedish foreign minister; Charles Bards, Swiss jurist; and Mynheer Von Kempen, Dutch colonial official. During today’s session, Foreign Secretary Henderson, of Great Britain, said that his government was not relaxing measures for maintaining order in Palestine. There will be no immediate reduction in the military and police forces in Palestine.

By The Associated Press. DESSAU, Germany, May 14.—The Junkers airplane, G-38, claimed to be the largest land plane in the world, started early this morning on its first extended cross country flight, with 20 passengers aboard.

PARIS — (#) — Rene Martineau, youthful Lyons motorcyclist, has completed a motorcycle trip of 700 miles across the Sahara desert. He made the trip with twelve tins of sardines as his only provision. Martineau said that near Reggan he went through a country where great rocks rise like “tombstones for the earth when it dies.” The stone shafts were polished like steel by the sand storms of centuries. “Then you strike the sand,” the youthful adventurer said. “I found the temperature 112 degrees at noon for three days. The sand caked on my machine. The oil would not run. I walked for sixty hours, sleeping days, trudging on. I took off the tires and rode on the rims through twenty-five miles of burning brush.”

Paris, May 15.—(AP) — The question of removing the League of Nations from Geneva to an especially created independent territory much like the Vatican City state has been raised by Matin, French Daily, and is arousing considerable discussion. The proposition is linked here with the idea of the proposed European confederation which also be placed in the same territory.

1930-03-27.text: LONDON, March 27. — The chief delegates to the naval conference, meeting at St. James’ palace this afternoon, decided to hold a plenary session a week from tomorrow. It was expected that the question of some form of a security pact for the benefit of the French would come up at that time. In the meantime important negotiations were understood to be proceeding among the British and French and British and Italians regarding a security pact.
