PLYMOUTH, England, Mar. 27.~ Captain William Rind of the United States Lines President Harding died suddenly of cerebral hemorrhage aboard his vessel here today. Captain Rind was taken ill on the bridge of his ship a few hours before arriving in harbor. His body will be sent to New York for burial.

Glasgow, Scotland, March 26. | (®)—A professional pipe lighter has been employed here to keep street railway laborers from wasting their time. His sole duty is to refill and light the men’s pipes as fast as they go out. His job was established by an efficiency expert. The men have to furnish their own tobacco and matches.

London, March 26 — From the breathless efforts being made to arrive at a five-power naval agreement at the London naval conference by means of a consultative political pact, which it is hoped will meet French demands for national security, there emerged tonight the following positions of the five nations represented here: United States — Appears willing to enter a purely consultative five-power agreement, which would involve no American obligation, either expressed or implied, to give military support on the occasion of any threat of war in Europe. Such pledge under no circumstances is to be made in return for reduction of French navy figures as presented here. Great Britain — Is prepared to proceed with a general five-power (Continued on Page 10)

LONDON; Mar. 27—(#)—Naval conference circles today looked for important developments definitely leading to success or failure of the parley within one next few days. All delegations were considering fixing a date for a plenary session next week with the hope that political developments of recent date will have become settled. Prime Minister Briand of France is seeking an offer from England and the United States in return for reduction of France’s excessive naval estimates. The United States, Great Britain and Japan are making a supreme effort to produce a five-power treaty which will mean definite armament reduction as well as limitation of programs. The three powers, with a three-power treaty within their grasp, are making a last desperate attempt to extend the agreement to France and Italy.

LONDON, Mar. 27.—(I.N.S.)—Captain William Rind, of the American liner President Harding, died this morning of apoplexy. He was seized while on the bridge of his ship directing her course into Plymouth. Captain Rind was stricken at midnight. Fellow officers carried him to his cabin where he died at 4 o'clock this morning, 45 minutes after the ship had anchored. The President Harding departed for Cherbourg two hours later under command of First Officer Malcolm Mackenzie. Captain Rind’s body will be prepared for burial in Cherbourg and taken home aboard his last command.

Lendon, March 27—/p—Aristide Briand, French foreign minister, was reported unofficially today to have told Arthur Henderson, British foreign minister, that France would be able to cut her naval tonnage program if the five power naval conference would produce a pact of mutual guaranty for the Mediterranean. M. Briand indicated that he thought such a pact should be on the lines of the League of Nations model treaties for mutual guaranty which to his mind, would not mean that Great Britain would undertake obligations other than those which she has already accepted under article 15 of the covenant of the League of Nations. Conference circles today looked for important developments definitely leading to failure or success of the parley in its broader conception within the next few days. The heads of the five delegations had under consideration the fixing of a date for a plenary session next w

PARIS, March 27.—Lita Grey, divorced wife of Charlie Chaplin, hinted today that she and the famous comedian may some day become reconciled and revealed that Chaplin has engaged rooms in Paris six weeks from now. Chaplin and Miss Grey were married in Mexico in November, 1924, when she was only 16. Mrs. Chaplin obtained a divorce in 1928.

Berlin, March 27. (4)—The Mueller cabinet resigned today. The resignation followed all day discussions of party leaders which failed to result in an agreement on the question of unemployment insurance. The ministry, which has been in office almost two years, has had difficult sailings of late, particularly with the financial program of Dr. Paul Moldenhauer, minister of finance.

TURIN, Italy, March 27—(— Crown Prince Humbert, who recently took Princess Marie Jose of Belgium as his wife, was in bed today with measles. Physicians said the disease, usually associated with children, was running its course, and there had been a noticeable abatement of fever. He is residing at the Palace, refitted at the time he brought Princess Marie Jose here.

BERLIN, March 27. (AP) — Professor Albert Einstein has presented to the Prussian Academy of Sciences a new paper he has written with Dr. W. Mayer on two strictly static solutions of the field equations of his uniform field theory. It connects gravitation and electricity. Solutions Three solutions were described as follows: These field equations can be rigorously solved in two cases. The first case is that of a spherically symmetrical field in space, for example, the external field of an electrically charged sphere of fixed mass. The other case is that of the static field of any number of uncharged mass particles at rest with respect to one another.

SHANGHAI, March 25, ()—Almost nation-wide telegraphic investigation during the past 12 hours disclosed tonight that 16 American Catholic missionaries—10 men and six women—are at Kanchow, Kiangsi province, isolated from the outside world and unable to come to coastal cities to obtain safety due to the depredations of uncounted hordes of Chinese bandits and communists. PEIPING, China, March 25, e—C. T. Wang, nationalist government foreign minister, today telegraphed the American legation here that renewed measures are being taken to protect missionaries in Kanchow where 11 Roman Catholic missionaries are said to be besieged by a communist band.

| BERLIN, Mar. 27. (AP)—The coalition ministry of Chancellor Mueller resigned today because of the inability of the parties represented in it to agree on a policy toward unemployment insurance. The cabinet had been in office since June 28, 1928, and had weathered numerous difficulties including such problems as the ratification of the Young plan and the new law for the safety of the republic. It could not reach agreement on the unemployment insurance problem and saw no other alternative save resignation. BERLIN, March 27. (AP) — President Von Hindenburg today accepted the resignation of Chancellor Mueller’s coalition cabinet.

VIENNA, March 26 (By A. P.)—Dr. Hermann (Ernst) Watzl, the Cleveland chemist who died in a suicide pact here with Mrs. Mary McGranahan of Cleveland, not only fired the fatal shots in time to save his life insurance for the wife and children whom he had abandoned in the Ohio city, but also tried to get a similar benefit for Mrs. Eva Horvath, mother of Mrs. McGranahan. This developed late today when the Vienna Tageblatt learned that Watzl bought an accident and suicide policy for Mrs. McGranahan on the second day after their arrival here. The policy named Mrs. Horvath as beneficiary. The insurance company, however, announced it would not pay the policy. The suicide clause is not operative until two years after issuance of the insurance and besides, the company explained, Watzl entered into the contract under the false name of Flassak. This was the name which he assumed when he married Mrs.

Canton, March 27.—(A)—The exact whereabouts of sixteen American Catholic missionaries, besieged for three weeks at Kanchow, Kiangsi province, by bandits and communists, was uncertain today. Belief was expressed they had evacuated Kanchow fearing the city would fall before the bandits who have been raiding, killing and looting throughout the southern part of the province for months. The belief was based upon a telegram sent by the Rev. Father Young, a missionary stationed at Kanchow, saying that the communists and bandits had entered Nananfu, about fifty miles away. Father Young said he was preparing to leave the city although he did not give his destination. Contrary to this, however, was an unofficial Chinese dispatch which stated the communists had been dispersed near Kanchow, thus relieving the situation. Meanwhile communication with Kanchow continued fragmentary, bandits having halte

(U. P. Staff Correspondent) Rome, Mar. 25.--(UP)--The discovery of four new planets—one of them 500 times the volume of the earth—was claimed today by Prof. Rafael Bendandi, the widely-known seismologist and astronomer. The vast astral bodies, lying hundreds of millions of miles beyond distant Neptune, were described by Bendandi as far beyond the range of past astronomical discoveries except the recently found planet reported from Flagstaff, Arizona. Bendandi said he believed the second of the planets he had discovered was the one found by Prof. Percival Lowell. Bendandi said he was ready to submit his data to any body of astronomers or scientists. “I have fully identified the four planets and they exist beyond a doubt,” he said. Bendandi's claims were first made known to the United Press correspondent six months ago but at that time the Italian expert refused to permit publication of hi

PARIS, March 27—The Young plan and Premier Andre Tardieu won victories in the chamber of deputies today when the body accorded the premier a vote of confidence on his financial program. The vote was 319 to 262. At the same time, the chamber voted in favor of proceeding immediately with discussion of the Young plan, which is before the deputies for ratification. Opponents of the plan had attempted to postpone the discussion until the return of Foreign Minister Aristide Briand from London. Premier Tardieu was accused of sending his foreign minister out of the country in order to be able to jam through the reparations measure.

SHANGHAI.—()— French missionaries were reported safe Wednesday night in Kanchow, Kiangsi province, which has been besieged for three weeks by communist and bandit armies. The fate of ten men and six women of the American Catholic mission in Kanchow remained unknown. The besieging banditry, said a nationalist government news agency dispatch, was scattered by a sortie of the provincial garrison. Efforts to communicate with the Americans were futile, the bandits halting telegraphic communication. Checked for the time at Kanchow, the lawless forces which have despoiled Kiangsi province for many months, attacked and captured the towns of Sinfeng and Taiyi in southern Kiangsi, said dispatches. Chu Teh, leader of the communist-bandit armies, educated in Canton in military tactics and formerly a student in several European countries whose languages he speaks, long has defied government troops as

| VIENNA, March 27, ()—An accident and suicide insurance policy taken out by Dr. Hermann (Ernst) Watzl of Cleveland for his bigamous bride, Mrs. Mary McGranahan of that city, a few days before he shot her and then himself in a hotel here was said by the insurance company to be void. The company said it would not pay the policy, which was made out to Mrs. Eva Hovarth of Cleveland, mother of Mrs. McGranahan, inasmuch as the suicide clause was not operative for two years after issuance of the policy, and because, besides, Watzl procured the policy under the false name of Flassak. It was secured on the second day of their arrival here, By shooting himself shortly before midnight Sunday, when the premiums on his own policy of $35,000 expired, Watzl is believed here to have assured collection of the amount by his wife and two daughters in Cleveland. Messina, Italy, March 27 (UP)— Thousands were reported homeless today and several villages destroyed in a violent earthquake which struck the islands off the North coast of Sicily. The authorities of the province of Messina reporting the quake said the village of Filicudi on the island of that name had been destroyed. The shock occurred at 11:42 a. m. yesterday. Destroyers and steamers were reported hurrying medicine and food to the island. All houses in the Lipari islands were said to have been rendered uninhabitable.

Berlin, March 28—President Von Hindenburg had accepted the resignation of Chancellor Mueller's coalition cabinet. The president requested that the cabinet continue in office until its successor could be appointed. Chancellor Mueller was understood to have recommended to Von Hindenburg that Heinrich Bruening, a Centrist member of the Reichstag, be asked to form a new government.

Paris, March 27..-Premier Andre Tardieu rallied his forces in the Chamber of Deputies today to fight off opposition to ratification of the Owen D. Young plan and the Hague reparations accords. The chamber passed, by a vote of 319 to 262, a vote of confidence in the premier, rejecting a proposal for postponement of discussion on the Young plan. The chamber previously had given the premier two votes of confidence by acclamation. Heated debate and threats of fist fights on the floor of the chamber preceded the voting.
WARSAW, Poland, Mar. 26. (AP) — Jean Pilsudski, brother of Marshal Pilsudski, and a member of the government bloc in the coalition, today was asked to form a cabinet. He accepted,

(By The Associated Press) Paris, March 27.—Premier Tardieu won his first skirmishes on the bill for ratification for the Young plan in the chamber of deputies today. He twice proposed a question of confidence and each was sustained, first by raised hands and second by a vote of 319 against 262.

1930-05-03.text: London, May 3—(AP)—The next move of the government in India was awaited here today with considerable interest. Feeling was widespread that it would involve the arrest of Mahatma Gandhi, leader of the civil disobedience campaign. Bombay dispatches indicated the arrest might be made whenever Gandhi fulfills either of two threats, the first to come to Bombay to lead personally his passive resistance movement, or the other to move on Dharsana and seize the government controlled salt depots there. A Bombay dispatch to the Daily Mail suggested that Gandhi knowingly had placed conditions on his going to Bombay which he knew would not be complied with. These conditions included a requirement of 100,000 followers, wearing homespun, forswearing violence, practicing rigorous self-denial and pledging themselves to devote one hour each day to hard spinning. The Mail said that fewer than 3,000 had res

CALCUTTA, Bengal. Play 3.—(?) —Police with lathis, or staves, injured several persons today when they broke up a procession in honor of the arrival of V. J. Patel, former speaker of the Indian Legislative Assembly. Patel, who resigned recently in collaboration with the civil disobedience movement of Mahatma Gandhi, was received at Howrah, a suburban station by authorities of the All-India National Congress and the municipal corporation.

London, May 3 (UP)—The British steamer Hollywood was damaged seriously and was in a sinking condition after a collision with the British steamer Maine, a Lloyd's dispatch from Greenheights, near London on the Thames river, said today. The Hollywood was damaged amidships and was making for shore above the Stoness lighthouse.

LONDON, May 3. — (AP) — Lloyd’s Gravesend wireless station said today the British Steamers Maine, from New York and Hollywood outward bound collided at Long Beach this morning. The Hollywood was put ashore seriously damaged. “The Hollywood's principal injuries were on her starboard side, abreast of No. 2 hold. The ship was a small coasting trade vessel plying between London and Sunderland. The Maine proceeded to Royal Dock, with extent of its damage unknown here.

LONDON, May 3.—(I.N.S.)—Martial law was declared in Harbin, Manchuria, today after a communist demonstration before the Japanese consulate, according to a dispatch to the Daily Telegraph. Rioting broke out and scores of agitators were arrested.

London, May 3.—It was understood today that the Prince of Wales probably would receive promotion in both army and navy during this year. Reports said he would be gazetted a major general in a few months and possibly promoted to the rank of Rear Admiral.

LONDON, May 3, (/)—Jennie Lee, veteran actress famous the world over for her impersonation of Jo, the crossing sweeper, in Dickens’ Bleak House, died today in London at the age of 72. In her youthful days she won a triumph in this part of San Francisco and other American cities. Her son was killed in the World War and her husband died soon afterwards. She has been put in recent years in reduced circumstances.

President Hoover tells the United States Chamber of Commerce, “While the crash only took place six months ago, I am convinced we have passed the worst, and with continued unity of effort we shall rapidly recover.” That will encourage many. And the banks, reducing interest charges here and abroad, will help. When money is cheap capital looks to new enterprises, which means hiring labor. Lowering the federal reserve discount rate to 8 per cent in the New York district surprised all that lack advance information. In accordance with our custom we followed the British, lowering our rate here when theirs was lowered. This gratifies England, which feared that a rate lower than ours would cause British gold shipments to this country. The late W. J. Bryan would be amazed to hear congress discussing tariff protection for silver. He thought silver, at sixteen to one, could stand forever as gold’s y

LONDON, May 28. (AP) — Viscount Bridgeman of Leigh, formerly lord of the admiralty, who headed the British delegation at the Geneva naval conference in 1927, has come out in drastic criticism of the London naval agreement. In a speech at Weymouth last night he assailed the London treaty as endangering the security of the British empire, and as providing for too great a cut in the British cruiser program. “I very much regret this agreement,” he said, “partly because it does very little in the way of economy, partly because it gives away the most important part of our fleet, and gives us practically nothing in return.”

BOMBAY, India, May 2—(AP)—While Mahatma Gandhi was making known today the conditions under which he will agree to lead his civil resistance campaign into the City of Bombay, all India awaited tensely the arrest of “the holy man” which usually well-informed persons continued to insist must occur before another day has elapsed. Conditions which the venerable leader announced he would exact from his followers as the price for continuing into the city were printed today by the “Bombay Congress Bulletin,” an unregistered sheet published daily by the Bombay Provincial Congress committee. The conditions comprise: observance of complete discipline, a permanent pledge to wear handspun khaddar and the actual spinning with “tokli,” a miniature spinning wheel for one hour daily. “If Bombay produces 100,000 such men,” the manifesto of Mahatma Gandhi concludes, “I shall lead them without the slightest

BOMBAY, May 3. (U.P)—A firmer attitude against Mahatma Gandhi's followers in his passive resistance campaign in India was urged on the British government today by the Bombay branch of the European association. A committee of the branch, in a letter to Sir Frederick Sykes, Governor of Bombay, asked that the government arrest all persons who invite the natives against the government. The present policy of the government is being interpreted as weakness, the committee said it believed, and the law is being brought into contempt. Counter propaganda is necessary in the campaign against Gandhi, the committee wrote, urging the government to issue communiques stating its real position throughout the presidency.

TOKYO, May 3.—(4)—The death toll in a typhoon which swept the southern portion of Saghalien island and the northern coast of Hokkaido reached nearly 200 today in reports to Rengo News agency from Odomari. The messages said the bodies of 94 victims had been recovered, and that 100 others were missing. The storm descended upon Odomari bay, at the southern end of Saghalien, just after 10,000 fishermen had been attracted to sea by the appearance of great schools of herring. About 2,000 fishing boats were out when the typhoon struck. Property damage has been estimated at $2,500,000.

Le Bourget, May 2.—(7)—A French girl flyer, Mile. Lena Bernstein, today hung up a new endurance mark of 85 hours, 46 minutes, 55 seconds for women. She beat by almost 10 hours the women's endurance record recognized here—that of Mile. Maryse Bastie, who flew for 26 hours, 46 minutes and 30 seconds last July. By almost the same margin she exceeded the American women's endurance record achieved a year ago by Miss Elinor Smith at Roosevelt Field, N. Y., a mark of 26 hours, 21 minutes and 32 seconds. For Both Sexes Mile. Bernstein took off at 7:18 o'clock yesterday morning and landed here at a fraction after 7:04 tonight when her fuel had been exhausted. It was announced her flight constituted a world record for airplanes of all categories having only one pilot, male or female.

TOKO, May 3. (UP)—Approximately 200 Japanese fishermen apparently lost their lives in a storm in Aniwa Bay last night, dispatches received here today said. Their herring hauls valued at $2,000,000 were lost when a number of fishing vessels went down. Half the fishing tools of boats which did not sink were washed away. Dispatches said 221 fishermen were aboard the vessels and only 25 were rescued.

LE BOURGET, France May 2 (UP)—Mile Lena Bernstein landed at the airport here today after breaking all women's records for endurance flight. She had been in the air 85 hours and 46 minutes when the plane landed at 7:04 P. M.—less than an hour short of the goal she had set for herself.

Tokyo, May 3.—(P)—Fears that a typhoon which swept Southern Saghalien and Northern Hokkaido Islands had taken a heavy death toll among the fishermen were reported today in dispatches to Rengo News Agency from To 2 and Otari. The typhoon hit the area last night. About 100 persons were missing and were believed to have drowned. Several bodies were washed ashore. Property damage was estimated at 5,000,000 yen (about $2,500,000). The storm struck just when the appearance of great schools of fish in Odomaria Bay had drawn 2,000 fishing boats, carrying 10,000 fishermen to sea.

BERLIN, May 3. (INS)—Fifteen guards and five soldiers were injured, some of them seriously, when political prisoners in the Riga jail staged a bloody but short-lived revolt, it was reported in dispatches from Riga to the Telegrafen-Union here today. Stirred to insurrection by alleged Communist propaganda, the prisoners attempted to battle their way out of the jail, and the riot was quelled only after heavily armed troops had been rushed to the scene. Similar revolts took place almost simultaneously at the Mitau and other prisons, the dispatches declared. LONDON, May 3. (INS)—Martial law was declared in Harbin, Manchuria, today after a Communist demonstration before the Japanese consulate, according to a dispatch to the Daily Telegraph. Rioting broke out and scores of agitators were arrested. All foreign consulates in Harbin were closely guarded. It generally was believed the disturbances

BERNE, SWITZERLAND, May 3.—(#)—The Swiss government today awaited the answer of President Hoover to its plea for consideration of the Swiss position in promulgation of the proposed new American tariff schedules. President Jean Marie Musy in a personal letter emphasized the importance of the branches of Swiss industry that he had been led to his direct step. He asked the president to consider the disastrous effects to Switzerland of the proposed duties, particularly on watches, shoes, cheese and silk.

Amsterdam, Holland, May 3.—(UP)—The British steamer Raven went down in the North Sea after a collision with the Greek steamer Cleopatra near the Island of Borkum today, advices from the Island of Terschelling said. The Cleopatra saved the crew of the Raven. The Raven is a steamer of 1,337 tons.

Paris —(4)— France had a round 2,000,000,000 budget this year, the largest it has ever had if war expenses are expected. In francs this is 60,298,159,195, which figures roughly as $50 for each of the 46,606,000 people. This is about one-third more than the per capita expense of the United States government. Half the French expense, however, is war debts and reconstruction. This big budget was adopted after several months of wrangling. Although it is the biggest and is twice the gold value of the previous budget, the beginning of taxation and deflation. Mend Poineare, former premier, who was called to the cue of the tumbling franc in 1928, demanded and was given a free hand in finance and his task was to load on some more taxes and cut a list of expenses. Surprise To Americans It was the most important development for some time in the conference activities and was the subject of discussion in all conference circles. | Ottawa, March 29.—(P)—Premier W. L. Mackenzie King announced to the House of Commons yesterday that Canada is negotiating with the United States for a treaty to suppress smuggling. He said the object of the treaty was not only to stop liquor traffic but was designed to prevent smuggling of all kinds of merchandise both ways across the border. The announcement was made in the course of the debate on the amendment to the export bill introduced by Mr. King for the purpose of denying customs clearances to craft carrying liquor to the United States. The measure has passed its second reading.

London, March 25 (#).—A formal plenary session of the five power naval conference next week will inform the world what has been accomplished in ten weeks of negotiations and what hopes are held out for naval disarmament. The chief delegates of the five powers decided upon this course this afternoon, the exact date of the plenary session will be fixed Thursday after Foreign Minister Briand returns from Paris to head the French delegation. Picture Changed In conference circles tonight the coming session was described by delegates as one of hope instead of despair, this indicating an entire change of the conference picture, since this morning. There is no talk of adjournment, and the reports of a six month interval, which today became tangled in a skein of confirmations and denials, the proposal for adjournment being credited both to the Italians and British, gave way to more constructive n

| LONDON, March 26 (UP). — Hope of a five-power naval agreement was revived today, at least temporarily, with official announcement that the United States is willing to enter into a “consultative pact” without pledging, either actually or in inference, the use of military or naval forces to protect France from aggression. Whether such an agreement will satisfy France's demands for a security pact as the price of reducing her tonnage figures appeared to rest today upon the question of how much farther than this Great Britain is willing to go in the way of military guarantees.

London, Today.—(P)—If France can obtain the military guarantees of security she wants from some other nation the United States delegation to the Five Power Naval Conference will consider a proposal for a so-called consultative pact “with an entirely open mind.” A statement issued by the American delegation shortly after last midnight reiterated formerly expressed unwillingness to enter into any treaty involving the United States in any sort of a military guarantee of French security. The consultative pact would merely involve consultation with the other five powers in the event of a threat of war. Denial was made in the statement!

LONDON— (Wednesday)—(1) Rumors current late Tuesday night that the naval conference had undergone a dramatic development by the fact that the American delegation had informed their colleagues that they were prepared to make a new proposal were published in the midnight edition of the Daily Herald, laborite newspaper close to government sources. The Herald said that this proposal was the result of a consultation between the delegation and President Hoover, who had decided to reconsider his decision that in no case would the United States be a party to any "security" treaty. The implication was that the United States had changed its attitude toward consultative pacts, and was willing to enter a pact on changed lines in order to save the conference. The Daily Herald's story, contrary to the American delegation’s statement that President Hoover had played no part in the discussions of politi

SYDNEY, N.S. W., Mar. 26—(INS)—A huge crowd stood in wonder today before a great festoon of lights in city hall. Lights that glowed and faded with the impulses of a radio wave sent 11,000 miles by Signor Guglielmo Marconi, from his yacht outside Genoa Harbor. When the spectators realized the significance of the marvel involved in this successful demonstration of radio wizardry they began cheering. Australian electrical engineers had successfully operated a two-way radio telephone between Australia and Italy. GENOA, Mar. 26.—(INS)—Aboard the yacht Electra, Signor Marconi today successfully lighted an electric exhibition in the city of Sydney, New South Wales, 11,660 miles away, by means of his new radio wave.

LONDON, Mar, 26.—Fanning the spark of life breathed into the London naval conference by the reinstatement of America’s willingness to center a consultative pact provided no military guarantees are involved, Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald today was reported ready to grant France at least some measure of the security she desires. Determined to keep the conference alive in order to maintain the prestige of his labor government, Premier MacDonald is understood to be prepared to grant some political concessions to France. Just what they will be is a matter for conjecture at the moment.

LONDON, March 26.—Another important step in the difficult task of nursing the five-power naval disarmament conference back to life was understood to have been accomplished today when the British cabinet approved Prime Minister J. Ramsey MacDonald's proposal for extending France security guarantees. According to the London Evening Star, the cabinet, meeting in full session, sanctioned the premier’s suggestion that Great Britain sign a pact guaranteeing France's interests in the Mediterranean if the United States will enter into a consultative treaty.

Ottawa, March 25.—(AP)— Premier W. L. Mackenzie King's bill to amend the export act was passed on the third reading by the house of commons today, by a vote of 173 to 11. The bill, which grants the government authority to refuse clearance to liquor shipments destined for the United States, now goes to the senate. The reading of the bill followed spirited debate. Representatives of several parties united to furnish the 11 votes which opposed the measure. Eight conservatives were joined by a single liberal, Maj. C. G. Power, member for Quebec, south; Henry Bourassa, Independent member of Lavelle, and A. A. Heaps, labor member for Winnipeg, north. Should Resign During the debate, R. B. Bennett, conservative leader, challenged the government to resign, declaring that self-respecting ministers would resign in a case of this nature. This demand followed a charge that the government had changed

Borach, Bombay, India, Mar. 25 (/P) —There are 18 invalids among the 79 devotees who are following Mahatma Gandhi from Ahmadabad to the sea at Jalalpur, where they will manufacture salt in defiance of the British monopoly. Gandhi leaving Samni for Tralsa today left general directions to be followed, and asked that prayers be said for the safety of his party.

Vienna, March 25, (4)--The mystery surrounding the disappearance of Dr. Hermann (Ernst) Watzl, Cleveland chemist and inventor, of Austrian birth, was cleared today after an inquiry in three continents for four months. The body of a man found shot dead in a dingy hotel room yesterday was definitely identified as that of the chemist by his father, H. Watzl. A woman lying near Watzl's body and also shot dead, was said to be Mrs. Mary McCranahan, of Cleveland. A rapid medical examination resulted in a statement that Watzl had killed the woman and then shot himself through the heart. A mysterious letter was thought by Vienna police to have had some thing to do with the missing chemist’s suicide and the killing of the woman. They said that the shooting had followed the receipt of this letter by Watzl, but searched everywhere for it unavailingly. They surmised that he had destroyed it. In any c

By Associated Press, Rome, March 26, The Society for the Propagation of the Faith, missionary organization of the Roman Catholic Church, today received a cablegram from Shanghai reporting that eleven American priests at Kanchow, Kansi, for whose safety there had been fears, had been freed by lifting of a communist siege there. All were well.

Sweeoe, 108i yer — Sonore 34 radio Waves, cutting across the Atlantic, America and the Pacific, Wednesday carried the voice of Marquis Guglielmo Marconi, inventor of wireless telegraphy, from his yacht Electra here to Sydney, Australia, to open the electrical exposition there. Marconi's assistant, Matthieu Beaman, tested the short wave apparatus at 8 a.m. As soon as the operation was concluded, Sgr. Marconi took the phone. He spoke across 11,000 miles to the direction of electrical association, reading a message which outlined what he intended doing later in the day—transmitting a small unit of power to Sydney in order to close a circuit there and light the electric lamps of the exposition. He then handed the phone to Andrue Berding, Associated Press Staff correspondent, who conveyed greetings of the newspapermen assembled for the ceremony at Genoa.

Vienna, March 26,--(4/P)--Although Dr. Wermann (frost) Watzl, chemist and inventor, died in a suicide pact with another woman, his last thoughts were of his American wife at home in Cleveland, and their two children. The exact time of the shots which first killed his bigamous bride, formerly Miss Mary McGrarahan, of Cleveland, and then took his own life, has not been determined, but it is believed they were fired just before midnight Sunday, when his life insurance premium would have expired. A letter to a Vienna fatimate, found near the body of Watzl as it was discovered in the Hotel Sacher, contained the passage: "Knowing the custom of insurance companies I realized that my wife would be unable to cash my policy of $35,000 unless she could establish my death officially. But I also knew that the claim would fail if my premiums were not paid regularly to my death. Then I remembered the i

By The Associated Press. Shanghai, March 25.—Sixteen American Catholic missionaries, ten of whom are men and six women, are isolated in Kanchow, Kiangsi province by bandit and communist armies, and their situation is reported serious. The red forces are said to surround Kanchow, refusing to permit anyone to depart or enter. In a telegram to the Associated Press from Nanking, Foreign Minister C. T. Wang said: "The national government has taken strong measures to suppress the Kiangsi communists. It believes the American missionaries are safe if they do not attempt to move about." Reinforcements Being Sent A small number of government troops is at Kanchow, said a message from the Chinese foreign office to the American legation at Peking, and the government is endeavoring to send reinforcements. Threats have been made by Kiangsi authorities to withdraw the garrison from Kanchow; however, sai

Aboard Yacht Electra, Off Genoa, March 26.—(U.P)—From a new special apparatus set up in his sea-going laboratory, Guglielmo Marconi today transmitted sufficient electrical power to Sydney, Australia, to close a circuit and throw on the current that lighted thousands of lamps at Australia’s electro-technical show. Previous to the test, at 11 a.m., Rome time, a United Press staff correspondent exchanged wireless telephone conversations with newspapermen at Sydney. He was informed that everything was in readiness at the Sydney city hall, where the electrical show is in progress, for the radio-mechanical action lighting the auditorium. Marconi, taking the radiophone transmitter before the test, read a message of greeting. He recalled that it was 30 years ago that he first transmitted faint signals across the Atlantic Ocean. Previous to the test, the Italian radio expert emphasized that his f

{BY Bons tovwwu STUTTGART, Germany, Mar. 25. —The seventh person died here today from eating bear ham sold here by a butcher last week without government inspection. Sixty cases of trichinosis have developed.

Shanghai, March 25.—The American Yangtse Rapids steamer, the Ifung, was fired upon late yesterday by Communists waving red flags, 200 miles above Hankow. . . The steamer was subjected to 2 sharp rifle barrages which were returned by the American armed naval guard aboard the vessel. F.C. Roberts, a member of the American guard, was wounded in the left arm during the skirmish.

Moscow, Mar. 26. (4).—Complete "Americanization" of its industries appears to be the goal of the Soviet government. Under the stimulus of American engineering skill and enterprise, the government today decided to erect this year, along modern American lines, a series of huge industrial plants costing $2,150,000,000. The government is scrapping most other methods of construction and adopting those which have given the United States first place in world industry. No less than 39 American engineering and technical firms are now operating in Soviet Russia, between them supervising nearly $3,000,000,000 worth of construction. Since withdrawal of W. A. Harriman & Co. from the big Georgian Manganese concession, no American financial interests have invested capital in Soviet enterprises, but the number of American engineering firms securing profitable contracts is increasing. The Red forces are said to surround Kanchow, refusing to permit anyone to depart or enter. In a telegram to the Associated Press from Nanking, Foreign Minister C. T. Wang said: “The Nationalist government has taken strong measures to suppress the Kiangsi Communists. It believes the American missionaries are safe, if they do not attempt to move about.” A small number of government troops is at Kanchow, said a message from the Chinese foreign office to the American legation at Peiping, and the government is endeavoring to send reinforcements. Threats have been made by Kiangsi authorities to withdraw the garrison from Kanchow, however, said missionary advices, which expressed th

Milan, Italy, March 20.—“Pluto” is the provisional name that Italian astronomers have given the new trans-Neptune planet discovered March 13 at Lowell Observatory, in Flagstaff, Ariz. Professor Emilio Bianchi, and his assistants of Brera Observatory, have photographed the new planet, despite the fact that the weather had been bad, and they hope with one more night to contribute somewhat to the American researches. Professor Bianchi sees the American discovery as substantiating Newton’s theory of the law of gravity. He also paid tribute to Professor Percival Lowell, who first predicted a planet would be found in the position of the new body, and paid tribute to the work of his successor in the last fourteen years.

BPE ERIS Rr ee Paris, March 26.—Aristide Briand, French foreign minister and head of his government’s delegation at the five-power naval conference at London, entrained at noon today for the British capital, where he will partake once more in the conference.

1930-05-25.text: PORT DARWIN, Australia, May 24—(#)—Miss Amy Johnson, 23-year-old English flier, reached this city this afternoon from Atamboea, Timor, after a flight of 400 miles across the adjacent sea. In reaching her destination, she has completed a 19 day flight from England to her destination. She left Croydon, England at the outset of her flight.

“London, May 25— (AP) — (Sunday) — Lord Davidson, former Archbishop of Canterbury and primate of England, died at 1:05 o’clock this morning. Lord Davidson resigned the “throne of Saint Augustine” November 12, 1928, after parliament had for the second time rejected the revised Anglican prayer book, acceptance of which he had sought as the crown of his long ecclesiastical career. His stout heart never recovered from this political blow, which had crushed his hopes and sent him voluntarily into retirement. His resignation came at a time when two forces in the Church of England, one moving toward modernism and the other toward stricter observance of the ritual and cere- (Continued on Page 1, 2nd Section)

DARWIN, Australia, May 24— Miss Amy Johnson, 22-year-old British flyer, completed a hazardous 9,900-mile solo flight from England when she landed here safely at 3:57 p.m. today (1:27 a.m. eastern standard time). Miss Johnson failed to break the solo flight record of 154 days made by Bert Hinkler three years ago, but in her trip across Europe, Asia and the Malay settlements she flew through storms and met with accidents which threatened at times to force her to return home in defeat.

LONDON, May 24 (#)—The news from India today showed that a new form of civil resistance was taking place in Calcutta. While the women in other parts of India are supporting raids on the government salt works or are picketing liquor and foreign cloth shops, the women of Calcutta decided to stop football play. Women pickets gathered on the main grounds where league football matches were to be played, and, by obstructing the main entrances to pavilions, prevented the players from entering or emerging and thus effectively stopped all play. Karachi was another new center. The police there raided a shop which had been selling contraband salt and seized a large quantity of the condiment. A melee developed in which several persons were injured and the police charged with their stocks to restore order. At Karachi also there developed Moslem sentiment for the campaign of the Hindu nationalists, so

BOMBAY, India, (UP).—The casualties of the volunteer raid on the Dharasana salt works were paraded through Bombay Saturday in an effort to arouse enthusiasm for renewed raids Sunday on the Wadala depot near here. Ambulances carried injured volunteers—some of them bandaged and garlanded with flowers—past cheering crowds. Nationalist flags were waved and traffic was paralyzed. The crowds rushed the street cars and took possession of them, disconnecting the power lines. Several hundred women marchers wore red robes. The congress leaders meanwhile arranged for a mass attack on the Wadala depot early Sunday, having enrolled about 40 prominent Mohamedans to aid them.
AMRITSAR, India, May 24 UT - Twenty persons, including several children, were injured by the explosion of a bomb today at a religious fair.

BOMBAY, May 24.—(UP)—A partial strike was observed in Bombay today as National Congress Volunteers prepared to stage another huge demonstration in protest against the British government’s action in sending troops to Dharasana. The customary daily raid on the Wadala Salt works, near Bombay, was abandoned today, but Congress leaders said they expected to make a mass raid on the works tomorrow, similar to the raid made there last Sunday. The raid tomorrow, however, may not be so good-natured as the previous one. The passive resistance campaigners have shown stronger tendencies to use force during the week than at any time since the independence drive started, and there were some fears that they may forget Mahatma Gandhi's teachings when they descend on the big salt works. Serves Sentence In addition, their post-leader, Mrs. Sarojini Naidu, now is serving a prison sentence as a result of her

PORT DARWIN, Australia, May 24—Amy Johnson, radiant spirit of the modern girl, slid into the airfield here today in a light sport plane and combed her hair. In back of her was the wholehearted adulation of the British empire. But it wasn't important. The 23-year-old aviatrix had spanned 11,000 miles of the hardest flying territory there is in temperate or tropic belts. “I'm so happy,” she said. “The last hop (a span of 300 miles from Timor Island to Australia) was excellent and I enjoyed it all the way.” Miss Johnson was a perfect example of what Australia likes—nonchalance. As soon as she cut the switch, Amy lifted herself over the cockpit. Port Darwin, nearly everyone that lives there was on hand and was prepared to help a weary girl to her well-earned rest. A radiant figure hopped to the ground. She took off her hat, and out came the pocket comb. Then, the crowd arrived. The “three ch

Fort Darwin, North Australia, May 24 ().—A slight 23-year-old English girl, dressed in khaki shirt and shorts with a green sun helmet, stepped from a diminutive moth monoplane here today finishing the last lap of a flight from England to Australia. The girl, Amy Johnson, made the long and perilous trip in nineteen days. She really required twenty flying days, but gained eight hours against English summer time in the journey eastward. Drowned by the sun and deafened by the roar of her motor, the blond young Briton made a spectacular landing to be greeted by a huge and cheering crowd.

| FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, Germany, May 21 (%.—The dirigible Graf Zeppelin wirelessed her home port this afternoon that she passed the Cape Verde islands at 6:16 p.m. mid-European time (12:15 p.m. B. S. T.) The Graf reported that all was well aboard the huge ship which now is headed across the South Atlantic for Brazil. The Graf, at the time of her message, was about 800 miles north of the equator and about 1400 miles from Pernambuco, Brazil, the first South American destination.

Paris, May 24—(®)—A dispatch from Jeddah, Arabia to the Petit Parisien today said that 50 Moslem pilgrims aboard the burning steamer Asia in Jeddah harbor Wednesday cut one another's throats rather than face death in the blaze. Their act, the dispatch which purports to be an eyewitness account of the disaster which is now said to have taken 200 lives, took place at the foot of the companion way and before the cry, “everybody for himself” was heard. Like Sacrificial Blood Flow The blood of the suicides flowed as if at a sacrifice. Their bodies blocked up the exit and prevented others praying with their faces toward Mecca in the dining saloon, finally from reaching the outside, causing their death, too. Fires, origin of which has not been determined, spread so rapidly it was possible to lower boats only on the starboard side. Two boats lowered were sunk immediately by pilgrims who jumped a

Vienna, May 26.—Prince Cantacuzene was killed in an airplane accident today, a dispatch from Bucharest reported. A small airplane carrying the prince and Princess Myrcea Cantacuzene fell 600 feet while flying at the Baniaza airdrome. The princess was slightly injured.

Auteuil, France, May 24 (AP) The powerful American combination of Helen Wills Moody and Elizabeth Ryan captured the French women’s doubles tennis championship today, defeating Mme. Simone Mathieu and Mlle. Yvette Parbier of France in the final at 6-3, 6-1. Bill Tilden and Wilbur Coen, America’s representatives in the men's doubles championship chase, were eliminated in the quarter finals by the French team of Jean Borotra and Rene de Buzelet. The scores were 6-2, 8-10, 5-7, 6-3, 7-5.

Paris, France, May 24. —The worst possible French weather, which sets most people to coughing and sneezing, seems to bother little the stout-hearted American Gold Star mothers and wives who came to France to visit the graves of their sons and husbands. Even as America’s khaki-clad youth slogged along in French mud in 1917-18 so have the Gold Star mothers and wives continued their tours of battlefields and cemeteries without flinching. A few have been induced to rest, principally because of chronic heart troubles, but that cannot be charged to the present tour.

MILAN, Italy, May 24.—(U.R)— Shouts of “Down with France!” were raised here today in the midst of a vigorous speech by Premier Mussolini, who reviewed 16,000 troops and then addressed a great crowd that gathered on the reviewing grounds. “We must be prepared for any surprises of tomorrow,” said the premier in defending the Fascist regime.

Shanghai, Sep 24. Scarred by civil war, banditry has become rampant in virtually every province of China south of the Yangtze valley and in several north of it. Bandit armies, freed of military control by Nationalist government troops now engaged in combatting the revolt by the northern alliance, are looting, killing and kidnapping in wholesale fashion. Foreign consuls have renewed their warnings to their nationals to evacuate the interior. The provinces of Honan, Hupeh and Kiangsi were declared dangerous by the British authorities, because of air raids by forces contending in civil war in Honan and the banditry in Hupeh and Kiangsi.

By The Associated Press. DETMOLD, Germany, May 24 Officials announced today that 56 persons had died here presumably as a result of eating impure ice cream. They showed symptoms of typhoid fever. The health department has begun an investigation.

1930-06-02.text: Bombay — A drizzling rain fell over Bombay presidency Monday, marking the first of the rainy season, which comes every summer with the arrival of the monsoon. This year the rain will mark the end of an important phase of the Indian nationalist civil disobedience campaign. The showers will be torrents Tuesday and the salt deposit areas, such as at Wadala and Dharasana, will become morasses of mud and slime, inaccessible to the raiders who during the last two months have harassed British police guarding them. The final raid of the year at Wadala was undertaken Sunday by 14,000 nationalist volunteers and spectators. The presence of troops was believed to have restrained the crowd somewhat, although about 150 persons were injured when the police charged with their bamboo clubs. Raids Will Cease There will be some further raiding at Dharasana but even this will cease within a few days. There

MM SENTIMENT MAJORITY ON TREATY ASSURED LONDON—George Lambert, speaking for the liberals in debate on the naval treaty, today supported the government, thus assuring a government majority on the treaty question.

Bombay, June 2.—(A4)—Official India today could cease to worry about ‘Indian nationalists’ raids on the government salt pans, but faced a problem of greater importance—non-payment of taxes, which is being instigated as the next step in the nationalist campaign of civil disobedience. A “final” salt raid was undertaken Sunday at Wadala by 15,000 nationalist volunteers and spectators who had prepared for a week for the occasion. One hundred and fifty of their number were injured by the police, but the remainder broke through the cordon and obtained bags full of salt. Holding the salt aloft, and with their bodies covered with slime and mud, the volunteers paraded the streets of Bombay calling aloud: “We have broken the salt laws.” The spirit of the crowd was subdued, however, in comparison with recent raids, a development which authorities attributed to troops which were on hand in the event

LONDON, June 1 (By A. P.)— For the first time in the history of England, Scotland Yard today enrolled eight women detectives. No hard-faced women are these. Known as the “mystery eight,” the women were chosen for their looks, education and knowledge of police work. They will work under Miss Dorothy Peto, who recently joined Scotland Yard as a staff officer for women police. The women will be assigned to the general work of crime detection, various police stations to assist in but at first will be detailed to investigate traffic in women and the peddling of narcotics.

LONDON, June 2.—Former Premier Baldwin, in moving a resolution in the House of Commons today that a committee be appointed to report on the Naval treaty, said the country wanted to know more exactly to what it had been committed. The former premier said that the Americans had investigated and were satisfied, adding: “Why should we have the same thing here in order that we may satisfy ourselves as to the effect of the treaty on ourselves.” The country wanted to know before it was committed to the treaty, continued the former premier, “whether our security in the first place remains, whether we shall be in a position in any circumstances to fulfill our own sacred obligations under the League of Nations, thirdly, which is the most important, how we stand and how we shall stand in the future with regard to European standards of naval construction.” Relying, Prime Minister MacDonald said that

LONDON, June 2-17). A dispatch to the Daily Herald today from its Bombay correspondent quoted a “high official” as saying that if by the end of the year the tax-resistance campaign is succeeding the government will be faced with considerable financial embarrassment. The dispatch added that hope prevailed that civil resistance would have been checked or abandoned by then, “although at the moment all signs point in the contrary direction. The correspondent said the growth of the Gandhi movement was shown by the increased number of persons wearing the Gandhi jeans, which is the symbol of the Nationalist campaign. Concurrently he said there has been an intensification of the boycott of British goods.

Eastbourne, Ene., June 2, — Fifteen members of the crew of the Swedish steamer Ingar were feared to have been lost today as the result of a collision with the Italian motorship Literno in the English Channel. The collision occurred off Reachy Head in a dense fog. The Ingar sank immediately, and although the Italian vessel cruised around for several hours in the vicinity of the crash only two survivors were picked up.

BOMBAY, India, June 2.—Wholesale defiance of the government's ordinance against picketing shops selling foreign goods or liquor was inaugurated today by the India Independence volunteers. More than 500 women volunteers renewed picketing of foreign cloth shops in Bombay and the local congress were organizing more volunteers for the work, which was expected to replace the practice of raiding salt depots. The picketing campaign was a direct challenge to the recent ordinance of the Viceroy, Lord Irwin, and was expected by many observers to decide definitely the strength of the home rule movement. The independence leaders also have planned to defy the viceroy’s order to halt propagandizing against payment of land taxes. Seventy-two makers of contraband salt from Worli, where almost 1000 Satyagrahis are in prison, were sen-

LONDON, June 2—British military forces moved quickly today in the Peshawar district in retaliation for the recent outbreak of violence there, in which seven persons were killed and nine injured. Troops occupied the villages of Charaadia and Prang, where a disquieting situation prevailed, threatening further outbreaks. Eight alleged Communist agitators were arrested, according to Yeshwar dispatches. The third month of Mahatma Gandhi's passive resistance campaign for Indian independence was ushered in yesterday with a raid on the Wadala textile works and renewed rioting at Peshawar, a strategic hub at the entrance to the Khyber Pass. Seven Indians were killed and nine injured at Peshawar, an official announcement from the government of India said, while at least 20 were injured in the Wadala raid. National Congress sources claimed 100 were injured at Wadala, although they admitted most wer

(By The Associated Press) Bombay, June 1—Fifteen thousand Indians surged through a two-mile cordon of police at the Wadala Salt works today and left behind 190 injured. So overwhelmed were the police that they called troops to assist them, but the area was quiet tonight and the soldiers were withdrawn. Staves Freely Used The police used their bamboo staves freely, thus accounting for the 150 casualties, but the Nationalists who were unhurt emerged with handfuls of salt and considered their onslaught triumphant. The attack had been advertised as a “final raid” by the Nationalist leaders, and they had spent a week in preparing for it. Many persons were arrested and among them were nine women, headed by Mrs. K. M. Munshi, wife of a former member of the legislative assembly.
SYDNEY, Australia, May 28. — Amy Johnson, the intrepid British girl flier, reached Charleville, Queensland, tonight. Motorists grouped their cars to light the flying field with their headlights.

ROME, June 2—(#)—The world’s non-refueling flight endurance record was brought to Italy this morning by Major Umberto Maddelena, who in 1928 first sighted General Umberto Nobile and the Italia survivors on the ice north of Spitzbergen. Landing at Montecelio aerodrome at fourteen minutes before one a. m. he and his companion flier, Lieutenant Fausto Cecconi exceeded by one hour and 49 minutes the previous record of the Germans, Johann Risticz and Hans Zimmerman, who in 1928 remained aloft for 65 hours and 26 minutes. The new record is 67 hours and 15 minutes, the flight having begun at 5:31 a. m. Friday morning at Montecelio. It was the culmination of long efforts for the two airmen, and represented their fourth attempt at the world record, three other attempts having been made in the latter two months of 1929.

DIJON, France, June 1.—In the French government's political keynote speech today, Premier Andre Tardieu told 1,500 leaders from all branches of life that France is strong and intends to remain mistress of her own destiny, needing neither to fear nor to boast. The premier’s address was awaited by all France, and by many other countries, because it follows closely on speeches by Premier Mussolini of Italy, which have been characterized in the French press as “bellicose” and as directed mainly against France. M. Tardieu made no specific mention of Italy nor Mussolini, but confined himself to a declaration of calm confidence in French democratic institutions, and French national strength, both physical and moral. He recalled Foreign Minister Briand’s long efforts to achieve peace. He added, however, that although “the government is passionately interested in this work, it has neglected nothi

PARIS, June 2.—(?)—All Europe is watching with interest and some anxiety a political situation which promises to develop into a duel between two European statesmen, Benito Mussolini, premier of Italy, and Andre Tardieu, premier whom France regards generally as a worthy successor of Clemenceau and Poincare. Mussolini has attracted attention again because of recent speeches in Northern Italy, wherein he warned the world that Italy's independence and Italy’s future cannot be neglected and that, if occasion necessitated, the world would find that the Italian people would form themselves into a solid mass to defend Italian rights. In another speech he declared that there is nothing more insulting to the pride of the Italian people than to suppose that Italy's recent naval program is a thing which will not be brought to its consummation. And he continued with the phrase that has rung around Eu

DIJON, France, June 21 - The French people today read into a speech of Premier Andre Tardieu the answer of the French government to recent speeches of the Italian premier, Benito Mussolini, in Northern Italy, which were regarded here as being unusually bellicose in nature. M. Tardieu's pronouncement, made before 1,500 leaders from all branches of French life, was that France is strong, intends to remain mistress of her own destiny, and needs neither to fear nor to boast. There was no specific mention of Italy but after calling attention to Foreign Minister Briand's efforts to assure world peace he added: "The government is passionately interested in the work (peace). It has neglected nothing which would enable France to participate actively by vigilantly safeguarding her security." "France is in a position which frees her from the need both to fear or to boast." Tokyo.—~ (*) —The longest and strongest earthquake of the year Sunday had left only minor damage in its wake. Of 25 minutes duration and 12 millimeters magnitude, the disturbance stopped clocks and caused frightened people to desert their homes but nowhere in the affected area were any casualties reported. The quake shook an area within a radius of 60 miles of Tokyo, An official communique issued by the Tokyo central meteorological observatory said the disturbance was centered in the Pacific Ocean eastward from Tokyo. The quake was perceptible to humans for six or seven minutes.

MONTECELLO, Italy — Major Maddalena Sunday night broke the world endurance record officially recognized for planes not refueling in the air, that of Johann Risticz and Hans Zimmerman, German fliers, who stayed up sixty-five hours and twenty-six minutes in 1928. Accompanied by Captain Cecconi, the Italian flier took off from the government field here at 4 a.m. Friday for Ostia and return, and by 10:25 o'clock at night had flown sixty-six hours and twenty-five minutes. At midnight he was still flying and it was believed he would exceed distance records also. For his record to be recognized, however, he must land at the point of departure. Major Maddalena, who participated in the reserve of Gen. Umberto Nobile’s crew of the dirigible Italia in the Arctic in 1928, is planning a flight to New York by way of the Azores.

PARIS, June 2.—The two American Gold Star mothers who became seriously ill while visiting their sons’ graves in France, today were nearly recovered. Mrs. Florence Williams, of Portsmouth, Ohio, who is at a Verdun hotel, it was announced, would get out of bed today and return to Paris shortly. Mrs. Florence Reynolds has left the American hospital and returned to a Paris hotel. She wishes to return to the United States with her original party, which is leaving Friday, so she is being taken daily to the cemetery near Soissons, where her son is buried.
Rome, June 2.—Italy won today the world's record for endurance flying without refueling which Germany had held for almost two years.

1930-05-11.text: BOMBAY, India, May 10.--(AP)— Unusual protective measures were put in force throughout India today to prevent communal rioting between Hindus and Moslems on the occasion of the Mohammedans feast of Bakrid, in commemoration of Abraham’s sacrifice of the lamb. Bakrid is an event which even under “normal circumstances carries with it the danger of disturbances. Today—the anniversary of the great Sepoy mutiny of 1857, and with Hindu-Moslem antipathies greatly accentuated by reason of Moslem abstinence from the civil disobedience campaign—there was particular apprehension, Moslem sacrifice of cows, Sacred to the Hindus, constituted another danger element. - ORDERS ISSUED: In Sholapur, scene of sanguinary rioting Wednesday and Thursday, in which unofficial estimates of 50 dead and 400 wounded are made, an order was issued forbidding assembly of more than five persons: “This applied only to Hin

BOMBAY, India, May 10.—(P) With Mahatma Gandhi in Yeroda prison and nearly a quarter of a million troops on the alert British authorities today safely got through the first part of an anxious weekend in the development of the Indian situation. With memories of Thursday’s rioting at Sholapur fresh in mind, they feared further trouble would break out today. But the principal event was political instead of violent. At Amritsar, the general meeting of the central Sikh league, chief organization of a fighting race famous for prowess in the Indian army, today resolved to support Mahatma Gandhi's civil disobedience campaign, chiefly conducted hitherto by Hindus. Such Muslim support for the campaign injected a disturbing but unpredictable element into the situation facing British authorities. Thus far most of the Muslims have held aloof from the Gandhi movement, being traditionally suspicious of

Indore City, Indore, India, May 12 (UP)—The stepson of an American-born woman, the former Nancy Miller of Seattle, Wash., has come into the full ruling powers of the Maharajah of Indore today. The Maharajah Yeshawant Rao attained his majority yesterday and was invested with all rights and privileges of Indore’s ruler at a ceremony of the most magnificent Oriental splendor. Yeshawant had been ruling with partial powers since his father was forced to abdicate in 1925. Yeshawant’s first official act was to declare several concessions to his subjects, including the revision of taxation.

(United Press Meat correspondent.) BOMBAY, India, May 10, (UP)—A series of secret conferences of independence leaders at Gujarat and widespread dissemination of revolutionary propaganda at Poona put the government on guard tonight against a surprise move in the passive resistance campaign against British rule. Precautions against disorders were strengthened, especially in the northern peril throughout Mohammedan India today with the celebration of the great (Continued on Page 2, Col. 2)

Shanghal.—(4)—Following previous dispatches reporting the massacre of 16,000 inhabitants of Yungyang in Honan province April 23, other Chinese press dispatches Saturday stated that bandit armies had destroyed 509 villages in central Honan, the inhabitants being “murdered, kidnapped and outraged to unknown numbers, while the countryside was reduced to desolation.” Flames of the burning villages, it was said, lasted for four days and could be seen for many miles. Many of those kidnapped were murdered and their mutilated bodies flung into creeks or left in roadways. The brigands were opposed by nationalist government troops, but only a few outlaws were killed. The notorious “Widow Chang” was believed to be the leader of a party of 200 brigands. Believed to have become revengeful as a result of the killing of her wealthy husband by bandits, she herself had turned brigand and long had ravaged

SHANGHAI, May 10.——National government armies battled today on two widely separated fronts in an effort to turn back the northern alliance rebels in their drives toward the Yangtse river. With heavy casualties on both sides after two days of fighting, the result was in doubt. Rebels in Chengchow were reported in grave danger as national airplanes bombed the city, destroying the railway station and northern headquarters, said Japanese sources. Contending for supremacy in China, the opposing forces battled on both the eastern and western frontiers of Honan province. The major engagement was along the Lunghai railway. (Continued on Page 4, Col. 4)

1930-05-01.text: London, May 1—(AP)—British newspapers today said that they understood that the Indian administration, working with the approval of the home government, would take immediate strong action to put down the civil disobedience campaign of Mahatma Gandhi and the all-India national congress. It was believed, the papers said, that Gandhi would be arrested. In some quarters it was recalled, however, that the Mahatma’s arrest often has been reported as imminent, but has never materialized. There is a widely held view that the government's refusal to grant the Satyagraha leader the ‘martyrdom of arrest has strengthened its position. Bombay dispatches said that Gandhi had another plan to harass the government which will be revealed on the banks of the River Tapti at Surat. The nature of the plan was a mystery but a special messenger was understood to have taken Gandhi's instructions for carrying it

(LONDON) Apr. 30. (AP) Unless all news of disturbances is being stopped at the source by British censors, two full days have passed without a serious breach of the peace in India. Closing to visitors of Khyber Pass, outlet from India to Afghanistan, was unexplained, but was regarded as a precautionary act adopted for the protection of Peshawar, which is but eleven miles distant. A surprise attack was made on Monday on the artillery magazine at Barrackpore which may have been intended as a repetition of the Chittagong incident, but it was unsuccessful. One Calcutta report said a sentry was shot in the leg by raiders, whose connection with the Indian nationalist cause was uncertain. Growing opposition among the native press developed to the government's security requirements for papers coming under the censorship. This amounted to 50,000 rupees, or about $18,000. Mahatma Gandhi, leader of
LONDON, May 1 (UP) - The Bank of England reduced the discount rate today from three and one-half to three per cent.

By The Associated Press. London, April 30.—Preparations for toning down the reds and pinks and other clashing hues which are expected to dominate the May Day celebrations throughout Europe tomorrow have been made by police and troops in the various capitals. In general the Communists, socialists and Laborites will be permitted to march and speak as long as the meetings are orderly. The most peaceful of all European celebrations is expected in London although as usual extra police will be on duty. Paris police took the view that anything might happen there and ordered thousands of troops and police to be under arms by daybreak. The cabinet tonight approved secret plans for protection of Paris and maintenance of order throughout the country. As a preventative the French government today expelled 22 persons accused of political agitation concerning May Day activities and caused the arrest o

Delhi, India, April 30.—(UP)—Devi Das Gandhi, son of the Mahatma Gandhi, leader of the Indian independence campaign, was sentenced to a year of rigorous imprisonment today on charges of seditious propaganda. The younger Gandhi pleaded guilty and delivered an impassioned oration against the British government, charging that he could not be patriotic in India without also being seditious in view of the British authorities. His elder brother already is serving a six months prison term.

LONDON, May 1. (P)—May Day racial demonstrations throughout Europe and the Far East drew to a quiet close today under the eyes of perhaps the heaviest military and police forces ever mustered on such an occasion. About 500 Communists paraded in London, marching to Hyde Park (Continued on page 8, col. 2)

BOMBAY, April 30.—Mahatma Gandhi had new plans today for attaining the elusive martyrdom he has sought since he instituted his passive resistance campaign for Indian independence more than a month ago. Disappointed but undaunted by the failure of his efforts to be arrested while superintending illegal salt-making activities, Gandhi prepared to lead a raid on a nearby salt depot at an early, but unannounced, date. He promised in a speech yesterday that he would notify the authorities well beforehand. The independence leader told his followers he did not wish the salt laws broken in the native states, which have a form of self-government.

SUNNINGDALE, ENG. May 1. (AP).--A British women's golf team today defeated a women’s team from the United States in all-day competition consisting of foursomes in the morning and singles in the afternoon.

SHANGHAI, May 1 (AP)—A reign of terror in Lungchow, southwestern Kwangsi province, was reported in dispatches from that area today. Communists were said to have gone on a rampage of burning, looting and massacring there. All foreigners were reported to have evacuated, but much missionary property, including buildings of the Seventh Day Adventists mission and the Christian Alliance was said to have been destroyed.

ROME, April 30 (UP)—Construction of 29 warships was approved today by the cabinet. The warships approved include one cruiser, two scout ships, four destroyers and 22 submarines. The cruiser will be 10,000 tons, of the Washington standard type and will be named the Pola. The two scout ships will be 5,100 tons each. The four destroyers will be 1,240 tons each. The keels of all 29 ships will be laid in the current year. The submarines will be divided as follows: Four of 1,890 tons each; six of 810 tons and 12 of 610 tons.

Tokyo, May 1.—An earthquake of unusual strength and duration was felt here shortly after midnight. There have been no reports of casualties nor any great damage from the quake. The central meteorological observatory said the center of activity was probably at sea, 75 miles northeast of Tokyo. The quake, which started at 12:58 a.m., registered on the seismographs for 30 minutes. It was perceptible to residents of Tokyo for five minutes. Scientists attribute the quake to activity in the “outer Tsukuba earthquake belt.”

Tokyo, May 1—(AP)— An earthquake of unusual strength and duration shaking Tokyo shortly after midnight did no great damage. There were no reports of casualties. Seismographs registered the quake for 30 minutes after its start at 12:58 a.m. Residents felt it for a full five minutes.

MARSEILLES, France, May 1— (LP)—Jean Mermoz, French flier, who proposed to fly to South America, started in a seaplane for Dakar, Senegal, on the African coast, at 5:15 a. m. today, but was forced to land. The landing was made at Perpignan, France, on the Spanish border at 7:15 a. m. Mermoz was forced down by a leaky radiator.

As preparations for May Day celebrations were in full swing throughout many countries of the world today, authorities took precautions to prevent disorders. All work ceased this afternoon in Moscow to give workers time to participate in the final plans for international labor day. Millions of yards of red bunting, hundreds of thousands of red electric light bulbs, and numerous other decorations were placed on government buildings, shops and homes last night. The activities in Moscow were to begin tonight with lectures in clubs, theatres, and conference halls on the labor movement. Tomorrow demonstrations by civilians will take place in all leading cities of the proletarian republic. Authorities in Athens have prohibited all communist gatherings tomorrow. Reports from Poland today stated that police are planning to concentrate strong forces to avert trouble when members of the rival socia

MOSCOW, May 1—(AP)—Red Moscow and the entire Soviet Union celebrated May Day with great processions of workmen, housewives, Red Army soldiers, young pioneers and the civilian population. Following a military parade led by Clement Voroshiloff, commissar of war, nearly a million proletarians marched in triple columns for seven hours through Moscow's historic Red Square, singing revolutionary songs and carrying thousands of banners and placards containing revolutionary slogans and inscriptions condemning capitalism. The gigantic massed spectacle was scarcely less impressive than that which assembled on the anniversary of the October Revolution.
Tokyo, May 1 (4) (Thursday)--An earthquake of unusual strength and duration was felt here shortly after midnight.

PARIS. May 1—()—Three incipient May Day demonstrations, one in Paris and two in the suburbs were quickly suppressed by the police today. Altogether about one-fifth of the 600,000 workers in the main industries observed a May Day strike. The police arrested 233 persons, of whom 43 were foreigners, on various charges.

1930-05-19.text: BOMBAY, India, May 18.—Elaborate police precautions failed today to prevent desultory raiding by Nationalist volunteers on the salt depots at both Dharasana and Wadala. Four hundred Hindus were arrested at Wadala alone by the officers. Others were taken into custody at Dharasana. At Dharasana a strange struggle occurred between the constabulary and the Nationalists. The latter, crowding to the small town from every part of Gujarat, waited passively until the attention of police was engaged elsewhere and then stepped in to loot the government salt bins. Mrs. Sarojini Naidu, who since the arrest of Mahatma Gandhi and Abbas Tyabji is in charge of the civil disobedience movement, declared the volunteers at Dharasana have "imprisoned the police behind their own bars." Every train brings hundreds of Nationalist volunteers to the little village where the silent bloodless battle with the police

SUNNINGDALE, England, May 19.—Bobby Jones today won the golf vase of Golf Illustrated in a 36-hole medal play competition with leading amateurs of the United States and Great Britain. The American open champion returned a 36-hole total of 143 to win the trophy. He followed a fair 75 in the morning with a brilliant 68 in the afternoon round. The other American Walker Cup players entered in the competition also scored well. George Voight had a total of 146, George von Elm 147 and O. F. Willing 159.

Plymouth, England, May 16.—()—The first contingent of American gold star mothers arrived here this morning aboard the steamer America from New York after a most pleasant Atlantic crossing. The mothers said the weather was delightful all the way over, The mothers, who are going to visit their sons’ graves in France and Belgium, kept about the decks a great deal and only one of the party had a single meal in her cabin. Captain Fried was a pleasant host and not a day passed that he did not receive a group on the bridge and provide plentiful entertainment, concerts and the like.

LONDON, May 19.—Forty-five persons were killed and the entire village of Likasan was destroyed by an eruption of Telemojo volcano, between Batavia and Surabaya, Dutch East Indies, according to a Central News dispatch received here today from Amsterdam.

(All Rights Reserved) LONDON, May 19.—(U.P)—Results of the London naval conference constituted the greatest step ever taken in the general evolution of disarmament, A. V. Alexander, first lord of the admiralty, said today in an interview with the United Press. “Alexander stressed three points in particular: 1. Whereas the Washington treaty resulted in a race for large cruisers to offset the loss of power due to the scrapping of battleships, the London conference by limiting all combatant categories of ships for the three greatest naval powers, eliminated naval competition between them. 2. The limitation figures actually agreed upon in London were much lower than those which Britain unsuccessfully proposed at Geneva in 1927. 3.
