LONDON, May 19.—(UP)—The first unofficial reaction to the definite plans of French Foreign Minister Aristide Briand for a union of European countries was hesitant, if not unfavorable. A survey of opinion in Britain and continental countries indicated little enthusiasm for the plan and many observers were pessimistic in view of several striking nationalistic occurrences of the weekend. The speeches of Premier Mussolini of Italy, and of Premier Andre Tardieu of France—both strongly nationalistic—were contrasted by observers with the Briand scheme for an international union by which Europe could "unite to live and prosper." Not Desirable The press of Great Britain indicated a belief that a federation such as Briand’s questionnaire of last Saturday proposed was not desirable at present and probably would not meet England later. The press of Rome reserved comment but the general opinion of ob

NEWPORT, R.I., May 19. — Three men barely escaped with their lives today when a gasoline explosion wrecked and set fire to the 60-foot speedboat Astrid, a former rum-runner, while the craft was about six miles off Seaconnet Point. G. H. Moreman, skipper of the Astrid, and two companions escaped in their dory and subsequently were reported to have been picked up by a fishing boat bound for New Bedford, Mass. The Astrid burned to the water-line but remained afloat and was towed by a coast guard patrol boat to the beach at Seaconnet Point.

London, May 18 (UP) — The Prince of Wales and Bobby Jones played 36 holes of golf together today and though rain fell during a part of the match, it did not interfere with either’s game. The match was played on Sir Philip Sassoon’s private course at Trent Park, High Barnet. Just who won the match, how many strokes Bobby gave the Prince and the totals for 36 holes could not be learned.

BY ASSOC Lr Ces PARIS, May 18.—Seventeen Gold Star mothers whose sons sleep their last sleep on the slopes of Mount Valerien at Suresnes, just outside Paris, had their first real test of fortitude today when they knelt and prayed beside their graves. Although plainly shaken with grief at first, many of them sobbing, pride for their soldier dead soon restored their composure. The cemetery visit was devoid of all official pomp and speeches, the mothers wishing to be alone with their sons buried on the beautiful green hill where every grave is marked with a white marble slab on which the name is engraved in black. Colonel G. G. Bartlett, who has been in charge of the pilgrimage, accompanied the mothers on their automobile trip from Paris to the cemetery, where the caretaker, James Duncan, a former A.E.F. lieutenant, gave each of them a huge wreath of flowers to place on the graves of their
VOEAMEN MATE VOI BERLIN, May 19.—The Reichsbank reduced its rediscount rate one half of one per cent to 4 1-2 per cent today.

Paris, May 19.--Orders for immediate evacuation of French troops from the third and last zone of the German Rhineland were given today by Premier Andre Tardieu to General Guillaumat, commanding the occupational troops. — Tardieu asked the German ambassador to assure his government that the last French soldier will have left the occupied area on June 30, the date agreed upon by German and French representatives at the Hague conferences. The evacuation plans—which will free German soil from foreign soldiers for the first time since the Armistice—have been ready for a month awaiting Germany’s fulfillment of her reparations obligations under the Owen D. Young plan on the first day possible, the date of formal opening of the international bank.

PARIS, May 19.— The American Gold Star mothers prepared today for the first extensive pilgrimages to their sons’ graves in France. The 16 women whose sons are buried at Sureanes, near Paris, visited the graves again today but the majority of mothers will start for the provincial cemeteries tomorrow morning by auto bus. The visitors were reported in good health by doctors who are assigned to accompany them.

(United Press Staff Correspondent) SEVILLE, Spain, May 19.—(U.P.)—The dirigible Graf Zeppelin, nearing the end of the first stage of flight to South America and the United States, approached Seville late today after an uneventful flight from Friedrichshafen. A crowded, enthusiastic city awaited the big ship which promised to make Seville the European terminal of a regular commercial air route across the Atlantic Ocean. Many tourists mingled with the Sevillanos and the interest in the flight was indicated by the fact that all air mail stamps were exhausted hours before the dirigible arrived. Six military planes from Granada arrived here shortly before the Graf Zeppelin circled over Gibraltar. The planes will participate in the welcoming ceremonies, which were scheduled for late in the afternoon after the dirigible toured along the Mediterranean coast to delay its arrival here. The Graf Ze

Friedrichshafen, Germany, May 19—The dirigible Graf Zeppelin pushed rapidly forward today bound for Seville, Spain, and a new, trailblazing commercial route to South America and the United States. The Graf passed over Cape Palos, Spain, 300 miles due east of its destination, at 6:45 a. m. today (12:45 a. m. (EST). The big airship made fast progress across Switzerland, into France and down the Rhone river valley after a delayed departure from Friedrichshafen. Four American passengers were aboard the ship when it departed from Friedrichshafen, and a fifth was to board it at Seville. The Americans were George Crouse, Syracuse, N. Y.; Mrs. Laura Crouse Durston, Syracuse, N. Y., his sister; United States Navy Officer Harry Shoemaker, and Karl Von Weigand, newspaper correspondent, Berlin. HAVRE, May 18.-(4%—Three cars and the engine of Great Northern passenger train No. 236, northbound between Butte and Havre, were derailed about a mile west of Box Elder early today. Passengers and the train crew were badly shaken up, and Fireman Arthur Bundstrock was injured. Great Northern officials here blamed the wreck on Mexican section hands who were laid off Saturday evening. The officials said they believed the laborers were intoxicated and loosened spikes holding the rails to the ties.

1930-04-03.text: LONDON, March 31. (AP) — The MacDonald government, for the second time in its ten months of life, today suffered a minor defeat in the House of Commons, but immediately rallied its forces and succeeded in carrying the day on a motion to adjourn the House. Today’s defeat was on a motion for suspension of the rule that the House adjourn at 11 p.m., the vote being 183 to 179. The defeat was one of procedure, and despite cries of ‘resign’ from the opposition benches, was not considered a vital matter.

London —Official announcement was made at American delegation headquarters today that the Americans, British and Japanese are in complete accord. The Americans and British, at a meeting with the Japanese at St. James’ palace, indicated acceptance of the Japanese reservations. The only points to be settled are details relating to Japanese reservations on the scrapping and replacing of ships in order to keep their dockyards working. It was said there would be no factor of difficulty in any of the Japanese reservations. Senator Reed, who was credited by his colleagues with having been instrumental in solving the American, British and Japanese problem, made the following statement to newspaper men after the meet- “I cannot too strongly impress upon you the fine spirit in which the Japanese and British have met as (Continued on Page 12)

DUBLIN, Irish Free State, April 3 — William T. Cosgrave was restored today to the presidency of the Irish Free State, an office he held from 1922 until last week, when he resigned after defeat in the Dail on an opposition measure. He was re-elected by the Dail Eireann last night by a vote of 80 to 65. In two preceding ballots his two opponents, Eamonn DeValera, of the Fianna Fail, and Thomas J. O’Connell, labor leader, were eliminated, DeValera by a vote of 98 to 54, and O’Connell by a poll of 78 to 13. Mr. Cosgrave’s name was proposed only after Mr. DeValera, who is in the United States on a lecture tour, had been nominated and defeated, and Mr. O’Connell had been put up and voted down. His election had been taken as almost a foregone conclusion since his resignation last week. The president of the Irish Free State is not president in the American sense, but is president of the cabinet
DUBLIN, April 2 VPA motion in the Dail to elect Amon De Valera, Fianna Fail leader, president of the Free State council was defeated late today, 33 to 74.

LONDON, April 3. — Three statements in rapid succession from leaders of the American, French and Japanese delegations, coupled with postponement of the plenary session, which had been scheduled for tomorrow lent further optimism to the London naval conferees today. First was a statement by Henry L. Stimson yesterday expressing belief that an agreement is nearer than ever. Second was the announcement by Foreign Minister Aristide Briand of France to the press that negotiations for a security pact based on an interpretation of the Locarno Treaty were proceeding "satisfactorily." Third was a statement by the Japanese delegation indicating that whatever reservations have been made by the Japanese to the agreement proposed by the United States are so slight they will offer no obstacle to an agreement. In the opinion of most observers, postponement of the plenary session indicates that the "Big

until some time next week and the delivery of the Japanese reply to proposals worked out in London today marked important developments in the naval conference negotiations. It was stated in American conference circles that the postponement of the plenary session was to be taken as a good sign rather than the reverse and as indicating progress in the negotiations. Conversations now proceeding between various groups, especially the French and British, were said to be progressing satisfactorily but were not yet in a state to permit a satisfactory plenary meeting for the present. The big five leaders want something more definite for the plenary session than they now have. Secretary of State Stimson, after a meeting of the chief delegations at St. James’ palace, said: “The situation is very much more improved than last week. LONDON, April 3, (®)—After ten weeks of difficult negotiations, during which obstacles often were encountered that seemed insurmountable, the naval conference this afternoon was recorded in American, British and Japanese circles as having achieved great success. This position was reached after a conference this morning wherein the Americans and British accepted the Japanese government's reservations to the American-British naval proposals. Thus was assured at least a powerful three-power agreement as an outcome of the conference even if France and Italy cannot participate. In this connection observers were much interested in a statement made this afternoon by A. V. Alexander, first Lord of the British Admiralty. Speaking at Brixton, Mr. Alexander said: "This week the conference is much more hopeful than it was a little time. Official announcement was made at American delegation headquart

DUBLIN, April 2—(7)—William T. Cosgrave was re-elected president of the Irish Free State council by the Dail Eireann. Cosgrave thus will resume after the brief interval of five days the important post which he held since 1922. When his ministry fell last week it had achieved a record for longevity among European cabinets by virtue of its eight years of continuous service. It lost by only two votes when that slender majority of the national legislature favored extension of old age pensions, a measure which the president opposed as constituting too great a burden on the present finances of the country. At that time it was predicted that Mr. Cosgrave would be returned to office.

LONDON, April 3 — Complete agreement on disarmament programs was reached by the delegates of Great Britain, the United States and Japan today. It was officially announced that the American and British representatives had accepted the reservations embodied in the Japanese sanction of the Reed-Matsudaira compromise agreement. 3-POWER PACT NEAR Acceptance of the Japanese reservations makes a tri-partite treaty between the three major naval powers of the world a certainty. If the security demands of France can now be satisfied, it is highly probable that a five-power disarmament treaty, the chief aim of the London naval conference, will materialize. The reservations set forth in the Japanese acceptance were technical, and regarded by British and American experts as not affecting the efficacy of the compromise agreement obtained here by Senator David A. LONDON.—M—Taking one great step forward Wednesday toward a three power disarmament agreement among the United States, Great Britain and Japan, delegates to the London naval conference hesitated to take another toward a five power pact until sure of their ground. Consequently they announced that the important plenary session set for Friday morning would be postponed until next week. Reijiro Wakatsuki met Secretary Stimson and Prime Minister MacDonald at St. James’ palace Wednesday afternoon. There he formally gave the long awaited answer to the American-British ratio proposals, accepting them with reservations. The reservations, it is stated, create no obstacle to a five power agreement. Outlook Is Better. The same three will meet again Thursday morning to discuss the Japanese reservations further. Dublin, Ireland, April 3,—(P)—William T. Cosgrave, ousted a week ago, was again in power today as head of the Free State executive council, having been re-elected by the Dail Eireann 8H to 6H. The political flurry which again brought prominence to Eamonn De Valera, now in the United States, apparently resulted in establishing more firmly than before the control of the Cosgrave support in the Dail. De Valera was nominated and defeated. There were three successive votes taken during more than eight hours of debate.

London, April 3—(#)—Mary Fitzgerald, Duchess of Leinster, was remanded by the Lambeth police court today on a charge of attempting to commit suicide. The Duchess who has been separated from her husband for some time, was taken to Lambeth hospital early (continued on page 7)

LONDON, April 3.--(UP)--Prime Minister MacDonald told the House of Commons today the British government would continue to administer Palestine in accordance with the terms of the mandate, as approved by the Council of the League of Nations. The Prime Minister, who was replying to a question by former Premier Baldwin, stated that administration was an international obligation from which there could be no question of receding.

Dublin, April 3—(INS)—After the brief interval of five days Wul-Nam T. Cosgrave returned today to the Presidency of the Irish Free State Executive Council, his policies vindicated and his position stronger than at any time since he first took office in 1922. Mr. Cosgrave was reelected by the Dail Eireann by a vote of 80 to 65. Mr. Cosgrave resigned after the Dail had favored, by two votes, a bill to extend old age pensions, a measure the President had opposed because it would cause too great a drain on the country’s finances.

Tokyo —()— More than 100 persons were believed drowned Wednesday when the ferry-boat Wakatomaru, carrying 300 Japanese from Wakamatsu to Tobata, capsized. The ferry boat was overcrowded and a high sea was running.

- TOKYO, April 3 —AP—Under the auspices of the famous “Black Dragon Society” and other nationalistic organizations an open air demonstration against the Japanese cabinet’s acceptance of the London naval formula was held in Shiba Park today. Although today was a national holiday, being the anniversary of the death of Japan’s legendary first emperor, Jimmu Tenno, and fine spring weather prevailed the attendance of about 2,000 was relatively small.
(By The Associated Press.) | Paris, Apr. 3—Premier Tardieu was taken suddenly ill at a coffee meeting today and had to be assisted to his automobile and taken to the hotel where he resides.

Tokyo, April 3.—(AP)— Dispatches from Wakamatsu said that when search was given up today at the scene where the ferryboat Wakato Maru capsized yesterday, 53 bodies had been recovered and 40 persons were missing. Two of those rescued died later in a hospital, making the probable death toll 95. The ferryboat, soon after leaving Wakamatsu for the town of Tobata, was lashed by a gale which swept huge waves aboard. The 200 passengers, twice the vessel's normal capacity, rushed to one side of the ship to escape drenching. Their weight caused the boat to turn over. Despite the storm, large crowds remained at nearby beaches throughout the night, many searching frantically for missing relatives. During the night scores of fishing boats, lighted with torches or kerosene flares floated at the scene of the disaster, looking for bodies.

Warsaw, Poland—(/)—An affair of honor between two fiery matrons of Warsaw which they attempted to settle with pistols in storybook style ended happily today when after several shots each discovered she was unable to hit the other. Both decided their honor had been saved and went home to cook breakfast. Two women acted as seconds while a woman surgeon was on hand in the event of casualty. One of the women was alleged to have found the other woman in a cafe with her husband, whereupon she administered a stinging slap. The other woman then demanded a duel.

Cherbourg, France, April 8.—(A. P.)—The North German Lloyd liner Europa, fastest ship on the seas, was delayed somewhat by heavy weather in the English Channel and took four days, 22 hours and 26 minutes—seven hours slower than the Bremen's eastbound record—to arrive here today from New York. The Europa established a new transatlantic record on its westward crossing, which it completed in 4 days, 17 hours and 6 minutes—eighteen minutes faster than its sister ship, the Bremen, which previously had held the record.

Berlin, April 3.—(UP)—Chancellor Heinrich Bruening’s coalition cabinet, supported by Nationalist votes, defeated the Communist and Socialist joint motion of non-confidence in the Reichstag today, 252 to 187. Victory of the new government was made possible by an eleventh-hour decision of the Nationalists to support the cabinet in return for a promise of farm relief measures, to be enforced before Easter. The result completely reversed predictions made after formation of the Bruening cabinet, when it was believed that Socialist and Communist opposition, mustering more votes in the Reichstag than the groups represented in the ministry, would immediately overthrow the government on the first test of strength.

Ry United Press BERLIN, April 3.—General Conrad Von Der Goltz, outstanding figure in the battle of Tannenberg in the World War, died today. Count Von Der Goltz, born in 1865, took a prominent part in World War campaigns in the Baltic region. After the war he led a volunteer army which was supposed to be opposing the Bolsheviks but he was suspected of planning an attack on republican forces in Germany.

Moscow, April 3—(UP)—Josef Stalin, the Soviet dictator, warned Russian communists today to avoid violence against the peasant masses of Russia. The Communist party leader said the party would be in danger of breaking with the peasant masses and undermining the proletarian dictatorship unless it quickly and thoroughly corrects its mistakes and excesses. The mistakes and excesses to which he referred were in connection with the campaign for collectivization of the agricultural regions. The entire front pages of the morning newspapers were devoted to Stalin's statement, which amplified his recent declaration that the collectivization drive had been sped too much and had stirred up discontent. He declared the party must admit its errors and permit withdrawal of peasants who are not yet ready for the campaign and must concentrate on the immediate task of sowing spring crops which must be succ

BERLIN, April 3.—(AP)—A motion of no-confidence in the new ministry of Chancellor Heinrich Bruening was defeated by the Reichstag this forenoon. It was proposed by the socialists and communists. The nationalists, who held the balance of power, refused to support the government's opposition. The motion was beaten 252 to 187. Mr. Hugenberg, leader of the nationalists, personally appeared on the rostrum and announced the decision of his party not to support the opposition move. Had the government fallen, Chancellor Bruening was understood to have had the authorization of President Von Hindenburg to dissolve the Reichstag.

Berlin.—(-P)—Chancellor Heinrich Bruening, whose new cabinet scored its first victory in the Reichstag today, defeating a non-confidence motion, called a cabinet meeting immediately after adjournment to decide on his government's position. He was reported to be concerned over the problem of obtaining a majority for the government’s complete program and to have consulted his cabinet as to whether it would not be better after all to dissolve the Reichstag and have new elections. The Nationalists, who did not support today’s non-confidence motion, which was defeated 252 to 187, made so many reservations that Chancellor Bruening was fearful their support might prove illusory when it came to practical work. It was understood that the cabinet shared Chancellor Bruening’s annoyance, but calmer counsel prevailed and the remainder of the cabinet session was devoted to working out detailed legisla

VIENNA—(7)—Albert H. Washburn, former United States minister to Austria, died Wednesday at a hospital here. Mr. Washburn recently visited the United States after Gilchrist B. Stockton was appointed minister to succeed him, but he returned to Austria to clean up some details. He was taken ill with a severe cold several days ago. He was seventy-four years old. Mr. Washburn, a native of Middleborough, Mass., entered the foreign service in 1890 as American consul at Magdeburg, Germany. Three years later he resigned that post to become private secretary to Senator Henry Cabot Lodge. Subsequently he became prominent in Republican politics in his native state and made a name for himself as an authority on international law, occupying a chair on that subject at Dartmouth. He was appointed minister to Austria in 1922 and rendered distinguished service as chairman of a mixed commission appointed t

TOKYO, April 2—Deaths exceeding 100 were believed to have occurred today in the capsizing of the overloaded ferry boat Wakato Mart off the island of Kyushu, southern Japan. Forty-eight bodies had been recovered a few hours later, and the search was continued. Soon after leaving the coal exporting port of Wakamatsu for the town of Tobata, the ferry boat was lashed by a gale that swept waves aboard. She was carrying at least 200 passengers, twice her normal capacity. These rushed to one side of the laboring ferry boat to avoid drenching. Their weight caused the little boat to turn over. With the exception of two Serbian girl dancers, who are missing, all of the dead are believed to be Japanese.

Berlin, April 3.—(A.P.)—General Baron George Konrad von der Goltz died here, aged 77. He took a prominent part in the battle of Tannenberg as commander of a Landwehr division, and also was known for his musical compositions:

1930-04-01.text: LONDON, APR. 1. (AP).—A British naval conference spokesman announced this morning that “distinct progress” was made during the past 24 hours toward finding a security formula satisfactory to Great Britain and France. The announcement represents a distinct change from the gloom which pervaded conference circles yesterday over the Anglo-French negotiations in which Great Britain has endeavored to satisfy France’s desire for guaranteed security in exchange for reduction of the French naval program. It was understood generally that the two delegations had reached an impasse. The difficulties of the situation, however, did not prevent the experts continuing to hammer on this complicated political problem with the apparent result that they have begun to see some light. Meetings were continued and this afternoon Foreign Secretary Henderson, of Great Britain, and Foreign Minister Briand, of Fran

Calcutta, India, April 1.—Five men were killed in rioting today which followed a passive resistance demonstration against enforcement of a new rule restraining carters from taking out buffaloes during the hottest hours of the day. One Hindu was killed when police fired on a large crowd of carters who had gathered at the Calcutta end of Howrey bridge. The crowd threw brick bats at the police and injured three sergeants. Four more were killed in rioting this afternoon in Harrison road which is the usual storm quarter in this region. The district between Howrey bridge and Harrison road presented the aspect of a battle scene and the streets were jammed with abandoned carts, many overturned and minus wheels. A tense atmosphere prevailed over the area and groups of natives gathered at various spots. A procession carrying black flags with defiant inscriptions appeared in some of the streets.

London, March 31 (P) — Advices received in London today from Tokyo regarding the Japanese answer to the American-British proposal has convinced American, British and Japanese conference circles that a three-power naval agreement will save the London negotiations from the failure which still threatens the European aspects of the parley. But a five-power agreement tonight still remained the goal of the delegates, even through the present hours of adversity. Prime Minister MacDonald assured the House of Commons of this today, while Secretary Stimson and the American delegation continued persistent efforts toward that end. Japan's reply has been drafted and should arrive in London for formal announcement at the plenary session Friday, although it is believed here it will be made known first in Tokyo. Advices from Tokyo today said Japan would make a reservation regarding her demand for 7% of

| Dunedin, N. Z., April 1—(AP)— In the stormy darkness of the lower harbor Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd tonight said farewell to 23 members of his Antarctic expedition who are bound for home on his party’s vessel, the Eleanor Bolling. Rain-laden clouds were scudding in from the sea when the Eleanor Bolling made her departure for New York via Panama. In the fading sunlight the ship steamed down the harbor and when night fell with the vessel still five miles from open sea, Byrd made his final calls to all parts of the craft to bid the voyagers au revoir. As he left the ship on a private yacht, the Admiral led in cheers for the safe return of the departing members of his party. The salute by the men aboard the ship indicated the high esteem in which Byrd is held. Dunedin's send-off to the ship evidenced the close friendships made by the men during their stay at the expedition’s winter base.

By United Press LONDON, April 1.—Weeping bitterly in a gas-filled room she had rented under an assumed name, the Duchess of Leinster, wife of the premier duke, was found this morning on the verge of death, and was taken to a hospital. The duchess, before her marriage, was May Etheridge, a musical comedy actress. She became engaged to the Duke of Leinster, then Lord Edward Fitzgerald, while she was playing a leading part in "Princess Caprice" at the Shaftesbury Theater in London. In 1913 she and Lord Edward were married, and in 1922, through the death of his brother, her husband succeeded to the titles, which include those of Earl of Offaly and Marquis of Kildare. The duchy was created in 1766, but the barony of Offaly goes back to 1205. The couple have one son, who holds the honorary title of Marquis of Kildare. At the hospital where she was taken, it was disclosed that the duchess had b

LONDON, April 1.—Solution of the naval conference deadlock to permit a five-power treaty appeared possible today. Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald and Foreign Secretary Arthur Henderson were said on reliable authority to have told the Italian foreign minister, Dino Grandi, that a new formula had been proposed to meet the French demands for security guarantees. The British leaders said they had hopes that France would accept. The British prime minister was said to have told Grandi that Aristide Briand had asked his government for instructions regarding the new formula. Briand received a reply from Paris late. The French delegates had refused to reduce their naval tonnage demands until the other powers grant them a security agreement. Earlier efforts to reach a formula for a security pact had failed.

LONDON, April 1.—The Labor government was defeated in the House of Lords today when the Lords by a vote of 60 to 12 accepted a technical amendment to the Scotland drainage bill. The defeat followed reversals in the House of Commons last month, but it was not considered of major importance.

(By The Associated Press) Johannesburg, Union of South Africa, April 1.—Professor H. E. Wood, astronomer of the South African union, flatly denied that the planet recently discovered by the Lowell Observatory at Flagstaff, Arizona, was the Trans-Neptunian planet long sought by astronomers. He declared it was only one-thirtieth the size of the earth and estimated it was forty times further from the sun than the earth.

LONDON, April 1—(#)—A mysterious woman known only to her neighbors in Brixton, London suburb, as “Mrs. Williams,” was revealed today at a hospital to which she was taken as the Duchess of Leinster. The landlady said she was aroused early today by a violent knocking and found an ambulance awaiting. “I was told,” she said, “that it had come to fetch the Duchess of Leinster to a hospital. I understand she was found in a semi-conscious condition and that there was gas in the room.” - The duchess was May Eheridge, an actress, who was married at the registry office, Wadsworth, in June 1913, to Lord Edward Fitzgerald, who succeeded to the title of Duke of Leinster in 1922. He is a premier duke, marquis and earl of Ireland. Their honeymoon was spent in a Canadian shack.

London, April 1—(AP)—Diplomatic advices reaching the American naval headquarters from Tokyo were said by an American spokesman this afternoon to have led to the conclusion that the Japanese government's reply on the naval proposals was a virtual acceptance. Press reports regarding reservations in the reply were read with interest by members of the American delegation and it was generally believed these reports were accurate. The American spokesman said there were no indications that the reservations would stand seriously in the way to at least a final American, British and Japanese agreement. Authoritative conference circles said that if the Japanese reply, when officially presented, is in effect acceptance, this means that the conference can secure at least a three power pact even if France and Italy stand out. Formal Report Tomorrow The Japanese government’s reply was received by the J
EDIN- Associated Press. DUNEDIN, New Zealand, April 1 - The Eleanor Bolling, the ship which Rear Admiral Richard Byrd used in his Antarctic expedition, sailed today for the United States.

(RAC Associated Press) SHANGHAI, April 1—Further dispatches today confirmed scattered reports that bandit armies were conducting a virtual reign of terror in several provinces of China south of the Yangtse River. From Hankow came information that the bandits who last Thursday raided and looted the City of Yuanchow, Western Kiangsi Province, besides capturing three missionaries, had boiled the district magistrate in oil, killed a Chinese Christian pastor and forced the residents to pay $60,000 Mexican “good will money” before they departed. Grave fears were expressed for the safety of the kidnapped trio, which included Miss Nina Eleanor Gemmel, 35, formerly of Girard, Kan., and Tacoma, Wash. The other captured missionaries were the Rev. and Mrs. R. W. Porteus, of England. An expected general evacuation of foreigners from Kiangsi province, long ravaged by lawless bands, was reported from N

Tokyo, April 1.---The Japanese government today instructed its delegation in London to accept the Reed-Matsudaira naval formula without altering tonnage figures but with reservations which it was authoritatively stated, should present no difficulties for an early conclusion of a tripartite naval limitation pact. As a result of its decision the Tokyo government confidently expects the success of the London conference, at least as far as Japan, America and Great Britain are concerned. With Premier Hamaguchi presiding, and Baron Shidehara, foreign minister, stating the case for an agreement, the cabinet decided to instruct Reijiro Wakatsuki, head of the Japanese delegation in London, to accept the Reed-Matsudaira formula with the tonnage figures unaltered but with reservations. After adjournment of the cabinet’s four hour session Premier Hamaguchi proceeded to the Imperial palace and receiv

BAYREUTH, Germany, Apr. 1—(P)—Frau Cots M. Wagoner, widow of Richard Wagoner and Dr. Franz Liszt, celebrated composers, died today at the age of 92. She had been ill for a long time and as long as a year ago was said to be unable to see, to hear, or to leave her bed. Her illness was said to be sheer weakness from her age.

Shanghai, March 31 ().— Bandit disorders, complicated by the capture of missionaries, and Communist activities, were indicated by reports pouring into Shanghai today to have created a grave situation in various parts of China. Radicals who apparently had subsided some weeks ago when Chiang Kai-Shek demonstrated the strength of the Nanking government, were reported active again, especially in northern China where Yen Hsi-Shan, governor of Shansi Province is heading military opposition to the Nationalist government. Much of the recent lawlessness in South China was attributed to Yen's indictments as he allegedly is trying to bring about the government's downfall. Information came from Suchow, about fifty miles from Shanghai that police and soldiers had united and ambushed boats carrying 500 bandits. The boats were raked with rifle fire until they were filled with dead and wounded, the repo

PARIS. (P) — William J. Locke, noted British novelist who underwent an operation this morning, was reported in a critical condition late today. He underwent 4 “very severe abdominal operations,” his doctors said.

TOKYO, April 1—(P)—The Japanese Government tonight forwarded instructions to its delegation at London to accept, with some minor reservations, the proposed American-Japanese naval agreement on naval tonnage, it was learned on high authority. LONDON, April 1—(UP)—The reported agreement of the Tokyo Government to the compromise terms laid down by the United States on comparative naval strength, with "slight reservations," was the outstanding development of the five-Power Conference today. The action of the Japanese cabinet assured the certainty of a three-power agreement, if efforts at framing the broader treaty fail. Meanwhile, the French and British continued their search for a formula which would satisfy the French people that their security was being guaranteed, without committing the British in advance to military action to protect her. KHEKLIN, April 1 --(INS) A bomb was seen this morning at the entrance to the city hall. With their typical efficiency, the Berlin police cleared the district of pedestrians, emptied the city hall of its workers, called out the fire department and then retreated to a safe distance. After a short wait and no action, a venturesome fireman approached the bomb and found attached thereto a card "April fool".
BEYREUTH, Ger. April 1--Frau Cosima Wagner, widow of the composer Richard Wagner, and daughter of the equally famed musician, Franz Liszt, died here today at the age of 3.

ISTANBUL, Turkey, April 1— “God sent me to Turkey at a critical moment when the nation was turning from Islam to drink,” Agnes Slack, secretary of the world’s Women Christian Temperance Union, who is here to organize the first Turkish branch of the W. C. T. U. said today. Two hundred Turkish women took the teetotalers’ pledge in forming the Union branch today, electing Madame Hussein Bey as their president.

BAYREUTH, Germany, Apr 1—One of the few remaining links with the “Golden Age” of German music was broken today with the death of Cosima Wagner, widow of Richard Wagner, at the age of 93. Frau Wagner died at her Bayreuth home, The Villa Wahnfried, shrine of music lovers of all nations who flock to this town by the thousands each year for the Bayreuth Festival of Music.

P)— Japan, it was believed today in well informed circles, will approve with two or three reservations the tentative agreement of Japanese and naval conference - for tonnage and ratios of naval strength of their respective countries. Instructions are expected to be cabled Tuesday to the Japanese delegation in London. Foreign Minister Shidehara was said to have completed a draft of instructions to the delegation that would authorize its acceptance of the American formula, provided other powers signatory to the agreement agreed to Japan's reservations. If the Japanese cabinet gives its expected approval and Emperor Hirohito sanctions the instructions, they will be cabled to Reijiro Wakatsuki, Japan's chief delegate to the London conference. Varly April 14—France has prepared a leader welcome for the planned pilgrimage of American gold star mothers who this summer will visit the graves of their slain and the battlefields over which they fought. French government cooperation was readily offered and many French women's organizations have joined with the United States quartermaster's department, which has charge of the pilgrimage, in compiling plans for the comfort of the women France regards as distinguished guests. In Paris, the first point of visit for most of the mothers, two of the most luxurious hotels have been reserved. In charge of the six American cemeteries in France, Romagne, Fere-In-Tardenois and St. Mihiel, stopping places have been erected and arrangements made for tea and other refreshments. French organizations have undertaken to decorate the graves with fresh flowers and French and American flags. The most com

1930-03-18.text: WOKING, SURREY, England, March 18 (P)— A change for the worse in the condition of Lord Balfour, veteran British statesman who has been ill several weeks, was reported today. A bulletin issued today by his physicians said: “Lord Balfour is not so well and his condition is causing anxiety.”

London, March 17 (®)—The naval conference, undaunted by difficulties today settled down to a new siege for a five-power disarmament treaty. The British official spokesman announced tonight that the conference was not going to break down this week nor was it going to succeed this week. He said the delegates still were determined to arrive at a treaty satisfactory to all, but no definite development was likely to occur until next weekend, when Premier Tardieu, of France, returns from Paris for another conference with Prime Minister MacDonald. Meanwhile, Foreign Minister Briand will continue to head the French exploration party scouting over new routes toward solution of the Franco-Italian parity problem, which today more than ever became the crux of the conference. Secretary Stimson, Ambassador Morrow, Ambassador Dawes and Senator Reed and others of the American delegation have enlisted in

| Dunedin, New Zealand, March 14. -(/P)-—In perhaps the most inclusive broadcast ever attempted in New Zealand, Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd addressed approximately 400,000 school children today telling them of his experiences during the year of exploration in Antarctica. The two islands of New Zealand were linked up by cable across Cook Strait and the address, made in the Town Hall before 7,000 children of Dunedin, was sent by land lines to Christchurch, Wellington and Auckland. Receiving sets were installed in practically every school in the country and Byrd's voice was heard equally well in all of them. His talk of adventure in the South Polar regions, which included a flight over the South Pole, won the friendship of thousands and when Admiral Byrd proposed that he take to the United States the greeting of the school children of New Zealand the applause was enthusiastic. London, March 18.—Success of the London naval conference appeared to rest today upon the ability of the powers to persuade Italy to abandon her demand for naval equality with France or, failing that, to present definite figures on her minimum tonnage requirements. Although the position of Dino Grandi, Italian foreign minister, has been unwavering, hope was expressed that the hint of France's willingness to consider reduction of her own estimates might lead Italy to reciprocate. Since publication of reports that Japan and the United States have reached a satisfactory understanding, Premier Andre Tardieu’s statement of Sunday night indicating his satisfaction at progress of the Anglo-French negotiations, observers now regard the Italian question as the sole issue of major importance that stands in the way of a five power pact.

LONDON, March 18.—The five power naval conference today entered its ninth week, apparently still a long way from its goal of a naval limitation treaty which will not really involve additional construction. In the words of Andre Tardieu, premier of France, leaving for Paris after a week-end with Ramsay MacDonald and his own delegation: "The conference continues;" but even his professed optimism and assurance of eventual success failed to convince observers that appreciable progress is being made. Most rigid secrecy has been invoked by the delegates to cloak their activities here at this stage, but it appeared today that the French situation and the Franco-Italian differences were still, as they have been for weeks, the crux of difficulty at agreement. Paris was understood to be negotiating privately with Rome for a better understanding of what the Mussolini government means by parity with

London, March 18. (#)--James E. Fenton, Australian minister for trade and customs and delegate to the naval conference announced today that the Australian delegation had provisionally booked return passage for Australia for April 12.

Shanghai, Mar. 18—(-1)—Bandits and communists, said delayed Chinese reports received here today, attacked and captured Fuan, a town near Kiangfu, central Kiangsi province, massacring all Fuan officials and 2,000 men, women and children, early this month. After slaying the populace, continued the reports, the bandits looted the town, carrying their plunder into the mountains of western Kiangsi. The outrage was reported by the magistrate of Kiangfu. He said the people of Fuan were paralyzed with fear and were afraid further to oppose the bandits, who were depicted as subjecting Kiangsi province to a merciless deluge of robberies and wholesale killings. The magistrate appealed to the Nationalist government at Nanking for military assistance.

Madrid, March 17, (4)—Funeral honors surpassed only by those rendered a Spanish sovereign will be accorded former Premier Primo De Rivera, who dominated Spain for six years, but died an exile in Paris. The cabinet decided today that Primo should be buried with the same ceremonials he would have had if he had been premier when he died, or as a captain-general dying in active command of forces. Premier Damasco Berenguer and his ministers officially resolved that their predecessor deserved this honor and paid tribute to his patriotic services, emphasizing particularly his ending of the Moroccan trouble.

PARIS, March 18.—(4)—Warning that the world of today faces the same risk of war as preceding epochs was issued by Senator Henry Berenger, former ambassador to Washington, in a report to the French parliament.

Berlin, March 18. (4)—The Reichstag today adopted the new law for the protection of the republic by a vote of 265 to 150. The law supersedes the old defense law which went out of operation on July 22, 1929. Under the old law the former kaiser was specifically forbidden to reenter Germany. The new law does not contain this provision and while under it the kaiser theoretically would be free to return, nobody, not even the monarchists, considers even the possibility of his return.

MADRID, March 18. The body of Don Miguel Primo de Rivera was brought back today to Spain, entering the country at Irun, the same frontier city through which so many of those he exiled when dictator left their homeland, and from which he himself departed just a month ago, discredited and cast aside. Friends and foes alike, their bitterness quenched at the bier, planned for him the highest honors the Spanish monarchy accords to one not its sovereign. The former dictator will be buried as if he at his death still was premier, and with the military pomp of his rank of captain general. The funeral party will remain at Irun, which is near San Sebastian, until late this afternoon. The body will be removed from the train at the border city to a special chapel in the railway station, where a mass service will be sung, departure for Madrid following. The funeral will arrive at the Norte station, M

Madrid, March 17 (4)—Sidney Franklin, Brooklyn matador, who was seriously gored by a bull yesterday, was resting easier late today, and his physicians said that unless complications developed, his recovery could be expected. The Brooklyn bull fighter, who has made a name for himself in Spain because of his fearlessness and skill, received many messages of good wishes from other bull fighters and enthusiasts of the Spanish sport.

Irun, Spain, Mar. 18.—(#)—The Spanish batteries topping the hills along the French frontier roared a 21-gun salute today as the body of Primo de Rivera crossed the border of Spain. © Thus, was the former dictator who died in Paris Sunday night, honored by the same salute that would be given a king. The train halted at the little railway station here, where sometimes exiles have seen their last of Spain. The coffin was removed and placed in state in a chapel of the station. Masses were said by priests and prayers were offered. Late this afternoon the funeral train will leave for Madrid, where it will arrive Wednesday morning. 1930-04-29.text: LONDON, April 29.—(I.N.S.)—Two hundred persons were drowned when the steamship Condor foundered in a cyclone in the Padma river, near Nagarbari, India, according to a Central News dispatch received here today. Only eighteen were saved, so suddenly did the vessel overturn from the fierce blast of the storm. Waves poured into the cabins and terrified passengers clung to the rails. The master of the ship and the crew made heroic efforts to weather the cyclone but the powerful gusts caught the ship broadside and she went over in the turbulent waters. All mails and cargo were lost.

| LONDON, April 29—(?)—Behind a bare announcement of unsatisfactory conduct by Garhwali native troops in the rioting at Peshawar last Wednesday, observers to- day saw a threat of mutiny with conse- quent danger of peace in India. Until now there has been no word that the loyalty of the native troops or sepoys had ever been questioned despite their hav- ing been called upon at various times to put down disturbances growing out of Mahatma Gandhi's civil disobedience campaign. An official India office communique published today, however said: “In view of the possibility of exagger- at ed and misleading rumors, the govern- ment of India thinks it advisable to make it known that during the recent disturbances at Peshawar when troops ‘had to be employed the conduct of a small element namely, two platoons of the second battalion of the eighteenth Royal Garhwali Rifles was found to be unsatisfac

Bombay, India, (*)—Two Pathans were killed and five seriously injured today near Nasik in a fierce encounter between a band of seven Pathans and villagers from Nangar. The villagers turned out in large numbers when the alarm of “robbers” was raised. The Pathans who are Afghan hillsmen, were armed with knives and pistols. They opened fire, but the villagers hemmed them in a ravine and used long range slingshots with deadly effect.

Calcutta, April 23—I, M. Sen Gupta, who now is serving a sentence of six months rigorous imprisonment for sedition and conspiracy growing out of the civil disobedience campaign, was today unanimously reelected mayor of Calcutta. This will be his fifth term.

LONDON, April 29.—(UP)—Rocco Fannelli, aide to “Scarface Al” Capone, Chicago beer king and gang leader, drank cocktails quite illegally here last night and boisterously bantered about the liquor laws of the United States. “So long as our folks have got a thirst we are the boys to quench it,” Fannelli confided. “Why should not the Americans enjoy a drink in America—the land of the free?” Fannelli laughed at the fact the Chicago crime commission has placed his name on the list of public enemies. That, to him, was “all bunco.” “We are able to take care of ourselves,” he said. “And what we say goes in Chicago.” Fannelli turned to the problem of gun shooting as found in Chicago. “Where there’s competition there's bound to be little tiffs at times,” he said reminiscently, with a touch of the philosophic. “The cleanest way out of them is passing a gun. We do not have them for ornaments in Chica

Bombay, India, Apr. 29—(AP) Orthodox Hindus and “untouchables” clashed before the temple at Nasik Sunday. The untouchables engaged in a demonstration against the higher caste Hindus, finally drawing from them a bombardment of stones and dirty water. There have been several reports recently of similar conflicts in other villages. It is said that many untouchables are determined to embrace Mohammedanism in the hope of securing relief from high caste Hindu oppression. A considerable effort has been made to have Mahatma Gandhi and the all-India national congress promise an improvement in their condition.

(International News Service) | LONDON, April 29.—Two hundred persons were drowned when the passenger Condor foundered in a cyclone in the Padma river, near Nagarbari, India, according to a Central News dispatch received here today. Only 18 were saved, so suddenly did the vessel overturn from the fierce blast of the storm. Waves poured into the cabins and terrified passengers clung to the rails. The master of the ship and the crew made heroic efforts to weather the cyclone, but the powerful gusts caught the ship broadside and she went over in the turbulent waters. All mails and cargo were lost.

Shenghal, April 23—(4)—Captured by bandits who looted the prosperous Hupeh province City of Scientaschen, on the Han river, 59 miles from Hankow, two American Catholic Priests were reported by Chinese sources today to have been shot by their captors. The priests, believed to have been Father Francis Murray and Father Patrick Lassan, were from the mission established by the Chinese mission of St. Columbus, Neb. Others of the mission were reported to have escaped the bandit attack. Bandits who have been ravaging northern Kiangsu province for several days, torturing peasants, looting and burning their homes, swept into Kingsuchen, posted machine guns and mowed down 1,000 helpless inhabitants. One thousand others were carried off with loot from the city. Kingsuchen, which was burned by the bandits before they departed, is within 100 miles of Nanking, capital of the Nationalist government.

Shanghai, April 28.—(AP)— Bandits armed with machine guns massacred 1,000 residents of Kingsuchen, northern Kiangsu province Saturday, it was learned today. One thousand captives were carried off with loot of the city which was burned. This latest massacre by outlaws who have recently slain thousands in other sections of China took place within 100 miles of Nanking, seat of the Nationalist government. The countryside about Kingsuchen was ravaged and peasants were tortured. Mounted upon horses, the bandits dashed into the town, posted machine guns and mowed down the helpless inhabitants, afterward looting their homes before setting fire to them. Priests Taken Two priests were kidnapped by brigands who sacked the city of Sientaochen, 50 miles northwest of Hankow. The priests were attached to the mission established by the Chinese Mission Society of St. Columbans, Nebraska. Most of the pers

Moscow, April 29.—(U.P)—The Soviet government, it was learned today, sent a note to Poland yesterday in reference to the recent discovery of an infernal machine in the Soviet legation at Warsaw. The note called attention to the “extraordinary danger of the situation.” The bomb, which was discovered in the Soviet legation at Warsaw before it exploded, was said by police there to have had only a small charge of explosive. News of the discovery, however, stimulated the recent opposition of some Soviet officials toward Poland, and the incident was widely discussed here.
—The former Crown Prince Frederick Wilhelm of Germany, traveling incognito as Count Von Golden, is spending a few days here en route to Germany after a trip to Egypt, NS ES, Italy, Apr. 29.—(AP)

1930-05-07.text: Delhi, India, May 6. — (AP)— Two persons were killed in rioting in the heart of Delhi today. The Delhi Indian infantry and eight armored cars established a state of armed defense this forenoon. The dead were natives. A virtual state of war prevailed in the Chandi Chowk—the principal thoroughfare of Delhi. Through this street the armored cars kept up a continual patrol. Entrances to all civil buildings were guarded by troops. The chief commissioner immediately following the riot promulgated section 144 of the criminal procedure code forbidding the assembly of more than five persons. —o— ° London, May 6—(AP)—Military and police arrangements were tightened everywhere today in India to prevent possible outbreaks in retaliation for the arrest yesterday of Mahatma Gandhi, leader of the civil disobedience movement by which Indian nationalists have sought independence from Great Britain. Hartals

By The Associated Press. Bombay, India, May 6—An almost endless list of outbreaks today marked the turning of the imprisoned Mahatma Gandhi's campaign of civil disobedience from peaceful into warlike progress. Bloodshed occurred in a dozen cities where hostile actions of the “holy one” followers were met with armed force. The home and Indian governments strengthened the hands of local police authorities with troops and armored cars. Outstanding among the day's disorders was a clash at Delhi in which two natives were killed and fifty or more seriously wounded. A half mile procession of Gandhi's devotees filed into the city’s principal thoroughfare, Chandi Chowk, refusing to disperse.

Bombay, India, May 7—®— Threat of a widespread Indian boycott of British firms today loomed as the outstanding feature of Mahatma Gandhi's non-violence campaign of civil resistance. The authorities viewed as an ugly feature the contemplated move by certain Indian commercial organizations. Indian businessmen heretofore, it was pointed out, had not allowed their political views to influence their business relations with the British and it was feared a boycott would lead to bitter feeling in the field of commerce and possible retaliatory steps by victims. Bombay was quiet today. Excitement has subsided sufficiently to permit the withdrawal of military pickets from the Indian quarters. Cotton mills generally were working with full forces. The intended activities of V. J. Patel, former president of the legislative assembly, were awaited with interest. There was speculation as to whether he wo

London, May 7. (4?)—Government circles in India were represented here today as confident, notwithstanding widespread rioting which has followed the arrest of Mahatma Gandhi, that they can control the situation there. British businessmen in India are said to share this view. While they approve of the internment of Gandhi, which many of them advocated for a long time prior to the government action, they believe that the government should refrain as far as possible from emphasizing forcible measures, lest matters be aggravated and the boycott on foreign goods and banks be strengthened. Modern Indian opinion is also represented as supporting the government and is still looking hopefully forward to the proposed round table conference. There is no expectation that the demonstrations will cease suddenly, and it is realized further serious trouble may break out at any time, especially in Bombay,

LONDON, May 7.—(LN.S.)—Three hundred casualties have occurred in the rioting at Delhi following the arrest of Mahatma Gandhi, nationalist leader, it was stated in official dispatches to the evening newspapers today. Scores were shot down when police, aided by soldiers in armored cars, fired into a mob which had attacked a police automobile. The exact number of dead is not known, but is believed to exceed twenty. Many of the others were seriously wounded.

Calcutta, India, May 7.— Troops clashed with revolutionary bands on the bank of the river Karnafuli, opposite Chittagong, today, killing four of the insurgents. A villager also was killed in the fighting and five others, including a constable, were reported seriously wounded.

RISTOL, R. I.—(4)—The Enterprise, the first of four prospective defenders of the America’s cup to be completed, was launched here Monday shortly after a similar event had disturbed the other side of the Atlantic at Gosport, England, where Sir Thomas Lipton’s challenger, the Shamrock V., slid down the ways. The Enterprise bore the name of a famous little navy schooner, “the lucky little Enterprise,” which helped bring the Barbary pirates to terms a century ago. She was designed by W. Starling Burgess for a syndicate of well-known New York yachtsmen and built by Merriweather. She is smaller than the other three defenders and slightly smaller than Sir Thomas’ challenger. The Enterprise is of bronze and the Shamrock V of wood. GOSPORT, England—()—Sir Thomas Lipton’s yacht Shamrock V with which he will make his latest attempt for the historic America’s cup, was launched Monday. The Countess o

Bombay, India, May 7 (UP)—The list of injured mounted today as Indian passions rose in revolt against the imprisonment of Mahatma Gandhi, the leader of the passive resistance campaign, and the passive resistance campaign for Indian independence turned into an orgy of violence. Reports from important centers such as Delhi and Calcutta and from other towns in India were that more than 150 persons were injured in outbreaks following Gandhi's arrest, at least three of them seriously. Delhi, India, May 7 (UP)—Business was at a standstill while supporters of Gandhi in his campaign for Indian independence paraded through the streets engaging in frequent clashes with police. More than 70 Indians and police were injured in the frequent clashes yesterday.

BOMBAY, India, May 7. — (AP) — Police charged a mob of weavers of the Standard Mill here today and dispersed them after the Indians, striking in protest at the arrest of Mahatma Gandhi, had stoned them. At first the weavers were more than a match for the constabulary but reinforcements were rushed up and the demonstration was halted. The mill is next to the textile mill where there were disturbances yesterday. A large crowd welcomed V. J. Patel, resigned speaker of the Indian Legislative Assembly, as he arrived here this forenoon from Calcutta. The crowd escorted him from Victoria station through the principal streets. Arrest Protested. He exhorted his audience to remain non-violent and to carry out the program which is to be laid down in a few days at a meeting of the all-India National Congress committee. A strong protest at Gandhi’s arrest was made here at a meeting of representatives

Sydney, May 7.—Two obsolete Australian battleships anchored in the shark-infested Hawkesbury River are to be used as prison quarters for hundreds of short-term prisoners who will build roads through the large Kuring-gai Chase National Park. The sharks will discourage plots to escape.

Paris, May 7.—(®)—Marshal Joffre, hero of the battle of the Marne, is seriously ill at his country residence at Louveciennes, near Paris. His friends have fears for his recovery. His condition was revealed only yesterday through circuitous sources, the 78-year-old soldier having expressly forbidden that information as to progress of his illness or his whereabouts be issued. Telephone queries to his home went unanswered and newspapermen were barred. It was learned, however, he was stricken upon his return a week ago from a visit to his birthplace on the shores of the Mediterranean, in the eastern Pyrenees region.

Paris, May 7.—(4)—Marshal Joffre, hero of the Marne, about whose health his friends have shown concern, insisted today that he was feeling quite all right. The 78-year-old soldier attended business at the Superior War Council this morning as usual and issued a denial of reports of his ill health. Marshal Joffre has been somewhat frail of late and his friends have shown some anxiety.

DOORN, Holland, May 6.—(U.P.) The former German Kaiser appeared in the role of fireman today when a blaze started in the villa of Brand Dwreibergen, a friend of the exiled monarch. Wilhelm himself dashed to the fire with his own fire engine from Doorn, only to find that the blaze was extinguished before he arrived.

LE BOURGET, France, April 30 (AP)— Adrienne Bolland, French girl who flew over the Chilean Andes in 1923, today landed her plane on the roof of a big shed when telegraph wires tossed it out of its course as she made a forced landing. Her motor failed during the air baptism of a woman passenger and she was unable to clear the wires. She steadied the plane sufficiently to set it down on the roof and in order to avoid rolling off maneuvered to turn the machine on its nose. Meanwhile she threw her arm around the frightened woman beside her to prevent her falling or jumping out. The plane was wrecked but the passenger, uninjured, descended a ladder.

MADRID, May 6.—Spain’s aggressive university students, responsible for several recent demonstrations protesting police methods, were quiet today and the government announced the entire country was tranquil. San Carlos medical college, whose students battled police yesterday with the result that a workman was killed and at least 15 other persons were injured, remained closed today by government order and strong forces of police guarded it to prevent any attempts at demonstrations. Some students went to the college as usual this morning, but left quietly after reading placards which announced the closing. In other parts of Spain undergraduates showed sympathy with their colleagues in the capital but no disorder resulted. Students of the University of Salamanca, believing some of the Madrid students had been arrested, attempted a sympathy strike, but returned to their classes when assured b

1930-05-23.text: London. May 23. —(AP)—J. Ramsay MacDonald, bolstered by an overwhelming vote of confidence by his own party, today turned his face toward political opponents, Friends were confident that he had so strengthened his own position that he would be able to ride out of the political storm which has gathered about the unemployment issue, and that there would be no general election for some time. Vote Is Overwhelming. The parliamentary labor party, meeting in closed session at which the life of the government was at stake, voted 210 to 29 last night to defeat a motion of censure on the ministerial unemployment policy offered by Sir Oswald Mosley, patrician laborite, who this week resigned his place in the cabinet as chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster. Sir Oswald's motion was offered in a speech of 55 minutes duration. In the succeeding two hours Mr. MacDonald and his labor ministers were under

By the Associated Press. Bombay, India, May 22.—British and Indian troops were so firmly established in control of the several salt-raid zones tonight that further attempts at civil disobedience and demonstrations by the natives became out of the question. Dharasana was under martial law. Troops were bivouacked on the scene of yesterday's serious encounters in which about 600 Hindu demonstrators were injured. If the followers of Mahatma Gandhi expected to execute further raids upon government salt pans they made no sign tonight.

London, May 23—(INS)—Lord Strickland of Sizergh, head of the ministry and minister for police and posts of Malta, was wounded today when a man fired three shots at him in an attempted assassination in Malta, according to a Central News dispatch. The dispatch did not say how seriously Lord Strickland was injured.

8 The Associated Press London, May 22—Prime Minister MacDonald won an overwhelming victory at a meeting of the parliamentary Labour party tonight to discuss the government’s unemployment policy. Sir Oswald Mosley’s motion of censure was defeated 210 to 29.

Star Correspondent. BOMBAY, May 23—For the first time in a week there was a lull in the Blayagrabia' salt raids today, but the peace was preserved only by British troops who held complete control in the Dharasana salt works area. The arrival of troops at Dharasana and the breaking up of the national congress volunteers’ camp at Unldl, nearby, forced an interruption, at least for the present, of Satyagrahis plans for massed raids on the salt pots, and scattered the volunteers from their center of activity. British authorities refused to grant bail to Mrs. Sarojini Naidu and other leaders who were arrested with her during the bloody Dharasana raid Wednesday, and remanded them to jail for a week.

London, May 23 (UP)—Prime Minister Ramsey MacDonald’s government survived the first of three serious threats against its life by a wide margin of votes last night. A motion put by Sir Oswald Mosley, returned member of the government, at the party meeting in the Commons Chamber and designed as a censure of the government for its unemployment policies, was defeated by a vote of 210 to 29.

/ Bombay, May 23 (UP)—A great procession in protest against the government's action in driving independence volunteers from their camp near the Dharasana salt depot, marched through the business district of Bombay today. The procession entered the business district only after police withdrew a blockade which halted the demonstration for several hours. The police first prohibited the parade, and national congress leaders authorized the volunteers to sit down in the streets. This stalemate was ended when all offices were closed in the business district and the procession was then permitted to continue.

LONDON, May 23. — (INS) — A plucky young British aviatrix who for 20 hours worried the English more than India or politics was safe today at the village of Hailioklik, near Atambua, on the Island of Timor, according to dispatches to the London evening newspapers. On a solo flight to Australia, which began at Croydon, May 8, Amy Johnson had reeled off her daily flights with precision, her flight plane performing excellently. Nearing her goal, she was unreported for nearly 20 hours, and the English public dropped everything else to follow and anxiously scan the newspapers for word of England's “girl Lindbergh.”

MARSEILLES, France, May 23. (AP)—The Fabre Steamship Line was informed by wireless today that 112 Moslem pilgrims perished when the Steamer Asia burned in Jeddah harbor yesterday. The crew was unable to get many of the pilgrims, who were en route from Mecca to Jibouti, to leave the ship. Advices said the pilgrims dropped on their knees on the deck and prayed as they were enveloped in flames. Most of the victims were inhabitants of Somaliland, returning from the great pilgrimage to the Holy City of Mecca. The origin of the fire was unknown. The Asia was a total loss. Somaliland is a region of East Central Africa.

Auteuil, France, May 23.—Helen Wills Moody and Elizabeth Ryan, America’s standard-bearers in the women’s doubles event of the French tennis championships, reached the finals today by defeating the strong British combination of Joan Fry and Ermyntrude Harvey by the convincing scores of 6-1, 6-2, 7-5.

Shanghai, May 23—The Nationalist government tonight claimed its forces had crushingly defeated the northern alliance rebel armies in northern Ho-nan province and had taken 20,000 rebel prisoners with field guns at Lanfeng. The rebel armies, said the government advices, were in general retreat toward Kaifeng, Honan province. Foreign dispatches stated that the fighting along the Haichow Tungkwan railway caused heavy casualties. The Nationalist artillery used shrapnel, which took a heavy toll among the rebels. The Chinese Red Cross of Shanghai issued an appeal for Chinese doctors to proceed to the battlefront to attend the wounded.

PARIS, May 23. — (IN.S.)--One hundred and twelve pilgrims perished on board the French steamship Asia afire in the Red Sea, according to a message received today at Marseilles from the captain of the vessel. The message said the Asia was still burning. It was assumed that rescue ships had removed the crew and the remainder of the 1,500 pilgrims who were reported to be on board the ill-fated vessel.

PARIS, May 23 (AP)—Ranks of the American gold star mothers in France to visit the graves of their sons were swelled today by another group of 106 arriving at Cherbourg aboard the steamer Republic. Everything was in readiness to welcome them. United States army officers went to meet them at the steamer and escort them to Paris, where they were due this evening. Meanwhile, the vanguard of mothers visited the cemeteries.

SHANGHAI, China, May 23.—(U. P.)—The government troops of Chiang Kai-Shek inflicted “heavy casualties” on the so-called northern rebel armies, the Kuo Min News agency reported today in describing the capture of Lan-Feng from the rebels. Chiang mobilized his forces in Honan province two days ago for the opening of a campaign against the northern armies with which Yen Hsi-Shan, “model governor” of Shansi, and Feng Yu-Hsiang have attempted to set up a new regime at Peiping. Lan-Feng was the immediate objective of the nationalists. The battle lasted two days. About 20,000 prisoners were captured, the government reports claimed.

1930-04-09.text: SIMLA, INDIA, April 9.—(—Government policy with reference to the civil disobedience campaign of Mahatma Gandhi, Indian nationalist leader, today was said in responsible quarters to involve suppression of the movement as quickly as possible but not at the price of disturbance. To date this has brought arrest of many of Gandhi's lieutenants and devotees, while the sexagenarian leader himself has been left strictly alone, although courting arrest from the very beginning of his march from Ahmadabad to Jalapur. It was said to be the government's plan to deal with each situation as it arose and in accordance with local conditions. The letter of the law probably will not be enforced, although it is not regarded that non-interference with Gandhi's person is to be taken as indicative weakness of the authorities, who are said to feel that precipitate action might give artificial stimulus to the go

London, April 8 ().—Agreement between Great Britain and France upon questions of national security in Europe, as indicated tonight by Foreign Minister Briand, after his conference with Prime Minister MacDonald, will permit the London Naval negotiations to continue with a five power disarmament treaty as the goal. Whether a five power agreement is really any nearer realization could not be determined tonight, however, in view of the very brief and restrained official announcement made by the British and French delegations after the conference of their chiefs. Briand, returning to the Carlton after the interview, declared to the French journalists that there now was agreement between the British and French regarding interpretation of Article XVI of the League of Nations covenant. That is the article which deals with measures to be taken should any number of the league resort to war in disr
LONDON, Apr. 9.--A full agreement on a three-power naval parity plan was reached today. The agreement was completed when Japan withdrew her request to transfer 23,000 tons to the submarine category.

| By The Associated Press Dandi, Bombay Presidency, India, April 8.--Mahatma Gandhi has decided to leave Dandi, where he led the civil disobedience movement by breaking the salt laws Sunday morning, and go to neighboring territory to continue his campaign for Indian Independence. | Gandhi said that Abbas Tyabji, his second in command, was going to Nadiad to take charge of the Kaira district, Although Gandhi himself has not been molested, numerous of his assistants and even his son have been given prison sentences for infringing the government salt monopoly. The British are refraining from arresting him to prevent his attaining the status of a martyr.

(United Press Staff Correspondent) LONDON, April 9—(UF)—Delegates to the naval conference looked today to their host, Premier Ramsey MacDonald of Great Britain, for a sign which would indicate whether a five-power treaty might yet be possible. As things stand at this late date, the United States and Japan are ready to sign a three-power pact with Britain, excluding France and Italy—but none of the three powers desires to close permanently the possibility of including all five nations represented here in a naval treaty of some sort. The return of Aristide Briand, French foreign minister, yesterday, has tended to dispel some pessimism. The statement issued by the French delegation that conversations with the British would continue today gave cause for further hope. London, April 5.—France having expressed satisfaction regarding the security accorded her by the British interpretation of Article 16 on the covenant of the league of nations, French and British experts this afternoon started discussion of how much could be lopped off the French naval tonnage figures. The British wish the French to slash 200,000 tons from the 724,000 originally demanded, but such a reduction is causing a raising of eyebrows among the French delegates. However, Jacques Dumesnil, French minister of Marine, and A. V. Alexander, first lord of the admiralty, tackled the problem and it was expected Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, of Great Britain, and Aristide Briand, French foreign minister, would meet again to discuss the situation.
