LONDON, April 8.—(4)—The Duchess of Bedford, who is 65 and an aviation enthusiast, made her first solo flight today in her own plane at her home, Woburn Abbey, Bedfordshire. The Duchess, who is believed to be the oldest woman pilot, expects to start on a non-stop flight to Africa Thursday.

BOMBAY, April 3—The government continued today its discreet but stern activities against the leaders of the “civil disobedience” campaign and while Mahatma Gandhi, “the holy man,” still enjoyed freedom his son and scores of his lieutenants and converts were languishing in prison. Having been disappointed yesterday when he was not arrested at the Village of Aat for making salt, Gandhi made a fiery speech urging the people to make salt and resist its confiscation “until the death.” He exhorted women to participate in the movement, declaring that if the authorities “touch our women” the whole country would be “ablaze.” Gandhi has announced his intention of continuing his march throughout the country, carrying the “civil disobedience” idea personally to every village, town and city. A boycott of British goods, inaugurated here by Gandhi supporters, apparently is gaining strength. Several lar

BOMBAY, India, (UP) - The government of India continued Wednesday its passive resistance to the efforts of the Mahatma M. K. Gandhi to force his arrest for breaking the salt monopoly laws. Gandhi, who dramatized his breach of the salt laws by marching for days across India to the sea near Jalalpur, proceeded to the village of Bhimrad Wednesday morning, where his son was arrested Monday in connection with the Elder Gandhi's civil disobedience campaign. The energetic Indian leader, accompanied by a group of selected volunteers, witnessed on the way his followers collecting salt, emulating his own example. Others have done the same in various localities during the week, and about ten have been arrested since Sunday.

Moscow, April 9.—A sensational order for modification of anti-religious demonstrations by the Soviet Society of the Godless will be published tomorrow. Indicating that worshippers would be less molested at Easter time than in any previous year since the revolution, the society’s magazine “The Godless” will instruct its members to “make less noise and less excitement” and to concentrate on more serious propaganda. The leaders of the anti-religious movement will seek to restrain enthusiastic members who have planned extensive demonstrations for the Easter season. The atheists were prepared to have anti-religious pageants and parades at the time the worshippers go to the churches. While the new instructions will not prevent anti-Easter pageants, it appeared certain that the hilarity and enthusiasm of previous years would be diminished.

1930-04-02.text: London, April 1—Japan has joined the American-British consortium for naval disarmament, thereby assuring the basic success of the London conference with at least a 3-power treaty. A five-power agreement, including France and Italy, still hangs in the balance. Both Foreign Minister Briand of France and Prime Minister MacDonald of Great Britain said tonight that the gulf was narrowing rapidly on the security issue. But even with that chasm bridged an old terror—Franco-Italian parity—still threatens difficulties. Formal Answer Tomorrow The Japanese government's favorable reply to participation in a five-year limitation program proposed by the United States and Great Britain was received by the Japanese delegation today. It was studied, and a formal answer to Secretary Stimson and MacDonald is expected tomorrow morning. Important reservations will be attached to the Japanese acceptance but t

LONDON, Apr. 2.—Reijiro Wakatsuki, head of the Japanese naval delegation, this afternoon delivered his government’s reply regarding tripartite agreement negotiated in London to Secretary of State Stimson and Prime Minister MacDonald. It was stated in conference circles that the answer, as already predicted from Tokyo, was a virtual acceptance of the agreement. The Americans, British and Japanese will meet again tomorrow forenoon to discuss the reply further. The American spokesmen said this afternoon there was every indication that the negotiations would result in a solution of the American-British-Japanese problem.

London, April 2. (4)—A formula opening the way for Franco-British agreement on French naval tonnage was under consideration today by the five power naval conference. If agreement should eventuate, the second of the three principal barriers to a five-power limitation treaty will have been removed, leaving only one, the Italian demand for naval parity with France. Japanese acceptance of the Reed-Matsudaira compromise schedule covering the Japanese-American relationship removed the first. Although apparently regarded favorably by the delegation itself, there was question as to what viewpoint British opposition would take to the formula, which it was understood France accepts as making more definite British military commitments under the League of Nations covenant. DUNEDIN, NEW ZEALAND, APR. 2. (AP).—Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd's party will leave Dunedin for Wellington on Monday, news having arrived that accommodations are available on the steamship Rangitiki sailing from Wellington on April 24. The Rear Admiral will leave for Christchurch where he will receive a civic celebration before embarking for Wellington at which place he will arrive Tuesday morning. Another civic reception will be given him here that evening.

London, April 20 (UP) — Delegates of the five world powers continued today their negotiations, confident that the turning point in the naval conference had been passed and that the obstacles which have threatened to wreck the hopes of the parley are now over. Acceptance, with certain reservations, by the Japanese government of the American and British proposals on naval tonnage ratios, together with indications that the British and French were about to arrive at a happy solution of the French demand for a security pact, brought the greatest single day of the meeting since January. The British spokesmen told the press that search for a formula to meet French demands continues satisfactorily. The chief delegates will meet at St. James Palace at 4 p.m., in preparation for a session at 10:30 a.m. Friday. The Japanese government’s reply to Anglo-American proposals for a naval treaty will be d

Ottawa, April 2.—(AP)—Opposition to the government bill to prohibit the export of liquor into the United States was voiced in the senate last night when the measure came up for second reading. A proposal by Senator Willoughby that a special committee be selected by the senate to secure information as to the probable effect of the bill on Canada’s national and economic life and on international relations met with opposition from Senator Dandurand, government leader, who refused to accept the amendment. Willoughby said while he believed in most friendly relations between the two countries, he did not think Canada should be too generous, declaring that the Volstead act was not being well enforced and that a straw vote now being taken in the United States showed opposition to it.

LONDON, April 2. — The conference appeared today to have found an avenue to success. The Tokio government’s cabled acceptance of Anglo-American tonnage proposals gave impetus to the negotiations between other delegations and there were indications that the more serious problems of the conference were nearing solution. Acceptance of those proposals by the Japanese makes certain accord between the three leading powers, Britain, Japan and the United States and regardless of whether a five power pact is written a tri-partite agreement is possible. Believe Accord Near Yet the security requirements of France, the big obstacle to the five-power pact, may be satisfied through interpretations placed on article sixteen, of the league covenant and agreed upon in principle by England and France. CALCUTTA, India, April 1 (®)—A new rule which forbids carters to take their buffaloes out during the hottest part of the day led to rioting here today in which five persons were killed. Fifty policemen and 50 civilians were injured, while 20 persons were arrested. Students also demonstrated in sympathy with the carters outside the student hotel in Cornwallis Road. They erected barriers formed from material taken from a road repair job and threw brickbats at the police. The police retaliated by dispersing them with barrel staves. Double police patrols were in the streets tonight to prevent further disorder.

By United Press LONDON, April 2.—The chief delegates at the naval conference decided today to postpone the scheduled plenary session from Friday until next week. At the same time, the Japanese delegates were informed that the United States and Britain had accepted the three-power naval understanding subject to minor reservations made by the Japanese government. Discussions on the three-power accord will be continued tomorrow. Jacques Louis Dumesnil, French minister of marine; Hugh Gibson and George A. Gordon of the American delegation met at the Ayace at 4 p.m., immediately after the Anglo-Japanese-American session. The Japanese spokesman said it was not likely the Japanese reply to the Anglo-American proposition would be published until the other delegates had discussed it. He said the reply should really be treated as "instructions" to the delegation. Meanwhile, the British cabinet met

DUBLIN, April 2 (AP)—A motion in the Dail Eireann to elect Eamon De Valera, Fianna Fail leader, president of the Free State council was defeated late today 93 to 74. DUBLIN, Irish Free State, April 2 (AP)—A break occurred within the ranks of Eamon De Valera’s own party today in the hour preceding the convening of the Dail when a new Irish president was to be elected to succeed William T. Cosgrave who resigned last week. Sean T. O'Kelly strongly urged the Fianna Fail and entire opposition to support Thomas J. O’Connell, labor party candidate for the office, as an alternative to either Mr. De Valera or Mr. Cosgrave, who was generally expected to be re-elected. He based his attitude on a statement by William Davin of the laborites, that they would not in any circumstances support De Valera, because they accepted the Irish treaty with England.

LONDON (Wednesday) —()— The Daily Herald, labor party organ, says that as a result of conversations between Foreign Secretary Henderson of Great Britain and Foreign Minister Briand of France a formula has been found that may give France the security she has been demanding and enable her to enter a five-power naval disarmament treaty. A draft of this formula, according to the Herald, was sent to Paris for thorough consideration by Premier Andre Tardieu and the French cabinet. The newspaper understands that in view of these new circumstances Italy has at last agreed to eliminate the contentious word “parity” with reference to her naval claims, which has been a rigid barrier in Franco-Italian negotiations. The Daily Mail, conservative, also reports that a draft formula was sent to Paris, adding that Foreign Minister Briand expressed approval of it in general terms. The Mail thinks that the

Bayreuth, Germany, April 1—The widow of the immortal Richard Wagner died peacefully this morning at the age of 92. To the last she insisted that she was happy and well. Frau Cosima, as she was generally known, had long been infirm. She contracted bronchial catarrh several days ago, but her death was unexpected. Three daughters—Isolde, Thode and Eva—were present. A son, Siegfried, who is conducting Wagner performances at the Scala opera house in Milan, could not reach the bedside in time. Much of the success of Wagner, who was author of the Ring opera, Lohengrin and other famous works, was attributed to his wife's aid. She was the daughter of Franz Liszt. The body will be cremated at Coburg Friday and an urn containing the ashes will be placed alongside Wagner's tomb at Bayreuth. The romantic life of Frau Cosima was notable for the unusual arrangement whereby she persuaded her first husba
TUTTGART, Germany, Apr. 2. —(AP)—The proprietor of the restaurant which a few days ago served bear meat to its patrons died today of trichinosis. He was the tenth victim of the repast.

Vienna, April 1. (ep cover) this part of Europe April fool jokes are sometimes no joke, Many persons were attracted to the Danube Canal here today to see three American marines, the arrival of which from the Black Sea was announced in an afternoon newspaper, with photographs. But there were no submarines; it was all a joke for All Fools’ Day. Much indignation was reported from Budapest, where afternoon newspapers announced the death in Egypt of Count Albert Apponyi. References to the sad event were made at the municipal council meeting and other public assemblies, but Apponyi proved to be alive and well.

1930-04-17.text: BOMBAY.—(4)—Civil disobedience with attendant battles, bloodshed and arrests spread from coast to coast in India Wednesday. One civilian was killed and nearly fifty other persons were injured in riots which occurred at Karachi, Calcutta and Peona. The number of arrests was mounting hourly. Nine Europeans who were stoned by mobs, two women among them, were on the casualty list. The only fatality reported was at Karachi. Thirty-three persons there were injured, seven seriously. The clash resulted when a mob, angered at the arrest of six nationalist leaders, stormed the city magistrate’s court. After the arrest of leaders the mob quieted. Police Station Attacked. Among those injured in the rioting at Peona were the city magistrate and the superintendent of police, who were stoned when a crowd of nationalists attacked police headquarters in protest against the conviction of the Pandit Jawaha

LONDON, April 17.—(4)—There was a great deal of hope, but little prospect, today that the five-power naval conference would be concluded at a plenary session Tuesday and that the treaty draft could be completed and made ready for signature by that time. Unless the work is finished the American delegation, save about 25 members of the entourage who need not stay, will not be able to take the Leviathan Wednesday morning for New York, and must wait over in England for some time further, since it is wished to use a ship flying the United States flag. British spokesmen particularly are pessimistic that the plenary session can be held Tuesday. Ramsay McDonald, arriving by airplane yesterday at Lossiemouth, Scotland, for his Easter vacation, told reporters. “I may go back to London tomorrow or the day after—it all depends—but at the moment I expect to be here ten days.” Ten days from Wednesday

London, April 17.--(AP)--Senator Joseph T. Robinson, member of the American Delegation to the Naval Conference, this afternoon issued a statement outlining the terms of the safeguarding clause in the naval treaty. His statement read: “The so-called safeguarding clause in the naval treaty will provide in general that if during the term of the treaty the requirements of national security of any of the three powers whose auxiliary vessels are limited are, in the opinion of that power, materially affected by new construction by any nation whose auxiliary program is not limited by the treaty, that power will notify the other two of the amount and kind of building it requires. Robinson stressed the necessity of all nations having a free hand to build in case of necessity. His statement said: "The so-called safeguarding clause will order, in general, that if during the time of the treaty, requirements of national security of any of the three powers whose auxiliary vessels are limited is, in the opinion of that power, materially affected by new construction of any nation whose auxiliary program is not limited by the treaty, that power notify the other two of the amount and kind of ships it requires. “Thereupon those other powers shall be entitled to make pro

By The Associated Press London, April 16.--The draft of the important safeguarding clause of the London naval treaty, which is to protect the United States, Great Britain and Japan—as signatories of the three-power pact—in relation to the naval building programs of the other powers was completed today and made ready for transmission to the home governments. More than 80 per cent. of the five-power treaty has been written and the remainder is expected to be completed tomorrow. The five-power delegations here intend to send various sections of the treaty to their home capitals, and upon the speed wherewith approving replies are sent depends the holding of the final plenary session for signature. Among farmers’ wives until recently the percentage of insanity was very high. Living isolated lives, working hard from dawn until long after dark, seeing nobody but the sometimes dull, tired husband and farm hands, was bad for the mind. Then came rural free delivery, bringing pictures of the latest fashions, and the telephone with news of neighbors; finally, greatest blessing of all, the radio. Farmers’ wives tune in, and retain their sanity. To the exceptional woman, rich, able to do what she pleases, but hitherto finding little amusing excitement after sixty, flying offers relief. The British duchess of Bedford, sixty-four years old, goes up and down the earth at a rate of speed that old Satan never dreamed of. ROME, April 17. (AP).-—-The bells of St. John Lateran, “Mother Church of Christendom,” rang out this morning, answered by those of all Rome's 400 churches on the occasion of commemoration of Holy Thursday, feast of the institution of the Eucharist, recalling the last supper of Christ and the Apostles. What is believed to be the very table used at the epoch-marking repast was brought forth from its repository in St. John Lateran and exposed for the veneration of the large congregation. Two skulls, regarded as those of Saints Peter and Paul, were also on view there, as well as a reputed portion of the pillar to which Christ was bound when scourged in the house of the high priest, and a bit of the Holy Sponge mentioned in St. Matthew's account of the crucifixion. The mass at the Lateran Basilica was sung by Cardinal Pompili assisted by 12 priests, seven deacons and seven sub-deacons, and a

FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, Germany April 17.—The giant dirigible Graf Zeppelin landed without a hitch at her home port at 7 o’clock this evening having completed a round trip to Seville, Spain. She made the entire trip in 53 hours.

Friedrichshafen, Germany, April 17.—The dirigible Graf Zeppelin landed at her home hangar today late after a 51-hour round trip to Seville, Spain, in preparation for her forthcoming flight to Brazil and the United States next month.

1930-05-13.text: BOMBAY, India, May 12.—(CAB)— Mahatma Gandhi's civil resistance movement today received its second great setback with the arrest of Abbas Tyabji and a large group of his immediate followers, at the moment when they were starting from Navsari to raid the Dharsana salt works. The government's abortive action followed Tyabji's refusal to call off the proposed raid after repeated warnings by government officials. Command of the forces of passive resistance immediately was taken over by Mrs. Saironji Naidu, Hindu poetess, selected by Mahatma to automatically succeed as leader. The seizure of Tyabji coincided with government plans for a tightening of control of the entire Indian situation. While the arrested leader and his cohorts were being transferred to the jail just outside of Navsari, the civil authorities in Sholapur announced that two more military detachments had been sent from Poona,

By The Associated Press. LONDON, May 12.—The Daily Mail tonight received a dispatch from its correspondent at Bombay saying that the entire city of Sholapur had fallen into the hands of rioters and that traders refused to open their shops fearing wholesale looting.

BOMBAY, India, May 13 (UP)—The government established military occupation and martial law today in the city of Sholapur, scene of the most serious fighting of the nationalist independence movement. Determined to suppress all centers of disorder before violence could spread to other districts, the government also made wholesale arrests at Shiroda and Belgaum, where Mrs. Naidu—woman leader who fell heir to the authority of Mahatma Gandhi—first indicated her determination to continue vigorously the passive resistance campaign. A serious situation arising out of rioting by natives at Sholapur had left the fate of the town, which is 220 miles southeast of Bombay, in doubt, and the government ordered a strong detachment of troops there to establish control in the district. Prisoners Riot in Court Precautions also were taken at Lahore where 18 Indian prisoners attempted to incite a fresh outbre

BOMBAY, India, May 12--(AP)— The dowager Begum of Bhopal, 72, known as "the Queen Victoria of India," died today and tonight the whole of her Indian state was in official mourning. At her bedside was her son, the Nawab Zada Hamidulla, for whom she abdicated in 1926. The dowager was weakened by an operation yesterday. Her title of "Queen Victoria of India" came from the fact that she developed a backward rural state with small income into a thriving modern territory with annual income of 5,000,000 rupees. She built railroads, highways, hospitals and schools, established modern sanitary methods and agricultural research, and formed her own small army to police the Moslem state of nearly 7,000 square miles. She was the last ruler in her own right in India prior to the abdication, and the last of a female dynasty of three generations extending back to 1844.

LONDON, May 13.—British troops regained control of Sholapur, important textile center 250 miles southeast of Bombay, today after rioting Indian Nationalists had ruled the city for several hours according to dispatches received by the London evening newspapers. Martial law was proclaimed throughout the city, the dispatches said. Traders, fearing the looting of their shops, remained indoors and refused to open up while the disorderly crowds milled through the principal streets. Urgent calls for assistance had been sent out and at the behest of the district magistrate, a full battalion of the Royal Ulster Rifles was sent from Poona by special train. Sholapur, an important center of the textile industry with a population of approximately 250,000, was the scene of bloody riots last Wednesday and Thursday. Official reports said five were killed and fifty wounded. Unofficial reports placed the

FORMBY, Eng May 13 (4) — Seven Americans survived today in the British women's golf championship when the field was reduced to 32. The survivors are Miss Glenna Collett, Miss Maureen Orcutt, Miss Helen Hicks, Miss Virginia Van Wie, Miss Edith Quier, Mrs. Lea Federman and four were eliminated. Miss Glenna Collett, New York; Miss Virginia Van Wie, Chicago; Mrs. Lea Federman, New York; and Mrs. Stewart Hanley, Detroit were through for the day as they won third round matches and will play fourth rounds tomorrow morning. Miss Maureen Orcutt, Englewood, N.J., Miss Helen Hicks, New York, Mrs. O.S. Hill, Kansas City, Miss Edith Quier, Reading, Pa had to play two rounds today. Miss Hicks was the first American player to hurdle the two obstacles, winning morning and afternoon matches by the same score seven up and five to play. Miss Louise Fardyce, Youngstown, Ohio, Miss Peggy Wattles, Buffalo, N.

[INTERNATIONAL NEWS SERVICE] LONDON, May 13.—Miss Amy Johnson, British aviatrix attempting a solo record-breaking flight from London to Australia, arrived at Rangoon from Calcutta today, according to dispatches to the London Evening newspapers. She negotiated without difficulty the hazardous crossing of vast stretches of open water and uninhabited jungle land.

Calcutta, Bengal, May 13, (AP).— Eighty persons were arrested this forenoon by police in a raid on the headquarters of the Bengal presidency of the All-India National Congress Committee and on a branch camp of the organization. The arrests were made on warrants.

Shanghat, May 13 (AP) — Chinese soldiers killed 29 persons and wounded scores of others in breaking up a riot today caused when a hungry mob attempted to loot food shops at Huchow, Chekiang province. Grain prices in most parts of China recently reached new high levels as the result of the depreciated value of silver. Banditry, which had raged in many of the provinces for months, ran rampant.

YOKOSUKA, Japan, May 12. (AP) — Japan’s newest cruiser, The Takao, was launched here today with Empress Nagako and a dozen other members of the imperial family as well as a large group of distinguished men and women watching the ceremonies. The Takao is a 10,000 ton craft, fifth of the famous Nachi class and ninth of Japan’s cruisers carrying eight-inch guns.

SHANGHAI May 13. (AP)—National government official sources tonight stated that what was considered as the “decisive initiating battle” against the rebellious northern coalition was raging along the northwest border of Anhwei province and along the Haichow-Tungkwan railway in northeastern Honan province.

FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, May 13- The Graf Zeppelin left here today on a flight over Switzerland at 7:55 A. M. The big dirigible is scheduled to leave here Sunday on her transatlantic flight to South America and the United States.

BASEL, Switzerland, May 18 UP The bank for international settlements today fixed the salaries of its heads. President Gates McGarrah will receive $50,000 a year; Leon Fraser, deputy chairman, $40,000, and Pierre Quesnay, general manager, $30,000 a year.

[SPECIAL TO THE TIMES] MUNSTER, May 13.—A clerical omission at national census headquarters in Washington, D. C., caused Munster’s population to be reported as 731 against the federal estimate in 1929 of approximately 1,500, it was learned here today after Glenn Surprise, assistant census supervisor for the 1st district, had busied himself in a check-up on the work of Mrs. Ellen Myer, local enumerator. Surprise, who was at work here yesterday when The Times appeared carrying a story of protests by Munster citizens, said the district census office was in no way responsible for the error. He placed the blame squarely on the national offices. HAD NO MAPS, The mistake resulted, Surprise said, because the national headquarters failed to provide Mrs. Alice Drake Jones, district supervisor, with complete maps and descriptions of the territory to be counted as Munster. Similar omissions occurred

1930-06-04.text: BOMBAY, INDIA, June 4—(?)—Nationalist leaders today foresaw increasing cooperation of Moslem elements in the civil disobedience campaign by which they expect to win independence from Great Britain. A mile long procession of Moslems last night paraded the street to demonstrate Mohammedan sympathy for the movement. Later they assembled on the Maidan Esplanade and unanimously adopted a resolution supporting the program inaugurated by the all India National Congress headed by Mahatma Gandhi. The resolution appealed to all Moslems to participate in the movement and to boycott British goods. Leaders said that as long as the congress and the Moslem council did not support London round table conference to discuss the problem, no Moslem should attend it as a representative of his people.

(By The Associated Press.) Dublin, Irish Free State, June 4.— Captain Charles Kingsford-Smith, famous Australian airman, arrived in his airplane, Southern Cross, at Baldonnel airdrome this afternoon from Croydon to make preparations for a projected trans-Atlantic flight to the United States.

Bombay, India, June 3. — King George's 65th birthday observance was the apparent cause of grave disorders today which caused injuries to 88 persons at the Worli concentration camp, which houses volunteers arrested for breaking the salt laws. Some thousand volunteers are detained behind a barbed wire barrier at the camp, which is in a suburb of Bombay, and this morning sympathizers on the outside demonstrated against the royal anniversary by hoisting black flags over lodging houses and parading near the concentration camp, shouting anti-imperialistic slogans. While they were demonstrating thus, a company of military sappers and miners marched up to repair the barbed wire surrounding the camp, which had been weakened by previous attempts at escape. Soldiers Are Stoned. The soldiers were jeered and stoned as they worked. Eventually their operations brought them to a place on the boundary wh

Sydney, N. S. W., June 4—(UP)—Miss Amy Johnson, 22-year-old British flyer, completed a 29-day flight from London today amid a tremendous welcome from the people of Sydney. Whistles on ships and factories blew long and loud as she piloted her tiny moth plane across the city, escorted by 20 Australian planes, and landed at Sydney airdrome. Miss Johnson flew here from Brisbane, where she departed at 8:50 A. M. and landed here soon after 2 P. M. The first part of the flight was made alone from London to Port Darwin, Australia, in 19 days. From Port Darwin to Sydney, she was accompanied by an escort of Australian planes, extended as a tribute to the young flier.

CAMBRIDGE, England, June 3. —(ADP)—Tragedy today enshrouded historic Cambridge University when Douglas Newton Potts, a first year undergraduate, shot and killed Dr. A. F. R. Wollaston, 55, noted English explorer, scientist, physician and tutor, and then fatally wounded himself. Young Potts also shot and severely wounded Detective Sergeant Willis, Hospital officials say he will recover. The shooting occurred in Doctor Wollaston’s room in Old King’s College. Dean Milner White this afternoon said Potts, who was an outstanding bright student, suddenly left the college ten days ago. ‘The faculty was much perturbed by his absence and a search was started. Yesterday a message was received from the London police saying Potts had been found there and was returning to college. Dr. Wollaston, it was understood, went to the station to meet the student and the two men returned to the tutor’s rooms wh

By The Associated Press. LONDON, June 4.—The MacDonald government safely weathered another “crisis” in the House of Commons today, a House of Lords amendment eliminating the district levy from the coal bill being rejected by 250 votes to 220.

Severe clashes between police and Hindu rioters broke forth anew in India today at three different points, with one killed and many wounded as the score in all cases the natives were repressed. Bombay’s Worli suburb, in which is the large internment prison with its barbed wire entanglements, was the scene of the fiercest encounter, in which 4 score or more congress volunteers were seriously injured, five of them being taken to a congress hospital in precarious condition. A village near Madras, Cholinganallur, hitherto quiet, listed the single early fatality, a Hindu engaged in inciting volunteers to raid a salt store. The police were heavily stoned. Dharasana reported several natives injured by police during repeated raids on the salt depots by two batches of civil disobedience cohorts.

London, June 4, ()—The London Daily Mail today carried an undated account of a demonstration at Poona by 5,000 men who marched through the streets openly abusing the government and carrying a portrait of King George, who is Emperor of India, garlanded with old shoes in token of their contempt. The authorities did not interfere in any manner, and the writer commented that the populace was left to draw its own conclusions. He saw in the incident an abdication of authority by the government.

dune tL. — The Aga Khan's Blenheim fought its way to victory in the 151st running of the derby today. Somerville Tattersall’s Tliad was second and Sir Hirs Diolite, the favorite, was third. Silver Flare was fourth. H. H. the Aga Khan led his proud colt to the Judge's stand after the finish while the throng, despite the disappointment of many over the failure of the favorite, Diolite, gave the well played Blenheim an ovation. The great riding of Jockey Har Wrage was given due credit for the victory. The victory was worth $47,890 net to the Aga Khan. Tattersall took approximately $6,900 for Tliad and Sir Hugo $3,000 for Diolite. The breeder of Blenheim received $2,500, the gross value of the race being just under $60,000. The closing price on Blenheim was 18 to 1, Tliad was 25 to 1, and Diolite 31 to 4.

Cambridge, England, June 3— (AP)—A. F. R. Wollaston, a tutor at King’s College, Cambridge, was shot and killed today by a student who later wounded himself. The student, whose name was temporarily withheld, was also stated to have shot and wounded Detective Sergeant Wilson of the Cambridge police. He then turned the revolver on himself and was reported in a dangerous condition.

Horta, Fayal, Azores, June 4,—(A. P.)—The Graf Zeppelin, bound from Lakehurst to Seville, Spain, passed over the Island of Flores, Azores, at 6 a. m., eastern standard time. All seemed well aboard. The Graf headed to the east as she passed over Horta and began the last water lap of her journey back to Europe. The weather was fine and there was a light wind. The sky was fairly clear although there were some low lying clouds. Visibility was good. Friedrichshafen, Germany, June 4.—(A.P.)—The Graf Zeppelin, riding the winds which blow from west to east, sailed along the fortieth parallel today toward Seville, Spain, and thence home. The winds which kicked up whitecaps on the blue Atlantic beneath, so accelerated the giant dirigible’s speed that there was possibility Dr. Hugo Eckener's estimate of 50 hours from New York to Seville might be bettered and a record set. Since leaving New York the

NAPLES, Italy, June 4--(UP)—Mt. Vesuvius was active again today, deafening explosions and frequent eruptions of incandescent cinders frightening the countryside. The fiery display was visible over a wide radius through the night and during the early hours today. It was recalled the volcano erupted violently from June 2 to 8, last year, the lava reaching the outer section of the village of Torzingno, damaging fruit orchards and vineyards.

ROME, June 4, (P) — Official announcement was made today that the pope will hold a secret consistory on June 30, and a public consistory on July 3, at which new cardinals will be created. No mention was made as to how many cardinals would be treated or whom they would be.

NAPLES, Italy, June 4—(AP)— Lordly Vesuvius, quiescent for a year, was in intermittent eruption today, with high fountains of lava being shot frequently into the air. The eruptions, accompanied by explosions, were visible for miles around. Earthworks were thrown up to prevent an outflow of lava, despite predictions of the Vesuvius observatory that the eruption will be less violent than those of last year at this time when several villages over the countryside were submerged.

SHANGHAI, June 3.— Rebel armies on four battle fronts today challenged the supremacy of the nationalist government of China. Fighting which began May 8, with but a few thousand men has reached huge dimensions, more than a half million troops being engaged. Strengthened by reinforcements, the northern alliance armies flung themselves at the nationalists in a general offensive along the Haichow-Tungkwan railroad in Northern Honan province. In this area it is said at least 400,000 men were fighting to determine the future of China. The nationalists, beaten back to Kweiteh, Honan, by fierce rebel on- (Continued on Page 2, Col. 6.)

PY S4848 4 & Madria—()— Bad weather lies ahead of the Graf Zeppelin. Storms thus far not of a dangerous nature, prevail generally in the Iberian peninsular and Mediterranean region, between the Azores, Spain and Southern France. The Spanish weather department Wednesday sent special reports which were transmitted to the Graf. Rain clouds await the Zeppelin at Seville. Tail winds, with squalls, generally were reported on the path the dirigible is following. There were indications a serious blow might follow.

FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, June 4.—(Wednesday).—The Zeppelin works at 1:00 o’clock this morning, mid-European time, (7 p. m., Tuesday E. S. T.) received a message from the Graf Zeppelin, bound from Lakehurst to Seville, saying she was at latitude 38 north and longitude 44.3 west. That position placed her about 900 miles from the Island of Fayal, Azores. (By The Associated Press) By midnight tonight the German dirigible Graf Zeppelin should be at Seville, Spain, the eighth ocean crossing added to her list of many laurels. Fifty hours it would take, Dr. Hugo Eckener said before lifting his great sky cruiser up against the stars at 9:12 P. M. S. T. Monday night, and scattered reports from ships and the dirigible itself have indicated that this schedule would be easy to maintain. During the first four hours of the flight, the most perilous of its journey above four continents and twice across the equa

ROME, June 4 (GAP)—What were considered as conflicting statements of Premier Mussolini and his foreign minister, Dino Grandi, with regard to the Italian navy excited some attention here today. Grandi, speaking in defense of the Italian naval program at the conclusion of a budget speech yesterday, said: “The Italian government is disposed to postpone laying down its program for naval construction in 1930 provided the French government does the same for the program for 1930. Considering the relative strength of the two fleets, such a concession would have a greater effect on the Italian navy than on the French.” Premier Mussolini in a speech at Florence a few days ago declared: “There has been some doubt abroad that Italy would carry out her naval program, but it will be constructed ton for ton with mathematical precision to the pride of the Italian people.”

HORTA, Azores, June 4.—Well past the halfway mark on its latest commercial conquest of the Atlantic, the giant German dirigible Graf Zeppelin soared over the island of Fayal, the Azores, at 9:30 a.m., eastern daylight saving time today. The mammoth dirigible, heading toward Seville on its return trip to Friedrichshafen after a journey which embraced three continents and more than 10,000 miles, was heading due east when it swept over the Azores. The weather was excellent, and the morning sun was shining brightly as the Graf loomed up out of the ocean blue over these pinpoints in mid-Atlantic whose residents have witnessed so many trans-Atlantic aerial conquests and not a few failures. In the various towns of Fayal, hundreds of persons turned out to witness and cheer the air monarch. The Graf swept due eastward, making excellent time, heading straight for its destination on the Spanish mai

Rome, June 3, (UP)—Italy is willing to suspend her 1930 naval building program pending the outcome of the proposed Franco-Italian conversations on naval limitation, if France agrees to do the same, Dino Grandi, the foreign minister, announced today. Grandi’s announcement was made during a speech in the senate. The Franco-Italian conversations were agreed upon at the London naval conference in an effort to reconcile differences and permit both countries to sign the limitations clauses of the treaty.

Shanghai, June 4(4)—Japanese dispatches today stated that the Nationalist Government armies had suffered reverses throughout Hon-Pan province. The northern alliance rebels attacked in heavy force, compelling the Nationalists to retreat. The Nationalists in northern Shantung province, the Japanese dispatches said, were withdrawing south of the Yellow River before the advancing northerners.

EVILLE, Spain — Unfavorable weather conditions were in the path today of the dirigible Graf Zeppelin, flying eastward from the mid-Atlantic Azores islands, toward the Portuguese coast. The Spanish weather bureau advised the dirigible that an unfavorable north wind prevailed between the Azores and Europe and that cloudiness was increasing. Storm areas and showers prevailed along the coastal region, and the Mediterranean zone was even less favorable. "In case the Graf Zeppelin follows the Mediterranean route the wind, although not violent, will be choppy, varying directions and at some points so strong as to be worthy of being taken into consideration," the bureau announced. Continuous rainfall here reduced interest in the arrival at Seville but the ground crew was ordered to report at 6 a.m. Thursday to await arrival of the ship, which will halt en-route to Friedrichshafen, Germany.

(By Associated Press.) PARIS, June 4—A decided lessening of the tension between France and Italy today was noticeable following the speech yesterday of foreign minister Dino Grandi concerning naval affairs.

1930-05-20.text: BOMBAY, May 19--Nerve worn and fatigued with a prolonged skirmish with Indian nationalists, police guarding the government salt depot at Wadala today resorted to more extreme measures to curb the increasing raids on the salt pans. The policemen used their lathis, or staves, to good effect in rounding up the raiders as they would seek entrance into the barbed wire enclosure containing the salt deposits. Seven of the nationalist volunteers were injured. Spectators, constantly increasing in number, who all Sunday sat on their haunches and laughed and jeered the constabulary at their efforts to check the raiders, were driven back across the railway lines and away from the salt area by the policemen. They turned from this task to find a party of 100 nationalist volunteers making a raid on the salt pans. Acting quickly they arrested seventy, but another thirty got away with hands full of salt.

Bombay—(#)—A partial hartal, or stoppage of work, was observed here Tuesday in protest at the arrest of nationalist volunteers who raided the salt depots at Wadala and Dharsasana. Dispatches from Karachi today said a British police superintendent and eight Indian constables had been injured by a bomb explosion in the bazaars at Multan, Punjab. Forty arrests were made. The police were dispersing a mob when the bomb was thrown in their midst and exploded. The crowd had gathered while the goods of a shopkeeper were being seized for non-payment of the local water tax. The Indian merchants’ chamber of this city has telegraphed the viceroy, Lord Irwin, asking that he institute a public inquiry, under a judge of the high court, of recent rioting and its handling at Sholapur.

CAIRO, Egypt, May 20 (AP) — Twenty-six persons were killed and 326 dwellings destroyed by fire in the villages of Timsahia and Benisaleh in the Man Falut district Saturday. The first outbreak of fire occurred at Timsahia where 226 buildings were destroyed and 20 people killed. Three other persons were burned seriously. While the entire Assuit province fire fighting machinery was quenching the blaze at Timsahia, a fire broke out at Benisaleh. About 100 dwellings burned and six persons were killed. Causes of the blaze were not reported.

Bombay, May 20 —(UP)— There has been a noticeable increase of bitterness in recent days between the Indian Swarajists, or independence seekers, and the officials of the government in India responsible for ‘preserving order in this vast empire of Great Britain. The bitterness has been aroused largely by the drastic measures the government has felt imperative to combat the growing independence spirit. The announcement of severe court martial sentences at Sholapur, disturbed mill town 220 miles southeast of here, especially added to the Indians’ resentment. The members and adherents of the congress were particularly angered by the heavy sentences given under the martial law regime at Sholapur to the president and secretary of the congress committee there. They were given five and seven years in prison respectively. The congress leaders claimed their only offense during the riots recently wa

BOMBAY, India, May 20—(UP)—Police met the renewed attacks of Indian Independence volunteers on the Dharasana Salt Works today by making wholesale arrests of raiders, who were released within a short time. More than 150 volunteers who invaded the prohibited area today were taken in custody but soon released. Another group of 100 raiders advanced to the wire fence around the depot, but were ignored by police when they failed to enter. Mrs. Sarojini Naidu, poetess and leader of the volunteers, made extensive plans for mass action against the Dharasana Works tomorrow, when the Gatyagraha or passive resisters will concentrate on the depot again.

Seville, Spain, May 19.—(AP)—The dirigible Graf Zeppelin landed here today at 5:40 p.m. (12:40 p.m. E.S.T.) completing the first lap of her flight to South America. The Graf took off from Friedrichshafen Sunday at 5:18 p.m. (11:18 a.m. E.S.T.). Her arrival here indicated a flight of about 24 hours for the approximately 1,500 miles she was estimated to have flown. The dirigible increased her mileage by lingering over the northernmost African coast for a considerable time. In doing so she passed out of the view of observers for about four hours.

(By The Associated Press) Seville, Spain, May 20.—The Graf Zeppelin rode peacefully at anchor here last night at the end of the first leg of her voyage from Friedrichshafen, Germany, across the equator to South and North America. Twenty-four hours from her starting point the Giant of the air had experienced as her first dif- iculty a heat wave that envelop- ed Spain, avoiding which she had been flown off her course two hours, adding the African contin- ent to her journey. Passengers Disembark The Graf nosed up to her mast at La Tablada Airport, her own specially constructed anchorage, at 5:40 p.m. (12:40 p.m. EST), (Continued on page eight)

Cadiz, Spain, May 20 (UP) — The dirigible Graf Zeppelin flew over Cadiz at 10:00 a. m. (4:00 a. m. central standard time) today and started out over the Atlantic Ocean on her flight to Brazil and the United States. Seville, Spain, May 20 (UP)—The German dirigible, Graf Zeppelin, left Seville at 8:22 a. m. (2:32 a. m. central standard time) on its 60-hour flight across the southern Atlantic to open a new commercial air route to South America. The Zeppelin’s next destination is Pernambuco, Brazil, the second stop on a tour which will carry it to Cuba and the United States. It paused here a limited time after a 25-hour flight from Friedrichshafen. Seville, Spain, May 19 (UP)—The Graf Zeppelin was moored at 4:45 p. m. for an overnight stop before starting the ocean flight to Brazil, at the mooring mast which was erected here especially for the German ship. Four or five passengers, who were a

SEVILLE, Spain (AP)— The Graf Zeppelin arrived at 4:40 p.m. (11:40 a.m., E.S.T.) Monday, completing the first stage of the first dirigible flight to South America. The airship was welcomed by the cheers of a large crowd of natives and tourists who had been watching the sky for hours to catch the first glimpse of it. Hugo Eckener, commander of the ship, delayed the arrival here to take advantage of the favorable landing conditions prevailing late in the day. After reaching Gibraltar, 100 miles from Seville, before noon, the airship made a flight over the African coast and pushed its way through stiff headwinds en route back to Spain. The Graf Zeppelin will remain here overnight, departing for Brazil Tuesday morning if conditions are favorable. Four American passengers were aboard the ship when it departed from Friedrichshafen at 5:18 p.m. Sunday (11:18 a.m., E.S.T.), on the flight to Sevi

PARIS, May 20 (AP)—Most of the first contingent of gold star mothers in France visiting the graves of their sons left in a drizzling rain today for the battlefront cemeteries where their sons lie. Medical officers reported there was no illness among them and that everyone was able to take her place in the sightseeing bus at the proper time. The journey to the former battlefields was made at a leisurely pace and the four groups were not expected to reach their destination until tonight. The first visits to graves will be made tomorrow. The small number remaining in Paris tomorrow will again visit the Suresnes cemetery on the slope of Mount Valerien near Paris. They spent today sight-seeing and resting.

The first pilgrimage of 252 gold star mothers, most of them from Ohio, left Paris Tuesday for the six battlefield cemeteries of France on their missions of remembrance. For one week beginning Wednesday, the American mothers and widows of soldiers killed in the world war will visit the graves of their dead, and return to Paris three days before sailing for home on the United States liner President Harding. The group en route to the Romagne cemetery, the largest and most distant from Paris, was scheduled to reach Verdun before nightfall. Another group, en route to the Somme cemetery, planned to see the spot in the Compiègne forest where the armistice was signed. Luxurious autobuses, with American army officers, an interpreter, and a trained nurse on each were used for the tours of the battlefields.

CONSTANTINOPLE, May 20.—(UP)—Thirteen Turkish women were killed instantly, and eight others were crushed when an ancient tower in whose shade they were, collapsing after working in the opium fields near Smyrna, collapsed yesterday. Only two women escaped the fall of the tower without injury. The tower once was used as a lookout for enemies. The governor of Smyrna has extended aid personally to the victims’ families.

NAPLES, Italy, May 20—The claims of a 15-year-old Italian youth to have discovered an entirely new principle of electrical power, which would eliminate all present fuels, were given serious consideration in responsible circles today when the government ordered an extensive investigation of the experiments. Saverio Natella, a student of Positano, near here, has carried out his startling and fantastic experiments with such remarkable results that one investigator, Professor Scholer of Belgium, said the town of Positano, which has no electric power, "will give light to the world." Natella recently had a narrow escape from electrocution during his experiments and authorities acted today to test the accuracy of his conclusions before permitting him to continue. The youth claimed to be able to draw any amount of electric power from space. He said he had discovered electric waves in certain par

Seville, May 20—Silvery and gleaming, the Graf Zeppelin rose from her mooring mast here at 8:32 a.m. (4 A.M. E.D.T.) and headed into the southwest bearing the old world’s greetings to the New. Heavily laden with passengers and mails, the majestic airship rose easily in fair skies aided by the calmness of the morning hours—well away on the journey to South America and the United States. Dr. Hugo Eckener, veteran commander of the dirigible, was at the controls. He smiled at the crowds below and waved cheerily from the windows where so much of the world {Continued on page three}

1930-05-12.text: POONA, India, May 12) (AP)— The entire second battalion of the Royal Ulster Rifles, including its commanding officer and a whole battalion of headquarters troops, was rushed from here to Sholapur early today. The increasingly serious developments following the score of killings and burnings in that city today caused the call for reinforcements.

BOMBAY, May 12—(U. P.)—Continuing its quiet but determined drive to end the Indian independence movement, the government of India today arrested Abbas Tyabji, Mohammedan successor to Mahatma Gandhi in the passive resistance campaign. Tyabji had succeeded Gandhi when the Mahatma himself was arrested at Surat exactly a week ago. Sarojini Naidu, a former president of the national congress—the body backing the passive resistance campaign—became leader of the movement with Tyabji's arrest. The arrest was made at Tyabji and 159 volunteers began a march on a Tharasar salt depot. Tyabji had threatened the salt raid last week, declaring it would be conducted peacefully and the government immediately warned him that it would take action if he attempted it. A number of casualties occurred in a village near Jalalpur when followers of Mahatma Gandhi, imprisoned independence leader, clashed with liquo

(By The Associated Press) London, May 12.—Peiping dispatches to the Daily Express today said that according to the headquarters of the Northern Alliance Generals, 10,000 nationalist troops had been killed and 15,000 captured during the heavy fighting of the past few days near Peng-Pu. The battle between the nationalists and the northern coalition has been proceeding along the Luaghai railway. The dispatch adds that the northerners are driving on towards Nanking.

CALCUTTA, India, May 12 (AP) — Miss Amy Johnson, British flyer, arrived here tonight from Allahabad. She is flying solo from England to Australia. Miss Johnson alighted smiling and said it seemed impossible that she had left London only May 3rd.

(Monday)——-Ab baa Tyabli, who succeeded Mahatma Gandhi as Leader of the Indian civil disobedience movement, and all his immediate followers were arrested this morning at Navsari, as they prepared for a raid on the government ante depots at Dharsana, NO ARDUOUS OUTBREAKS alapur. LONDON, May 12.—(P)—A British airplane raid was made yesterday against the forces of the Haji of Turvangsa on the northwestern frontier of India, Wedgewood Benn, secretary of state for India, announced in the House of Commons this afternoon. Mr. Benn added that the results of the raid were not yet known. Previously, dispatches from Bombay said that British authorities in the Gujarat district had served an ultimatum on the Haji, notifying him to remove his followers from the vicinity of Peshawar immediately. Peshawar is the key city of the northwestern frontier and the surrounding country is inhabited by war-

Bombay, India, May 1—(AP)-- The death of the Dowager Begum of Bhopal, one time the only woman ruler of an Indian state, was announced today. She was 72 years old. The Begum of Bhopal abdicated in 1926 in favor of her son, the Nawab Zada Hmidulla. The Begum was much beloved by her people. She made many gifts to educational institutions and while on a visit to London once ordered 2,500 watches for her people in India. She was known as a strong believer in the prohibition of liquor and once was quoted as saying that in Bhopal men no longer beat their wives now that her country was dry. The abdication of the Begum in 1926 brought to an end a period of eighty years of female rule in the little state of Central India which has a population of about 700,000. The Begum had ruled Bhopal for a quarter of a century with vigor.

BOMBAY, May 12.—Ahbas Tyabji, retired high court judge and acting leader of Mahatma Gandhi's civil disobedience followers in India, and 59 volunteers were arrested today at Kavadi as they started their march toward Dharasana where he planned to raid government salt depots. Tyabji, who took over leadership of the Indian nationalists when Mahatma Gandhi was arrested by the British Indian government, had announced that he and his followers would reach Dharasana Wednesday night and begin their raids on Thursday. After religious ceremonies, eluding the painting of forehead caste marks and the delivery of blessings by Mrs. Gandhi, wife of the arrested leader, the Tyabji volunteers set out from Kavadi at 6 a.m. Mrs. Gandhi and hundreds of villagers accompanied the procession. It had proceeded but a few miles when the arrests took place. Several inspectors, a district magistrate and three hundre

GENEVA, May 12—(/4’)—Resignation of Charles Evans Hughes, now chief justice of the United States, as a member of the Permanent Court of International Justice, was accepted by the council of the League of Nations as its first important act after assembling today under the presidency of Marinkovitch, Jugo-Slavian foreign minister. The council voted to hold a special election at the next assembly in September to select a successor to Mr. Hughes.

Istanbul, Turkey—(#—Sale of the crown jewels of the Ottoman empire, valued at about $300,000,000 today was forecast by the semi-official daily newspaper “Bjumour-eit,” to raise money to relieve Turkey’s economic crisis. The jewels, part of which are on exhibition in the museums of Istanbul and the remainder hidden in Angora, include the peacock throne, studded with 30,000 jewels. This single relic is estimated to be worth $13,000,000. There is still another throne in the collection containing one of the world’s largest emeralds and a whole box full of diamonds and pearls.

MUNSTER, May 12.—Protest that the population of Munster is above 1,000 rather than a mere 731 has been made by various local civic leaders since announcement of the enumeration was made last Thursday from the offices of Mrs. Alice Drake Jones, supervisor of the census for the first district. Those who aver the enumeration was not complete cite the vote in the election last Autumn and the recent school census as proof that numerous families were not counted by the local enumerator, Mrs. Ella Myer. FAMILIES NOT COUNTED Hugo F. Kaske, local civic leader, in a signed statement given to The Times, said he knew of three families that had not been counted and that he was positive there were numerous others. “In the last election there were 420 or more votes cast. The school census this spring showed 3356 persons between the ages of 6 and 21 living in Munster,” Kaske said. “Unless ratios are all

PARIS, May 12.—On the heels of the ill-fated attempted long-distance flight of the Mexican ace Pablo Sidar, an adventurous French airman, Jean Mermoz, took off from St. Louis, Senegal, today, in an effort to fly across the south Atlantic to Natal, Brazil. A dispatch from the Senegal port stated Mermoz started at 11 a. m. Paris time (6 a. m. Eastern Daylight Saving Time.) Mermoz is attempting the hazardous flight in a new type of hydro-airplane constructed especially for him. He is carrying a cargo of mail and hopes to cut down by days the usual time required for shipment of the post from the African to South American shores. In an effort to ensure the flier's safety, four speedy sea-going tugs were stationed along the trans-Atlantic route to aid Mermoz should he be forced down on the crossing. The flight is being made to determine the practicability of regular airplane mail and cargo ser

1930-05-18.text: Bombay, India, May 17.—The “salt war” in Bombay presidency tonight appeared to be working to a crisis. While successive groups of civil resistance volunteers poured into Dharasana to carry on the campaign against the government salt depot there begun by Mrs. Sarojini Naidu, 400 other volunteers assembled this afternoon in Bombay and planned to march tomorrow on the salt depot at Wadala, six miles away. A large force of police has been called out to frustrate the attempt, the nucleus of their concentration being at Jacob Circle, on the line of march to Wadala. The volunteers changed their plan of marching en masse and decided to split into small groups so as to spread out the police. A third raid is projected at the Shiroda salt works and the police have made preparations to meet any contingency there.

FRIEDRICHSHAFEN— (If weather permits, the Graf Zeppelin will float upward at 5 o'clock Saturday afternoon (11 a.m. e.s.t.) and turn its nose in the direction of Seville for another flight to the new world and return. The first stop will be the Spanish city, where a fifty-foot mooring mast has been erected. The great German dirigible expects to reach there late Monday and remain all night, taking off early Tuesday morning for Pernambuco, Brazil, in its first flight across the South Atlantic and across the equator. It will stop at Rio de Janeiro, then head northward for Havana and Lakehurst, where it will prepare for the return flight to Seville and Friedrichshafen. Twenty-two passengers, including four Americans, will make the voyage. Best known among the latter are Mrs. Mary Pierce of New York who was on the zeppelin flight of last May that ended when the big airship became crippled and

BERLIN, May 17 (AP) — Three persons were killed during the night in brawls between Communists and Fascists going home from their political meetings in various parts of Berlin. Such clashes have become so frequent that the police have forbidden meetings of the hostile parties to be held simultaneously.

BERLIN, May 17—()—Max Valier, German pioneer in experiment and research with rocket motors, was fatally injured today while working on a model of a new liquid oxygen rocket. A piece of the recoil motor blew out and struck Valier in the neck. His jugular vein was severed. Two scientists working with him at the time were uninjured. Valier and the German, Paul Hevlandt, had been developing the new motor together and only recently made successful tests with it. It was Valier’s ambition one day to attempt flying the Atlantic with a rocket airplane equipped with these motors. He believed he could do it in a few hours.

Friedrichshafen, Germany, May 17—The dirigible Graf Zeppelin, veteran of a record-breaking flight around the world, will start its spring travels Sunday, sailing for Seville, en route to Brazil and Lakehurst, N. J. As the forerunner of what the Zeppelin company expects will be regular trans-Atlantic mail and passenger service, the ship is scheduled to fly to the Spanish city, halt there for additional passengers and cargo and then head out across the ocean to the northeastern tip of the South American continent. Six Americans will be aboard, some of them being expected to join it at Seville. William B. Leeds of New York has gone to Brazil, where he will board it for the trip to Lakehurst. The flight from Seville to Rio de Janeiro will require two and a half days, and, after an hour’s pause there, 24 hours will be consumed in the flight to Pernambuco, where it will remain two days. SPY BSBA R AR SESMKAV FIR, (United Press Staff Correspondent) PARIS, May 17— The American gold star mothers arose today ahead of most Parisian workers, and went out into the brilliant sunshine to start three days of sightseeing before visiting the graves of their sons who were killed in the world war. The weather, which had been rainy for two weeks, suddenly cleared, and as the first of the mothers left their hotels today, they saw the rising sun reflected on the roofs and pavement. Several of the mothers hurried to the Rue De Rivoli. Others carried little slips of paper, on which they had listed everything they should see before starting on to the battlefields. The oldest members of the party, Mrs. Lydia Lindsay, 75, of Hamilton, Ohio, and Mrs. E. M. Brasher, 77, of Cincinnati, were two of the earliest risers. Mrs. Brasher, with good forethought, carried on her arm a large fruit basket,

Paris, May 17 (42)--The American Gold Star Mothers who arrived in France yesterday to visit the graves of their sons today paid tribute to France’s nameless World War dead. Mrs. Sarah Thompson of New York laid a huge wreath of white lilies and red carnations on the tomb of the unknown soldier at the Arc de Triomphe. Surrounding her at the simple ceremony were the members of the first gold star pilgrimage and a large crowd of sympathetic French—many of the Gold Star Mothers themselves—brought tears to the eyes of the American women with their kindly friendliness.

The proposed European federation, most ambitious project which has been considered since the setting up of the league of nations, will be far from the close union such as exists among the United States of America, according to M. Briand’s memorandum. There will even be little similarity between the two groups since the most that is suggested for the European union is a type of regular conferences, without charter or constitution. The foremost practical questions such a union might deal with, in Minister Briand’s conception, are economic, and comprise eventual efforts to lower customs duties of European states among themselves. Paris, May 17. (AP)—The last Rhine bridgehead held by the French army of occupation was today ordered progressively evacuated. Premier Andre Tardieu, who has been discussing the evacuation of the third occupied zone with Ambassador Von Hoesch of Germany and high French military authorities this week, announced in a communique that Germany had carried out all the necessary conditions for acceptance of the Young plan. Under the plan, it was provided that the French troops should leave the Rhineland by June 30, 1930, but in case Germany ratified the plan with the other countries earlier, the way was left open for speedier French withdrawal. Two important steps in all were taken today to efface survivals of wartime policy. United Press Start Correspondent FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, Germany May 17--(UP)—Dr. Hugo Eckener, white-haired commander of the Graf Zeppelin, issued an order tonight for the dirigible's decks to be cleared for action at 4:45 p.m. Sunday in preparation for the first commercial flight to South America. The dirigible will fly from Brazil to Lakehurst, N.J., on the return trip. The famous ship is scheduled, barring unexpected developments, to rise from her hangar here about 5:30 p.m., en route for the first stop at Seville. Mrs. Mary Pierce of New York and perhaps the infant Alfonso De Orleans, cousin of King Alfonso of Spain, are scheduled to join the passengers aboard the dirigible at the Spanish terminal. There will be 22 passengers on board the ship when it leaves here. Mr. Pierce was aboard the dirigible on one of its previous flights across the Atlantic, the protests raised by her family when

PARIS, May 17, (UP)—The nations of Europe were asked by France today to join in definite plans for creation of an economic and political "United States of Europe." Two lengthy documents embodying the project of Foreign Minister Aristide Briand for a European federation were delivered to the 26 continental nations, belonging to the League of Nations, and also were made public by the foreign office here. Replies from the nations are not expected before mid-June but the more optimistic of Briand’s supporters hope for concrete results soon, and the calling of a European committee to organize the federation in the autumn. They also hope to see Briand’s efforts recognized by his election as the first president of the union, although the veteran diplomat himself was unambitious for such personal honors. 1930-03-23.text: LONDON, March 22. (A.P.)—With tomorrow’s meeting at Chequers between Prime Minister MacDonald and Premier Tardieu definitely canceled, the five-power naval conference has reached the point where it is a conference in name only. The stubborn deadlock of France and Italy over parity and the delay in obtaining Japanese approval for the American-British-Japanese tri-party agreement have resulted in a complete suspension of the London meeting. Japan’s favorable reply next week will save the conference as far as a three-power treaty is concerned and will enable material contribution to be made to the cause of disarmament. An unfavorable reply from Tokyo—which neither the British nor the American delegations apprehend for a moment—would present an alarming prospect of the conference either blowing up as did the Geneva conference in 1927 or fizzling out completely unless a naval pact between the

By The Associated Press. London, England, March 22.--The Earl of Balfour, last of Great Britain's Victorian statesmen, was buried with simple services at his ancestral home in Whittingehame, Scotland, today. Relatives, villagers and farm folk assembled at the little church for the last moments with the man who had brought fame to the district.

ROME, March 22 (AP).—The eleventh anniversary of Premier Mussolini’s founding of fascist combat groups, designed to deal summarily with communists and other subversive elements, will be commemorated throughout Italy tomorrow. Foglio d’Ordinl, the fascist order sheet, today published a nation-wide message from the premier saying that every attempt against the united will of 42,000,000 inhabitants was bound to fail. "During eleven years fascism prevailed over a thousand difficulties of every sort, but many others, no less grave, are before us," said the premier. "They impose upon us always more peremptorily the command and united discipline by which the fascist Italian people ought always more and more to unite into a single group. Today the first battle legions find themselves side by side with the young men who have grown up to a life dedicated to a faith which unites two ages and two hi

SHANGHAI, March 22.——— Eleven American Catholic missionaries reported besieged at Kanchow, Kiangsi province, by Chinese communist disorders were declared here today by Bishop Sheehan to be in "no" imminent peril. Bishop Sheehan, a native of Streator, Ills., who is in charge of Catholic missionary activities in northern Kiangsi, said the missionaries at Kanchow had been carrying on their work in the midst of continual depredations by communists and bandit hordes. Present conditions, he said, are no worse than had existed for many months. A telegram received here last Wednesday from the Kanchow Vicariate described the situation as "quiet." Bishop Sheehan did not mention any plans for withdrawal of the missionaries as suggested by the state department in Washington, which has requested that the Chinese government send troops to protect the missionaries. Tonight the result of their labors for naval limitation, completed in treaty form, was in the hands of the governments of the five great sea powers, awaiting approval by those home governments so the London treaty may be signed at the scheduled time Tuesday. The salient points of that pact, which will rule the seas until the next disarmament conference, scheduled for 1935, is called into session, are under scrutiny in Washington, Paris, Rome and Tokyo.
