By The Associated Press Bombay, April 17.-The government bore down heavily today on the leaders of the civil disobedience campaign in India. Government magistrates all over the country spent the day in sentencing followers of Mahatma Gandhi charged with violating the salt laws. A total of 27 prominent nationalists were sentenced to varying terms—12 at New Delhi including Davi Das Gandhi, son of the Mahatma; three at Allahabad, 10 at Karachi and two at Surat. Gandhi's son was sentenced to three months simple imprisonment. Deetor Choithram, president of the provincial congress committee at Surat, received the longest sentence--two years of rigorous imprisonment. Gandhi himself still was unmolested by the police. He took advantage of the lull in rioting, which yesterday spread to the three important cities of Calcutta, Karachi and Poona, to make a long speech to volunteers at Navarsi, accus

LONDON, April 18. (UP)—Definite and vigorous action by the British government to end unrest in India became nearer today, with the report that findings of the Simon investigating commission probably will be issued within two weeks instead of late next month. The first section of the Simon report, which is said to have a slight pro-Indian tinge, already is in the hands of the printers, and drafting of the second section is nearly completed. — Experts on colonial affairs ex (Turn to Page 2, Column 2)

ROME, April 18—(AP)—Before altars stripped of their ornaments and surmounted by veiled crucifixes, with the tabernacles in the center standing open and empty, black-vestmented priests solemnly prostrating themselves today commemorated the death of Christ in all the churches of Rome, and as throughout the Catholic world. Rome's commemoration of Good Friday was, as always, particularly impressive because of the number of purported relics of Christ's passion and death to be found there. A great “procession of penitents” composed of thousands of clergy and laymen wended its way to Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, where a comparatively large piece of what is said to be the cross of Calvary has been kept for centuries. Between the hours of noon and three o'clock, corresponding to the time that Christ is supposed to have suffered his agony, all business was at a standstill, and traffic largely suspe

|By United Press - || VALENCIA, Spain, April 18.—Nine persons were dead and 20 badly hurt today following a collision between a train and a passenger bus near Gilet, a mining town in this vicinity. It was impossible to identify the bodies.

Valencia, Spain, April 18.—2— Eight members of a holiday party were killed yesterday and 16 injured in a collision between their auto-bus and a freight train near the village of Samagreli, between Sagunto and Valencia. Four of those injured were in a serious condition. Aid has been rushed from Valencia, and the authorities have begun an investigation into the collision, which occurred at a grade crossing. The crossing guard, apparently holding himself responsible for the disaster, committed suicide late in the afternoon. Witnesses said the driver of the bus apparently did not see the oncoming freight train until it was too late to avoid a collision.

1930-05-28.text: London, May 27.—(4)—For the first time in a 12-month, British people tonight were scanning the press for reports of the illness of their sovereign. Confined to his quarters in Buckingham Palace with a painful attack of inflammatory rheumatism centering in his right hip, King George was obliged to forego the third court of the season, this evening, his place being occupied by the Prince of Wales. Otherwise, according to official announcement, the king was maintaining his usual schedules. He is nearly 66 years old. He has had two severe illnesses in the last two years, the present illness, however, was only indirectly related to these, due to his somewhat depleted vigor.

By The Associated Press. Bombay, India, May 27.—Riot and tumult, or their aftermath of chaos and uncertainty, reigned today in four great cities of Britain’s Indian possessions. Official estimates showed that in Rangoon, Lucknow, Dacca and Bombay, 82 persons had been killed, 865 injured and hundreds upon hundreds arrested. Rangoon Beleaguered Over the weekend the riots have broken out of the bonds of the civil disobedience campaign. They overshadowed the salt raids of Mahatma Gandhi’s volunteers and made of “non-violence” a merely academic term. Rangoon, the Burmese capital, not yet recovered from the heavy earthquake of several weeks ago, tonight was a beleaguered city. Soldiers and police were striving desperately to maintain a hold, already precious, ever fighting coolies and lawless hands. Death List At 60 Fifty-four bodies lay in the city mortuary, and many others are believed to ha

LONDON, May 28—The city of Rangoon, Burma was in a desperate plight today as rioting continued and more than 60 persons had been killed and nearly 800 injured according to Exchange Telegraph Dispatches received here. All shops and bazaars were closed and the specter of famine was present among the native population of the city. Throughout the night British and Indian troops stood by police in an effort to quiet fighting, which originated between striking dock workers and imported Indian strike-breakers. Shots and volleys of firing were heard throughout Rangoon all through the night, while troops continued their efforts to maintain a semblance of order.

| LONDON, May 28. (WU) — The rheumatism which has affected King George's right hip shows a definite improvement, an official announcement from Buckingham Palace said today. The King, however, received no visitors this morning. The improvement, the official announcement said, was the result of the massage treatment which was prescribed by the King’s physician, Lord Dawson of Penn.

LONDON, tap The Second British labor government faced a battle for its life Wednesday without the aid of 58 liberal votes on which they have depended heretofore to maintain a majority in the house of commons. The parliamentary liberal party, meeting Tuesday, voted to abstain from voting on the conservative motion of censure leveled at J. H. Thomas, lord privy seal and minister for unemployment. The action left labor alone to confront the conservatives. While the MacDonald government numbers a voting strength of 288 against 262 conservatives, with seven independents, the outcome of today’s battle would seem to lie with the socialist left-wing members, who last week in a secret parliamentary party meeting voted no-confidence in Mr. MacDonald's leadership. These left-wingers number 29, and by refraining from voting or by voting against the government probably would bring its defeat, and sub

(By The Associated Press) LONDON, May 27.—The Daily Mail's correspondent at Rangoon, Burma, reported today that fifteen Indian coolie women had been massacred by fighting coolie mobs during the rioting that has taken such a heavy toll of life. Some of the women were said to have been tortured before being killed.

RAMAGNE-SOUS-MONTFAUCON, France, May 28,—(#)—Mothers whose sons served in the fifth division today went over part of the historic Meuse-Argonne battlefield where most of their boys fought and fell in the grim days of the world war. A bright sun brought out the people of the surrounding regions in large numbers and many of them waved flags as the American cars went by. One woman came out of a house where the men of the fifth division had once been billeted and waved her hand to the passing gold star mothers. Then, apparently overcome by the vivid memories of the war, she burst into tears and rushed back into the house holding her face in her hands. Many of the American women to whom the battle was explained by Captain Saulier were able to identify the spots where their sons had fought. Then, visiting the cemetery, they knelt solemnly at the graves of their boys and prayed silently. Floral

Madri.—(#)}—Two Spanish army aviators who had been reported missing since last Wednesday were found Tuesday to be in the hands of wandering tribesmen in the vicinity of Cape Bogador, State of Rio De Oro, a Spanish-African colonial possession near the western region of the Sahara desert. The fliers, Commandante Ricardo Burguete and Capt. Nunez Maza, in two airplanes, left Cape Juby, in the same state, last Wednesday as part of a military squadron en route to Morocco for inspection by Gen. Balmes, chief of the Spanish army air service. They were accompanied by Vincente Ferrer, a mechanic, who is a fellow captive with the officers now, and Mehammed Hen El Buya, a Moorish chieftain, whose fate has not been learned. It is not known whether the fliers are being held for ransom, or even if they are considered captives. The government is moving with delicacy in the matter, since peace officially

San Sebastian, Spain, May 27.—(AP)—A parade of 20,000 citizens of this royal resort city, seeking the reopening of gambling facilities at the casinos, this afternoon turned into a political demonstration against the Berenguer government and rioting broke out. Police fired into the crowds in attempting to quell the demonstrators, injuring 30 persons. Four civilians, including a woman and a child, were reported to be badly wounded by the bullets. Troops Out. The rioting lasted through most of the afternoon and the streets were heavily patrolled by police and soldiers tonight. Twenty arrests were made. The parade had been organized in protest against continuance of Primo de Rivera’s order suppressing gambling in the casinos. The citizens said they had lost much tourist trade through the suppression and they became disorderly when mounted police attempted to break up their demonstrations. Th

; By The Associated Press. Shanghai, May 27. — The northern alliance of the rebel army, numbering 200,000 men, independent dispatches said tonight, badly defeated the nationalist government forces in heavy fighting in Honan Province during the last three days. Forced to give way before furious onslaughts, the nationalists dug in, awaiting reinforcements before renewing the conflict.

Paris, May 28.—General John J. Pershing has absolutely no political ambitions, he declared emphatically today when he read of a move in the United States to draft him as senator from Nebraska. “I can assure anyone I'll resign if I am elected against my will,” General Pershing said.

GENEVA, May 28 — Premier Benito Mussolini, dictator of Italy, is ill and soon will undergo an operation it was learned today from travelers who came here from Rome. These travelers declared it would be announced that Mussolini only was taking a rest, while Minister of Transportation Ciano assumed his duties. Many of Mussolini's speeches have been censored, it was averred by travelers who had heard him address Fascist groups in Italy. They said that this was particularly true during his provincial tour when he told of storm troops prepared for action at Lucca as soon as war should be declared. This, he hinted, according to reports, would be soon a war to be fought along the east side, apparently referring to Jugo-Slavia. There was a tendency to credit Mussolini with "sword-rattling," but this, according to the travelers, was merely "camouflage" to hide the serious economic situation of th

1930-06-08.text: Cairo, Egypt—()—Two policemen and two rioters were killed Tuesday at Masourah in a furious and prolonged encounter between armed forces and followers of the recently resigned Premier Nahas Pasha. The police fired into the mob which offered stubborn resistance, A pitched battle was raging in the center of Masourah which the police and a detachment of troops appeared unable to end. The Nahas Pasha, who was in his motor car, was in the thick of the fighting. Masourah is a notorious Wafd stronghold. The Wafd executive committee held a meeting Monday night to discuss its future program. A prominent member of the Wafd executive body informed the newspapers that the Wafd would do its utmost to hold its meeting in Masourah notwithstanding a prohibition by the government on the use of the Delta railways.

DUBLIN, Irish Free State, June 7.—(AP)—Captain Charles Kingsford Smith and his three comrades of the air tonight deferred their proposed flight to America and flew back to Baldonnel Airdrome from Curragh Camp to await suitable weather for the take off. The flight had been set to start at dawn Sunday but weather reports from London dashed the hopes of the Australian air pioneer who in 1928 spanned the Pacific ocean in the “Southern Cross,” the same plane in which he intends to try to fly the Atlantic.

Toronto, June 9—(AP)—A wreath was laid today by Leo V. Youngworth of Los Angeles, Imperial Potentate of the Nobles of the Mystic Shrine, on the cenotaph in City Hall Plaza which honors Canada's war dead. The ceremony followed a welcome by the mayor to the 30,000 Shriners from the United States and Canada, here for their annual convention. The official party journeyed from the cenotaph to the Canadian Exposition grounds, where 12,000 Toronto cadets and 2,000 girls staged a "Young Canada" day parade.

DUBLIN, Irish Free State, June 9 (AP)—Captain Charles Kingsford-Smith and the crew which will pilot the Southern Cross with him in a trans-Atlantic flight attempt, are passing the time leisurely at Baldonnel airdrome awaiting weather reports which will determine their plans for a takeoff. They have been delayed two days thus far by adverse reports. Captain Saul, the navigator, has insured his life for the trip, and is paying a premium of 400 Pounds Sterling (about $2,000). The capital sum involved has been kept a close secret but it is believed to be £5,000. He is a master mariner and has crossed the Atlantic many times.

LONDON, June 9. (4—Paavo Nurmi, the famous flying Finn who holds more track records than any other man, smashed the world’s mark for the six-mile run at Stamford Bridge today. The great Finn covered the distance in 29 minutes, 36 3-5 seconds as compared to the record of 29:59 2-5, set by Alfred Schrubb of England, which had stood since 1904. Running in a handicap event, Nurmi finished third behind opponents to whom he had conceded more than three minutes start.

By The Associated Press. Bombay, India, June 7.—British airplanes, loaded with bombs, have driven from their caves the wild Afridi tribesmen who for a month have been menacing the strategic city of Peshawar on the northwestern frontier of India. Eighty airplanes have participated in the attacks and have dropped 5,000 bombs. British troops made a thorough search of the area southwest of Peshawar today and found that the hill warriors had withdrawn. Europeans were cheered today by the news that two British officers and the wife of one of them had been released by raiders who carried them into Afghanistan Wednesday. Those kidnapped were Major E. L. Farley, Captain J. C. Frere and Mrs. Frere. News travels slowly in India and not until tonight was it learned that a serious riot occurred Thursday in Gheehnagat, a village in the Daspur district of Midnapore. Two police sub-inspectors and four c

DUBLIN, Ireland, June 7. (UPI)—The start of the airplane Southern Cross over the Atlantic to New York was postponed indefinitely tonight because of unfavorable weather. Capt. Charles E. Kingsford-Smith, ready for the most ambitious east-to-west flight since the partial success of the Bremen, was advised that the weather would not be propitious for the next 36 hours. Kingsford-Smith hopes to reach New York in about 36 hours. He had planned to start early tomorrow until the adverse weather reports were received.

CALCUTTA, India, June 7.-Police fired on a crowd of 1,500 rioters in the Midnapore district of Bengal today, injuring 17 persons. The demonstrators were indignant over band salt. They refused to disperse despite commands of police. Police charged them with batons, but they continued to resist until fired on. Police reinforcements were asked for last night under Police Chief Lowman of the Bengal force. The Midnapore district is 68 miles southwest of here.

1930-06-07.text: DUBLIN, JUNE 7. (AP) -- Captain Charles Kingsford-Smith hopes to take off in his attempted trans-Atlantic flight tomorrow, Sunday, morning at 2 o'clock if weather reports at that hour are favorable, he announced today. Captain Kingsford-Smith will have as his navigator an Irishman, Captain J. P. Saul, a sea captain who has crossed the equator under sail and also has served as observer in the British air force in the Great War. J. W. Stannage will be the plane's wireless operator and M. E. Van Dyk will be assistant pilot.

The Associated Press. Bombay, India, June 26.—Unrest of tribesmen on the northwestern frontier continues to focus the anxious attention of the Europeans here. The news that two British officers and the wife of one of them have been kidnaped by trans-border Achakzai raiders, also was a disturbing factor. Three Kidnaped The Europeans kidnaped were Major E. L. Marley, a sapper stationed at Quetta, Captain J. C. Frere of the twelfth Secunderabad infantry brigade and his wife. The incident occurred Wednesday afternoon at a point seven miles from Chaman on the main Quetta Chaman road. The first news of the event was received in Chaman from the engineer of a train which passed close to the spot shortly afterward. Flee to Afghanistan Police and troops sped to the spot but were unable to overtake the raiders before they crossed the border into Afghanistan six miles distant. It was learned that th

BOMBAY, INDIA, June 17.—(AP)—Undeterred by the arrest of their leaders in the government's raid on the nationalist congress headquarters, Bombay civil disobedience campaigners today strengthened and made effective their picketing on European shops in the Fort area. During the night the Satyagrahis, as the nationalists are called, met to elect from their number a new “war council,” or executive, to direct and manage the campaign against the British government. Yesterday's raid by Indian and European police against the all-India National Congress headquarters seems to have resulted in the arrest of every hitherto unimprisoned member of the war council except the only woman member, Mrs. Perin Captain. She appealed to police to arrest her too but they smilingly refused. She seemed disappointed at their refusal. Only fifty picketeers were sent out yesterday but it was planned today to send ou

DUBLIN, June 18 (UP)--The start of the Southern Cross on its attempted flight to New York was postponed indefinitely again today on receipt of late weather reports showing unfavorable conditions over the Atlantic. Previously Capt. Charles E. Kingsford-Smith had hoped to start in the morning.

LONDON, June 7—By today surrounded cancellation of the court presentation of Mrs. Christopher Courtney at the first royal court at Buckingham Palace May 14, The official London Gazette published the sparse three line notice: “Lord Chamberlain's Office, St. James’ Palace, “Notice is hereby given that the presentation of Mrs. Christopher Courtney at Their Majesties’ court on May 14 has been cancelled.” The London Morning Press republished the announcement, but made little hazard as to the identity of the Mrs. Courtney, evidently fearing to name the wrong person. Only two papers ventured to name the person they believed to be the presenter, now disavowed. Reports of the May 4 court presentation indicated that Mrs. Courtney was presented by Lady Salmond, wife of Sir John Salmond, the air marshal. The Daily Express today, seeking communication with Lady Salmond, was told by her husband, “My w

Nottingham, Eng., June 7.—U.R— Prof. Albert Einstein, noted German scientist, said last night he was on the eve of a new relationship between space and matter. In a lecture at University College here, Einstein, famous for his theory of relativity, said he expected to discover a series of equations showing that space with its metric structure is a primary thing from which matter in all its forms is derived. The new idea came to him while he was seriously ill two years ago, Einstein said. Stated briefly, the idea was: "If one considers two elements in space (usually they are compared only as regards size) a further element comes into it which may give a clue. That is, he could compare the two elements in the matter of direction. "Space is the consideration of first importance, and matter only of secondary interest. Space is a primary phenomenon, and matter is derived from it as a secondary

LONDON (UP).—The first instance during King George's reign, of a cancellation of a court presentation was announced in London Friday. The Lord Chamberlain issued a brief announcement that the presentation of Mrs. Christopher Courtney, wife of Captain Courtney, deputy director of operations and intelligence in the air ministry, had been cancelled. No reason was given. Mrs. Courtney was presented at the court held May 14. She was presented to King George and Queen Mary by Lady Salmond, wife of chief air marshal, Sir John Salmond. The last parallel case was the incident in 1903, when the presentation of Mrs. Eric Gordon, later Lady Granville Gordon, to Queen Victoria was cancelled by King Edward. While no official explanation for the cancellation was given, it was pointed out that there is a strict rule against presentation of divorcees. The Somerset house records showed that Mrs. Courtney

By The Associated Press. Friedrichshafen, Germany, June 6.—The Graf Zeppelin rested tonight at her home base, at the end of a history-making voyage which had carried her to North and South America, over a portion of Africa and twice across the equator in 19 days. Dodging terrific electrical storms that threatened her with disaster over southern France, the Graf detoured to Germany, turning aside from her customary course in the Rhone valley and passing over Soleuvre, near the Swiss frontier. The last two days of the voyage saw the most unseasonable weather Spain has witnessed in years. Just as such an atmospheric disturbance all but wrecked Dr. Hugo Eckener’s dirigible in 1929, when she was forced to abandon an Atlantic crossing at a point near the suburbs of Valence and finally landed near Toulon. A wildly enthusiastic throng greeted the returning voyagers at the end of the dirigible’s

Friedrichshafen, Ger., June 7. —Trans-oceanic commercial service with airships can begin forthwith as a result of the technical observations made on the Graf Zeppelin’s tour of three continents, Dr. Hugo Eckener said today. The Zeppelin’s tour clarified many problems of trans-oceanic flying which previously had been unsolved, Dr. Eckener said, and the technical questions dealing with the feasibility of such a service were answered satisfactorily, hence, from a technical standpoint, commercial air routes could be opened at once, he said. The Graf Zeppelin returned to its home field yesterday after an absence of 19 days, covering 18,000 miles over three continents.

Shanghai, June 6.—(AP)— The Nationalist government's armies fought hard today to hold back the rebel tide rolling from both north and south toward central China. After battling for a month to halt the Northern Alliance rebels driving through Honan and Shantung provinces toward Nanking, the capital, the government was called upon to meet the menace from the south, Kwantung province rebels and bandit hordes numbering 60,000 from several provinces, advanced today to attack the Nationalist forces. Continued on Para 27

| FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, Germany, June 6 (UP) —The Graf Zeppelin dodged terrific storms today to complete a 15,000 mile voyage linking three continents in 19 days. A tremendous ovation greeted the dirigible as it appeared over Friedrichshafen and Lake Constance at 7:10 p.m. (1:10 p.m. EST). Thousands of members of the German Automobile Club, making a special run to this city from all parts of the land, joined with Friedrichshafen residents in cheering Germany's greatest single implement of international goodwill.

VIENNA, June 7 (UP).—Queen Marie of Roumania expressed “the greatest happiness” today when informed that her son, Prince Carol, had returned to Bucharest. “As a mother and one who always wished the best for the Roumanian people, I feel the greatest happiness,” the dowager queen said when she arrived here, en route to Germany.

Paris, June 7.—(P)— The oldest American gold star mother visiting France, Mrs. Elizabeth Hutchins of Oakland, Calif., exchanged visits today with Madame Nungesser, mother of the French flier who was lost on a flight to New York. The 92-year-old American woman called at Madame Nungesser’s home. They embraced each other, tearfully, and sat together for an hour, almost in silence.

1930-05-14.text: By The Associated Press. | LONDON, May 14.—Bombay dispatches to British newspapers today indicated steadily growing hostility to the British government in India. It was said that unrest growing out of civil disobedience campaign continued unabated.

A government Tuesday night assembled in hurried conference, India’s recalcitrant civil disobedience cohorts bided the call of Mrs. Sarojini Naidu, their woman leader, to “new efforts of resistance.” Sholapur, under martial law, seethed with activity. Its more than 100,000 population scurried to cover with the arrival of 1,000 additional troops and enactment of martial law. Under the surface of complete military control followers of Mahatma Gandhi sought means of thwarting the increased threat over them. Throughout the Indian domain arrests of illegal salt makers and depot raiders went on relentlessly. Courts sentenced the offenders to extreme penalties. Only Abbas Tyabji, the eighty-year-old disciple who succeeded Gandhi, and a few irresponsible boys, apparently escaped severe prison labor terms. The tightening of government attitude everywhere was in evidence. It was estimated from 200

BOMBAY, May 14.—Mrs. Sarojini Naidu, poetess and successor of Mahatma Gandhi as leader of the Independence movement, arrived today from Allahabad to gather her volunteer forces for an assault on the government salt works at Dharsana. She was determined to carry out the raid in the face of the most drastic measures which the authorities might take. She will leave tonight for the Gujerat district to make the raid.

BOMBAY, INDIA (7) The government of Bombay today took steps to prevent the contemplated raid of Nationalists on the Salt Depots at Dharsaana. The district magistrate at Surat issued an order under the criminal procedure code prohibiting for one month the assembly of more than four persons and prohibiting carrying of knives, sticks or dangerous weapons within the villages of Dharsaana, and Cheravada and Unmarsada, both within two miles of Dharsaana. The Nationalists have planned the raid to take place tomorrow under the leadership of Mrs. Sarojini Naidu, successor to Mahatma Gandhi as head of the civil resistance movement. Mrs. Naidu arrived here from Ahmadabad, where she conferred with the executive committee of the all-India national congress. She is leaving tonight for Karadi, enroute to Dharsaani. Jamnadas Dwarkadas, formerly a member of the legislative assembly, was arrested today wh

BOMBAY, India, May 14—(U.P) The government ordered a strong detachment of police to proceed immediately to the Dharasana salt works to resist the raid which Mrs. Sarojini Naidu, leader of the independence movement, will make there. The entire police force stationed at Jalalapur was sent to the salt depot and a strong barbed wire barricade was erected. Mrs. Naidu gathered volunteers for the raid before leaving Bombay tonight. The district magistrate reported that the Dharasana authorities were well prepared to deal with the threatened raid there. Police ordered from Jalalapur headquarters had been stationed there three weeks.

FORMBY, Eng., May 14.()—Helen Hicks, long hitting New York girl was the first American to advance to the sixth round of the British Women’s championship, winning her way through a defeat of a fellow countrywoman, Mrs. Leo Federman, also of New York, four up and three to play. Maureen Orcutt, New York, was eliminated in the fifth round by Enid Wilson, former English native champion, six up and four to play. The New Jersey girl could not cope with the brilliant golf played by her opponent. Glenna Collett won an easy victory from Beryl Brown, seven up and six to play, and followed Helen Hicks into the quarter-finals of the championship, to be played tomorrow morning.

SHANGHAI, May 14—The Nationalist government armies today captured 10,000 northern rebels and hurled the invading forces out of Anhwei province, government dispatches announced. Numerous field guns and seven thousand rifles were seized, said the dispatches, as the government troops pressed back the foe in northwest Anhwei and along the railway west of Suchow to across the Honan province border. The Nationalists, said Nanking advices, are attacking Kweiteh and expect by its capture to shatter the northern alliance rebel resistance in eastern Honan province. Fall of the city would cause the rebels to retreat westward to center their defense about Kaifeng, it is claimed.

SHANGHAI, China, May 14.—(U. F.)—The national government at Nanking announced today that the so-called northern armies of Marshal Yen Hsishan, governor of Shansi, had been defeated at Puchow. The announcement said 10,000 prisoners were captured by the government troops. Six field guns and 7,000 rifles also were captured. The right and left wings of the rebel lines collapsed and the government aviators opened a vigorous air raid over Chengchow, which was bombed.

Shanghai, May 13.—(>)—The Nationalist government announced tonight that its forces had driven the northern alliance rebel army westward along the northern borders of Anhwei and Honan provinces in a 'decisive initial battle.' Much ammunition was captured from the rebels in their precipitate retreat. The battle for supremacy in China has lasted five days.

GENEVA, May 14 (AP)—Measures for strengthening the forces fighting the illicit opium traffic by calling for help from the “victim” countries, including Latin America, were taken today by the council of the League of Nations. It was voted to invite Mexico, Uruguay, Spain, Poland, Belgium, Austria and Egypt to sit in the league’s advisory committee on opium traffic. It had been urged by humanitarian workers that hitherto this committee has been composed largely of representatives of countries which manufacture narcotics. The council tentatively set Dec. 1 for holding an international opium conference at which the chief matter for consideration will be a proposal to limit the world’s manufacture of narcotics to the world’s medical scientific needs.

1930-06-05.text: BOMBAY, India, June 4.—(#—India’s intermittent fever of discontent swung back today to its quiet phase following 24 hours of bitter clashes between police and followers of Mahatma Gandhi's program of passive resistance to British authority. From the Punjab to Madras there was a paucity of either news or events. Only in Delhi was a suspicious incident reported, the burning of the National Bank of India and several shops, with damage of about $550,000. The cause of the fire was not made known. Politically the congress volunteers believed their position strengthened today by alignment with them of a strong section of Moslem sentiment. This was expressed in a mile-long parade of Moslems in the streets of Bombay and the adoption, afterward in a mass meeting, of a resolution supporting the all-India national congress program. The group appealed to all their fellows to support the Mahatma.

Landon, June 4.--The Labor government of Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald today won its second victory within the span of a week by defeating a House of Lords amendment 20 votes to 220. Just a week ago today the Labor government beat off a conservative motion with a majority of 20, the vote being 270 against 241. The amendment defeated today would have eliminated the district levy from the coal bill, an extremely controversial measure which has troubled the MacDonald administration throughout this session of parliament.

london—i?)—Details of the conflict between the British government in Malta, important Mediterranean naval base, and the Holy See at the Vatican were revealed today with publication of an official blue book on the subject. The blue book, which contains correspondence regarding the Maltese situation, charges the Vatican with acting in a manner "which constitutes nothing less than a claim to interference with the domestic politics of a British colony." The trouble arose about eighteen months ago when the prime minister, Lord Strickland, himself a Catholic, prevented ecclesiastical authorities from transferring a Franciscan priest, who was a native Maltese, to a Sicilian monastery against his will. Maltese Catholics then were forbidden by the churchmen to vote for the government party in the forthcoming elections. A concordat between the government and the Holy See was put into draft form. I
LONDON, June 5 (1.—-Prime Minister MacDonald informed the House of Commons this afternoon that the government had decided against the construction of the proposed English Channel tunnel.

Friedrichshafen, Germany, June 4 (P)—The Graf Zeppelin notified the Zeppelin Works here tonight that she was not certain she would land at Seville because of bad weather and was heading for Lisbon. If the airship did land at Seville, it was added, the landing would not be made before 6 p. m., tomorrow, Spanish time, or 1 p. m., z. &. T. When the Zeppelin sent the message she gave her position as about 450 miles east and slightly north of San Miguel, most eastward island of the Azores, and about 500 miles directly west of Lisbon.

Shanghai, China, June 4.—Nationalist government forces were defeated today in heavy fighting both in Honan and Shantung provinces, said Japanese dispatches, and retreated before northern alliance rebels. Four hundred thousand men are battling in this area to determine the future government of China. Bandit armies devastating the Yangtse valley cut telegraphic communications, shutting off news from areas about Chengchow, Honan province, and Changsha, Hunan province, where the Nationalists were hard pressed by rebels yesterday. Menaced on four battle fronts by rebellion, with bandit and communist armies ravaging several provinces, the Nationalist government was struggling to maintain itself despite a depleted treasury, crop failure and demoralized business. Heavily reinforced along the Haichow-Tungkwan railway in northern Honan, the northerners inflicted a severe reverse upon the Nationali

SILVER PRESS AGENTS, Seville, Spain, June 4 (4)--Stormy night descended upon Seville, with the Graf Zeppelin plowing its way peacefully toward the Spanish coast through fine weather conditions that promised to bring the returning dirigible to this city by daybreak. Heavy rains swept most of Spain and the Mediterranean region tonight. The evil weather gave no sign of abating. It chiseled a populace accustomed at this season to brilliant sunshine and balmy air. Tidings from the Graf just at nightfall cheered official circles, where there had been anxiety. No previous message had come since mid-forenoon. It had been assumed that wireless communication was impossible because of the inclement weather. The infante Beatriz, wife of the infante Don Alfonso, the king’s cousin, who is in Seville to greet her husband, a passenger on the Zeppelin, had asked the government to inform her immediately o

FRIEDRICHSHAFEN (4) — Stormy winds off the Iberian peninsula, which buffeted the Graf Zeppelin about like a plaything of the elements, today delayed for hours its arrival at Seville, port of call en route to its home here. Radio advices from the Graf told of greatly decreased speed, and said the dirigible was heading toward Lisbon, Portugal. It was by no means sure that an attempt would be made to land at Seville, since advices from there indicated the landing field was water-logged and that a three-day blustery rain continued. In any event, the Graf’s advices said, no attempt at landing would be made before 6 P. M., M. E. T., (12 noon E. S. T.), which is at least 17 hours later than the preceding midnight Spanish time by which Dr. Hugo Eckener, the ship’s master, had expected to reach Seville. There are 22 passengers aboard the Zeppelin, and 43 officers and crew. The ship has not consta

1930-04-26.text: Bombay, April 25, (4?)--The atmosphere of India continued ominous today, with evacuation of all European women and children from Peshawar, the most serious feature of the situation. Peshawar lies far up on the northwestern frontier, commanding the entrance to the famous Khyber Pass. The hills around it are the home of the most dangerous Indian tribes, chief among them being the Afridis and Mohmands, who are born fighting men.

LONDON, April 26. (INS)—A German Zeppelin today zoomed across the London sky for the first time since the hectic war days, when the Graf Zeppelin appeared over Piccadilly at 4:13 p.m. (10:13 a.m. eastern standard time). The huge German airliner described a graceful circle over the city, dipping momentarily over Westminster Abbey. LONDON, April 26. (UP)—The dirigible Graf Zeppelin, continuing its series of test flights prior to departure on a flight to Brazil and the United States next month, flew over England today on a trip from Friedrichshafen. The big ship crossed the channel from France after a speedy flight from Germany and was sighted over Brighton at 3 p.m., heading for Wembley. The Graf Zeppelin was received with mixed feelings especially in Kent, where 14 years ago on April 26, 1916, the residents of that area were awakened by the roar of Zeppelin motors and the shattering explo

London, April 26 (UP)—Two companies of the Essex regiment and two machine gun sections have arrived at Peshawar to strengthen the garrison there, a United Press dispatch from Lahore said today. The troops were ordered to Peshawar where British authorities fear wild Afghan tribes might cross over the border into Peshawar to plunder, taking advantage of the rioting there early this week.

BRIGHTON, Eng, April 26 - England saw its first Zeppelin since the war today with the passage of the great dirigible Graf Zeppelin over Brighton at 3:15 p.m. en route to London and Cardington. PARIS, April 26 - The Graf Zeppelin, bound for London and Cardington to pick up its master, Dr. Hugo Eckener, was sighted over Paris at 11:58 a.m. (5:58 a.m. E.S.T.). It left Friedrichshafen at 6:00 a.m.

London, April 26.—Wul Thorne, 72, who has been in the House of Commons for 25 years and is one of the characters of that body, today married for the fourth time, his bride being Miss Beatrice Nelly Collins, 42, one of his constituents. “I have had three wives and they have all been jolly good ones,” declared the bridegroom, “married life is all right if you pull together.”

LONDON, April 26—(UP)—The Prince of Wales, world reveler, was back home today to settle down to business. Increasingly heavy obligations await the prince as heir to the throne, and his return from his latest 18,000-mile African hunting trip is expected to mean that he will enter into them with even more vigor than in the past. Fourteen public entertainments already have been scheduled for him between May 13 and July 17, and in addition he doubtless will be present at the dinners of four regiments of which he is an honorary member. Early in June, the prince will unveil the London statue to Marshal Ferdinand Foch, generalissimo of the allied armies.

Shanghai, April 25 (4)--Communistic and bandit armies today were reported looting, burning and slaying by wholesale in several provinces of China. Numerous missionaries were said to be in jeopardy and thousands of Chinese were reported massacred. Nationalist Government officials, whose troops have been ineffective, offered rewards for the capture of Communists, who in turn offered prizes for the capture of foreigners, being quoted by missionaries as saying that “all foreigners should be killed.” No deaths of foreigners, however, were reported. Fresh from the bandit-scarred province of Kiangsi, Fathers Gately and Flaherty at Hongkong substantiated tales of depredations told by fellow priests, and gave no assurance of safety of sixteen American Catholic missionaries held in the city of Kanchow, besieged since early in March by Red armies.

Apr. 26.—(#)—Retracing in peace time the route flown with deadly intent during the war by the imperial army Zeppelins, the dirigible Graf Zeppelin today cruised northwestward from Friedrichshafen to pay London a visit. The giant airship left its hangar here at 6:02 a. m. (12:02 a. m. E. S. T.) in brilliant sunshine for the 4590-mile trip to London, and from there to Cardington, where, grounding momentarily, her master, Dr. Hugo Eckener, will be picked up and brought back to Germany. Twenty-two passengers were aboard the dirigible, among them Lady Grace Drummond Hay. Others were to be picked up for the return trip to Cardington, where the R-100, which transcends the Graf in size and which will fly to Canada next month, is housed.

VIENNA, April 26—(INS)—Ex-Chancellor Ignaz Seipel barely escaped death by assassination today when an unidentified assassin, hurling himself upon the statesman before the door of the Capuchin church, burial place of the Hapsburgs, attempted to strangle him with bare hands. Passersby seized the assailant and dragged him away. Authorities stated that the man apparently was demented. The police, however, immediately launched an investigation to determine whether the assassin was the tool of a band of conspirators. He was subjected to a lengthy questioning at police headquarters, but it appeared he had acted independently in the abortive attempt. Dr. Seipel was succeeded as chancellor last year by Dr. Johann Schober. He attracted international attention some time before his resignation by his bitter controversy with Premier Mussolini over the status of Austrian-born residents of the Upper Ad

PARIS, April 26—(AP)—Henry Ford, and not Lindbergh or President Hoover, is the American best known to the millions of the masses of Europe. Inquisitive editors set about to find out for themselves in just which Americans their readers were interested, and Henry Ford ran away with the results. His biography in book or newspaper serial form, is known to more Europeans than that of any other contemporary American. Europe has adopted into many languages the word ‘Fordize’ which means to adopt the Detroit manufacturer's methods of production to old world factories. His ideas about prohibition, and automobiles, high wages, prosperity and automobiles, bear more weight abroad than those of any other American. The ten best known Americans as far as Europe is concerned, are: 1. Ford, 2. Hoover, 3. Pershing, 4. Chaplin, 5. Lindbergh, 6. Edison, 7. Dempsey, 8. Borah, 9. Colonel House, 10. John D. Ro

PARIS, Apr. 26. (U?).-Fear was expressed in responsible quarters here today that the revolt in India might spread to other parts of Asia, particularly French Indo-China. Growing concern was felt over the trend of events in India, where scores have been killed in the past few weeks in sporadic outbreaks. Violent native unrest allegedly has been fanned by Red propaganda. While not discussing the merits of the campaign of civil disobedience now being conducted by Mahatma Gandhi, persons in semi-official quarters consider his aims cannot be achieved without a most terrific upheaval, affecting not only India but the whole world. In the first place the French think an open revolt by the Indians would lead to guerrilla warfare between the Hindus and 70,000,000 Indian Moslems. The latter it is asserted here are alarmed at the prospect of Hindu control. In the second place it was felt Bolshevik p

1930-04-25.text: (By The Associated Press) The anxiety with which the British government views recent disturbances along the mountainous northwest frontier of India was indicated today with reports that censorship had been established and that women and children were being evacuated from the vicinity of Peshawar. Peshawar, where riots Wednesday resulted in the killing of three British soldiers, the wounding of eight and the death of twelve natives, is now said to be quiet although virtually in a state of siege. Troops and police are alertly patrolling the city. Some of the political prisoners held at Peshawar were moved to a jail at Charsadda, where slight demonstrations followed their transfer and the arrest of Abdul Gaffar Khan, but the police restored order without difficulty. While reports came from official circles that troops had been moved to the disturbed regions of Resalpur and Nowshera, that th

Windsor, Eng., Apr. 25. (AP). ~ The Prince of Wales, home from his African hunting trip, landed on Smith's Lawn in the Windsor Great Park today, making a perfect landing. On his arrival in England the prince was as close as he could get to his new country residence, Fort Belvedere at Sunningdale. From the front door a private road is being built to the private royal airdrome at Smith's Lawn. Fort Belvedere has been in the hands of builders and decorators for some time in preparation for the prince's return from Africa. The Duke of York and Prince George were awaiting their elder brother and greeted him. Then they drove to the prince’s country house where King George and Queen Mary welcomed him home.

CALCUTTA, India. Apr. 25. (AP) A mob of 4,000 rioters nationalist independence demonstrations at Nella, near Diamond Harbor today and clashed with a strong police detachment. The police fired buckshot into the ranks of the rioters but there were few casualties. Diamond Harbor is 4 miles from Calcutta.

Bombay, India, April 25. (P)-A state of siege was understood here today to exist in Peshawar, buffer barbarian hinterland, as an outgrowth of rioting. Wednesday in which three British soldiers were said to have been killed, eight wounded, and twelve natives killed. Reports were that the Indian government had clamped down a censorship on news from Punjab and northwest frontier province, in which Peshawar is located. An official statement at Simla, summer capital, said some of the political agitators jailed at Peshawar were taken to Charsadda to prison. A crowd collected outside the jail but the constabulary dispersed them without bloodshed.

Simlad, India, April 25.—British authorities are taking a serious view of the recent events in India, especially the troubles at Peshawar, along the northern border, and all women and children are being sent from that place. It was believed that military leave from India would be stopped. Casualties in the serious rioting at Peshawar are estimated at more than 50. Three British soldiers were among the dead. Peace has been restored, however, and the British troops, rushed up for an emergency, are gradually being withdrawn. Since the beginning of the rioting, public gatherings and meetings of more than five persons have been forbidden. The situation is now under control but British authorities said the discontent over the arrest of Abdul Kahn, leader of the Youths’ League, was causing trouble.

Bombay, April 24. (P)—With riots, demonstrations and arrests steadily increasing in India, the most disturbing feature of the situation tonight was the spread of trouble to Peshawar, key city of the northwest frontier. Soldiers Killed. Latest reports said that three soldiers were killed and eight wounded in the rioting there yesterday when troops turned machine guns on demonstrators to quell the disturbance. Twelve natives also were killed. Business is at a standstill and the city bears the appearance of an armed camp. Other less authoritative accounts say trouble is spreading on the frontier itself, with rioting at Kohat and Charsadda. Troops are said to have been moved into the disturbed regions of Risalpur and Nowshera, and the guard has been increased in Kohat Pass, which leads through the mountains of Afghanistan. No serious trouble was reported from the larger cities today, but ten

. London, April 25 (P)—The Bombay correspondent of the London Daily News today said that the growth of strength of Mahatma Gandhi, Indian nationalist leader, during the past fortnight, had been almost phenomenal. The correspondent declared the situation was growing worse steadily throughout India. The Mahatma, he said, was planning new aspects of civil disobedience in anticipation of the early arrival of the Monsoons, which will flood Gujerat and make salt collections impossible.

Southampton, England, April 24 "The Bremen, one of the Atlantic's largest and swiftest liners, was en route to New York tonight after an alarming collision with the tanker British Grenadier about five miles off Dungeness this morning. The collision occurred in a dense fog. The ships struck with a resounding crash. The Bremen moved slowly to Southampton, where she anchored off the Cowes entrance. Here an official surveyor boarded the ship and issued a certificate enabling her to proceed. The British Grenadier, said reports from Deal, was not so lucky. She was severely damaged on the port side, but was able to limp into Downs without assistance. When she anchored, oil was pouring from her tanks into the water. A woman passenger on the tanker was out. She was taken to shore by a motorboat in care of the physician who went out to the ship.

LONDON, April 25.—INS—The Prince of Wales arrived at Windsor Park by airplane at 4 p.m. today, completing the last leg of his return trip from the African jungle. The British heir was greeted by his brother, Prince George, and the party immediately motored to Belvedere Fort, where the King and Queen greeted him.

LONDON, April 20.—Apparently despairing of achieving martyrdom through arrest, Mahatma M. K. Gandhi has about decided to give up his campaign against the Indian government's salt monopoly and proceed to another method of civil disobedience, an Allahabad dispatch to the London Daily News said today. Gandhi possibly will intensify his efforts to boycott the use of foreign-made cloth in India and his anti-liquor drive, this dispatch reported. In the meantime, while the country remained comparatively quiet during the past 24 hours, the All India Congress issued a statement declaring 52 were killed and 30 wounded in the rioting two days ago at Peshawar. These were mostly villagers, but that none were volunteers following Gandhi, who had preached peaceful disobedience as definitely opposed to any form of violence. Ten persons were reported killed in an explosion in a fireworks shop at Rohri, U

LONDON, April 25.—The Prince of Wales returned today from the big game jungles of Africa, ending what probably will be his last extended vacation trip as Prince to the outposts of the British Empire. The Prince reached England at 8:20 p.m., flying over Dover en route from Paris, escorted by British fighting planes which had accompanied him on the last stage of his journey. Ten French military craft had escorted him from Paris to mid-channel, where they turned back. The Prince's airplane landed at Windsor Castle, where the royal family is in residence, late this afternoon.

British government in India took new repressive measures today to halt the independence movement which has claimed 51 lives in less than two weeks. It clamped down on the northeast city of Peshawar, the scene of a clash in which three British soldiers and 20 natives were killed. The rolling up a total of 20 casualties. A mob had invaded the Balaghat mine and stoned the police before the local magistrate ordered the latter to respond with bullets. (Continued on Page 20, Col 6.

LONDON, Apr 25 —LP;—The Daily Express today said that Princess Marie Louise, cousin of King George, who recently returned from a trip to South America, was living a simple, modest life in an Anglican convent called ‘The House of Mercy’ near Horbury, Yorkshire. The convent is headquarters for the order which does rescue work, and the princess, the Express said, is spending a short time each year within the convent. She follows the rules of the order, rising early with the nuns, sharing simple food, and assisting in the daily routine of looking after sixty girls within the convent. The paper said there was nothing in her convent life to distinguish her as a princess.

LONDON, April 25.—Evacuation of women and children from the troublesome Peshawar district in India, where already more than 30 deaths have resulted from violent fighting between troops and natives, was ordered by the government today. The most serious conflict was that at Peshawar, northern gateway into Afghanistan. Twenty native rioters are reported to have fallen before machine gun fire, turned upon them after they had surrounded an armored car, drenched with gasoline, set it afire and burned two soldier occupants to death. At Chittagong, scene of Friday's armory raid, in which six troopers were killed, an armed rebel was reported shot to death. At Mysore, in the south, 2 strikers were wounded when they attempted to storm the Kolar Gold mines. Peshawar is under martial law. Several Congressmen, charged with making inflammatory speeches, were imprisoned in the Peshawar fort. Entry into

Canton, China, April 24.—-(4)— Two American missionaries who fled here today from Sinfeng, Kiangsi province, reported that "Red" bandit leaders were offering a reward of $200 for every foreigner captured, saying that: "all foreigners would be killed." Sixty thousand peasants, the missionaries said, had enlisted recently in the Communist army which had been despoiling the province for many months. Soviet propaganda, they asserted, was making great headway among the masses, who were paid in Russian currency. The missionaries, Father McLaughlin and Father Moehringer of Brooklyn, N. Y., said that 16 American Catholic missionaries at Kanchow were in danger of capture by Red troops and possible execution, as the city was near surrender after a siege since early last month. Kate in Doubt Chinese troops were reported about to evacuate Kanchow, according to reports at Sinfeng when the priests lef

NAPLES.—(4)—In the idyllic surroundings of the Isle of Capri, where the Roman Emperors Augustus and Tiberius spent their holidays, Edda Mussolini, daughter of Italy’s dictator, and her husband, Count Galeazzo Ciano, Friday began their honeymoon. Arriving secretly from Rome late Thursday night they proceeded on board a motorboat to the island, which bears the Italian name of “Goat” and dots the western horizon of the beautiful Bay of Naples.

Rome, April 24 (/P)—Benito Mussolini, dictator of Italy since 1923, today like a private Italian citizen saw his 19-year-old daughter, Edda, become the bride of Count Galeazzo Clano in a ceremony that despite all its attendant magnificence was really but a wedding in a private family. In Il Duce’s parish church, St. Joseph's on the Via Nomentana, the daughter of the dictator and the son of the Italian minister of communications were married by the parish priest, Monsignor Pasquale. Their wedding, except for the picturesqueness of Fascist ‘Black Shirts” with glittering bayonets, was simple, in accordance with Il Duce’s preference for keeping his family life in the background. Pope Pius XI sent the bridal couple a solid gold rosary and his blessing. King Victor Emanuel, signing himself “Your most affectionate cousin,” sent congratulations to the premier from the royal family. King Zogu I o

Yokohama, April 25 -- With his big plane lashed to the after deck Van Lear Black, Baltimore publisher, sailed today for San Francisco aboard the Japanese liner Tatsute Maru, a new ship of the N. Y. K. line making its maiden voyage across the Pacific. The plane was not dismantled. Black, who recently completed a flight from London to Tokyo, intends to fly from San Francisco to Baltimore.

“Traitor” from opposition member interrupted Foreign Minister Baron Shidehara’s exposition on the naval treaty in the House of Representatives this afternoon. The foreign minister's speech was the same as that delivered in the House of Peers this morning and was greeted with much excitement, the Minseito majority section cheering and the Seiyukai, the chief opposition, raising a chorus of hostile shouts. Unperturbed, Shidehara read his speech to the end. Thereafter the opposition began a more orderly assault upon the government's acceptance of the London pact by reverting to regular parliamentary tactics. Ki Inukai, veteran president of the Seiyukai party, fired the opening gun with a scathing interpellation on the naval policy. “Our delegates.” TOKYO, April 25.—Cries of “Traitor” were heard from the opposition as the state for debate: “Is the empire not endangered by the treaty?” Premie

AUGUSTA, Ma.—(4)—The population of “township 5, range 12” in Discatacuis county has dropped 99.5 per cent in the past 10 years. The present population is one. The 1920 federal census showed a population of 147. Ten years ago there was a good sized lumbering operation under way. Since then lumbering has been abandoned and the lone resident is the keeper.

1930-05-30.text: (By The Associated Press) London, May 28.—An official Buckingham Palace statement today said that King George's rheumatism, which is preventing his attendance at the last two courts of the season, shows definite improvement.

BOMBAY, May 30.—()—Alarming reports were received here today of renewed rioting yesterday between Moslems and Hindus at Dacca, 150 miles from Calcutta, capital of Bengal. A large number of Hindus were arrested and the city superintendent of police, commanding Gurka troops was Neighboring villages were said to have taken up the communal conflict, which, since it began Thursday of last week has taken 14 lives at Dacca and caused injuries to 40 others. Thursday's renewed disturbances seemed to center on the Rair Bazaar, western suburb of the city. At Lillooah, also in the Calcutta area, police opened fire upon a mob of 4,000 rioters, most of them railway workers from the East India workshops. Four persons were wounded in the disturbance which grew out of the introduction of a new wage scale. The mob besieged the company office and injured several European officials slightly before the situa

BOMBAY, May 30.—The death toll at Rangoon, Burma, reached 168 today as a result of the violent riots among dock workers during the week, reports reaching here said. More than 700 were injured during fights. Meanwhile, the independence agitators in Bombay decided to defy the martial law proclaimed by the Government at Sholapur, a fortnight ago, after riots in that disturbed hill town 220 miles southeast of here. The situation was much easier with the exception of spasmodic outbursts which resulted in occasional killings. The military continued in control of Rangoon.

DHARASANA, BOMBAY, May 30.—(%) Ten nationalist volunteers were taken back to their camp at Untadi today on stretchers after a sortie against the salt depot here. One hundred volunteers participated in the raid. They had reached one of the salt heaps and had started to pick up salt when the police made a lathi charge, injuring several, ten of them badly. The remainder of the volunteers were dispersed by the lathis, or staves, in the hands of the police and driven outside the boundaries of the depot. They went back to the Untadi camp where other volunteers were arriving and sitting around in batches of four or five in the ruins of the camp which the police several times have demolished. Large numbers of volunteers arriving at Bulsar from various parts of Gujarat are expected at Untadi tomorrow to participate in further raids.

Mahatma Gandhi is sweeping onward despite that leader's internment and the arrest of his lieutenants daily. While the war council of the Bombay Nationalist Congress has decided to renew the mass raids begun against the government salt works at Wadala last week, raids on the salt pans and resultant arrests continue at Dharasana. Paris —(AP) — American Gold Star mothers in France for visits to the graves of sons who died in the World War gave an impressive background Friday for the most extensive observance of Memorial Day yet held abroad. Troops fired volleys in salute of the dead at the American cemeteries throughout France. Taps were sounded and dignitaries spoke. But the feature of the day were the trips before and after the ceremonies by the war mothers to the graves of those they lost more than 11 years ago. At Suresnes cemetery, outside of Paris, Ambassador Edge made the principal address, referring to them as those "who had given those who were dearest to them that others might live in the full enjoyment of their liberty." Taught Sons Loyalty. "You mothers instilled into these young men the principles for which they laid down their lives," he said. "You taught them the fundamentals of loyalty, courage, tr

PARIS, May 29.—(4.—The first contingent of the American gold star mothers and widows to visit France was homeward bound, tired but content at having a pious visit to the last resting place of soldier sons and husbands. One hundred twenty-seven were in the group which sailed. Four were left behind, one because of illness, the other will tour Europe. The second group, meanwhile, is still in France and will conduct special Memorial Day services over soldier graves, while the third contingent today left Belgium for military cemeteries in France.

PARIS, May 30—(LP)—The graves of 30,000 American soldier dead and of nearly a million French and British comrades were decorated today in the most elaborate memorial day ceremony that has occurred in Europe since the war. "The presence in the battlefield cemeteries of Gen. John J. Pershing, several hundred gold star mothers and war widows, and several hundred veterans of the fighting 27th division lent added impressiveness!" In a drizzling rain, U. S. Ambassador Walter L. Edge delivered the principal address of the entire ceremony in France at Suresnes cemetery near Paris. The ambassador pleaded for permanent peace.

SHANGHAI, May 30.— (UP)— Chiang Kai-Shek, head of the National government at Nanking, was reported wounded today while inspecting troops at the front in his campaign against the northern rebel forces at Peiping. The wound was in the leg and not serious, being described as “slight.” Chiang went immediately to Hsuchow headquarters, where he refused to permit any comment on the reports, which were said by local sources to be accurate.

1930-03-25.text: London, March 24.—Despite dissension within the naval conference in the form of the Franco-Italian parity dispute, and steady sniping from without by critics, Secretary Stimson and Prime Minister MacDonald intend to defend their banner of a five-power treaty to the bitter end. Thus today started the third month of negotiations, keeping busy even though the day’s work was fruitless as far as any reports made public. It’s understood that Signor Grandi feels pessimistic and expressed the opinion that adjournment of the conference might enable settlement of Italy’s argument with France in a cooler diplomatic atmosphere than that of London at present. Help from Japan, which may arrive Thursday in the form of approval of a three-power pact for Great Britain, Japan and the United States, would give the conference leaders a chance to pull at least partial success out of the stalemate.

Ottawa, Ont., March 25.—(LP)—Actual negotiations between the United States and Canada for a reciprocal “liquor” treaty have been opened, Prime Minister Mackenzie King told the House of Commons. The statement came last night during a warm debate on the pending King liquor bill during which the prime minister had been vigorously attacked by members who accused him of succumbing to “American pressure.” Replying to the charges that he had been coerced into sponsoring the bill by the United States, King declared that a treaty was not an impossibility and would prevent smuggling both from the American and Canadian borders. Cc. H. Cahan, of Montreal, who had been one of those who opposed the bill which would in effect give the Canadian authorities power to control exports of liquor if it desired, said he had been approached by a “high” official of the United States and told that if such legisla

United Press Staff Correspondent London, Mar. 25 (UP)—Chief delegates of the five-power naval conference, which convened on January 21 to limit the world's warships, considered today a proposal to adjourn for six months to prevent collapse of their negotiations. Prime Minister J. Ramsay MacDonald summoned the American, French, Italian and Japanese chief delegates to discuss the next step. A conference crisis has been created by failure of France and Italy to agree and the adjournment was urged to enable them to come to terms. The British spokesman said the adjournment suggestion was viewed as “worthy of consideration” under certain contingencies which have not yet arisen. He reiterated the conference was making a last effort to reach a five-power agreement. Decision on adjournment might be delayed because the French foreign minister, Aristide Briand, was not scheduled to return until tom

London, Mar. 25—Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald summoned a meeting of the five chief delegates to the London Naval Conference for 5:30 P.M. today. It is assumed they will discuss Dino Grandi's proposals to adjourn the conference for six months. London, Mar. 25—Adjournment for six months, after creation of a three-power pact and an agreement not to increase building programs in the interval, was under consideration today as a means of saving the face of the naval conference. The proposed solution was offered by Foreign Minister Dino Grandi of Italy, who outlined to Premier J. Ramsay MacDonald four reasons for the adjournment. First, he argued, the halt in the five-power negotiations would not preclude arrival at an agreement between America, Great Britain and Japan. Second, the six months could be used by France and Italy in an endeavor to settle the question of navies and tonnage which has h

Luxor, Egypt, March 24.—(P) The King and Queen of the Belgians today defied the reputed curse of the Pharaohs. With Howard Carter, excavator of the tomb of Tut-Ankh-Amen, King Albert and Queen Elizabeth visited the tomb in the Valley of the Kings and neither indicated any bad luck was expected. Thereafter the king walked nearly two miles from his yacht into Karnak. He will go to Cairo Wednesday.

LONDON, March 25.—Possibility of a full year's suspension of the London naval disarmament conference loomed today as the delegates met to discuss the proposal of Foreign Minister Dino Grandi of Italy that the parley adjourn for six months to permit France and Italy to settle their differences. British officials were outspoken in their belief that if the proposed adjournment were taken, it would be at least a year before the five powers could be convoked into a conference again. For this reason it is regarded as highly probable that substantial efforts will be made to reach some sort of a tentative agreement as speedily as possible. Once scattered, it is believed, the conference would be almost impossible to call together again. Prime Minister J. Ramsey MacDonald called a meeting of the heads of the five delegations for this afternoon, following an hour and a half's conversation with Secr

VIENNA, March 24.—Doctor Ernest Watzl, prominent chemist and inventor of Cleveland, who disappeared near Pottstown, Pa., on November 7, 1929, was found dead this afternoon in his hotel room here. Josefa Eropej, also of Cleveland, was discovered dead with him. The authorities said it was a case of double suicide and believed that financial difficulties were the reason. They were both shot dead. According to the police, Dr. Watzl left a number of letters addressed to people in various countries. They said the news of the deaths were communicated to the American authorities and refused to make further statements. The career of Dr. Ernest Watzl, Cleveland chemist, was as colorful as his disappearance November 7, 1929, was mysterious. He had invented a new process for the purification of water, which was said to be revolutionary and in great demand by waterworks in various parts of the countr

VIENNA, (UP) Ernst Watzi, brilliant young Austrian chemist, and a young woman believed to be Mrs. Mary Macgranahan of Cleveland, O., died some time in the darkness of Sunday night, in the royal suite of the Hotel Sacher here, in a suicide pact that ends a police mystery of two continents. The body of Watzi was identified at the police morgue Tuesday by a Viennese watchdealer, Franz Watzl, who said the dead man was his son, Herman Ernst. The watchdealer said his son usually used his other name, Ernst. Their deaths, through the instrumentality of Watzl's big army revolver, came only a few hours before $60,000 worth of insurance policies, in favor of the chemist’s wife and children back home, would have lapsed. It was Watzl’s last grand gesture, for the former Cleveland president, according to the police, had come to the end of his financial resources in the course of his four months’ wande

VIENNA, March 25.—As strange a story as any from fiction's pages was being unfolded by the police here today as they probed the deaths of Dr. Ernest Watzl, Austrian chemist and inventor who made a fortune in the United States and a woman identified as Mrs. Mary Horvath MacGranahan, of Cleveland, Ohio. The pair were found dead in the fashionable Hotel Sacher here. Police believe Watzl shot his companion and then turned the gun on himself. The couple had registered at the hotel, which in pre-war days was the rendezvous of Austrian aristocracy, last Wednesday as Mr. and Mrs. Johann Flassak of Cleveland. Further investigation showed the woman had masqueraded as Mme. Josefa Kropej, but she was later identified, according to the police, as Mrs. MacGranahan. The body of Dr. Watzl was identified by his father, a well-known...

Vienna, March 25.—(AP)—The strange career of Dr. Ernest Watzl, monocled Cleveland chemist and inventor, was pieced together by police of two continents today, while the inventor's body awaited claimants at a morgue here. The body was found yesterday in a dowdy room of a hotel, with a bullet hole through the heart. In the same room, and believed to have been shot by Watzl before he ended his own life, was the body of a woman known here as Josefa Kropej, but thought possibly to be Mrs. Mary McGranahan of Cleveland. The woman was said to have joined Watzl in Europe and to have come to Vienna with him. Among the effects of the trio, who were believed to have been dead since before Sunday, when Watzl's insurance policies would have expired, were letters to various people in different countries, one of them to Mrs. Watzl in Cleveland. Police said they believed financial difficulties caused the

Berlin, March 26.—(A.P.)—Pooling of interests by the Hamburg-American Line and the North German Lloyd was officially announced today in the form of a joint communique issued in Hamburg and Bremen. From this communique it was clear that a fusion in fact, if not in name, has been consummated, thereby placing German shipping on an entirely new basis and ending a rivalry of many decades between Germany’s two greatest lines. The joint fleet will number 3850 steamers aggregating more than 2,000,000 gross registered tons.

TOKIO, March 24 (#)--There were strong indications here Monday night that the Japanese government next Thursday would accept the tentative agreement of Japanese and American delegates to the London naval conference providing that Japan's total naval tonnage shall be a maximum of 69.6 per cent of the American total. The American quota is expected to be the same as the British. This expected decision of the cabinet permitting a Japanese-American agreement at London is believed here to be the forerunner of a naval treaty at least between Japan, the United States and Great Britain, even though France and Italy should not become parties to the program for reduced naval tonnage.

(By Associated Press) MILAN, March 25.—Feodor Chaliapin, operatic basso, is seriously ill here. He has had to cancel special performances of the Russian Opera Boris Godunov, in which he sings the title role at La Scala.

1930-05-24.text: BOMBAY, India, May 23, ~ Mrs. Sarojini Naidu was sentenced to nine months of simple imprisonment as leader of the Gandhi salt raiders at Dharsana Wednesday.

BOMBAY, May 23.—(4)—Two hundred and fifty nationalist volunteers, arrested in the recent salt raids and held in the detention camp at Worli, have begun a hunger strike in protest at the diet which is offered them. All India National Congress officials visiting the camp today tried to dissuade them from their course. Undeterred by the moving of troops to Dharasana, Surat and other localities where government-operated salt depots are located, Indian nationalists today planned further mass raids against the salt pans. The raid projected for today at Wadala was called off but only to complete preparations for a mass raid Sunday there. Another mass raid has been planned for Sunday at Dharasana. The government yesterday moved 250 Indian cavalry into the Surat district. Previously a large contingent of Hyderabad troops had been sent to Dharasana to hold the salt raiders in check there.

Bombay, May 23, ().-Today was more exciting in Bombay than any time since the opening of the civil resistance campaign, what with news of the imprisonment of Mrs. Sarojini Naidu coupled with a great procession of Indians. The procession of upward of 200,000 persons was organized by the leaders of various Indian commercial bodies and started marching from the Dullion exchange. Mrs. Naidu, who was leader of the civil disobedience campaign after the arrest of Mahatma Gandhi and Abbas Tyabji, was sentenced to nine months simple imprisonment, as a result of her activities in the recent salt raids at Dharasana.

Bombay, India, May 24—(A P)—Indian nationalists today observed “Dharasana Day,” making it an occasion to celebrate “victory” there against British police and armed forces, and of mourning for those arrested in the course of the raids against the Salt Pans. A partial hartal, or stoppage of work, was in effect in most of the native city. The usual daily raids against the Wadala Salt Pans were suspended temporarily, but will be resumed Sunday, it was understood, with a new mass raid. Instead the crowds which Friday staged a procession into the foreign area which was declared to be one of the most impressive demonstrations of Nationalism ever seen here, were called again to the Explanade Maidan where eye witnesses of the Dharasana raids were to address the crowd. The number of demonstrations were swelled by employees of the railway workshops and cotton mills who are observing “Empire Day.”

Manchester, England.—Charles Dawes, American ambassador, today was given the honorary degree of Doctor of Laws of Manchester University. He was one of several upon whom the honor was conferred. The ceremonies were in connection with the jubilee of Manchester University and its eightieth Founders’ Day as Owens College. General Dawes, accepting the degree, said, “This community and country well may rejoice that it has developed a character which, if this were a convocation of the universities of the world to confer degrees, would entitle it to one of the highest.” The ambassador described the degrees as “degrees in the school of life as well as in the university.” He spoke for all of the honorary graduates, expressing their appreciation.

LONDON, May 24 (AP)—Waving American flags, 156 Gold Star Mothers and 116 veterans of the 27th division arrived in London today on a pilgrimage to the graves of their sons and "buddies" buried in England. Landing from the steamship Republic at Southampton, the visitors came to London by train and were given a great ovation at the railway station. Most of the veterans, who fought with the 4th British army at Ypres and on the Somme, today were returning to the scene of their wartime activities for the first time since the Armistice. Practically all of the mothers were making their first trip abroad. Eight Gold Star fathers who are with the party were almost lost in the excitement of the reception. Officials of the British Legion, representatives of the war office and Colonel Jatin R. Thomas, military attache of the American embassy were in the greeting party. On Final Visit BERE-EN-TARDENNE
London, May 24—Archbishop Lord Davidson, former archbishop of Canterbury and primate of the Church of England, lapsed into unconsciousness this noon. He is seriously ill and is not expected to live.

By SALI PALE (Associated Press Staff Writer) DOVER (England), May 22— Sir John Fagge, former handyman of Pepperell, Mass., but present baronet of Dover, wants a job. Sir John came to England ten weeks ago to assume the title he inherited from his elder brother, John Charles, who died in January. Sir John's life has not been that exciting during these ten weeks. He got no money with the title and he is getting a little bored with his role of leisured country gentleman who has to live in a boarding house. In fact, he would like a job in London or any city in the United States except Pepperell, Sir John says. He doesn't know yet whether he is going back to the United States soon although he is sure he will return eventually. "But not to Pepperell," he says, "for it's very different now, you know. My position has changed. In other words, I won't work in Pepperell." The publicity of his acqui
