(World Copyright, 1930, by United Press) Bombay, May 24.—(UP)—Representatives of 50 Bombay mercantile associations at a mass meeting, which followed the big demonstration here yesterday, adopted a resolution urging a general boycott of British goods, demanding the release of Mahatma Gandhi, and urging the national congress not to participate in the round table conference in London next fall. The resolution was significant because of the prominence of the groups taking part in the meeting. A millionaire merchant, J. D. Birla, presided at the meeting. The national congress war council at the same time decided to follow up the demonstration yesterday with another today, in protest against the British action at Dharasana, while the volunteer camp was evacuated and military guards established. The entire Indian press gave space to a dispatch recounting a protest in London by Rob

Paris, May 23, ().-The arrival of 106 Gold Star Mothers today to visit the shrines of their dead sons’ heroism in the military battlefields has brought the total now in France to more than 235. That number will be maintained as a high point all summer, with one group on the battlefields, another arriving and another preparing to leave America for the pilgrimage at the same time.

SHANGHAI, May 23.—()-~Nationalist government forces have severely defeated the northern alliance rebels with heavy casualties, said government dispatches today, and are driving in general retreat toward Kaifeng, Honan province. The nationalists took 20,000 prisoners. Defeated in a series of engagements which began May 8 in Northern Kiangsu and Honan provinces, Gen. Yen Hsi-Shan, governor of Shansi province and head of the revolt against the central government, is said in government dispatches to be planning flight to a foreign country in anticipation of the collapse of the insurrection. The nationalists, advancing northward on the railway beyond Hankow, are reported thrusting the rebel armies before them on an axis front to converge at Changchow. (Continued on Page 2. Col 4.)
SHANGHAI, May 23 —(P) Five hundred bandits today looted two northern Kiangsu Province towns killing one hundred villagers, and kidnapping 400 for ransom.

PARIS, May 24.——-(#)--Tomorrow will be 'Mothers Day' in France. Mothers of America and mothers of France will join in the observance of a holiday which the French republic has set aside to honor the women who gave their sons to the cause of freedom in the Great War. There will be ceremonies, with processions, religious services and distribution of many flowers,

AUTEUIL, France, May 24.— (CUP.) —Mrs. Helen Wills Moody and Miss Elizabeth Ryan, California tennis stars, won the women’s doubles hard courts championship of France by defeating the French team, Mme. Mathieu and Mlle. Barbier, 6-2, 6-1. Mrs. Moody wore a sweater throughout the play. Both Americans played indifferently.

1930-06-10.text: Dublin, June 10.—(/Pj-- Wireless tests were made at Baldonnel airdrome today between the Southern Cross and another plane in preparation for Capt. Charles Kingsford Smith's proposed trans-Atlantic flight. The Southern Cross remained in the hangar while a Free State plane tumbled about in the air for an hour, three miles away. The messages were handled by J. W. Stanage, radio expert of the Southern Cross.

Bombay, June 10 (UP) — Three Indians were killed and more than 20 wounded when police fired on a group of Hindus and Moslems rioting at Vellore during the Mohurum feast, dispatches from Madras said today. Three of the wounded natives were in a serious condition. Police mastered the situation but only after two riots developed.

LONDON, June 10—(UP)—A firm conviction that the time is not ripe to grant immediate self-government to India was clearly the British reaction today to the first half of the discursive report of the Simon commission, made public last night. The report, which furnished a broad survey of the historical background of India’s political and social institutions, apparently was designed to give the whole story, with all the evidence, of India under the empire. The second half of the commission’s report, which will include recommendations by the commission, will be made public on June 24. The division into volume one and volume two, with a fortnight’s interval, was planned to permit study of the survey and the facts therein, that the people might understand the reasons for the recommendations. The reaction in the press today pointed to an almost unanimous belief that Britain should not move too r

| CALCUTTA, India, June 18 UP A mob reported to have been bearing firearms attacked a party of police at Chechusahat near Ghatal today and the police were stated to have returned the fire. The number of casualties was unknown. The police party had gone to Chechusahat to investigate a report that mob violence had broken out there and that one sub-inspector had been killed and another had disappeared.

LONDON — (#) — Lord Riddell, chairman of the British Newspaper Proprietors’ Association, told delegates to the Imperial Press Conference here today that in his opinion the increase in America’s foreign trade was due largely to that country’s advertising. He urged home manufacturers and merchants to advertise both at home and abroad, declaring: “It gives one a pang to look at overseas and colonial newspapers and see the preponderance of American advertising. I love America and love Americans, but I don’t want to see the world Americanized.”

| Bombay, India, June 9.— (AP)—Encouraged by reports that the war office had dispatched troops and warships to India, harassed officials today assumed a more optimistic attitude toward a situation in the Peshawar district, which was regarded as critical. With their hands full coping with the irritating massive resistance campaign for which Mahatma Gandhi is interned in Yerada prison, Poona, Indian government officials surveyed the reported massing of thousands of Afridis be- (Continued on Page 2)

By The Associated Press. PARIS, June 10—The fourth group of American gold star mothers to visit the graves of their war dead finished their pilgrimage today and started for home. Numbering 257, they will embark on the President Roosevelt at Cherbourg this evening. As they sail out of the harbor they will pass the sixth group, which is expected to land tomorrow morning. The fifth group of mothers made their first visits to graves today.

VIENNA, Austria, June 10, ()— Five mountaineers have been killed as the result of a sudden storm in the “Gesäuse” mountains, a deep defile 12 miles in length. Three bathers were drowned during the progress of the storm and three persons lost their lives in road accidents.

By United Press SHANGHAI, June 10—The amputation of General Chiang Kai-Shek’s left arm has been advised by Chinese surgeons, the United Press learned from private sources today. General Chiang, the head of the Chinese national government, was wounded by a bullet recently while engaged in a battle against forces of the northern coalition near Kweitch, the report said.

LE BOURGET, France, June 10 (7) —Madame Maryse Bastie passed the half-way mark today in an airplane endurance flight by which she is seeking to regain the world record recently taken from her by a young Russian girl, Lena Bernstein. Madame Bastie took the air at 8:18 p. m., last night in a small 40-horse power monoplane with enough gas for 40 hours. She hopes to stay aloft until noon tomorrow in an effort to beat Mile. Bernstein’s record of 35 hours, 46 minutes, 55 seconds. “All going well,” say notes she has dropped from time to time.
HEIDELBERG, Germany, June 10—(?)— Adolf Von Harnack, German theologian, died today after a fortnight’s illness.

(International News Service) BERLIN, June 10—Seemingly impenetrable wall of censorship surrounded Roumania today screening the dramatic events in the struggle involving the new King Carol III, his divorced wife, Princess Helen, and the Crown Prince Michael, their 9 year old son, who last week was King. Telegraph and telephone communications between Bucharest and other continental capitals have been blocked since late yesterday afternoon. The only regular communications to reach Vienna, Budapest and Belgrade have been brief, semi-official and colorless reports dealing with political and government affairs, but saying nothing of the bitter duel between Carol and Helen over Michael. Threatens Princess Reports reaching Budapest late last night through special channels from Bucharest confirmed the news which reached the world before the censorship, which had been partial, became complete. PARIS—(/)—Agreement between France and the United States to abolish double taxation was said today in official quarters to be almost in sight. Remaining details may be ironed out within the next few days, although no accord is likely for a week or so. American and French experts have negotiated the matter for some time. The agreement will afford relief to American subsidiary firms in France which have suffered through being taxed both at home and abroad.

1930-04-12.text: London, April 11, (P)—The London naval conference, with its treaty within a treaty built as a new beacon on the road to disarmament, is rapidly nearing its close and may end at the plenary session next Thursday with the signing of the London treaty. This will follow a similar plenary meeting of brief duration Monday and the drafting of a five-power treaty—which embodies the three-power agreement reached by the United States, Great Britain and Japan—is being rushed day and night. The only thing that might delay the windup Thursday would be inability of the pact writers to agree upon terminology in so short a time. Secretary Stimison and his American colleagues confidently expect to sail home on the Leviathan. The ship normally would sail April 22, but the United States Lines offered to hold her 24 hours if necessary, and the Americans are investigating to see if sailing could be delayed 4

BOMBAY, India, April 11 —(P)— Violations of the Indian government's silt monopoly by the civil disobedience volunteers of Mahatma Gandhi were reported today from widely scattered points in India and were attended with an increasing number of arrests, injuries and severe sentences. Despite prudent efforts by the government, the non-violent resistance movement appears to be making headway, particularly in Bengal, where the Mahatma himself has not yet personally campaigned.

LONDON, April 11 (AP)—The United States lines today offered to adopt the almost unprecedented measure of holding the great liner Leviathan 24 hours beyond her scheduled sailing date, April 22, for the American delegation to the London naval conference. Secretary Stimson greatly desires not only to sign the naval treaty here in London but also to catch this boat home. In order to make more certain that he might not miss the boat, Secretary Stimson inquired whether the United States lines would be willing to defer sailing 48 hours if necessary and this was being considered. This race of the American delegation against time has seized the imagination of conference circles and has rather taken the center of the stage. Until today the secretary had been about the only one of the delegation who believed it humanly possible to catch the Leviathan, but he stuck to his guns, now he has the whole

POTNEY-ON-THAMES, England, April 12, ()—Steered by a little American, Robert E. Swartwout, of New York, Cambridge today swept to a two-length victory over Oxford in the 82nd rowing of their historic boat race on the Thames. It was the first time that an American had ever steered a shell in the famous event and also was the first time that an American had earned a place in the Cambridge boat. By today’s victory Cambridge became one-up on Oxford, breaking the tie of 40 victories each and one deadlock which had been entered on the rowing books ever since 1829 when the great event was first held.

LONDON, April 12.—The so-called first committee of the naval conference adopted a report today under which the United States would scrap the Battleship Florida, of 21,825 tons, and the Utah of the same tonnage. Both ships were built in 1911. The report also provided that Great Britain would scrap the battleships Marlborough, Emperor of India, Benbow and Tiger, all of 25,000 tons and all built in 1914. The report adopted by the first committee deals with immediate scrapping of capital ships. In stipulating that the United States scrap the Florida and Utah, it specifies that one will be rendered unfit for war-like service within twelve months of ratification of the treaty being drawn up today and which it is hoped by the delegates, will be signed next week. The first ship would be finally scrapped within twenty-four months after the ratification. The second would be rendered unfit for war

LONDON (UP)—Technical advisors and international legal experts attached to the London naval conference began an intensive effort Saturday to frame the actual five-power naval agreement in time for its acceptance and possible signature at a plenary session next Tuesday. If, because of the magnitude of the task, it is impossible to have the document completed at that time, as was feared in some quarters, the actual signing may go over until after Easter. It was understood the experts would construct the new treaty in accordance with American suggestions, in three sections. The first would deal with those agreements to which all five powers subscribe, including “humanization” of submarine warfare, extension of the present battleship holiday until 1936, and other minor matters. The second, to be signed by Great Britain, Japan and the United States, would establish Anglo-American parity and l

LONDON, April 12+)—A clothes closet in the suite of Ambassador Morrow at the Ritz hotel has undone the dignity of at least one attache to the British foreign office. Several times the ambassador has mistaken the door of the vestibule closet of his suite for the exit and has walked into the closet, but his personal staff has carefully avoided it. H. W. Malkin, legal adviser to the foreign office, leaving Mr. Morrow's suite after a consultation on the naval treaty draft, mistook the closet door for the exit and cheerfully went inside and started to close it behind him. He finally untangled himself from the overcoats inside and left, somewhat flustered at his experience.

Bombay, April 12.—Two bomb explosions in which several persons were hurt and monster demonstrations throughout Bombay marked the closing day in the first week of Mahatma Gandhi's campaign of civil disobedience. Two persons were hurt when struck by pieces of bombs thrown into the waiting room of the Byculla Railway station. Another bomb was tossed into a milk train, slightly injuring several members of the crew. More than one thousand persons participated in a demonstration of illicit salt making.

BERLIN, April 12. () — By the its insistence that finance and farms must be linked. The government received 217 votes while there were 206 against, and one abstention. Loud cries of “shame” from the left benches greeted the announcement of the result by Paul Lobe, president of the Reichstag.

TOKYO, April 20 (AP)—Owing to inquiries from London and elsewhere regarding yesterday’s stock exchange closing, it is understood the Bank of Japan has cabled an explanation to the effect that investigations indicate the closure was due to private manipulations and had no relation to the general economic condition of the country.

Rome, April 12—The four hundred churches of Rome were filled today with countless flowers and palms for the celebration of tomorrow's ceremony of Palm Sunday. The largest crowd is expected at St. Peter's, where the palms will be blessed and distributed by the archpriest of the Basilica. At the Lateran Basilica, the archpriest, Cardinal Pompli, who is also vicar of Rome, will officiate. Pope Pius will celebrate the occasion quietly, receiving his palm from the hands of one of the prelates of the pontifical court. The palm offered to the Pope is a specially prepared work of art elaborately plaited and ornamented with flowers. It is, however, painted with miniatures in the medieval manner by the Benedictine nuns of St. Prisca on the Aventine Hill. The palm leaves of the Pope's palm are provided by the historic Bresca family of San Remo, according to a privilege conceded to them by Pope Sixt

TOKYO, April 11. (4)—Japan’s long period of depression in trade and industry was reflected today in the one-day closing of the Tokyo stock exchange and the strike of 5,000 cotton mill hands in Osaka and Kyogo. Shapes listed on the exchange were said to have declined 30 percent in value in two years, causing a paper loss of $4,000,000. The strike of mill employees was precipitated by the announcement of the Kanegafuchi

Tokio, April 12, WAKA brief but sharp crisis in Japan's industrial and financial quarters was believed past today. The stock exchange, which closed yesterday after a sensational decline in quotations on Kanegafuchi spinning company stocks, reopened today and trading was resumed. The market opened uneasily, however, with a background of hostility between the government and Yamaji Muto, former president of the Kanegafuchi’s great mill interests.

1930-05-04.text: Tokyo, May 3.—(AP)—Nearly 200 Japanese fishermen were believed today to have perished in a sudden typhoon which lashed their big fleet last night between the islands of Saghalien and Hokkaido. Dispatches to the Rengo News Agency stated that 94 bodies were recovered, but more than 100 men were missing. Five hundred fishing boats were wrecked and damage estimated at $2,500,000 was done. Lured by herring schools within the bay, 10,000 fishermen aboard 2,000 boats put to sea from Odomari, a fishing town of southern Saghalien. A majority of the male population of the town was aboard the boats. Suddenly and without warning, the typhoon struck with terrific violence. Some boats went down quickly, others were swamped as they ran for the harbor, while still others were smashed upon the rocky shores of Odomari bay. One-fourth of the boats were lost. Catch Gone. The typhoon came at the peak of a pr

Tokyo, May 5.—Dispatches from Toyohara yesterday estimated deaths from a typhoon in the Odomari and Tomitaka districts on the island of Saghalien would total 159. This included the known dead and the missing for whom no hope was held. The typhoon swept the rim of Aniwai bay at the southern extremity of the island. The damage was estimated between $2,500,000 and $5,000,000. Most of the dead were fishermen from the village of Odomari, who put to sea just before the storm, lured by reports of huge schools of herring within the bay.

1930-05-02.text: London —(P— Plans of Mahatma Gandhi, to lead his civil disobedience movement personally in Bombay if 100,000 followers wearing homespun can be assured him, were regarded here Friday as tending possibly the most serious developments yet of the present unrest. While there has been no act tending to confirm published statements Thursday that arrest of the Satyagraha leader was imminent there was general opinion the government could not hold its hand much longer if the Mahatma persists in this intention. Gandhi has thousands of followers in Bombay already enrolled, with recruits coming constantly.

(By The Associated Press) LONDON, May 1.—May Day throughout England and Ireland proved to be about as innocuous as a workers’ holiday, while from the remainder of Europe the incidents reported were chiefly minor in character. Hunger marchers of England converged on London, where they held peaceable demonstrations in Hyde Park and demanded interviews with the prime minister or some other cabinet member on plans to alleviate unemployment. Police Not Needed There were numerous communists in the crowds, openly wearing red rosettes and carrying red banners along the embankment, but large squads of police had little to do. Some youths reported to be Fascists attempted to start trouble with the demonstrators in Hyde Park, but the police quickly chased them out and averted a clash. Workers celebrated peacefully in Belgium except for a scuffle near Liege, where police halted a procession that was

(INTERNATIONAL NEWS SERVICE) FRIEDRICHSHAFEN, May 2.— The giant German dirigible Graf Zeppelin was converted into a private “air yacht” for the first time today. A Swiss businessman, reputed to be a multi-millionaire, chartered the airship for a long journey over the face of Europe. He kept his identity a strict secret. Under the command of Captain Von Schiller, the Graf took off the air at 8:10 a.m. (2:10 Eastern Daylight Time) for its private cruise. Aboard the airship were thirty-five guests of the Swiss millionaire who had accepted his lavish invitation to participate in the first dirigible joy-ride in history.

Friedrichshafen, Germany, May 2—(UP) dirigible Graf Zeppelin left here at 8 a. m. today on a privately chartered flight for the first time since it was built. Alwin Schmid, of Kuessnacht, Switzerland, chartered the big air liner for a joy ride over Switzerland, and invited 36 of his Swiss friends to accompany him.

Madrid, May 2.—Fifty persons were reported injured last night in Madrid when police broke up a demonstration in honor of the arrival of Miguel de Unamuno, celebrated Spanish author and philosopher, from Salamanca, where he is rector of the university. Señor de Unamuno returned to Spain about three months ago from several years’ exile in France under the de Rivera dictatorship.

1930-06-03.text: LONDON, June 3. — King George celebrated his sixty-fifth birthday anniversary today, remaining quietly in Buckingham Palace while his eldest son, the Prince of Wales, took the royal salute at the “trooping of the colors.” The king's uncle, the Duke of Connaught, witnessed the ceremony from a balcony overlooking the Horse Guards Parade. Hundreds of messages of congratulation from all over the empire and from other countries all over the world poured into the palace from early morning. The members of the royal family called early to convey their greetings and the grandchildren brought little flags.

London, June 3—(AP)—The London naval treaty today seemed well on its way toward final British approval. A conservative motion which, if passed, at least would have delayed approval, was beaten last night in the House of Commons by a vote of 282 to 201. The liberals voted with the government. The motion was presented by Stanley Baldwin, former conservative prime minister, who asked that the treaty be subjected to rigid inquiry by an especially appointed board of House members. In presenting his motion Mr. Baldwin stated that he had been made nervous as to Britain's safety by certain provisions of the treaty, and felt that it should be subjected to the same kind of inquiry it was receiving in the United States. In answering him Ramsay MacDonald, prime minister, said that the fact the "die-hards" in each of the three countries signatory to the treaty were fighting it was an indication to hi

- Cambridge, Eng., June 3.—In a sensational shooting tragedy in historic Cambridge University this afternoon, D. N. Potts, a first-year student at King’s College, was alleged by police to have shot and killed his tutor, A. F. R. Wollasten. Potts also was charged with having shot and wounded Detective Sergeant Wilson of the Cambridge police force, before turning his revolver on himself. Wilson is in a hospital in a serious condition.

BOMBAY, India, June 3.—(U.P.)— Police charged Independence Day demonstrators at the Worli prison today, injuring at least 12 persons. Several charges were made after the crowd had attempted to halt the work of soldiers who were repairing the barbed wire fence around the prison.

: By The Associated Press. | Bombay, June 2.—In the Peshawar, beset by a three-fold threat of civil resistance, wild tribesmen and communism, Britain today made the outstanding move in the strategy that is advancing her arms across the map of India. British troops, without warning to the communities, charged into two villages of the northwest frontier, gateway to the Punjab, Charsadda and Pranga. It was “Tommy Atkins” turn to try his hand at stamping out the Reds who for weeks have kept that district in a turmoil and aided the attacks of the other two disturbing elements. | They arrested eight leaders of the agitation and established martial law throughout the areas. Peshawar City itself today was quiet, as was most of the rest of India, in nearly every center of which Mahatma Gandhi's “Day of Silence” was as usual made the order of Monday. Salt raiding came to a virtual end with yesterd

Bombay, June 3.—(AP)—Twelve salt raiders were seriously injured in a bitter clash. The number of others injured in the clash was not made known. Troops were concentrated at Worli Sunday after attempts by hundreds of prisoners to force their way out of the prison enclosure. Repairs to the barbed wire fences occupied their attention at day yesterday. Today a procession from the congress went to the prison. While the troops and police were engaged in erecting a stronger barrier about the internment place, the natives, instigated by agitators, attempted to block the work of the troops. The mob insulted the police and military by spitting on them. This immediately led to strife, which was increasing steadily. The encounter occurred when a large group of prisoners within the barbed wire enclosure in the detention pen at the Bombay suburb made a rush for freedom. The congress volunteers within

Bombay, June 3.—(#)—Picketing of all shops in Bombay dealing in British goods was ordered today by the "War Council" of the Indian nationalist movement, The orders also called upon nationalist volunteers to picket the liquor shops, a move which has not been taken heretofore in Bombay city. Five hundred Bombay women yesterday picketed the city’s cloth shops in inauguration of the new campaign. The move of the council was in open defiance of one of the two ordinances promulgated last week by Viceroy Lord Irwin, which intended by the government to restrict the civil disobedience campaign, have been hailed by the nationalists as affording them two more laws to disobey. There seemed little question today but that the open defiance of the provisions against picketing and boycotting would lead to innumerable arrests, but this the satyagrahis, or nationalists, welcomed, it being their plan to fi

By The Associated Press. London, June 2.—Prime Minister MacDonald tonight won his first victory on the London naval treaty in the House of Commons, defeating a conservative motion to appoint a committee which would examine the treaty. The government defeated the motion by 282 votes to 201. The motion offered by former Premier Stanley Baldwin was to appoint a committee of 11 members to examine the provisions of the London agreement. The government was supported by the liberals.

CAMBRIDGE, Eng., June #.——- (#) -—Historic King’s College, Cambridge, today was the scene of a double tragedy which ended in the death of A. F. R. Wollaston, famous explorer and Cambridge tutor, and D. N. Potts, an undergraduate who died in a local hospital at 6:30 p.m. from a bullet wound. Detective Sergeant Willis is in a local hospital seriously wounded. The police theory was that Potts shot and killed Wollaston, wounded Willis and then turned the weapon on himself during an interview in the college at which Willis was present. The student had been away for a week allegedly without permission. The dead explorer was senior tutor of King’s College, he was a member of the 1921 Mount Everest expedition and had also traveled in central Africa and New Guinea. He held numerous scholastic distinctions and was at the age of 55 one of the best-known men in Cambridge. It was the expressed police

LONDON, June 2—(AP)—King George will celebrate his 65th birthday anniversary tomorrow, and on the eve of the celebration numbers of subjects have been gladdened by inclusion of their names in the birthday honors list. The girl aviator, Miss Amy Johnson, who flew alone in a tiny airplane from England to Australia in 19 days, was made a commander of the British Empire. Sir Esme Howard, widely known in the United States as former British ambassador at Washington, was awarded a barony.

SHANGHAI, June 2. (AP)—After an apparently brief cessation of hostilities between the Nationalist government and the Northern alliance, which is seeking to create an independent government in North China centering at Peking, advices from the Honan province zone of police today indicated renewed fighting is imminent. Dispatches indicated that at least 400,000 troops might oppose each other on the Honan front. Despite the multifarious claims of each group claiming victories, independent advices intimated that the opposing armies continue virtually deadlocked along the 10% line in the province. The northerners seemingly were holding a slight advantage, reports disclosed, having forced the Nationalists to retreat as far east as Kweiteh in the northeastern part of the province. The Nationalists were reported to have increased their forces to at least 150,000 indicating that Chiang Kai Shek ha

1930-05-16.text: BOMBAY, May 15.—The eyes of India centered today on the village of Dharasana, where the strangest scene of all the extraordinary drama witnessed recently in this country was enacted. A contest in "civil resistance" took place between Mrs. Sarojini Naidu, heading a group defying the salt laws, and police. Mrs. Naidu, who leads the civil disobedience movement now that Mahatma Gandhi and Abbas Tyabji are in jail, headed her volunteers for the government salt deposits at Dharasana and intended to raid the salt pans. The police halted the party, whereupon Mrs. Naidu and her followers squatted on the road while the police formed a cordon around them. The odd situation continued all day. No one was allowed to pass the cordon with food for the volunteers, and no volunteer who left the police lines was permitted to return. Meanwhile, the woman leader and her flock sat in the road, chatting and sp

LONDON, May 16.—Unusual weight was accorded today to criticism voiced in the House of Commons by Winston Churchill against the London naval treaty, but there was question as to how completely Mr. Churchill, a former conservative chancellor of the exchequer, spoke for his party. A series of attempts were made by labor members to draw Stanley Baldwin, the former conservative prime minister, into the debate which began last night with Mr. MacDonald's praise of the treaty as laying the foundation for international disarmament. Mr. Baldwin, who technically at least, is leader of his party, refrained. "I submit," said Mr. Churchill, "that in proposing a treaty binding ourselves to definite naval inferiority to any power, the government has gone beyond what was right or wise. Signature and ratification of this treaty will be a memorable and melancholy event in our history.

BOMBAY, India, May 16, (UP) —Great Britain's intention to disregard sentiment in suppressing the was shown today when Mrs. Ladevi Chatepadhyaya, sister-in-law of Mrs. Sarojini Naidu, independence leader, was arrested on a charge of violating the salt laws. Mrs. Chatepadhyaya was tried immediately, convicted and sentenced to nine months and two weeks imprisonment. Mrs. Chatepadhyaya was the first woman arrested in Bombay since Mahatma Gandhi instituted his passive resistance campaign against British rule two months ago. She was arrested less than 24 hours after she was chosen to lead a raid of 2,000 independence seekers on the Wadala salt depot near here Sunday. By the arrest the British government apparently wished to indicate that because a woman now heads the passive resistance campaign it would not soften in its determination to put down the revolt.

LONDON, May 15 (Pi--The London naval treaty was hailed by the government today as it was debated in the House of Commons, but ran into heavy Conservative opposition. Prime Minister MacDonald spoke at length for the treaty, asserting that upon its foundations were laid the hopes for future disarmament. But the Conservatives, with Winston Churchill leading them, declared that with the treaty Great Britain had not attained parity with the United States in the sense that both should be equal on the seas, and instead had given formal acceptance of definitely inferior sea power.

LONDON, May 16: (INS.)——After 28 hours of “passive” struggle for supremacy in one of the strangest contests in history, police removed Mrs. Sarojini Naidu and her salt-raiding followers bodily from the dusty road outside Dharasana today, according to an Exchange Telegraph dispatch from Bombay. Mrs. Naidu, successor to Mahatma Gandhi and Abbas Tyabji as leader of the civil-disobedience or passive resistance campaign against British rule in India, was taken by automobile to the base camp of the salt raiders at Untadi. Woman Raider Gets 9 Months LONDON, May 16, (INS.)—Mrs. Kamaladevi Chattopadhyaya, who was arrested in Bombay today with 100 volunteers as she was about to embark on a steamer to proceed to Shiroda on a salt raid, was sentenced to nine months and two weeks imprisonment according to a Central News dispatch from Bombay. The 100 volunteers were released. 40 Wounded By Police Fire

LONDON, May 16,—INS—With newspaper dispatches reporting fresh outbreaks of violence in India today, no confirmation could be obtained from any authoritative source of reports reaching London from Bombay that the British Government might seek a compromise with Indian nationalist elements. These reports said the government was considering opening negotiations shortly with Mahatma Gandhi, Indian Nationalist leader, now in jail, looking to a settlement of the political situation in India. FORMBY, Eng., May 16.—Many a slip twixt cup and lip—. “Blue-eyed, flaxen Diana Fishwick, an obscure 19-year-old school girl, is the champion woman golfer of her Motherland today, not the world famous Glenna Collett, of America. Little Miss Fishwick won in the final round of the British championship this afternoon by the score of 4 up and 3 to play, while Glenna, no longer the assured, confident champion who wiped out the great Enid Wilson and the greater Molly Gourlay on successive days, was giving the performance of a neophyte. Thus, for the second year in succession, the cup was at the fair American's lips but, just as in the 1929 final round with Joyce Wetherad, the potion she quaffed was no better than the dregs. The nectar of victory had been claimed by another. Her defeat was the most disastrous she had sustained since coming to int

CHERBOURG, France, May 16—(UP)—The S. S. America steamed into Cherbourg roads under a bright sun today, bringing the first contingent of Gold Star mothers to visit the graves of their soldier sons in France. French officials went out to meet the pilgrimage. The wharves and welcoming boats were decorated in honor of the mothers and their journey. There were few dry eyes as the mothers and wives of men who died on French battlefields looked on the sunny harbor where many American troops landed a dozen years ago. France gave them a sympathetic welcome and reassured them the nation has not forgotten the sacrifice of America. Army officers who have spent weeks preparing for the tour of soldier graves in France took charge of the visitors, most of whom were from the mid-west. Officers conducted them on the first stages of the trip, which was laid through the bright Normandy countryside where f

Paris, May 16.—A 6,000-word questionnaire and outline on the constitution of a "European Federal Union," prepared by Aristide Briand, French foreign minister, will be delivered to the governments of the 26 members of the League of Nations tomorrow. All other nations of the world, including Russia, will receive copies later, it was announced. Many European statesmen have long worked for an agreement which would knock down the tariff walls that now interfere with commerce between European states. Differences of language, in race, in monetary systems, in tariffs, and even in the gauge of railways, have, in their opinion, prevented the old and historic European nations from keeping up with the economic progress attained by their younger brother across the Atlantic. It is emphasized that while an economic agreement is sought, the proposed federation will not be hostile to the United States no

PARIS, May 16. (AP)—The pen which created “The Beloved Vagabond” today was stilled forever. William J. Locke, eminent British novelist, died at his home here at 9:35 p. m. last night after a long illness. He was 67. His adopted daughter, Sheila Locke, who forsook her own parents to live with him, was at the writer’s bedside.

PARIS, May 15.—(UP)—William J. Locke, one of the best loved of British novelists, died tonight at his home here after a relapse from a serious operation performed six weeks ago. The writer's adopted daughter, Miss Shiela Locke, was with him at the end. He was 67 years old. Mr. Locke had been ill for many weeks and had submitted to two operations for abdominal trouble. The last operation relieved the condition, but left him so weak that he could not combat the relapse successfully.

SENUIN, May 15, (2)—The step toward temperance taken by the German Reichstag, placing a few mild restrictions on the sale of hard liquor, will go into effect July 1. The new alcohol act rings the curfew for the sale of liquor at 1 a.m. and forbids the sale of intoxicants on pay days and election days, but enforcement thereof is left to the discretion of local authorities. One definite provision is that alcohol is barred from juvenile sports meets and similar gatherings. Debate prior to the adoption of the bill was furious. Wets and drys bombarded each other with statistics, lauding or condemning America’s example, each according to his lights. Robert Hampe, nationalist deputy, vehemently denied that alcoholism was a German national vice. There would naturally be exceptions, he said, but less beer was drunk now than before the war; the consumption of spirits was going down all the time. W

1930-04-20.text: - LONDON, April 19.—(AP)—The duchess of Leinster, who was the former May Etheridge, musical comedy star, was bound over to the court today for two years on her own recognizance after recent convictions on a charge of attempting to commit suicide. Friends came forward and said they would take her and not only look after her but nurse her back to health and strength. “I will put you on probation for two years,” said the magistrate to the ‘famous stage beauty. “If you fall into bad habits or frequent bad company or fail to keep in touch with the probation officer, you will be brought back here and dealt with in another way. You will have to see that no nonsense of this sort happens again.”

Calcutta, April 19. ()— British troops and police tonight were swiftly pursuing the insurgents who this morning raided the police arsenal at Chittagong and killed seven persons. Raiders Fully Equipped The magistrate at Chittagong reported that the raiders, who are believed to be in the surrounding hills, are fully equipped with modern arms and that the pursuing forces are scantily equipped. A detachment of British troops was sent out from Calcutta after the raid, however and expects to reach Chittagong tomorrow morning. Calcutta authorities, meanwhile, began a wide search for hidden arms and ammunition. Armored motor cars carrying machine guns were stationed at strategic points throughout the city and environs. The raid today ended a week which already had produced disorders in Calcutta, Karachi and Poona. The death roll rose to eight, for one Indian was killed in the fighting at Karachi

CALCUTTA, India, Apr. 19. WU.P —A sergeant-major of the Anglo-Indian forces and four Indians were shot and killed in an outbreak of insurgents at Chittagong, Bengal, last night. Insurrectionary mobs attacked the railway station and police armories in a violent attack, leaving them wrecked. The sergeant-major and his men were killed in a spirited defense of the buildings. One train was derailed by the mob and the telegraph wires were cut, interrupting communications. Women and children, endangered by the attack, were hurried to refuge on the decks at the port. Sir Francis S. Jacksen, governor of Bengal, who was on his way to the Summer capital at Darjeeling this morning, received a telegram at the Siliguri station explaining the threatening situation at Calcutta and elsewhere throughout the province, and decided to return to Calcutta immediately.

CALCUTTA, India, April 21. (UP) —The arrest of Mahatma Gandhi “in the near future” will be the “crowning act of British policy in India,” Pandit Nehru, who has accepted the presidency of the national congress committee predicted today. Nehru said the many arrests of independents in Bengal and other districts were merely so many points in favor of the people's struggle for freedom against the British government. “The arrest of Gandhi is a consummation devoutly to be wished,” Nehru declared, but he said the fight for independence would “continue with ever growing intensity until the freedom is achieved whether Mahatma is arrested or permitted to carry on his program of civil disobedience unmolested.”

LONDON, Apr. 19.—The 1930 Naval Arms treaty already accepted in its entirety by Japan and in the hands of other powers for approval was completed today.— The preamble was drafted after much discussion and constitutes a victory for the United States in that it does not mention the League of Nations, but does refer to the work of the Washington conference. The draft of the preamble begins with the names of the powers participating who "desiring of re- danger and desiring of carrying forward the work begun by the Washington conference and its achievements and to contribute towards achievement of general disarmament have resolved with a view to accomplishing these purposes to conclude a treaty for further limitations of naval armament and accordingly have appointed as the plenipotentiaries— the names of the delegates then follow after which the terms are set down numbering five chapters and

LONDON, an announcement from Tokio by the Central News agency that the Japanese government has approved the draft of the London treaty, without alteration, was received joyfully today by all the delegates to the naval conference. It is now assured that the treaty will be signed, Tuesday morning, at the final plenary session. Proofs of the naval treaty were being scrutinized today by leaders of the naval conference delegation and it was indicated the document would be given to the printers tonight for the “first edition.” There is the possibility that some last minute changes may be agreed upon necessitating another printing but at any event it seems assured that the treaty will be ready for signing, Tuesday morning, when the plenary session is called at 10:30 o'clock. The American delegation is packed up and ready to leave on the Leviathan, Tuesday night, while the Japanese delegates pla

London, April 19. (4)—Secretary Henry L. Stimson, chief American delegate to the London naval conference, devoted much of his Easter recess from naval activities to preparing the address which he will broadcast from London Monday to the luncheon of Associated Press members in New York in connection with the annual meeting of the Associated Press. The talk, which will begin at 2 P. m. Eastern standard time and will last a half an hour, will be available to listeners throughout the United States and is expected to be the most important pronouncement of the five power conference Mr. Stimson has made. He will review and interpret the actual proceedings of the London meeting. The secretary's Easter headquarters are in his country home at Stanmore but this afternoon he took a respite from work, and, with Mrs. Stimson, visited Cliveden, the country home of Lord and Lady Astor. In Scotland this

London. April 19.—Six native Indian police including 2 sergeants were killed outright today when a frenzied mob stormed the railroad police armory at Chittagong. It was stated in a Central News dispatch from Calcutta. The mob, consisting of more than one hundred demonstrators heavily armed with rifles, clubs and stones, stormed the armory after derailing a train near the vicinity of the armory. Women and children in the vicinity of the armory were immediately herded together under a strong guard and saved from injury. Detachments were rushed to the scene as soon as word of the conflict reached Calcutta. The soldiers are expected to be on hand tomorrow. While the situation is now believed to be under control of local authorities, fears are expressed that serious rioting may break out. Any available police have been sent to the scene from nearby towns and efforts are being made to round up

BAYEUX, France, April 21 (UP) - A bottle containing a message signed with the name of Francois Coli, French aviator who disappeared on his attempted Paris-to-New York flight with Charles Nungesser in 1928, was picked up on the beach here by an old woman. The message said: “Prisoners of Indians in the region of Lake Lawrence. Help. Thirty thousand franc ransom. April, 1932. Nungesser very sick.”

Warsaw, Poland, April 19— (AP)—John W. Willys, newly-appointed American ambassador to Poland, has leased the famous Potocki palace in Cracow suburb for his private residence. The palace is one of the most magnificent residences in Warsaw.

MOSCOW, Apr. 19. (U.P)—Russia’s anti-religious forces gathered today in a mighty effort to counteract the spiritual significance of Easter, and by lecture, theatrical performances, masques and dances to lure away the new generation from the churches. In contrast to the last few years, however, there was curtailment of the open street demonstrations that have provided wild and clamorous discord to plague and harass the devout churchgoers. The government’s orders are that the church people are not to be molested. On the other hand, the “educational” propaganda against religion will reach its height simultaneously with the climax of the orthodox festival. Special atheistic lectures will be given. The theaters will give special performances, while concerts and other distractions will be offered throughout the city.

VIENNA, Apr. 19. (P)—Advices received here tonight said approximately 100 women who lost children in the fire at Costeshti, Roumania, on Good Friday announced their resolution tonight to commit suicide by starving themselves at the common grave in which the victims will be buried tomorrow. The grief of the bereaved mothers was pitiful, advices received here said. One woman lay on the ground in front of the single door of the 100-year-old church and refused to move unless the frightened, milling crowd about her saved her two children, sitting on the front benches in the church. Meanwhile, a priest, after attempting to quiet the people, prayed for the souls of the doomed victims until he was overcome by smoke. A census of the countryside for miles around will be necessary before the exact number of the dead is known. Many of the children came long distances to attend the special Holy Week

Moscow, April 19, (4)—All churches of Moscow were crowded tonight with devout Christians eager to celebrate the resurrection of Christ with the fervor shown in by-gone days, before the atheistic movement got under way in Soviet Russia. Long before midnight, the hour set for the Easter masses, tens of thousands of devout could be seen making their way through the darkened streets, carrying light to guide them over the pavements to their favorite churches. The only noticeable mark of changed conditions this year was the absence of bells and chimes. A recent decree of the government silenced them forever.

1930-04-04.text: LONDON, April 3.—Complete satisfaction of the United States, Great Britain and Japan over their three-power naval construction agreement served today to veil to some extent the Anglo-French-Italian political problems which still delay complete success of the conference. The American spokesman declared today that the American-British-Japanese accord is much better than could have been expected from the Geneva arms conference, where the same three powers failed dismally in their 1927 negotiations. Senator Reed, the principal American negotiator, said the discussions were frank and fair, and that the result was not a victory for anyone but an honorable and reasonable settlement between the three. The committee of American, British and Japanese experts named yesterday needed only a one-hour session this morning to accept the Japanese reservation in principle, and tomorrow morning will meet a

LONDON, April 4—()—Prime Minister MacDonald, Foreign Secretary Henderson, and Foreign Minister Briand of France had lunch together today to discuss the proposed agreement for security which the French demand, and it was understood final decision of the possibility of achieving a security agreement might be made at the lunch table. For several days the British and French have been discussing a draft formula for security prepared by the British. This formula has now come back from Paris with French counter suggestions and today’s luncheon was to give the British a chance to reply. While there was no indication yet of how the discussions were trending, the feeling was expressed in conference circles this morning that the negotiations were nearing a finish, good or bad. Many Rumors Heard All sorts of rumors were being carried about the conference quarters today. All of them tended to the sam

LONDON, April 4. (U.R.) - The United States delegation to the naval conference was said in American sources today to have made tentative reservations to sail for home on the Leviathan April 22. LONDON, April 4. (U.P.) France hopes to receive a reply from Great Britain on her proposals for a security pact before tomorrow night, Foreign Minister Aristide Briand has announced, as the result of the past week of negotiation. The optimism of this statement was counterbalanced, however, by indications from the Italian delegation that Italy will not recede in her flat demands for naval equality with France, regardless of the proposed security pact. Still Questionable Thus, while undeniable progress has been made towards a solution which will permit France to reduce the estimates of her naval requirements, it still remained a question today whether a complete five-power treaty can be drawn. Effor

Ottawa, April 4—(AP)—The government amendment to the export act to deny clearance to craft carrying liquor to the United States was in the final stages of passage through the senate today. It already has passed in the house of commons. The measure was passed on second reading without a division last night and will be brought up for final action after the Easter recess. The opposition sought to delay action on the bill and have a committee appointed to investigate the possible effect of the measure, which not only will withhold clearance for liquor cars destined for the United States but will prevent withdrawal from warehouses of liquor for export across the border.

International News Service Staff Correspondent London, April 4—A luncheon table in a fashionable hotel here today formed the setting for one of the most critical phases of the London naval conference, Prime Minister J. Ramsay McDonald and Foreign Secretary Arthur Henderson were the guests of Foreign Minister Aristide Briand of France. They discussed in great detail the deadlock over the demands of Italy which now darken the hopes of formulating a five-power disarmament treaty. The British negotiations aimed at giving France the Mediterranean security she desires are threatened with failure, as Italy, through its Foreign Minister Dino Grandi, has declined to participate in any political pact based upon interpretation of the League of Nations covenant. Such interpretation, Grandi believes, should be discussed at Geneva and has no place in the London conference. In addition, Grandi steadfas

LONDON—A dingy police court in the drab London district of Lambeth Thursday had before it the wife of the Premier Duke of the Irish peerage, charged with attempted suicide in a two-room flat at Brixton April 1. She was the Duchess of Leinster, formerly the beautiful musical comedy star, May Etheridge, and a police inspector testified how he had found her in the flat at 3:15 o'clock in the morning, attired in a nightdress and with her head against an oven door from which gas was pouring. Thursday's proceedings were short and ended in the Duchess, known in court as Mary Fitzgerald, being remanded on bail of £50 (about $250). The case has created great interest in England, for many recall the stage and society sensation of 1913 when young Lord Edward Fitzgerald, as the Duke of Leinster then was, took the striking May Etheridge from the leading parts in "Princess Caprice" to a honeymoon in a

(International News Service) AUCKLAND, NEW ZEALAND, April 4.—Severe earth shocks, felt early this morning here, swayed buildings and terrified the residents of Opotiki township. First reports from the affected districts said the damage to property was extensive but there were no casualties.

SHANGHAI, April 4—(/)— The Nationalist government at Nanking took war measures against the northern militarist alliance which has declared for its overthrow. Nanking’s state council approved a mandate for “the arrest and subjugation” of General Yen Hsi Shan, governor of Shansi province, leader at the alliance.

(International News Service) TOKIO, April 4—The bodies of seventy-one persons drowned yesterday when a ferryboat carrying a capacity load of holiday merrymakers capsized off the coast of Fukuoka. Ten others died of exposure and 35 are missing.

BERLIN, April 3 (By A. P.)— Victorious by 65 votes in its first skirmish with parliament, the new Bruening cabinet today began work immediately on pressing legislation but was none too assured of its future. The government, headed by Dr. Heinrich Bruening, defeated by 252 to 187, a non-conference motion offered by the Communists, Fascists and Socialists. While the Nationalists, led by Dr. Alfred Hugenberg, gave support to the cabinet, they made so many reservations that the government feared Nationalist support might prove illusory when actual work began. Dr. Hugenberg told the Reichstag his party was willing to give the cabinet a trial only because it had promised farm relief. He said his party assumed no responsibility whatever for the cabinet’s action; that it would decline to vote, among other things, for a German-Polish trade agreement, and for many sections of the financial program

ADDIS ABABA, Abyssinia, April 3 (P)—The Empress Saditu, co-ruler of Abyssinia and descendant of a line that traced its ancestry to King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, died here yesterday. She was about 54 years old. She was the daughter of the Emperor Menelik II, who died in 1918, and succeeded her nephew Lij Yasu, dethroned in 1916. Her successor is the Ras Taffari, great nephew of Menelik, who has been the real ruler of the country for several years.

PARIS, Apr. 4.—(AP)—Premier Tardieu was said today to have had a comfortable night. He probably will rest today and save his strength to attend at the senate tomorrow when the Young plan ratification may be fought out. He was taken suddenly ill yesterday.

ADDIS ABABA, Abyssinia, April 4 — This ancient empire today planned its most impressive honors for Zaudits, its empress and co-ruler, who died here Wednesday at the age of 54. Zanuditu, whose name means Judith, was a descendant of a line which traced its ancestors to King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. Her death leaves Ras Taffari, her nephew, and Negus (King) since 1928, in supreme control of the country. The Ras has transferred his following to the imperial Guebbi, or palace, which he has occupied with troops. Both the capital and the country are tranquil. Zaudits was the daughter of Menelik II who died in 1913. She succeeded her nephew Lij Yasu who was dethroned in 1916. On October 7, 1928, the Ras Taffari, one of the world’s most picturesque rulers, made her co-sovereign, and crowned “King of Kings of Ethiopia, the conquering line of Judah and the elect of God.”

1930-05-08.text: LONDON, May 7—(AP)—As suddenly as it had flared up Mahatma Gandhi's campaign of resistance to the government today had simmered down to a few widely separated clashes. The worst of these, costing nine lives, occurred at Chittagong, scene on April 18 of a battle in which two Europeans and several natives were killed. Again at Calcutta armed police were compelled to act when a mob raided the police station. Simla reported officially that four deaths had occurred in yesterday’s riots. In the Civilian hospital 96 persons were treated. To this number were added 18 police injury cases. The arrival of V. J. Patel at Bombay and his pronouncement for a widespread boycott against British goods was the outstanding development in that district. Dispatches did not indicate how Mahatma Gandhi's followers would accept this attitude. More and more Patel, who recently resigned the speakership of the legi

LONDON, May 6.—George V, “by the grace of God, king of Great Britain, Ireland and the British Dominions beyond the seas, defender of the faith, and the emperor of India,” today celebrated the twentieth anniversary of his accession to the throne. The day was observed, for the most part, quietly. Twenty-one guns in Hyde Park boomed a salute, and naval stations throughout the empire took up the refrain. Bells of St. George's chapel, Windsor chapel, and Windsor parish hall were rung, and flags were flown from public buildings. In the morning his majesty received a number of servants from the London, Windsor, and Sandringham staffs and presented them with medals “for long and faithful service,” after which he left Buckingham palace to attend the races at Newmarket today and tomorrow. It was the first occasion his majesty has been to a race meeting since his serious illness of 1928-29. The rac

London — () — Anglo-Egyptian negotiations for a treaty collapsed Thursday. While no official communique was issued, it was authoritatively stated the rupture took place over Egypt's claims regarding the Sudan. Nahas Pasha, the Egyptian premier, demanded the whole Sudan be recognized as Egyptian territory, to be administered jointly by Egypt and Great Britain. Arthur Henderson, the British foreign secretary, refused to concede this.

LONDON, May 8.——The Anglo-Egyptian negotiations for settlement of the status of Britain in Egypt and the Sudan collapsed today. An official announcement, stating that the negotiations had ended, failed to give the cause, and government sources declined to discuss the breakdown. It was understood, however, that the discussions reached an impasse regarding continuance of British authority in the Sudan.

SUDTUDEGaIe, FBI, MAY Ben ‘AP)—-The Prince of Wales played as the partner of Bobby Jones in a four ball match this afternoon. Wales arrived at Sunningdale shortly after lunch, was introduced to Jones and the other members of the American Walker Cup team and soon was deep in conversation with Jones over golf. The Americans had completed their morning practice and a four-baller was quickly arranged so Wales could play with Jones.

Paris, May 8.—(A.P.)—The Young plan will be declared in force tomorrow. Its enactment into effectiveness depends only upon arrival of papers concerning ratification by Italy. The deposit by Germany and at least four creditor nations of their ratification is required to make the plan effective. The papers of France, Great Britain, Belgium and Germany have been received and Italy’s are on the way, it was announced today.

Rome, May 7. (®)—Italy today ratified the Young Plan as evolved by the two Hague reparations conferences in 1929. The ratification is effective as of May 5, 1930. With Italy’s approval registered, all the big nations but Great Britain involved in the reparations question have accepted the Young Plan.

1930-03-30.text: MELBOURNE, Victoria—(4)—With almost 90 per cent of the votes counted, opponents of the prohibition of alcoholic liquors in the state of Victoria Saturday night had rolled up a lead of more than 100,000 votes over those in favor in a compulsory referendum whether the liquor licenses in that state should be abolished. The terms of the referendum required a three-fifths majority in favor of abolition to secure that result. The industrial areas generally voted strongly in favor of the retention of the liquor licenses. When the count closed just before midnight those opposed to abolition of the liquor license were 422,581 and those in favor of it were 326,553. There are still about 200,000 votes to be counted. Victoria, which has an estimated population of 1,800,000, is the second largest state in Australia. The city of Melbourne and some of its suburbs are dry and an intense campaign was hel

LONDON, March 29—(4)—As the tenth week of the London naval negotiations closes, the fact that disarmament is fundamentally more political than technical is increasingly impressed upon the delegation. So far the experts have made little progress in their formula hunt. If they succeed, navies of the world can be standardized, limited and reduced under plans which have been worked out in the two months here and can be put into force at once.

BERLIN, March 29.—()—After more inter-party wrangling than had been at first expected, Dr. Heinrich Bruening, Centrist party leader in the Reichstag, today got together a new coalition government to succeed that of Heinrich Müller, resigned. Ministers submitted by the new chancellor to President Von Hindenburg, Germany's aged but sturdy leader, showed a shift toward the right of the Reichstag. Though the political center of gravity in the government is nearer the Nationalists, the retention of Dr. Julius Curtius at the ministry of foreign affairs, gave assurance that Germany's foreign policy would not be changed from that inaugurated by the late Gustav Stresemann.

Paris, March 29.— (7) — After three days of discussion the French chamber of deputies tonight adopted the Young plan elaborated by the experts of the United States and the great European powers in Paris last spring and finally approved the Hague conferences. The deputies approved the plan by the overwhelming vote of 539 to 55. This practically means the acceptance of the plan, already approved by the German reichstag, by France. Little opposition is expected in the senate, Anent Rhine An agreement with Germany regarding the occupation of the Rhineland was also voted. The final outcome of the voting on both measures was never in doubt during the debate, which was directed for the government by Premier Andre Tardieu. Making a vigorous appeal to the deputies, M. Tardieu asked for unanimity in approving the Young plan legislation, so that the world might understand that France was united on

1930-04-14.text: By ENS SLOG ene London, April 14.—The Duchess of Leinster, former chorus girl and wife of the premier duke of Ireland, was found guilty of attempting to commit suicide today in Lambeth police court.

Melbourne, Australia, April 14 (AP)—The final count on the question of whether the state of Victoria should go wet or dry showed today that the drys had 419,005 votes and the wets 552,286. It was a record poll, with ballots cast by 95 percent of those entitled to vote. The election, held March 29, was a compulsory referendum on extension of the prohibition of alcoholic liquors throughout the state, which is the second largest in Australia. A three-fifths dry majority would have been necessary for prohibition victory.

LONDON, April 14—Delegates to the naval conference met in plenary session at St. James Palace at noon and were told by Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald, chairman of the conference, that it would be impossible to have the draft completed by Thursday. The session lasted only 21 minutes. Mr. MacDonald did not bother to read the texts of the various reports, perfunctorily referring to each by number. Among the reports adopted were those concerning the battleship building holiday, the unit tonnage of submarines, the characteristics of destroyers and special “exempt” ships and the methods of scrapping. Dino Grandi, the Italian foreign minister, was sufficiently recovered from his illness to attend. The meeting was held in the Queen Anne’s drawing room, the same setting as the previous plenary session on February 11. Secretary of State Stimson, head of the American delegation announced that as t

(By The Associated Press) London, Apr. 13 (#)—Broadcasting to America today, Colonel Henry L. Stimson, American secretary of state and chief of the United States delegation to the naval conference, today proclaimed the success of the conference to his fellow countrymen. The secretary outlined the moral as well as the material advantages achieved by the five delegations, concluding with a special tribute to his own colleagues, Senator David A. Reed, Senator Joseph T. Robinson, Secretary of the Navy Charles Francis Adams, Ambassador Charles G. Dawes, Ambassador Dwight W. Morrow and Ambassador Hugh S. Gibson. Of the work that the conference as a whole has accomplished, Stimson spoke with restrained enthusiasm. He still holds to the principle he announced at the first conference meeting, last January, that naval limitation is a continuous process, and disarmament a goal to be reached by succ

London, April 14—(UP)—Philip Snowden, Chancellor of the Exchequer, announced to the House of Commons today a budget for 1930-31 of £781,909,200 (about $3,909,545,000). The financial year ended with a deficit of 14,522,000 pounds, he announced, instead of the surplus of £4,096,000 estimated by Winston Churchill when he presented the Conservative budget last year. Snowden proposed to raise the additional revenue chiefly by increasing the standard rate of income tax to four shillings sixpence, an increase of sixpence of 234 percent, making the tax 2284 percent. The surtax on incomes over 2,000 pounds would also be increased (it runs in an ascending scale). The lowest grade of income taxpayers, however, will be given relief. Snowden announced that he proposed a reduction of 2 shillings sixpence in the rate of taxation on incomes up to £250 a year ($1,250). He said that out of 2,225,000 peopl

CALCUTTA, India, April 14.—(UP)—J. M. Sen Gupta, mayor of Calcutta, was sentenced to six months imprisonment today for reading extracts from radical books at College Square, where a demonstration was held several weeks ago in support of Mahatma Gandhi's independence campaign. Sen Gupta declined to participate in the court proceedings but repudiated a police suggestion that his followers used criminal force to instigate violence against the British government.

ALLAHABAD, Bombay, April 14. — Pundit Jawaharlal Nehru, president of the All-India National Congress, was sentenced to six months simple imprisonment this afternoon by a British court after conviction on a charge of violation of the Indian salt laws. He was arrested only this morning. The trial of the Pundit was held in the central jail while Indians staged a demonstration in front of the structure. A large crowd waved national flags. Nehru appeared at the window and thanked the demonstrators. BOMBAY, India, April 14, (4) — News of the arrest of Pundit Jawaharlal Nehru, president of the All-India National Congress, spread like wildfire through Bombay this morning. Within a few minutes the cotton, bullion, seeds, and share markets had suspended business. Sixteen persons were arrested at Lucknow, United Provinces, for offenses against the salt laws. They included Mohanlal Saxena, chief exe

London, April 14. (AP)—Philip Snowden, chancellor of the exchequer, presented his eagerly-awaited Laborite budget, estimated the expenditures for 1930-31 at £781,909,444 (about $3,909,000,000.) The chancellor estimated the revenue for the year on the existing basis of taxation of £739,645,000 (about $3,698,000,000.) Thus the difference he had to make good was £42,364,000 (about $211,000,000.) The chancellor, in the course of his speech, indicated he did not anticipate a general election this year, saying he had not found it necessary to provide in this financial year for such expenses.

London, April 1 (ar). Before a tensely interested house, Philip Snowden, Chancellor of the Exchequer, today brought down the second laborite budget in British history involving new taxation in order to balance the budget. The Chancellor said that new taxation was unavoidable because receipts under the existing laws would show a deficit of £42,000,000 against the estimated expenditures. He announced there would be an increase in the standard rate of income tax, a new assessment of all property in the country, an increase in the duty on beer, an increase in the surtax rate, an increase in death duties on estates exceeding £2,000,000 from 40 to 50 per cent, and measures to prevent the avoidance of estate duties.
| MOSCOW, April 11-1). Vladimir Mayakovsky, regarded by many as Soviet Russia's greatest poet, committed suicide today.

FREIBURG, Germany, April 14 (AP)—Sigurd Ibsen, former Norwegian premier and son of the great playwright, Henrik Ibsen, died today, aged 71. The former premier, who had been living in Germany for some time, underwent an operation recently, but showed no improvement and complications set in. Dr. Ibsen in 1906 was appointed a member of the Hague court of arbitration and served on that court for some time.

PARIS, April 14.—-(4)— Premier Tardieu escaped injury in an automobile accident last night. Leaving the chamber of deputies, his car collided with a taxicab; both conveyances were smashed, but the premier, unhurt, walked to his hotel.

Berlin, April 14.—Chancellor Heinrich Bruening’s new cabinet won an outstanding victory in the Reichstag today when the government financial program compromise plan was adopted on the third reading, 250 to 204. The compromise plan couples farm relief with the cabinet’s plan for financial reform, thus forcing such doubtful supporters as the Nationalist party deputies to support the financial reform program in order to carry through farm relief measures.

1930-06-01.text: SYDNEY, N. W., May 31, A pilot and his passenger were killed when the propeller of his plane shattered at 500 feet and the plane fell into the middle of Main Street at Tamworth. The pilot was Frank Mitchell, one of the most widely known airmen in Australia. Splinters from the propeller injured a child in the street below.

Bombay, May 31—(A.P.)—The casualty list resulting from raids by Indian Nationalists on government salt deposits was swelled by 106 names today, while plans were made for a huge “final raid” on the Wadala Salt Works Sunday. Today's injuries resulted when British mounted troops charged to break up an attack on the salt pans at Dharsane, where similar raids have occurred almost daily for two weeks. Nationalist volunteers numbering 156 started for the pans and were driven back several times by the sticks of foot police following a warning each time. The mounted troops finally charged to break up the attack. Meanwhile, other violence was reported from the far north of India—at Peshawar, on the frontier, where much trouble occurred about a month ago. A woman and two children were among the victims today when soldiers fired into a mob which had reassembled after being dispersed. Prior to the in

BOMBAY, May 31, — Three national congress volunteers, who rode to Sholapur eager to violate the rules of the British martial law there, went back to Poona today clothed only in loin cloth. Authorities of the city, which has been under martial law since fierce rioting three weeks ago forced evacuation of all European women and children, met the volunteers and confiscated the green shirts and red shirts the volunteers wear as emblems of the national congress. Dhotis—loin cloths—then were handed the independence seekers, and they were put aboard another train headed towards Bombay.

DHARASANA, Bombay, India May 31. (AP)—British mounted troops and foot police injured 106 volunteers who attempted to raid the salt pans here today. One hundred fifty-six volunteers attempted the raid and police with sticks made fruitless attempts several times to disperse them, warning them each time to disperse. Then the cavalry rode down the group to break it up. Most of the volunteers were sent to hospitals.

London, May 31 (4)—Reports emanating from Indian nationalist sources that Prime Minister MacDonald has sent a special representative to India to negotiate with Mahatma Gandhi for settlement of the political upheaval there was denied officially at both the India office and 10 Downing Street today. One official stated emphatically: “The prime minister has no representative in India other than the viceroy of India,” indicating that any negotiations must be directed by or through Lord Irwin. Whether this was being done could not be ascertained since a categorical statement was not available. British Troops Engage Natives Dhavasana, Bombay, India, May 31 (A)—British mounted troops and foot police injured 106 volunteers who attempted to raid the salt pans here today. One hundred fifty-six volunteers attempted the raid and police with sticks made fruitless attempts several times to disperse the

TOKYO, June 1—(Outides)— (AP) — An earthquake, the longest and strongest of this year was felt in this city at 2:59 a. m. today. Clocks were stopped and frightened people ran from their houses. A half hour later there had been no reports of serious damage nor of casualties. Japan in the past has experienced a long series of devastating earthquakes, with great loss of life. The earthquake and fire of September 1, 1923, the most disastrous in modern history, caused a loss of 120,000 lives and property damage of about $2,500,000,000 about Sagami bay on which Tokyo is situated. It was estimated that 400,000 persons died in Tokyo in the collapse of approximately 10,000 buildings.

| FARIS, May 31.—(VP)—A Havas dispatch from Montereau stated that the Paris-Marseilles express was derailed tonight at Montereau and that six persons were killed and 30 were injured, er Monday; showers in east,

| TORYC, May 31 (AP)—A South Korea dispatch to the Rengo News Agency says that a band of South Korean communists early today bombed and set afire Korean association buildings and schools and Japanese consulates in the Chientao district of Kirin province, Manchuria.

BERLIN--(CP)—German politicians of the extreme right, who cannot refrain from bursting into sarcastic comment against President von Hindenburg for his signing of the Young Plan, must hereafter be prepared to pay an occasional forfeit. This, in effect, was the decision of a Berlin court which Saturday fined Dr. Paul Goebbels, national-socialist Reichstag member and editor of a fascist periodical, $200 for an article which asked, “Is von Hindenburg still alive?” Attorneys for the president, plaintiff in the suit, asked a prison sentence for the defendant, but the court took into consideration that he was fighting the von Hindenburg policies of government administration rather than the president personally. The trial was conducted quietly in spite of the assembly of a throng of Goebbels’ sympathizers outside the building. The police refused them admittance to the court. The defense was accu

AMSTERDAM, Tolland, May 31. —Captain Charles Kingsford-Smith, transpacific aviator, left Schiphol aerodrome this morning in his famous plane, the Southern Cross, for Croydon, England, en route to Ireland. He is planning to start a transatlantic flight attempt from there some time next month, Kingsford-Smith flew over with his three companions, who will accompany him on his forthcoming attempt. The Southern Cross was completely overhauled while in Holland. The pilot said: "We shall stay for a couple of days in London and then fly to Ireland. The start of our Atlantic flight is up to the weather. We shall get off at the earliest possible moment."

More than 90 Gold Star mothers of the United States, the fourth group to land, Saturday paid tribute at the Arc De Triomphe to France's Unknown Soldier. In traditional fashion they paused at the altar of freedom before beginning their trip to the battle cemeteries where their dead rest in Flanders fields. Mrs. Eliza Wilson of Detroit, Mich., and Mrs. M. L. Smeaton of Fall River, Mass., acted for their comrades in the ceremony at the tomb, placing two beautiful wreaths on the memorial, which after Friday's celebration and previous visits of delegations, is fairly hidden in blossoms. Quartermaster General B. Frank Cheatam, U.S.A., and a number of dignitaries of the French civilian and military branches were present. After the brief ceremonies, the mothers went to a restaurant in the center of Paris for tea. There they were guests of honor with Walter E. Edge, American ambassador, who, with

1930-04-21.text: LONDON, April 20—(#)—The heads of the delegations to the Five Power Naval conference have approved the wording of the preamble to the London Naval treaty, and on receipt today by the Japanese delegation of authorization to sign the treaty, they were ready to meet tomorrow to examine and finally approve the entire text. Approval by the Tokyo government was considered today to preclude any last minute hitch in the arrangements for the final plenary session in St. James’ palace. It is expected that the treaty will be formally signed at 10:30 A. M. Tuesday, thus permitting the American delegation to leave for home on the liner Leviathan. Colonel Henry L. LONDON, April 21.—(U.P.) — The lowest temperature in 83 years, accompanied by snow, hail, sleet and rain, dimmed the brilliance of Easter Sunday in the British Isles and caused heavy financial losses to hotels, resorts and transportation companies. It was estimated approximately 10,600,000 pounds sterling were lost because the British people were unable to make their customary Easter visits to the seashore and the country. The famous fashion parade on Rotten Row, which the stenographers of the American naval conference delegation had planned to watch, was rained out.

BOMBAY, India, April 21. Self-rule or independence within eight days was promised by Mahatma Gandhi today if the Indian people would follow his counsels strictly. Gandhi made his promise at a meeting at Bardoli, center of the civil disobedience campaign for the Gujerat district. He told his hearers that if all village officials would resign in a body; that if a boycott of liquor and foreign cloth were established; and that if the manufacture of homespun were begun, they would have self-government within a week, if not complete independence. The Mahatma’s campaign meanwhile was attacked by Maulvi Mahomed Yakub, deputy president of the Legislative assembly, who charged in a speech before the All-India Moslem conference for Palestine affairs that Gandhi had changed his attitude towards Indian Moslems during recent weeks.
